Preface:
The Programme for International
Assessment of Adult
Competencies – An Overview
Policymakers have become increasingly concerned not only over the levels of traditional literacy skills in
their populations but also the growing importance of human capital and the broadening of the skills needed
to sustain productivity and social cohesion. The increased importance of human capital and the learning
that is associated with it has led to a critical need for information about the distribution of knowledge, skills
and characteristics of the adult population. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
(OECD), in recognition of this need, initiated the development and implementation of an international
comparative survey of adults named the Survey of Adult Skills as part of its Programme for the International
Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) in 2008, with the following goals and objectives:
•

provide policymakers in each participating country with a baseline profile of adults in their country
in terms of the knowledge, skills and competencies that are thought to underlie both personal and
societal success

•

assess the impact of these competencies on a variety of social and economic outcomes at the
individual and aggregate levels

•

gauge the performance of education and training systems in generating the required competencies

•

help clarify some of the policy levers that could contribute to enhancing competencies.

The Survey of Adult Skills, now in its second cycle, represents one of the key sources of empirical evidence
to support policies focused on developing relevant skills, activating skills within the labour market, and
ensuring their effective use to drive economic growth and social equity. By offering direct measures of key
skills beyond traditional indicators like levels of education and work experience, the survey helps
policymakers understand skill acquisition, retention, and use, shaping strategies that foster sustainable
development and equal opportunities.

Key features of the Survey of Adult Skills
The Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) has been planned as an ongoing assessment programme. The first
cycle of the survey involved three "rounds" of data collection. The first occurred in 2011-12, the second in
2014-15, and the third round in 2017. The second cycle of the assessment – the 2023 Survey of Adult
Skills – has had one round of data collection implemented in 2022-23.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

9
The main features of the second cycle of PIAAC are described below.

Skills assessed in the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills
The 2023 Survey of Adults Skills assesses the following three domains of cognitive skills:
•

literacy (including reading components)

•

numeracy (including numeracy components)

•

adaptive problem solving (APS).

Panels of subject-matter experts developed the conceptual frameworks for each domain, guided the
development and selection of items, and informed the interpretation of results. The complete domain
frameworks can be found in OECD (2021[1]). The frameworks define and describe the underlying latent
skills the assessment aims to measure. To inform item development, they identify the key task dimensions
that should be used to build the assessment and report results. Across the domains, the dimensions focus
on:
•

Content – the various representations of information, or types of materials and tools, that adults
use to complete tasks.

•

Cognitive processes – the information-processing strategies required to use specific materials to
meet task demands successfully.

•

Contexts – the social and situational contexts in which tasks are embedded.

Literacy and numeracy were also assessed in the first cycle of the Survey of Adult Skills. The frameworks
used in the second cycle build on past frameworks but have been revised and extended to ensure
relevance to contemporary reality and understanding of the phenomena measured (Rouet et al., 2021[2];
Tout et al., 2021[3]; Tout et al., 2017[4]). Adaptive problem solving is a new domain assessed for the first
time in the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills. The results from the second cycle for adaptive problem solving
cannot be compared to those from the first for problem solving in technology-rich environments due to
differences in the underlying constructs.
The assessment tasks in the survey focus on respondents' ability to draw on information-processing
strategies to perform tasks in real-world contexts. Successful completion of these tasks does not require
specialised knowledge or more specific skills: in this sense, the skills assessed in the Survey of Adult Skills
can be considered "foundational" or, more appropriately, the general skills required for a broad range of
situations and domains. They should not be seen as basic skills that are less complex than other higherorder or specialised skills.
Another key feature of the assessment is that it is designed to reflect the increased reliance on digital
devices in professional and personal life and the new demands this poses for accessing, processing and
evaluating information. The literacy assessment in the second cycle encompasses a broader spectrum of
digital texts, including texts with multiple sources, and emphasises the evaluation of the accuracy and
relevance of information. The numeracy assessment places a strong focus on interpreting mathematical
information presented in dynamic forms (e.g. interactive websites) and structured forms (e.g. infographics)
and making judgments based on critical evaluation of mathematical information.
A brief overview of the domains of competence assessed in the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills is provided
below.

Literacy
The framework used in the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills defines literacy as "accessing, understanding,
evaluating and reflecting on written texts in order to achieve one's goals, to develop one's knowledge and
potential, and to participate in society" (Rouet et al., 2021[2]).

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

10 
The framework identifies three cognitive processes that support the range of adult reading activities that
are the focus of the literacy assessment:
•

Accessing texts involves identifying one or more texts that are relevant to a presented task and
locating information within them. Readers must navigate across texts or passages, or within texts,
as a function or task demands. In an assessment context, the complexity of an access task is
driven by the interaction between the question posed to the test taker and the features of the
presented texts.

•

Understanding consists of constructing meaning and representations. This aspect includes both
literal and inferential comprehension of material with a single text, as well as across multiple texts.

•

Evaluating involves assessing the accuracy and credibility of information in a text; evaluating the
soundness of a text (i.e. the completeness and consistency of the information); evaluating the
relevance of one or more texts for a given task; and reflecting on the author's intent, purpose and
effectiveness.

To provide more detailed information about adults with lower literacy skills, the assessment of literacy was
complemented by a test of "reading component" skills. Reading components represent the basic set of
decoding skills necessary for gaining meaning from written text. Two types of reading component tasks
are included in the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills: sentence comprehension and passage comprehension.
Sentence comprehension tasks ask respondents to identify if a sentence does or does not make sense.
Passage comprehension tasks ask respondents to read a short passage as it displays on screen sentence
by sentence. For each sentence with a pair of underlined words, respondents are asked to identify the
word that gives meaning to the sentence.

Numeracy
The framework for the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills defines numeracy as "accessing, using and reasoning
critically with mathematical content, information and ideas represented in multiple ways in order to engage
in and manage the mathematical demands of a range of situations in adult life" (Tout et al., 2021[3]). The
phrase "represented in multiple ways" was included to reflect the importance of digital information,
representations, devices and applications in meeting the numeracy demands of everyday life.
Three cognitive processes are associated with numeracy skills:
•

Access and assess situations mathematically require adults to examine a contextual problem and
determine if and where they can extract the essential mathematics to analyse, set up and solve
the problem.

•

Acting on and using mathematics includes the processes of ordering, counting, estimating,
computing, measuring, graphing and drawing. Adults must use their knowledge of mathematical
processes, facts and procedures to solve real-world problems. Where relevant, they must also
select and use appropriate tools, including those present in digital environments.

•

Evaluating, critically reflecting and making judgements is the process of evaluating whether a
solution to a real-world problem is reasonable and relevant to the original problem situation and
context. Based on these judgements, a decision can be made about whether to accept the solution
or revise and adjust it.

Like reading components, the assessment of numeracy was complemented by numeracy components,
basic numeracy skills that form a prerequisite to developing the more advanced numeracy skills measured
in the numeracy assessment. Numeracy components include two fluency-based measures, each focusing
on different aspects of number sense: how many and which is biggest. How many tasks ask respondents
to look at an image and identify how many items are shown. Which is biggest tasks ask respondents to
identify the largest of four numbers.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 11
Adaptive problem solving
The conceptual framework defines adaptive problem solving as "(…) the capacity to achieve one's goals
in a dynamic situation, in which a method for solution is not immediately available. It requires engaging in
cognitive and metacognitive processes to define the problem, search for information, and apply a solution
in a variety of information environments and contexts" (Greiff et al., 2021[5]).
Within this definition are key features specific to adaptive problem solving compared to problem solving
more generally. One critical feature of adaptive problem-solving tasks is that these problems involve
dynamic situations, where resources and information needed to solve a problem are not readily available,
or some aspect of the problem changes while the solution is being developed. Additionally, it emphasises
the importance of metacognition. Metacognitive skills are called upon to monitor the problem-solving
process and adapt solution strategies as a problem changes.
Different cognitive and metacognitive processes may be required within each of the three stages of
problem solving: defining the problem, searching for information relevant to the solution, and applying a
solution.
•

Defining the problem – The three cognitive processes associated with this stage of problem solving
are: selecting, organising and integrating problem information into a mental model; retrieving
relevant background information; and externalising an internal problem representation by creating
a table, making a drawing, etc. The two metacognitive processes are goal setting and monitoring
problem comprehension.

•

Searching for information relevant for a solution – The framework identifies two cognitive processes
associated with searching for a solution: searching for operators, within the mental model and in
the environment, and evaluating how well these operators satisfy the problem constraints. The
metacognitive processes associated with searching for a solution involve evaluating resources with
respect to whether they can be executed. In the artificial problem-solving context of an assessment,
this evaluation process is difficult to distinguish from the cognitive processes described above.
Therefore, the expert group specified that items that tapped into this process should be coded for
analysis as requiring both cognitive and metacognitive processes.

•

Applying a solution – The primary cognitive process in the third stage is to implement the selected
operator(s) to solve the problem. As part of the metacognitive processes associated with applying
a solution, problem solvers must evaluate whether they are progressing towards the goal and take
actions if they are not. This involves monitoring progress, regulating the application of the operators
and reflection.

Other information on skills
Literacy, numeracy and APS constitute a subset of essential skills and competencies demanded in the
labour market and play a crucial role in accessing resources and services more generally in society.
Alongside technical and professional skills, other generic skills – such as communication, interaction (such
as the capacity to relate to others and work cooperatively), the ability to learn and share knowledge, and
physical skills – are valued to varying degrees on the labour market. To provide a more comprehensive
picture of adult skills, the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) collects extensive information on the skills adults
possess and use in addition to their proficiency in literacy, numeracy and APS. This information is collected
in the form of self-reports.

Qualifications and work experience
Educational qualifications and work experience are commonly used proxies to assess individuals' skill
endowments. The Survey of Adult Skills collects information on respondents' educational attainment, work

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

12 
experience and job mobility. Additionally, it incorporates respondents' perceptions of the educational
qualifications and work experience typically required to obtain and effectively perform their current job.

Use of skills at work
Information was collected from respondents regarding four broad categories of generic work skills:
•

Cognitive skills encompass reading, writing, mathematics and the use of information and
communication technology (ICT).

•

Interaction and social skills cover collaboration, cooperation, time and task management (for
oneself and others), communication, negotiation, and customer contact (e.g. selling products and
services and advising).

•

Physical skills involve the use of gross and fine motor skills.

•

Learning skills cover activities such as the instruction of others, engaging in formal and informal
learning and staying updated with developments in one's professional field.

The approach used in the Survey of Adult Skills relies much on the Job Requirements Approach (JRA)
pioneered in the UK Skills Survey (Felstead et al., 2007[6]). The JRA method consists of asking individuals
about the importance of different types of tasks performed at work and subsequently inferring the types of
skills that are required from their answers. Focusing on job tasks provides a more objective description of
these skills than methods relying on subjective self-assessment skill levels.
Respondents were also asked to evaluate the extent to which their overall skill set (considered globally)
aligns with the requirements of their current job.

Work-related training
Recognising the importance of work-related training as a potential source of skill development and as an
element of a broader strategy for maintaining and enhancing workforce skills, information was also
collected on respondents' participation in formal and informal training over the 12 months prior to the
interview.

Social and emotional skills
The 2023 Survey of Adult Skills background questionnaire assesses social and emotional skills through
the BFI-2-S and BFI-2-XS instruments developed by Soto and John (2017[16]). These instruments assess
five domains commonly known as the "Big Five": open-mindedness, conscientiousness, extraversion,
agreeableness and emotional stability. A number of studies highlight the significance of social and
emotional skills on key life outcomes. Data from the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills will facilitate analysis of
how social and emotional skills relate to information-processing skills, economic outcomes, lifelong
learning dispositions and behaviour, and past educational qualifications.

Personal characteristics, background and outcomes
The background questionnaire fathers extensive information on the factors that influence the development
and maintenance of skills including education, social background, engagement with literacy and numeracy
and ICT (both in and outside of work), and language background. Information is also collected on the
economic outcomes related to skill such as respondents' current activity, employment status and income.
It also explored non-economic outcomes, including health status, volunteering, political efficacy and social
trust.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 13
Test delivery
In the first cycle of the Survey of Adult Skills, the default delivery mode was a computer-based assessment
(CBA), with a paper version available for respondents who either lacked the necessary digital skills or were
reluctant to use a laptop. The CBA approach has several advantages. It enables using items more closely
resembling real-world digital information processing (e.g. reading digital texts or interacting with
mathematical information on digital devices). It also enables automatic scoring and supports adaptive
testing, allowing for more efficient and tailored test designs. However, some 25% of respondents
completed the paper-based version of the assessment in the first cycle.
In the second cycle, tablet devices were introduced to fully leverage the benefits of a CBA. Both the
background questionnaire and the direct assessment were delivered via tablets. The background
questionnaire was administered as a computer-aided personal interview where trained interviewers asked
respondents the questions from the background questionnaire and recorded the answers using a tablet
and keyboard. The time needed to complete the background questionnaire varied depending on
respondents' characteristics; for instance, certain questions were only relevant to employed adults or those
who had emigrated to the country.
After completing the background questionnaire, respondents participated in a short tablet tutorial to
familiarise themselves with the device and interface. This ensured that all respondents could complete the
assessment on a tablet. The direct assessment of literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving (APS)
was then completed autonomously by respondents using the same tablet. This component was untimed,
allowing respondents to take as much time as needed to complete the assessment.

Adaptive testing
The tablet-only design enables adaptive algorithms to optimise the delivery of assessment items. These
algorithms leverage information from the background questionnaire – such as age and educational
attainment – along with responses to previous assessment items to select and administer assessment
items that are neither too easy nor too difficult for the respondent.
The first step of this adaptive process is a locator test (also referred to as Stage 1), which includes eight
literacy and eight numeracy items. Based on their answers to these items, respondents are sorted into
three different paths:
•

Respondents who fail the locator test proceed to the assessment of reading and numeracy
component skills.

•

Respondents who pass the locator test with a low score first complete the reading and numeracy
component skills assessment, then proceed to the direct assessment of literacy, numeracy and
adaptive problem solving.

•

Some respondents (12.5%) who pass the locator test with a high score are randomly assigned to
the component skills assessment before proceeding to the direct assessment of literacy, numeracy
and adaptive problem solving. The rest proceed directly to the assessment.

In the direct assessment, each respondent is only assessed in two of the three domains: literacy, numeracy
or adaptive problem solving. In the adaptive path, each domain assessment consists of two stages. The
difficulty of the questions that respondents receive at the first stage depends on their performance on the
locator test and personal characteristics collected in the background questionnaire (such as level of
education). The question difficulty at the second stage depends on the performance at the first stage.
Additionally, one-quarter of the respondents are assessed using a linear design (non-adaptive path),
ensuring a diverse group of respondents attempts each item from a wide proficiency range.

The first cycle of the Survey of Adult Skills was conducted in three rounds, covering 39 countries and
economies and surveying approximately 250 000 adults. The first round (2011-12) included 24 participants,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 15
the second round (2014-15) involved nine additional participants, and the third round (2017-18) covered
six participants. The second cycle of the Survey of Adult Skills has been conducted once so far, in 20222023, surveying around 160 000 adults in 31 countries and economies. Twenty-seven countries and
economies participated in both cycles of the survey. For these countries, comparisons of results across
cycle are possible.

Relationship to previous surveys
The Survey of Adult Skills is the third of a series of international adult skills surveys implemented since the
mid-1990s by OECD countries. It was preceded by the International Adult Literacy Survey (IALS, 1994-98)
and the Adult Literacy and Life Skills Survey (ALL, 2003-06) (Statistics Canada, 2024[12]; Institute of
Education Sciences (IES), 2025[13]).
IALS assessed three literacy domains: prose, document and quantitative literacy. Prose literacy is the
knowledge and skills needed to understand and use continuous texts – information organised in sentence
and paragraph formats. Document literacy represents the knowledge and skills needed to process
documents or information organised in matrix structures (i.e. rows and columns). The type of documents
covered by this domain included tables, signs, indexes, lists, coupons, schedules, charts, graphs, maps
and forms. Quantitative literacy covers the skills needed to undertake arithmetic operations such as
addition, subtraction, multiplication or division, either singly or combined using numbers or quantities
embedded in printed material.
The major change between IALS and ALL was the replacement of the assessment of quantitative literacy
with that of numeracy and the introduction of the assessment of problem solving. Numeracy represented
a broader domain than that of quantitative literacy, covering a wider range of quantitative skills and
knowledge (not just computational operations) as well as a broader range of situations in which actors had
to deal with mathematical information of different types (not just situations involving numbers embedded
in printed materials).
The Survey of Adult Skills has been designed to link to IALS and ALL in literacy and to ALL in numeracy.
To ensure strong links in literacy and numeracy with IALS and ALL, approximately 60% of the assessment
items in these two domains in the first cycle of the Survey of Adult Skills have been drawn from these
previous surveys.
The literacy domain in the Survey of Adult Skills differs from IALS and ALL in two main ways. First, literacy
is reported on a single scale rather than two (prose and document literacy) scales. For comparison, the
results of IALS and ALL have been rescaled on the literacy scale of the Survey of Adult Skills. Second,
while the measurement framework for literacy in the Survey of Adult Skills draws heavily on those used in
IALS and ALL, it expands the kinds of texts covered to include electronic and combined texts in addition
to the continuous (prose) and non-continuous (document) texts of the IALS and ALL frameworks. In
addition, the literacy assessment was extended to include a measure of reading component skills, which
was not included in previous assessments.
The numeracy domain in the Survey of Adult Skills remains largely unchanged between ALL and the
Survey of Adult Skills. Problem solving in technology-rich environments in Cycle 1 in adaptive problem
solving in Cycle 2 of the Survey of Adult Skills constitute new domains.

Management structure
The development and implementation of PIAAC are overseen by the Board of Participating Countries
(BPC). The BPC is formally constituted as a body of the OECD and operates under a mandate approved
by the OECD Council. OECD member countries participating in PIAAC are automatically members of the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

16 
BPC, while non-member countries participating in PIAAC may be invited to join it. Each member country
has only one vote, most are represented by delegates from both ministries of labour and education.
The BPC is the main decision-making body for PIAAC, responsible for setting project priorities, developing
programmes of work and budgets, monitoring implementation, evaluating its impact and disseminating
results. It usually meets twice a year, reviewing and approving all key elements of PIAAC's design,
implementation and reporting. When decisions must be made outside of the regular meeting schedule,
they are handled through a written procedure.
The OECD Secretariat supports and advises the BPC, ensuring its work programme and decisions are
effectively implemented. It also manages the Consortium contract, covering the development and
international implementation of PIAAC. Finally, it is also responsible for the dissemination approach and
preparation of the international comparative report.
The Consortium, led by ETS, reported directly to the OECD and coordinated its subcontractors, the
Technical Advisory Group (TAG), and the subject matter expert groups. The subcontractors working on
PIAAC included: cApStAn, DIPF (the German Institute for International Educational Research), GESIS
(Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences), IEA (the International Association for the Evaluation of
Educational Achievement), ROA (the Research Centre for Education and the Labour Market) and Westat.
Each organisation had particular areas of responsibility associated with the instrument development,
delivery platform, operational procedures and standards, translation verification, quality assurance, quality
control, sampling, scoring, interview training, platform testing, data processing, scaling, data analysis, and
data analysis tools.
At the national level, PIAAC implementation is managed by various organisations within participating
countries, including national statistical offices, public or private research and survey organisations,
universities, and government ministries. Each participating country appoints a team responsible for
implementing PIAAC, headed by a National Project Manager (NPM) to oversee the survey implementation,
including translation, adaptation, sampling, data collection, scoring, coding and database preparation.
Throughout the project, the Consortium maintained close contact with national implementation teams.
NPM meetings were held at key stages over the project's life (approximately two meetings per year),
serving as forums for information exchange, training, progress discussions, and addressing concerns from
participating countries. The Consortium managed these meetings while the OECD Secretariat provided
regular updates on BPC discussions and decisions.

20 

Introduction
This chapter provides an overview of the field trial (FT) and main study (MS) assessment designs for the
second cycle of the Survey of Adult Skills, part of OECD’s Programme for the International Assessment of
Adult Competencies (PIAAC). PIAAC is a household survey that assesses the proficiency of noninstitutionalised adults aged 16 to 65 in key information-processing skills – literacy, numeracy and adaptive
problem solving (APS) – through tablet-based administration, focusing on skills essential for active societal
participation and economic growth. A primary objective of this second cycle of PIAAC was to report results
that can be compared with those from prior adult assessments, such as the first cycle of PIAAC. PIAAC
Cycle 1 had already established links with previous international adult surveys, such as the International
Adult Literacy Survey (IALS) and the Adult Literacy and Life Skills Survey (ALL). This was documented in
the Survey of Adult Skills 2019 Technical Report (OECD, 2019). To continue supporting these linkages,
the assessment design in PIAAC Cycle 2 included trend items in literacy and numeracy from PIAAC
Cycle 1.
Additionally, new items were developed for literacy and numeracy, along with new measures for numeracy
components, and the newly introduced APS domain – each aligned with their respective frameworks. The
MS assessment design allocated approximately 45 minutes for the background questionnaire (BQ) and 60
minutes for the direct assessment. The BQ collected contextual information on respondents, including
demographics, education, labour market experiences, skill use at home and work, and social and
emotional skills.

Field trial goals
A field trial is designed to yield information to verify instrument quality, platform delivery, survey operations,
scaling and psychometric characteristics of the instruments. To support the development and
implementation of both the PIAAC FT and MS, a set of standards and guidelines were developed and
observed during various phases of the assessment including survey development, implementation and
analysis and reporting of the data. The outcomes of the PIAAC Cycle 2 FT were used to evaluate the
tablet-delivery platform, assemble the final instruments for the MS, modify or refine any of the operational
issues detailed in the Technical Standards and Guidelines document 1 to improve the overall quality of the
assessment, prepare for the MS analyses methods and procedures, and examine relationships among BQ
variables and skills.

Operational goals
One of the purposes of the FT was to evaluate survey operations and procedures. This included an
examination of the efficiency and accuracy of data collection procedures, the functionality of the delivery
system, and the efficiency and accuracy of data processing, including recoding and data transmission. In
particular, the following tasks were conducted to collect information regarding field operations as they
relate to the direct assessment:
•

Collect data regarding how well respondents were able to use the tablet based on their
performance on tasks in the tutorials and their ability to engage with and complete the direct
assessment.

•

Evaluate the coding of non-response interviews to determine the percentage of respondents who
did not participate for literacy-related reasons and/or lack of technical skills.

•

Identify and develop plans for correcting any operational difficulties.

•

Evaluate the efficacy and accuracy of data capture, processing and transmission.

•

Review and approve quality assurance mechanisms.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 21
Instrumentation
In addition to informing survey operations, the FT must also provide quality information related to the survey
instruments, including adequacy of the scoring procedures, examination of national translation and
adaptation outcomes, and an evaluation of the scaling and analytic procedures that were planned to be
used in the MS. The following tasks were conducted in the FT to collect information regarding
instrumentation:
•

Review the accuracy and comparability of survey instruments and all supporting materials. This
includes providing initial estimates of item functioning among all newly developed cognitive items
as well as checking the stability of all PIAAC Cycle 1 item characteristics.

•

Evaluate the timing and flow of questions in the direct assessment.

•

Evaluate the appropriateness of questions based on the comparisons of the item characteristics
across participating countries.

Tablet-delivery platform
In the first cycle, PIAAC represented an innovation in large-scale assessment methodology in that it was
the first technology-based household survey of adult skills. In the second cycle, that innovation continued
as PIAAC moved to a tablet-based system. The tablet-delivery platform integrated the computer-assisted
personal interview (CAPI) tool to be used for the administration of the BQ with the tool that delivered and
scored the cognitive instruments. This integrated PIAAC system needed to work in conjunction with either
the international case management tool that was provided to countries or, in some cases, with a national
case management system used by the survey organisation selected by the national team. Thus, in addition
to looking at survey operations and instrumentation, the following set of tasks were completed to collect
information related to the tablet-delivery platform:
•

Test and evaluate the functioning of the delivery platform, particularly in regard to response
capturing and automatic scoring in the direct assessment.

•

Test and evaluate the workflow and routing for the direct assessment.

•

Verify the integration of the PIAAC platform with the international case management system that
the Consortium provided or, when preferred, with the national case management systems.

Scaling and psychometric characteristics
The FT data were used to examine scaling methodologies to determine the psychometric characteristics
of items and scales. This included the evaluation of the equivalence of item parameters among the trend
items taken from the first cycle of PIAAC. As discussed later, this equivalence is important in supporting
trends and verifying the absence of mode effects. The FT data also provided initial IRT item parameters
that were used to select items and construct the adaptive testing algorithms that were implemented in the
MS. In particular, the following tasks associated with IRT scaling and psychometric characteristics were
the focus of the FT:
•

Examine the stability of item parameters among the trend literacy and numeracy items that are
carried forward from PIAAC Cycle 1.

•

Evaluate the quality and performance of the reading and numeracy component items to select a
final set for the MS.

•

Estimate initial item parameters for all new literacy, numeracy and APS items.

•

Evaluate the overall psychometric characteristics and quality of the FT items to guide the selection
of items for the MS.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

22 
•

Select literacy and numeracy items that can be assembled to work as a locator instrument in the
MS and determine the cut points that will be used for routing respondents to one of several paths
in the MS design.

•

Examine the expected proportions of subsamples routed to the different stages of the tabletdelivered testlets based on their performance on the locator.

In the second cycle of PIAAC, a tablet design was used for the first time. Therefore, the FT was viewed as
a “dress rehearsal” for all newly developed aspects of the survey. In terms of sampling procedures, the FT
sample is not a full probability sample. However, critical aspects of sampling (e.g. sampling individuals
within households), as well as other aspects of the overall sampling plan (e.g. descriptions of the sampling
frames) and sampling guidelines, must be tested in this phase of the project. All quality control forms and
procedures were developed and tested, including monthly reporting on data collection progress and issues
and the capture and use of paradata that were uploaded on a weekly basis through dashboards designed
to support project monitoring. Finally, even though sampling weights were not required for the FT, the
weighting process was tested using the FT data.

The field trial assessment design
In PIAAC Cycle 2, all countries administered the assessment using the tablet-based assessment (TBA).
For one new country, the same approach was followed with an additional sample assigned to the paperbased assessment (PBA).

Tablet-based FT design
The PIAAC Cycle 2 FT was designed as a fully tablet-based survey. All respondents began by responding
to the BQ, which included a set of questions designed to collect information on a broad range of topics,
including familiarity with electronic devices. The BQ was delivered by the interviewer using a computerassisted personal interview (CAPI) system adapted for the tablet. Upon completion of the BQ, the
interviewer converted the machine into tablet mode and handed the tablet and stylus to the respondent. A
tablet skills section demonstrated to the respondents the basic skills required to complete the direct
assessment tasks (e.g. tapping, using drag and drop and highlighting), and the respondents were given
the opportunity to practice each skill. Following the tablet skills demonstration and practice, respondents
were randomly assigned to either the literacy, numeracy or APS path for the direct assessment, as shown
in Figure 1.1 below.
As part of the FT, respondents took a three-minute assessment of either reading or numeracy component
measures. These measures collected data on foundational literacy and numeracy skills. Respondents
routed to the literacy assessment took reading components, and those routed to the numeracy assessment
took numeracy components. The 33% of respondents routed to the APS assessment were randomly
assigned to either reading components or numeracy components.
The reading components measure consisted of two types of tasks: (1) reading sentences of varying lengths
and complexity and deciding whether the sentence makes sense or not, and (2) identifying the appropriate
word from a provided pair that best completes each sentence in a short passage. A total of 44 sentences
and four passages were included in the FT reading component assessment. The sentence items were
organised into four clusters of 11 items each. Each respondent received two clusters of sentences and
one passage, taken from one of 24 forms as shown in Table 1.1.

The numeracy components assessment for the FT also included two types of tasks: (1) identifying how
many objects were displayed in photographs of real-life items and (2) selecting the biggest number from a
set of four choices. The assessment included 18 ‘how many’ items and 24 ‘which is biggest’ items. The
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

24 
items were organised into four clusters. Each ‘how many’ cluster contains four or five items, and each
‘which is biggest’ cluster contains six items. Each respondent received four clusters in total (two ‘how many’
and two ‘which is biggest’) containing 20-22 items, taken from one of 36 forms as shown in Table 1.2.
Following the administration of the components, respondents received a tutorial that introduced them to
the various item types they would encounter during the assessment. These included single-selection and
multiple-selection multiple-choice items, items where respondents must tap on the stimulus (e.g. tap on a
sentence in a passage or on a cell in a table), drag and drop items, and numeric entry items where
respondents used an on-screen keypad to answer. For each item type, respondents could view an
animation showing how to answer a sample question, and they were asked to complete the required steps
on their own. The tutorial also included an orientation to the location of key elements of the assessment
screen, including the instructions about how to answer the question (e.g. “Tap on a choice to answer the
question below”), the question and the stimulus, as well as the navigation and help tools.

Next, respondents were asked to complete the locator tasks. The locator included some of the easiest
tasks in the assessment, along with a few tasks of medium difficulty. During the MS, these tasks were used
to inform routing decisions for the adaptive assessment. While these tasks were not functioning as locator
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 25
tasks in the FT, they were included to gather empirical data about their overall properties. This provided
the foundation for the selection of the locator items for the MS and, most importantly, for determining the
cut points to be used to route respondents to one of the available paths in the MS.
The FT item pool included 16 literacy and 16 numeracy locator items, each comprising two trend items
from PIAAC Cycle 1, and 14 new items per domain. From this item pool, eight literacy and eight numeracy
items were targeted for the MS locator. This increase over the three literacy and three numeracy items in
the “cognitive core” of PIAAC Cycle 1’s computer-based assessment was intended to enhance the
measurement of skills for lower-performing adults. The 16 FT locator items per domain were organised
into four clusters of four items each and presented in a rotated design, resulting in 12 pairs of clusters, as
shown in the 12 shaded cells in Table 1.3. Each respondent took either eight literacy or eight numeracy
tasks (i.e. two clusters). As shown in the overall design (Figure 1.1), respondents assigned to the literacy
assessment took the literacy locator, and those assigned to the numeracy assessment took the numeracy
locator. Respondents routed to the APS assessment were randomly assigned to the literacy or numeracy
locator.
A short orientation provided domain-specific information for each of the cognitive domains. The literacy
orientation included information and practice screens for using tabs to view multiple texts, navigating
through simulated websites, and scrolling. The numeracy orientation repeated the information and practice
screens for using the keypad to provide numeric responses, as this was required for almost half of the
items in the numeracy assessment. For both domains, the orientation concluded with information about
how respondents would be able to navigate back and forth among items. Respondents were told that once
they left a unit, they would not be able to go back to questions in that unit, and they were shown the
confirmation screen that would be displayed at the end of each unit. The APS orientation also provided
information and practice for using tabs to view multiple texts and navigating through simulated websites.
For APS, respondents were told that once they went to a new question, they could not go back to any
previous questions in a unit. The confirmation message that would be displayed near the NEXT arrow was
shown so that respondents were familiar with how to navigate through the APS tasks.
Following the relevant orientation, two 25-minute clusters of either literacy, numeracy or APS items were
administered to each respondent. The number of items in each cluster by domain were 16-17 literacy
items, 16 numeracy items, and 12-14 APS items. As shown in Table 1.4, within each domain, each cluster
was paired with every other cluster, and the positions of those clusters were balanced, resulting in 20 forms
for each domain.

Paper-based operational design
Previous surveys of adult skills were based on paper-based assessments. While the first cycle of PIAAC
was mainly conceived as a computer-based assessment, it still included a paper-based option for the direct
assessment. It was unclear whether that option would be necessary for the second cycle of PIAAC, given
that the use of technology among the adult population had increased in the intervening ten years and the
fact that PIAAC Cycle 2 employed a more user-friendly tablet-delivery platform, which is similar to the
technology used in smartphones.
However, it was agreed that the final decision on using a paper-based assessment for the MS would be
based on findings from the FT. As a result, countries that did not participate in PIAAC Cycle 1 and were
interested in potentially using the paper-based instruments in the MS for PIAAC Cycle 2 were given the
option to participate in an operational test of the paper-based instrument. This test allowed participating
national centres to practice the organisation, administration, scoring and data entry procedures required
for the paper instruments. Of all the participants, Croatia was the only country in the FT that participated
in the operational test of the paper-based instruments.
The additional FT target sample size for countries participating in the paper-based assessment was 300.
For the country participating in the paper-based assessment, one-sixth of the respondents were randomly
assigned to the paper-based assessment. As shown in Figure 1.2, the paper-based instruments were also
administered following the BQ. Each of the paper-based respondents took the core tasks, which included
four literacy and four numeracy items. Respondents were then randomly assigned to take either the literacy
or numeracy booklet, each containing 20 items.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 27

Figure 1.2. Paper-based field trial assessment design

Item development needs
The item development requirements used in the FT and final MS item pools for the literacy, numeracy and
APS domains are shown in Table 1.6. Overall, the MS required about 75-80 items for each of the literacy
and numeracy domains and 65 items for APS. Of these, some 30-32 trend items were needed to serve as
linking items for each of the literacy and numeracy domains. These trend items were used to evaluate their
utility in linking the computer-delivered and tablet-based assessments. Linking items refer to items selected
from PIAAC Cycle 1. They were used to establish the link between PIAAC across cycles. To meet the
goals for each domain, it was necessary to develop and assess a larger pool of items for the FT for each
domain.

Numeracy components

Problem solving in technology-rich environments was a new domain for adult surveys in PIAAC Cycle 1.
APS, the new domain in PIAAC Cycle 2, builds on this foundation but is a distinct construct. All APS tasks
tested during the FT were selected for the MS, encompassing 65 items across 15 units. The APS
assessment in the MS was organised into a pair of clusters, similar to its FT design.
Reading and numeracy component measures were included in PIAAC Cycle 2. Reading components
included items from PIAAC Cycle 1 and the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018,
while all numeracy component items were newly developed for PIAAC Cycle 2 (OECD, 2015[1]). Unlike in
PIAAC Cycle 1, the components were scaled onto the existing PIAAC scales, comprised of items from the
locator and main assessment. In the MS, the reading components had two types of tasks: sentences and
passages. A total of 36 sentences and four passages were included in the MS assessment. The sentence
items were organised into four clusters of nine items each. Each respondent received two clusters of
sentences and one passage. The numeracy components had 16 ‘how many’ and 14 ‘which is biggest’
items in the MS. The ‘how many’ were organised into four clusters, each containing four items. The ‘which
is biggest’ items were organised into four clusters, each containing three to four items. All clusters were
balanced in difficulty and response time as best as possible.

Main study goals and design
The MS assessment design served two primary goals: (1) to provide valid, reliable and comparable
measurement of all the domains included in PIAAC and across all participating countries; and (2) to provide
measurement outcomes comparable across cycles for all participating countries for assessing trends or
changes over time. The direct assessment design for the MS was based on an assumption of about
60 minutes of testing time; however, as it was not timed, some respondents were allowed to take longer
to complete it.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 29

Figure 1.3. General main study assessment design

The MS assessment design was implemented following the design illustrated in Figure 1.3. This design
evolved from the one used in PIAAC Cycle 1 as a result of choices made for PIAAC Cycle 2 regarding: (a)
the mode of delivery, (b) the general design of the assessment, including a longer locator, and (c) the
characteristics of the updated literacy and numeracy item pools and the new APS item pool and their
specific designs. The outcomes of the FT data analysis informed its development and implementation.
The general MS assessment design had the following key features:
•

A single tablet-based delivery design that was used by all participating countries. This tablet-only
design was chosen to reflect the increased use of digital technologies and better data quality
compared with a paper-based option and to avoid many challenges associated with the latter. FT
results confirmed tablets as suitable for the entire PIAAC population, with respondents adapting
well regardless of their experience with technology. A tablet-only design minimised errors through
a uniform delivery platform across countries, maximised construct coverage and ensured
assessment across all three domains, including reading components, numeracy components and
APS. It also enabled the capture of timing data and other process data variables, enhancing data
quality and insights into test-taking behaviours.

•

An abbreviated version of the BQ, known as the "doorstep interview," was developed for
respondents with language barriers in cases where interpreters or translators were unavailable to
assist with administering the full BQ. This doorstep interview was provided in multiple minority
languages and included essential questions on age, gender, educational attainment, employment
status, and immigration status.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

30 
•

A streamlined version of the tablet skills and tablet tutorial sections from the FT was incorporated
into the MS design to provide an effective introduction to the tablet-based tasks. This MS tablet
tutorial section was optimised to allow respondents familiar with tablets to progress quickly while
still offering support for those with less tablet familiarity.

•

PIAAC Cycle 2 included a locator test comprised of eight literacy and eight numeracy items, which
was administered after the BQ and tablet tutorial. The two sections of the locator were balanced in
sequence, with respondents randomly assigned to begin with either the literacy or numeracy items.
Performance on the locator determined respondents’ routing to Path 1, Path 2 or Path 3. Path 1,
for those likely to perform below Proficiency Level 1, included only reading and numeracy
component measures. Path 2, designed for respondents projected to score between Level 1 and
the midpoint of Level 2, included component assessments followed by either the literacy, numeracy
or APS assessment, with each respondent randomly assigned to two of the three domains. Path 3
followed the same design as Path 2, but only 12.5% of respondents were randomly assigned to
take the component assessments. Table 1.7 details decision rules for path assignments:
respondents scoring two or less on both literacy and numeracy sections of the locator were routed
to Path 1, those scoring seven or more on the literacy locator or six or more on the numeracy
locator went to Path 3, and the remaining respondents were directed to Path 2.

•

Each respondent who was assigned to the reading and numeracy component measures took two
sentence clusters and one passage in the reading components section, two ‘how many’ clusters,
and two ‘which is biggest’ clusters in the numeracy components section. The sections were
balanced in position, with respondents randomly assigned to begin with either the reading
components or numeracy components.

•

The first assignment to a domain: The first selection of a domain (literacy, numeracy or APS) was
random. The choice was determined by a random number between 0 and 1 that was generated by
the system. Literacy was chosen if the random number was less than 1/3, numeracy was chosen
if the number was equal to or greater than 1/3 and less than 2/3, and APS if the random number
was equal to or greater than 2/3.

•

The second assignment to a domain: After completing a domain, the respondent proceeded to a
second one, and the domain selection was also based on random probabilities. Thus, a random
number between 0 and 1 was generated again, and the following rules were applied:
o

If the respondent first completed literacy, he or she was assigned numeracy (starting with
numeracy orientation) if the random number was less than 1/2. Otherwise, he or she continued
with APS (starting with the APS orientation).

o

If the respondent first completed numeracy, he or she was assigned literacy (starting with the
literacy orientation) if the random number was less than 1/2. Otherwise, he or she continued
with APS (starting with the APS orientation).

o

If the respondent first completed APS, he or she was assigned literacy (starting with the literacy
orientation) if the random number was less than 1/2. Otherwise, he or she continued with
numeracy (starting with the numeracy orientation).

 31
•

Notably, PIAAC was the first international comparative survey to fully incorporate -MST in the MS
(OECD, 2019). In PIAAC Cycle 2, the literacy and numeracy assessments used a hybrid design,
combining adaptive and linear test components, as shown in Figure 1.4. The assessment began
with a locator test where all respondents received the same 16 items (eight literacy and eight
numeracy items, in a balanced order). The adaptive part of the hybrid design for each domain used
a 1-2-3 MSAT structure: Stage 1 included a single difficulty level for routing, with eight items in
literacy and eight in numeracy. Stage 2 presented two difficulty levels with six different testlets
(three low-difficulty and three high-difficulty), assigned based on locator test performance. Stage 3
included six testlets (two low-difficulty, two medium-difficulty and two high-difficulty), with
assignments based on performance in the locator and Stage 2 testlets. This design took advantage
of the longer locator to improve routing decisions to Stage 2. Its Stages 2 and 3 were fully balanced
in that all items appeared in both stages. Tables 1.8 and 1.9 report the adaptive paths for literacy
and numeracy instruments. To improve routing decisions, the PIAAC Cycle 2 design randomly
assigned a portion of the respondents to the linear part of the design, which featured clusters of
items with average difficulty that spanned a broader range of item difficulties. Annex A of this report,
which is available online, provides detailed information on the testlets and clusters used at the
different stages of the assessment (i.e. units included, number of items included).
Based on the locator test and different adaptive paths developed for literacy and numeracy, the
design parameters (e.g. locator threshold) for routing respondents in the MSAT were established,
see Table 1.10. The approach for determining these locator thresholds was based on the expected
proportions of subsamples routed to the different formats and the various stages of the tabletdelivered testlets in the MS.
The linear part of the hybrid assessment design was developed to be a non-adaptive path of
medium-difficulty clusters in Stage 2 and Stage 3, where the assignment of testlets depended on
the respondent’s performance on prior stages of the assessment. The linear component ensured
a minimum number of responses per item across proficiency levels. After the locator, 25% of
respondents were randomly assigned to this linear component, which included six Stage 2 and six
Stage 3 testlets, detailed in Table 1.8 for literacy and Table 1.9 for numeracy. Note that
respondents were randomly assigned to Design A or Design B, explained below in the context of
the assembly of instruments.

To support the proposed hybrid MSAT design, optimal test design methods were applied to perform
all assemblies (Ali and van Rijn, 2016; van der Linden, 2005). A stepwise assembly approach (Ali,
van Rijn and Robin, 2023[2]) was implemented to break down the assembly problem into
manageable steps, as illustrated in Figure 1.5. The first step was to partition the main item pool (all
items other than the locator items) into two parallel, non-overlapping sets (i.e. item sets 1 and 2).
This step was followed by assembling the Stage 2 and Stage 3 testlets from each item set.
Similarly, the linear clusters were assembled from each item set, followed by assembling linear
forms. This approach lends itself to building a more balanced MSAT design that rotates all items
across all relevant test positions (i.e. Stages 2 and 3 in our case). In each of these steps, statistical
(e.g. difficulty, precision) and non-statistical constraints (e.g. testlet length, the number of trend and
new items, content domains, item format and expected response time) were considered.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

Linear Clusters

Linear Clusters

The APS assessment design was different from the one developed for literacy and numeracy.
Based on discussions with both the Technical Advisory Group and the APS expert group, a
decision was made to employ a linear design with rotated clusters for this domain. This decision
was based on a number of factors. First, the locator does not contain any items designed to provide
information on the expected proficiency of respondents on the APS scale. Additionally, the adaptive
design required that units (not items) be classified as easy, medium or difficult. This was
challenging for APS since the sequence of items was designed to introduce new features of a
problem that required respondents to adapt their problem-solving strategies. Removing items to
produce units of more uniform difficulty would not only be challenging given the number of available
items in the FT but, more importantly, would compromise the measurement of the construct. For
these reasons, the APS assessment was non-adaptive and a balanced incomplete block design
was applied, so all respondents assigned to it received a set of items of similar difficulty.
Accordingly, APS items/units were divided into five clusters. Respondents assigned to APS were
exposed to two randomly selected clusters of items, as illustrated in Table 1.11.

•

After completing the direct assessment, respondents were asked two questions about their
perceived performance and effort. These questions gauged respondents' views on how well they
thought they performed, with five options ranging from answering a few items correctly (20% or
less) to almost all (81-100%). The effort question had a scale from 1 to 10, with 1 representing the
least effort and 10 the most. The interview then proceeded to post-interview questions, during
which the interviewer thanked the respondent for participating and provided an incentive, if
applicable.

FT data analysis and simulation studies to implement the literacy and numeracy hybrid MSAT designs
were critical for the development and validation of the MS design. Analyses of the MS data confirmed the
measurement characteristics of the hybrid MSATs. Results are reported in Chapter 10.

Summary and conclusions
This chapter describes and illustrates the goals and assessment design for both the FT and MS in the
second cycle of PIAAC. The multiple goals of the FT illustrate its importance in successfully implementing
the MS. It was intended to help evaluate four key areas – survey operations, instrument quality, tabletdelivery platform, and scaling and psychometric characteristics. The fact that the results of PIAAC were
being linked to previous surveys of adult skills, mainly the first cycle of PIAAC, while being implemented in
the new delivery mode (tablet) – while also including enhanced MSAT design – added to the importance
of the FT. The information generated during the FT was used to help establish the adaptive portion of the
MS for literacy and numeracy assessment.
The general MS design in PIAAC Cycle 2 included many new features across the cognitive domains. As
the OECD and the participating countries identified the feasibility of moving to tablet-based assessment in
the presence or the absence of a paper-based option, alternative designs were also illustrated for the FT
and described in this chapter. The introduction of doorstep interview to include a special subpopulation
(Ali, 2024[3]) was described as well. Within the cognitive domains in PIAAC, the described designs brought
innovation and important benefits to the overall goal of producing outcomes that are both valid and
comparable across countries and over time.

2. Sampling design
Wendy Van de Kerckhove, Lin Li, Tom Krenzke and Leyla Mohadjer, Westat

The PIAAC Cycle 2 standards required countries to select a probability
sample of non-institutionalised adults from age 16 to 65, limiting exclusions
to under five percent. The choice of sampling frame, sampling stages and
sample selection methods differed between the countries depending on the
specific situation, such as the availability of population registers and the
geographic size. Countries needed to ensure that the initial sample was
large enough to achieve the target number of completes, after accounting
for non-response and ineligibility. These considerations influenced the
country’s sample design. This chapter provides details on each participating
country’s sample design and selection results.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 41

Introduction
Participating countries and economies were required to develop their sample design and selection plans
according to the standards provided in the PIAAC Cycle 2 Technical Standards and Guidelines (TSG) 1
and to submit their plans to the Consortium for approval. The sample design and selection plans included
information about sampling frames and their coverage, stages of sampling, probabilities of selection,
sampling units, sample sizes and the processes for sample selection at each stage of sampling. In addition,
the countries were required to complete and submit quality control sample selection forms to the
Consortium. These were used to verify that the sample selection was conducted in an unbiased and
randomised way consistent with PIAAC standards.
The target population for PIAAC consists of all non-institutionalised adults from age 16 to 65 who reside in
the country at the time of data collection. Countries were allowed to expand the target population to include
additional subpopulations of interest to the country, provided they followed the TSG on such
supplementation. The next section provides more details on the PIAAC target population and on national
target populations that expand beyond the PIAAC standard definition. This is followed by a review of
sources of country sampling frames and their coverage of the target population.
The TSG allowed each country to choose a sample design and selection approach that is most optimal
and cost-effective as long as it applies full selection probability methods to select a representative sample
from the PIAAC target population. The rest of this chapter presents descriptions of the standard PIAAC
and national sample designs and probabilities of selection; the definition of sampling units and sample
selection methods; the PIAAC sample size goals and description of the process applied to determine the
initial sample sizes; sample selection results and a summary of the sampling quality control procedures;
and finally, a brief description of the incentive plans for PIAAC and recommendations for future cycles.

Target population and sampling frame
A clear and precise definition of the target population is necessary to ensure that each participating country
adequately covers the population of interest and to maintain consistency and comparability across
countries. The PIAAC target population consists of all non-institutionalised adults between age 16 and 65
(inclusive) who reside in the country (their usual place of residency is in the country) at the time of data
collection. Adults were to be included regardless of citizenship, nationality or language (standard 4.1.1).
The target population excludes adults residing in institutional collective dwelling units or group quarters
such as prisons, hospitals and nursing homes, as well as adults residing in military barracks and military
bases. However, full-time and part-time members of the military who do not reside in military barracks or
military bases are included in the target population.
Adults in other non-institutional collective dwelling units or group quarters, such as workers’ quarters or
halfway homes, are also included in the target population. This includes adults living at school in student
group quarters, such as a school dormitory. Adults who were unable to complete the background
questionnaire (BQ) or assessment because of hearing impairment, blindness/visual impairment or physical
disability are considered in scope; however, they were excluded from PIAAC response rate calculations
(i.e. subtracted from the denominator) because the BQ and assessment do not accommodate such
situations. Similarly, adults who were unable to complete the doorstep interview because of an
unaccommodated language or were unable to complete the BQ because of a learning/mental disability or
reading/writing difficulty are in scope but excluded from PIAAC BQ response rate calculations. Also, adults
who were unable to complete the assessment because of a lack of tablet skills are in scope but excluded
from the PIAAC assessment response rate calculations.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

42 
For countries selecting persons from population registries, the midpoint of the data collection was used to
define the age-eligible population. The use of the midpoint considers and accepts that some newly 16year-olds and some 65-year-olds would be outside the 16-65 range at the time of the interview – about
0.3%. For countries selecting persons from a household roster via a Screener questionnaire, eligibility was
determined based on age at the time of the Screener.
The target population does not cover the entire geographic area for the following countries:
•

Belgium – The target population consists of the Flemish Region of Belgium only.

•

United Kingdom – The target population consists of England only.

Sampling frames and their coverage
The sampling frame is the list from which the sample is selected, so the quality of the sampling frame
affects the quality of the sample. In addition, adequate information on the frame must be available to
conduct sampling, data collection, weighting and non-response bias analyses. Most countries with multiple

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 43
stages of selection had specified multiple frames. The Consortium reviewed these frames to ensure they
included sufficiently reliable information for sampling individual units and ultimately locating individuals for
the interview and assessment. In the next sections, we provide information about the sampling frames
used at each stage of selection and the coverage of these frames.
In PIAAC, the non-coverage rate, combined over all stages of sampling, could not exceed 5%
(standard 4.2.1). Thus, the sampling frames for each country were required to include 95% or more of the
PIAAC target population. Frame non-coverage rates were limited as much as possible to avoid biases due
to non-coverage of some subgroups of the population.

Sampling frames
PIAAC standards require that sampling frames are up to date and include only one record for each
sampling unit. Countries had to examine their sampling frames and eliminate duplicate records when lists
were combined to create a sampling frame. Countries were required to assess the extent of duplication
and the proportion of out-of-scope units on the frame and, if necessary, develop a plan to correct these
problems. In addition, countries also evaluated and developed plans to address any non-coverage in the
frame that was not addressed in the documentation of country-specific exclusions (see Tables 2.5 and 2.6).
The methodology used to create these frames was also reviewed by the Consortium.

Multistage sample designs required a sampling frame for each stage of selection. Some countries used
national population registries as sampling frames, which contain useful variables for stratification,
weighting and non-response bias analyses. If the country had a list of residents that was of sufficient quality
and covered the PIAAC target population, no frame of households or household sampling was necessary.
Such countries directly sampled eligible persons from the registry, or first selected geographic areas and
then selected eligible persons within the geographic areas. Table 2.3 provides the full list of sampling
frames employed by countries with population registry samples. Information about the sampling units at
each stage can be found in Table 2.7 later in this chapter.
For multistage area sample designs in which a person registry is not used, dwelling unit registries might
be available. Otherwise, listing procedures are necessary to create a frame of households within the
selected geographic clusters. A frame of geographic clusters can be formed by combining adjacent
geographic areas, respecting their population sizes and taking into consideration travel distances for
interviewers. Within selected households, field enumeration (screener) is necessary to create a frame of
people. Table 2.4 contains sampling frames for the countries without population registries using screeners
for PIAAC. The exception is that Spain is included in Table 2.4 among the countries without population
registries, even though it has a population registry. Spain used a population registry as the sampling frame
for the first two sampling stages only and used a household screener for the third sampling stage.

Non-coverage of the target population
As mentioned earlier, the non-coverage rate for PIAAC, combined over all stages of sampling, may not
exceed 5% (standard 4.2.1), and thus, the sampling frames for each country were required to cover 95%
or more of the standard PIAAC target population. All exclusions to the PIAAC target population, whether
they exceed the threshold, were reviewed by the Consortium. Exclusions are acceptable only if they occur
because of operational or resource considerations, such as excluding persons in hard-to-reach areas. The
Consortium asked each country to identify possible exclusions before sample selection. Adjustments for
any non-coverage of the target population in each country were made through benchmarking during the
weighting process (see Chapter 8). A complete list of exclusions for countries using population registries
is presented in Table 2.5; Table 2.6 includes a similar list for countries using screeners. Note the noncoverage rate in the tables accounts for excluded subpopulations such as undocumented immigrants or
non-institutionalised collective dwelling units. Other exclusions that will occur as a natural part of the survey
process (e.g. dangerous areas that were not known in advance) are not included in the estimated noncoverage rate.
In addition to PIAAC-eligible persons not included in sampling frames, persons who were included in the
frame but in practice were impossible to be interviewed were treated as exclusions conditional on the total
exclusion rate staying at or below 5%. Chapter 19 provides more information about this group, with
Table 19.1 showing the overall exclusion rate for each country.

National sample designs and probabilities of selection
The PIAAC standard sample design is a self-weighting design of persons (or of households, for countries
without person registries). A self-weighting design is achieved when each sample person (or household, if
sampling dwelling units) has an equal probability of selection (standard 4.4.3). For geographically large
countries, the typical sample design is a stratified multistage clustered area sample. For geographically
small participating countries, the sample design had less clustering and fewer stages of sampling. Also,
several countries had lists of households or persons already available from national registries or registries
managed by municipalities.
The TSG allow each country to choose a sample design and selection approach that is most optimal and
cost-effective if the sample design applies full selection probability methods. Each participating country
was required to produce a probability-based sample, representative of the target population of the country.
The PIAAC standards require probability-based samples, which are essential for two main reasons. First,
probability sampling encompasses a set of designs that leads to a variety of unbiased sampling
approaches that allow analysts to generalise the results to the target population. Second, measures of
precision related to survey estimates (i.e. standard errors, margins of error, confidence intervals) can be
computed under a probability design only. Hence, statistical tests for differences between survey estimates
are possible only under a probability-based design.
The PIAAC standard probabilities of selection as applied to each country’s design are presented in this
section.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 47
Each person in the PIAAC target population must have a nonzero probability of selection resulting from
the application of established and professionally recognised principles of scientific sampling
(standard 4.4.1). That is, every in-scope person must have a chance of being selected into the PIAAC
sample. The following presents the PIAAC approach that was recommended for selecting the ultimate
sampling unit for one-, two-, three- and four-stage sample designs, respectively. The approach is based
on the PIAAC standards and guidelines.
Countries were sent the formulae prior to their sample selection process, and they were asked to confirm
or provide formulae showing their deviations from the self-weighting design. The Consortium conducted
checks during and after sample selection. Some countries deviated from these formulae due to
oversampling (as given in Table 2.2) or alternative sampling formulae. Another reason for varying sampling
weights is that a few countries also conducted the deselection of open cases toward the end of data
collection to reduce their workloads so that cases could be worked fully. Table 19.11 provides the variation
of the base weights, which identifies the countries that achieved self-weighting or near self-weighting
designs (a coefficient of variation of less than 0.05). Among the 18 registry countries in Cycle 2, selfweighting or near self-weighting designs were achieved by Croatia, Estonia, the Flemish Region of
Belgium, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Singapore and Sweden. Among the 13 screener countries,
self-weighting or near self-weighting samples of dwelling units was achieved by Korea and Latvia.

Zealand, Portugal, the Slovak Republic and Spain. Canada applied both an alternative design
implementation strategy and an oversample that caused variation in the resulting household base weights.

across strata based on expected response rates. Ireland’s weights varied mainly due to not releasing
reserve samples uniformly across all areas. New Zealand’s weights varied due to oversampling and
applying a deselection approach. Portugal’s weights varied due to selecting a small PSU with certainty.

household base weights. Spain’s household base weights varied slightly due to selecting the same number
of households across PSUs.

All countries with three- or four-stage designs selected samples of dwelling units before the enumeration
and selection of persons within households. Although the goal was to select one person per household,
the selection of more than one person per household was preferred for countries with a large variation in
household size (standard 4.4.4). Countries that selected two persons aged 16 to 65 in large households
include Czechia, Latvia, Portugal, the Slovak Republic, Spain and the United States. In addition, New
Zealand selected at most one person from each of the three age strata (16 to 24, 25 to 65, 66 to 75) within
a household. Also, the United States had two strata (16 to 65, 66 to 74) where two persons could be
selected from the 16 to 65 stratum if there were four or more eligible individuals, and one person was
selected among the 66 to 74 year-olds. Details regarding the selection methods for countries with threeor four-stage designs are presented in Table 2.8.
Stratification groups sample units into homogeneous sets (strata) and reduces sampling variability
between such strata and thus reduces the overall sampling variance associated with the resulting survey
estimates. To maximise the benefit of stratification, stratification variables should be reliable and related to
the survey outcome. Many of the countries utilising population registries benefit from the person-level
characteristics available as stratification variables. The stratification and/or sorting variables for countries
with one, two, three and four stages of selection are detailed in Table 2.9.
