Sample size determination
Adequate sample sizes are needed to establish stable item characteristics, estimate separate population
models for each tested language in a participating country and, ultimately, report results for multiple groups
within the population of interest. Population modelling is a critical step in obtaining appropriate proficiency
values to be used in describing the distributions of skills in a country and in reporting national and
subpopulation data.
The overall goal of the sample design for the main study was to obtain a nationally representative sample
of the target population in each participating country that is proportional to the population distribution across
the country (i.e. a self-weighting sample design). As mentioned earlier, countries had the option to increase
sample sizes to obtain reliable estimates for groups of special interest (e.g. 16- to 29-year-olds), for
geographic regions (e.g. states and provinces) or extend the age range (e.g. 66-plus). However, the
minimum sample size required was for a self-weighting design, and any sample size attributable to
oversampling, or subgroups outside of the PIAAC target population, was additional. PIAAC sample size
requirements are presented below.
To determine the initial sample size for the main study, the sample size had to be adjusted to account for
survey ineligibility in the field, expected non-response to the BQ, doorstep interview and the assessment,
and the expected BQ language barrier rate. For countries with a household screener, sample size goals
had to be constructed for the screener to account for ineligibility and screener non-response, in addition to
non-response to the BQ, doorstep interview and assessment.
In most highly clustered surveys or those with a high degree of variability in sampling rates due to
oversampling, initial sample sizes must be increased to retain the desired precision. For PIAAC, countries
were asked to estimate the design effect of their design with such an increase in mind (guideline 4.3.1B).
The estimated design effect could be based on their Cycle 1 experience, field trial data or other similar
surveys.

PIAAC required sample sizes
The minimum sample size requirement was 4 000 to 5 000 completed cases per reporting language,
depending upon the sample design. These requirements are shown in Table 2.10. The number of
completed cases that countries achieved can be found in Table 17.2 in Chapter 17.

Sample size goals and reserve samples
The eligibility rate and response rate assumptions specified by countries were reviewed to help ensure
that initial sample sizes were large enough to achieve the required number of completed cases and meet
the reporting precision requirements. Some adjustments to these expected rates were made based on
field trial experience. At the person level, eligibility was defined as being part of the target population.
Countries that included a dwelling unit sample as part of their sample design were further required to
provide an estimated screener eligibility rate. Selected units found to be vacant, for seasonal use only, not
actually dwelling units, or without persons aged 16 to 65 were considered ineligible for the survey and had
to be accounted for in the derivation of the final sample size.
It is difficult to predict the non-response and ineligibility rates for a survey like PIAAC. As a result, the
Consortium encouraged each country to consider selecting a reserve sample of at least 50% of the size of
the main initial (original) sample. The requirement was to select the reserve sample at the same time as
the original sample and then set it aside and not use it unless sample monitoring showed potential for
shortfall. Reserve samples were recommended over supplemental samples because computing the
selection probabilities is simpler with a reserve sample than with supplemental samples. The same concept
was used if a country was concerned about exceeding the sample size goal by a significant amount. After
selecting a sample 50% larger than the required sample size, the country was able to release to the field
a sample that was less than 100% by randomly selecting (subsetting) from the original sample and then
releasing more cases as needed. Also, the countries could split the reserve sample randomly into several

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 59
“release” groups as long as the release group by itself was representative of the country and not a handpicked group.

Sample selection results
Table 2.13 below provides the final sample sizes for each stage of sampling for each country. Chapter 19

Twenty-three countries used a portion of their reserve sample. In addition, four countries opted to deselect

be used in the later phase of data collection to reduce cost and possibly non-response bias as well.

and randomly deselected some of the not-worked cases about one to two months before data collection
ended. The United States randomly deselected some of the cases with low influence on potential nonresponse bias so that interviewers could focus more on the remaining cases. Design weights were adjusted
to account for the release of the reserve sample and deselection.

Sampling quality control checks
The Consortium developed a comprehensive set of quality assurance and quality control checks to ensure
PIAAC produced high-quality data that were comparable across countries. Chapter 21 contains a
description of the quality assurance and quality control procedures developed for all sampling activities,
including sample design and selection results. Countries were required to complete quality control sample
selection forms, which collected sampling information for each stage of selection using standard templates.
The templates were designed to capture aggregated information that was necessary for verifying that the
sample was representative of the target population and that sampling was conducted in an unbiased and
randomised way. For example, at each stage, countries were asked to estimate and report the total target
population within each stratum so that distributions by stratum could be reviewed at each sampling stage.
The Consortium carried out all sampling quality control checks as listed in Chapter 21 and informed the
countries of the approval of their plans/procedures or asked for revisions to aspects that did not meet the
PIAAC standards.
Table 2.14 provides a summary of the sample design and selection quality assessment. For the sampling
plan, it was essential that a complete sampling plan was provided and that the country responded to
feedback from the Consortium. As it relates to the sample selection process conducted in the country’s
home office, it was important that complete Quality Control (QC) sample selection forms were provided
prior to data collection to check that each person in the PIAAC target population had a nonzero and known
(calculable) probability of selection resulting from the application of established and professionally
recognised principles of scientific sampling, and that there was no substitution of sampling units. Regarding
sample selection processes that were conducted in the field, countries were assessed according to the
following criteria, ensuring that:
•

persons were selected from within households using a fully enumerated grid of household
members

•

each person in the PIAAC target population had a nonzero and known (calculable) probability of
selection resulting from the application of established and professionally recognised principles of
scientific sampling

•

no more than two persons in the PIAAC target population (age 16-65) were selected in a household

•

no more than 10% of households had two persons selected

•

there was no substitution of sampling units.

Cautionary remarks were given to Lithuania and the Slovak Republic. The age and gender distributions of
respondents differed substantially from Lithuania’s initial expectations. Through validation, Lithuania
identified interviewers who were only listing a single household member to ensure that person got selected;
the identified cases were flagged as falsified. Lithuania also explained that in some regions, household
respondents may also underreport the number of people living in the household in order not to jeopardise
the financial incentives received from the government. For the Slovak Republic, the average number of
eligible persons per household was much lower than expected. A possible explanation, provided by the
National Centre, is that interviewers listed on the screener the number of people who were present at home
at the time of the screener interview, not all eligible people.

Respondent incentives
Respondent incentives have been shown to be effective in improving response rates without affecting the
respondent’s performance. As a result, the use of incentives can potentially reduce bias in the estimates.
As such, countries were permitted to offer modest incentives to obtain respondent cooperation, such as a
monetary or non-monetary incentive (e.g. pen, notepad, candy, mug, voucher, gift certificate). A variety of
incentives were offered across most participating countries, with the exception of Denmark and France,
which did not offer any incentives. Chapter 19 provides details about the type of incentives used during
the main study data collection in PIAAC.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 63

Recommendations for future cycles
Based on the field trial and main study experience of PIAAC Cycles 1 and 2, the Consortium is proposing
a series of recommendations for future cycles of PIAAC as it relates to sampling activities.
•

Countries should follow the TSG on the qualifications of the National Sampling Manager.

•

Countries should evaluate the quality of the frames from the start so they have adequate time to
look for alternatives if the quality (and coverage) of the frame does not meet the standards.

•

Before countries move forward with the sample that has been selected, the QC sample selection
forms must be reviewed by the Consortium, with feedback provided.

•

Countries should use the results of PIAAC to improve upon the stratification and sorting scheme.
The non-response bias analysis and the scores can be used to identify better stratification and
sorting variables, such as education, employment and other variables that are correlated with the
scores.

•

Countries should use the design effects to identify ways to improve the sample design. That is,
countries should evaluate how to reduce the clustering and unequal probabilities effects as plans
occur for the next cycle.

•

Countries need to follow the schedules of all QC sampling activities so there is adequate time to
identify problems and incorporate changes to correct mistakes in a timely fashion.

•

Countries should put more emphasis on adaptive survey design (ASD) and provide timely reports
on what ASD procedures they are implementing.

•

Countries need to start validation of screeners earlier to identify and correct any issues with
household enumeration.

3. The development of the PIAAC
cognitive instruments
Mary Louise Lennon and Laura Halderman, ETS

This chapter describes the development of the cognitive instruments used
to assess adults’ skills in literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving.
The framework of each domain is briefly summarised with a focus on how
the frameworks defined the constructs and guided item development. The
stages of item development are described, including trend item selection,
new item development, reviews of new items by subject-matter experts and
national teams, and the main study item pool selection process following
the field trial. The chapter also highlights the adaptation of the assessment
for tablet-based delivery, enhancing accessibility and user experience.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 65

Introduction
The first cycle of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) was
the largest and most innovative survey of adults ever conducted. PIAAC Cycle 2 built upon that foundation
to develop an assessment focused on the types of everyday tasks adults encounter at work, home and in
their communities. These are tasks that increasingly require skills related to navigating, critically analysing
and the flexibility to solve problems when presented with sudden or unexpected changes.
More specifically, Cycle 2 was designed to:
•

include instruments developed to assess literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving skills,
many of which incorporate digital resources that respondents likely encounter in their everyday
lives

•

collect information about the skills of individuals with low levels of numeracy proficiency by
developing the first large-scale assessment of numeracy component skills

•

expand the number of adults who could participate in a technology-based assessment by
developing instruments that could be delivered on tablets using a familiar and intuitive interface

•

improve measurement by employing an adaptive design that both increased the number of items
in the overall item pool for each domain and administered a subset of those items to individuals
that was targeted to their skills

•

introduce innovations in the translation and adaptation process to better ensure comparable
measurement and support the work of National Centres

•

involve and support countries in the instrument development process so that the assessment tasks
reflect a cross-linguistic and cross-cultural perspective.

The Terms of Reference issued by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)
for PIAAC Cycle 2 characterised the direct assessment as the core of the survey. The cognitive items that
make up the direct assessment provide policy makers with information about the skills and knowledge of
adult populations − from those with limited literacy, numeracy and problem-solving skills to those who can
effectively manage complex tasks. While PIAAC introduced significant new elements to the development
of the direct assessment, key aspects of previous surveys were employed as well. In particular, as was
the case in Cycle 1 and the earlier assessments to which PIAAC was linked, this development work was
based on frameworks that defined the assessment constructs for each domain as well as features of the
tasks designed to measure those constructs.

Developing the PIAAC cognitive frameworks
Assessment frameworks provide the foundation for developing a coherent assessment. In a coherent
assessment, the framework, assessment instrument and scheme for interpreting the results of the
assessment are linked, as shown in Figure 3.1.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

66 

Figure 3.1. The Components of a Coherent Assessment

The framework defines the construct to be measured, identifies the characteristics of items that will
measure that construct, and specifies how the scale or scales will be interpreted and reported. The overall
goal of this process, which is based on Messick’s (1994[1]) construct-centred approach, is to explicitly lay
out the inferences and assumptions about what is to be measured and how the results will be interpreted
and reported.
The frameworks for each of the three PIAAC cognitive domains – literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem
solving – were developed by groups with expertise in each domain following a model that consisted of the
following five steps.1

Define the domain
Each expert group began by developing a working definition of the domain and the assumptions underlying
that definition. Such a definition was an important step in developing the assessment framework as it set
the boundaries for what would and would not be measured and explicitly communicated the assumptions
underlying the design and development of the assessment.

Identify the core dimensions of the domain that should be used in building the assessment
and reporting results
Expanding upon the domain definition, the experts next identified the dimensions or components of the
domain that were used to guide the construction of the assessment tasks and helped to differentiate
performance at each level of proficiency on the reporting scale. The goal of this step was to develop a
coherent representation of the domain to ensure that assessment tasks cover the core dimensions so that
policymakers and others can summarise and report information in useful ways.

Further specify each of the dimensions
In order to use the core dimensions to develop the assessment and, later, to interpret the results, each
dimension needed to be further specified and defined. Using subject-matter expertise, existing literature
and experience from other large-scale assessments, the experts provided detailed information that allowed
item developers to categorise stimulus materials and items so this information could be used in reporting
results.
An example taken from the work of the numeracy expert group may be helpful in understanding how steps
two and three were implemented in the framework development process. In step two, the numeracy experts
identified four core dimensions of numeracy: cognitive processes, mathematical content, representations
and contexts. In step three, each of these core dimensions was further specified. For example, the core
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 67
dimension of mathematical content specifically includes these four key areas: quantity and number, space
and shape, change and relationships, and data and chance. These specifications allow item writers to
develop items targeting particular aspects of each dimension, which ultimately allows for more precise
understanding and reporting of numeracy proficiency. Note that each numeracy item was classified to one
of the specific aspects for each of the four core dimensions. A similar process was used to further specify
the other core dimensions.

Specify the distribution of tasks across each of the dimensions
To provide a clear blueprint for test developers, the expert groups were asked to specify targets for the
percentage of items that should fall into each of the elaborated categories. For example, in numeracy, the
experts decided on the following distribution for the cognitive processes: 25-35% of the items should
require respondents to access and assess situations mathematically, 30-40% should require acting on and
using mathematics, and 25-35% should require respondents to evaluate, critically reflect and make
judgments. While it was not always possible to meet these targets precisely, due to the constraint of
balancing linking and new items, these targets made the aspirations for the assessment explicit.

Identify variables within each dimension that are expected to drive difficulty
Finally, given their experience and knowledge in their respective fields, the experts were asked to include
information in the framework about the variables that were expected to influence task complexity. In
numeracy, for instance, complexity factors can include textual aspects (such as how explicitly the
mathematical information is given in a problem) and mathematical aspects (such as the type of operation
or number of steps required to solve the problem). Elaborating such factors, or variables, guided test
developers in targeting items at different points along the difficulty scale and informed the interpretation of
the assessment results.
Finally, the expert groups and test developers used main study item-level data and the framework
classifications to describe the proficiency levels in each domain. The definition of the proficiency levels for
each scale are reported in greater detail in Chapter 5. For previous large-scale literacy assessments,
including the International Adult Literacy Survey (IALS), the Adult Literacy and Lifeskills (ALL) survey and
PIAAC Cycle 1, describing the proficiency levels in each domain provided a useful means for exploring the
progression of information-processing demands along each of the scales, and for defining what scores
mean at particular points along the scales. In this way, the descriptions of proficiency contribute to the
construct validity of inferences based on scores from the measure on which it is based (Messick, 1989[2]).
The following sections summarise key aspects of the frameworks (OECD, 2021[3]) for the three cognitive
domains assessed in PIAAC Cycle 2: literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving.

Literacy framework
The OECD specified in the Terms of Reference for PIAAC Cycle 2 that the conceptual framework for the
literacy domain was expected to be largely unchanged from Cycle 1. The Literacy Expert Group (LEG)
reviewed the Cycle 1 framework and suggested updates to reflect the evolution in the field over the past
ten years, primarily reflecting the growing importance of reading in digital environments. For example, the
framework discusses the need to account for the skills required to interact with multiple texts effectively.
That is, adults need to be able to extract, use, and evaluate the quality of information across multiple text
sources. Thus, the ability to work with multiple texts was deemed critical to incorporate in the Cycle 2
framework.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

68 
Definition of the literacy domain
In Cycle 1, literacy was defined as understanding, evaluating, using and engaging with written texts to
participate in society, to achieve one’s goals, and to develop one’s knowledge and potential.
For the second cycle of PIAAC, the LEG proposed the following definition (OECD, 2021[3]):
Literacy is accessing, understanding, evaluating and reflecting on written texts in order to achieve one’s goals,
to develop one’s knowledge and potential, and to participate in society.
Changes from the Cycle 1 definition included:
•

The inclusion of “accessing” as an important component of reading includes retrieving information
within a text and, in the case of reading situations that involve multiple texts, searching and
selecting relevant texts.

•

The inclusion of “reflecting on” includes reflecting on both content and form. Reflecting requires
readers to draw on their own experience or knowledge to compare, contrast or hypothesise about
different perspectives or viewpoints.

•

Deletion of “engaging with”. The LEG discussed this change in detail but decided to delete this
process as it is not specifically measured in the cognitive assessment. It is an aspect of literacy
that relates to achieving one’s goals and, as such, was included in the framework as part of a
discussion about engaging with and using texts for that purpose.

Core dimensions of literacy
Three core dimensions of literacy were defined for Cycle 2: cognitive task demands, texts and social
contexts. These align with the dimensions referred to as aspects of tasks, categories of texts and social
contexts in the framework for Cycle 1. Cognitive task demands, text and their interactions are primary
difficulty drivers for literacy, while social contexts are not. Social contexts were included to ensure a variety
of content that appropriately reflects a range of experiences in adults’ lives. The dimensions related to the
difficulty are further elaborated as follows.

Cognitive task demands
The literacy framework in Cycle 2 identifies three broad cognitive strategies that support most reading
activities: accessing text, understanding and evaluating. Each is defined as shown below:
•

Accessing text: searching and locating texts or information within texts. Two types of search
processes are explained in the framework: identifying a relevant text or texts in a set and locating
information within a text. Access tasks range in difficulty from those that require a simple match
between text contained in a short paragraph and the questions phrasing to tasks that involve
searching information across multiple texts.

•

Understanding: constructing meaning and representations, which includes literal comprehension
and inferential comprehension both within a single text and across multiple texts. Literal
comprehension tasks involve a direct or paraphrased match between the question and target
information in the text. In contrast, inferential comprehension requires a reader to integrate
information across entire text passages in order to perform tasks such as identifying the main idea,
developing a summary, and providing or recognising an appropriate title for a passage. In more
complex understanding tasks, a reader may be asked to draw inferences across multiple texts.

•

Evaluating: assessing the accuracy and credibility of text information, evaluating the soundness of
the text (i.e. completeness and consistency), evaluating the relevance of one or more texts for a
given task, and reflecting on the author’s intent, purpose and effectiveness.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 69
Texts
The literacy framework in Cycle 2 defines texts as either static or interactive. Texts are also classified in
four ways: by text type (or genre), text format, text organisation and source.
•

Text type – While many real-life texts cannot easily be classified by genre, largely because they
tend to cut across categories, the framework specifies that six text types were to be kept in mind
to ensure a general distribution across the assessment. As in the first cycle of PIAAC and PISA,
those six types included description, narration, exposition, argumentation, instruction and
transaction.

•

Text format – In previous large-scale adult assessments, as well as in PISA, texts were classified
as continuous or non-continuous. This was viewed as an important distinction, as each format
requires different text knowledge and a different approach to text processing. In keeping with this
understanding, texts included in the PIAAC Cycle 2 assessment included continuous, noncontinuous and mixed texts.
o

Continuous texts have sentences organised into paragraphs. Examples include newspaper
articles, essays, brochures and announcements.

o

Non-continuous texts include tables, graphs, forms and diagrams, where information is often
displayed in lists. Examples include restaurant menus, television schedules, tables showing
interest rates or sports rankings, and lists of navigation links shown on a webpage.

o

Mixed texts include both continuous and non-continuous elements. A web page or article with
paragraphs of information supported by a table or graph is an example of a mixed text.

•

Text organisation – This aspect focuses on the ways of presenting content and facilitating access
to information of interest. These include layout features and content representation, such as titles,
headings and, in the case of longer texts, chapters and indices. Digital texts may include tools such
as windows, scroll bars, tabs and hyperlinks.

•

Source – As noted earlier, the literacy framework for Cycle 2 emphasises the importance of
including both single and multiple texts in the assessment tasks. Single texts are defined as those
that originate in a single source – e.g. a single author, publication medium and date of publication.
Multiple texts have different authors or are published through different authors or at different times.

Factors that impact difficulty for literacy tasks
Findings from previous large-scale adult assessments suggest that the difficulty of a given task depends
on the characteristics of a text, the characteristics of the task or question, and the interaction between a
question and text(s). In the literacy framework, the LEG provides a table showing general factors that could
impact all tasks, as well as factors specific to accessing, understanding and evaluating tasks. The general
factors are described below; Table 3.5 in the framework document provides the elaborated set of difficulty
drivers across different task types.
•

Text factors include the amount of information to be searched, the visual and rhetorical organisation
of the text, the density and plausibility of distractors or competing information 2, and the number of
texts included in the task.

•

Task factors include the number of targets to be located, the number of criteria or conditions to be
fulfilled and the precision with which those criteria are specified in the task. An example of the latter
is a question that contains a table listing mountains and their heights. The question, “What
mountain is higher than 5 000 feet?” is more precise and makes locating the requested information
easier than, “What is the highest mountain?” where the different heights need to be compared in
order to locate the highest one.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

70 
•

Text-by-task factors are driven by the type of match required to answer the question. Tasks
involving a literal match between wording in the question and the text are easier than those that
require the reader to infer the link between the question and the relevant part of the text. In addition,
texts that contain distracting information, such as multiple keywords that match the wording in the
question, tend to be more difficult.

Item development goals for literacy tasks
To guide test development efforts, the LEG recommended that the item pool be distributed across
framework categories as follows. For cognitive task demands, the targets for the item pool included 35%
in the accessing category, 45% in understanding and 20% in evaluating. Additional targets included having
60% of tasks associated with a single text or source and 40% with multiple sources.
To ensure a range of contexts in the assessment tasks, the overall targets were to have 15% of items in
the work context, 40% in personal, 30% in community, and 15% in education. No specific
recommendations were provided for text types or response formats beyond requesting diversity across
those categories.

Reading components
Reading components were used to assess Literacy proficiency in Cycle 2; however, only the sentence
processing and passage fluency from Cycle 1 were included. The assessment design for Cycle 2 assigned
reading components to respondents across the entire range of skills (see Chapter 1 for details). Extending
the measure of components to a larger population of respondents made it possible to generalise the results
to the total population in each participating country and put them on the same scale as the literacy items –
something that was not possible in Cycle 1.
Performance and timing data were collected for both tasks, with timing data included as a measure of
fluency. The LEG noted that collecting both types of data would provide important information, particularly
about the skills of those at the lower end of the literacy proficiency scale.

Numeracy framework
Work on the numeracy framework for Cycle 2 was informed by a review of the Cycle 1 framework
conducted by an expert panel commissioned by the OECD Secretariat (Tout et al., 2017[4]). Several
members of that panel agreed to serve on the numeracy expert group (NEG) for Cycle 2, helping to ensure
that the panel’s recommendations were implemented in the updated framework.

Definition of the numeracy domain
In Cycle 1, numeracy was defined as the ability to access, use, interpret, and communicate mathematical
information and ideas, in order to engage in and manage the mathematical demands of a range of
situations in adult life. An explanation of numerate behaviour, which was also included as part of the
definition, stated that “numerate behaviour involves managing a situation or solving a problem in a real
context, by responding to mathematical content/information/ideas represented in multiple ways.”
For the second cycle of PIAAC, the NEG proposed the following definition (OECD, 2021[3]):
Numeracy is accessing, using and reasoning critically with mathematical content, information and ideas
represented in multiple ways in order to engage in and manage the mathematical demands of a range of
situations in adult life.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 71
Key changes from the Cycle 1 definition included:
•

The elimination of the word “ability”, as that was thought to imply an innate ability that some people
may not possess. Such an implication was not aligned with the NEG’s belief that all adults have
the capacity to learn mathematics and apply it successfully in their lives.

•

The phrase “interpret and communicate” has been replaced with “reason critically” to align with the
NEG’s view that one core cognitive process for numeracy, particularly in the context of technology
environments, is the ability to evaluate, critically reflect and make judgments.

•

The phrase “represented in multiple ways” was included to reflect the importance of digital
information, representations, devices and applications in meeting the numeracy demands of
everyday life.

Core dimensions of numeracy
Four core dimensions of numeracy were defined for Cycle 2: cognitive processes, content, representations
and contexts. These have been updated from the Cycle 1 core dimensions, referred to as facets, which
included mathematical ideas/content, responses, representations and contexts. Like literacy, contexts
were not expected to drive difficulty and were included to ensure a range of content relevant to adults’
lives. The dimensions that drive difficulty are elaborated as follows.

Cognitive processes
The NEG wanted to more explicitly describe and address the way adults have to solve problems in reallife contexts. Therefore, the experts reworked and elaborated the “response” facet from Cycle 1 to include
three cognitive processes associated with numeracy skills: accessing and assessing situations
mathematically, acting on and using mathematics, and evaluating, critically reflecting and making
judgments. Each is defined below:
•

Access and assess situations mathematically (assess, identify, access and represent). Adults
examine a contextual problem and determine if and where they can extract the essential
mathematics to analyse, set up, and solve the problem. They translate from a real-world setting to
the domain of mathematics and provide mathematical structure, representations and specificity for
a real-world problem.

•

Act on and use mathematics (order, count, estimate, compute, measure, graph and draw). Adults
utilise mathematical processes, facts and procedures to derive results and solve real-world
problems. In order to do so, they need to select and use appropriate tools, including technology.

•

Evaluate, critically reflect and make judgments (evaluate, reflect, justify and explain). Any solution
to a real-world problem needs to be evaluated against the original problem situation in terms of its
reasonableness and relevance to the original context, and a decision must be made about whether
to accept the solution or revise and adjust it.

No changes were suggested for the four key areas of mathematical content, information and ideas used
in Cycle 1. However, the Cycle 2 framework includes updated descriptions for each content area.
•

Quantity and number: understanding ordering, counts, place value, magnitudes, indicators, relative
size and numerical trends.

•

Space and shape: understanding and using measurement systems and formulas, dimensions and
units, location and direction, geometric shapes and patterns, angle properties, symmetry,
transformations, and 2D and 3D representations and perspectives.

•

Change and relationship: understanding ways to describe, model and interpret mathematical
relationships, quantitate patterns, and change. This involves understanding, using and applying

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

72 
proportional reasoning and rates of change, including the use and application of ratios, and
recognising, describing and/or using a relationship between different variables.
•

Data and chance: includes topics such as data collection, data displays, charts and graphs,
measures of central tendency and variance, and understanding and knowing about chance and
probability.

Representations
This dimension, which was not explicitly included in the Cycle 1 definition of literacy, was elaborated in the
Cycle 2 framework to include four classifications for the representation of real-world numeracy situations.
In the assessment context, these representations guided the selection and development of stimuli for the
items.
•

Text or symbols – the stimulus is based on text that can include symbols and numerical information.

•

Images of objects – the stimulus is based on photos or images of physical objects.

•

Structured information – the stimulus is based on data or information that is represented in tables,
graphs, charts and maps and may include calendars, schedules, timetables and infographics.

•

Dynamic applications – the stimulus is based on interactive applications, animations and
applications supporting calculations, such as loan calculators, currency or measurement
convertors, spreadsheets and drawing programmes.

Factors that impact difficulty for numeracy tasks
For each of the three cognitive processes, the NEG identified factors that drive the complexity of the
cognitive processes. For example, accessing and assessing situations may be more or less difficult
depending on the reading demands associated with the problem or the format in which the mathematics
is represented. Acting and using may be more or less difficult depending on the complexity of the
mathematical concepts or processes that need to be used or the number of steps required to solve a
problem.
The NEG also adopted the complexity scheme used in ALL and in PIAAC Cycle 1 to inform item
development and interpretation for Cycle 2. That scheme includes two aspects of the text or stimulus
material presented in a task (type of match/problem transparency and plausibility of distractors) and three
factors associated with the mathematical aspects of a task (complexity of mathematical information/data,
type of operation/skill and expected number of operations/processes). It is noted that these five factors,
which are described in full by Tout et al. (2020[5]), are not independent but interact in complex ways.

Item development goals for numeracy
As was the case for literacy, part of the development work for the numeracy expert group included defining
item development goals across the core dimensions of numeracy. For cognitive processes, the targets for
the item pool included 25-35% in the access and assess situations mathematically category, 30-40% in
the act on and using mathematics category and 25-35% in the evaluate, critically reflect and make
judgments category. Targets for the content categories were as follows: 20-30% quantity and number, 2030% space and shape, 15-25% change and relationships, and 25-35% data and chance.
For the four representation categories, the NEG acknowledged that it set aspirational targets with relatively
high goals for the two categories – structured information and dynamic applications – associated with 21stcentury technology-based representations. The full set of targets included 15-25% text or symbols, 1525% images of physical objects, 35-45% structured information and 15-25% dynamic applications.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 73
Finally, the NEG recommended an equal spread across the three context areas of personal, work and
social/community, with about one third of items in each context.

Numeracy components
The Terms of Reference for PIAAC Cycle 2 included a request for the numeracy expert group to consider
the inclusion of a measure of numeracy components in this cycle. Like the assessment of reading
components, this would allow for better measurement at the lowest end of the scale and provide some
information about whether adults who were unable to perform the easiest locator tasks could demonstrate
basic numeracy skills.
The Cycle 1 data showed that a significant percentage of adults perform at the lowest level in numeracy
proficiency (OECD, 2019[6]). The NEG agreed that these findings presented a strong argument for
developing an assessment that is equivalent to the reading components assessment.
Members of the NEG reviewed existing adult numeracy standards and frameworks as a starting point for
defining the scope of an assessment of numeracy components, noting that such component skills have
been much less researched, theorised and examined compared with component skills for literacy. As
discussed in the numeracy framework, the NEG identified a number of conceptual issues and constraints
that would need to be considered when undertaking the development of a numeracy components
assessment. These included:
•

Defining the breadth and level of the mathematical content that should be considered foundational
skills.

•

Determining how the assessment tasks could be embedded in real-world contexts that would be
relevant for adults. One recommendation to accomplish this was that the stimuli be based on
photos and realistic representations of real-life objects.

•

Developing tasks in which the reading demands would be as minimal as possible, while also
providing support via audio or video embedded in the system was considered as one solution.
However, constraints related to the required translation and recording of audio tracks across all
languages represented in PIAAC were acknowledged.

•

Avoiding tasks that were based on recognising and using money, given that monetary systems
vary significantly across countries, it would be difficult to maintain mathematical comparability.

Based on their review of the literature and consideration of both conceptual issues and delivery constraints,
the NEG recommended the development of a numeracy components assessment that focused on number
sense. Number sense relates to the understanding of quantities and of how numbers represent quantities.
The numeracy component items, therefore, would ask participants to determine quantities from real-life
pictures of objects and to identify the largest number from an unordered set of numbers.

Adaptive Problem Solving (APS) framework
As part of the background work for the innovative domain in Cycle 2, the OECD Secretariat commissioned
the development of a conceptual framework for adaptive problem solving in 2017 (Greiff et al., 2017[7]). A
conceptual model was developed that defined three stages of problem solving (definition, search and
application), the cognitive and metacognitive processes associated with each stage, and the information
environments in which problem-solving tasks are situated. It was agreed that this model highlighted
important aspects of adaptive problem solving that should be a focus of the assessment, but these needed
to be further specified to define the scale and inform test development.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

74 
Definition of the adaptive problem-solving domain
Using this conceptual model as the starting point, the expert group discussed some of the key ideas to be
included in the definition of adaptive problem solving for PIAAC. One important task was to identify the
features that are specific to adaptive problem solving.
To this end, the experts agreed that one critical feature of adaptive problem-solving tasks is that such
problems involve dynamic situations. In dynamic situations, resources and information needed to solve a
problem are not readily available, or some aspect of the problem changes in the course of working to
develop a solution. For example, new information is presented part-way through a problem, which requires
the respondent to modify the process they had initially chosen to find a solution. Thus, it was agreed that
some of the adaptive problem-solving tasks should require respondents to decide what information is
relevant versus irrelevant to solving the problem and to take steps to access relevant information. These
steps might involve accessing social, digital or physical resources.
The importance of metacognition was a second defining characteristic of adaptive problem solving that the
expert group emphasised. Metacognitive skills are called upon in order to monitor the problem-solving
process and adapt solution strategies as a problem changes.
Both of these aspects were incorporated into the following definition of adaptive problem solving (APS) for
PIAAC Cycle 2:
Adaptive problem solving involves the capacity to achieve one’s goals in a dynamic situation, in which a
method for reaching a solution is not immediately available. It requires engaging in cognitive and metacognitive
processes to define the problem, search for information, and apply a solution in a variety of information
environments and contexts.

Core dimensions of adaptive problem solving
The expert group reviewed the ways in which task dimensions were defined in the PIAAC domains of
problem solving in technology-rich environments (Cycle 1) and literacy (Cycle 2) as examples of how the
core dimensions for adaptive problem solving might be defined. Overall, the experts agreed that the APS
assessment should focus on assessing an individual’s capacity to flexibly adapt their problem-solving
strategies to dynamically changing environments, identify and select among a range of available physical,
social and digital resources, and monitor and reflect on their progress.
Several core dimensions of APS were defined for Cycle 2: cognitive and metacognitive processes, and
several task dimensions. Contexts were not expected to drive difficulty but were included to ensure a range
of situations relevant to adults’ lives. The dimensions related to difficulty are elaborated as follows.

Cognitive and metacognitive processes
As stated in the definition, adaptive problem solving involves both cognitive and metacognitive processes.
Metacognitive processes become more important to the extent that problems are complex and have
aspects that change during the solution process. These processes may be required within each of the
three stages of problem solving: defining the problem, searching for information relevant to the solution of
the problem, and applying a solution.
•

Defining the problem:
The three cognitive processes associated with defining the problem include:
o

Selecting, organising and integrating problem information into a mental model – Available
information must be evaluated to determine what is needed to understand the problem, the
relevant information must then be organised and integrated into an accurate mental model
focused on what the problem is about.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 75
o

Retrieving relevant background information – In the real world, effective problem solvers
activate relevant memories from past problem-solving activities. The framework notes that, in
an assessment context, problems that require specific background knowledge must
necessarily be avoided in order not to confound the availability of expert knowledge with a test
taker’s problem-solving abilities.

o

Externalising internal problem representation – Examples of this process include creating a
table or making a drawing that reflects a problem solver’s mental model of the problem.

Two metacognitive processes are associated with defining the problem:

•

o

Goal setting – In real life, goal setting involves reflecting on one’s own cognition and motivation.
This process was not defined as one that could be assessed in the adaptive problem-solving
tasks as it would not be practical to allow test takers to define their own goals and, therefore,
reach different solutions. Instead, goals were defined as part of the description for each task.

o

Monitoring problem comprehension – Problem solvers need to monitor whether their
understanding of a problem is sufficient to solve it. The experts believed this could be assessed
by requiring test takers to indicate whether they need additional information in order to solve a
presented problem.

Searching for information relevant for a solution:
Two cognitive processes associated with searching for a solution are defined in the framework:
o

Searching for operators in the (mind and) environment – This involves using appropriate
devices, tools or information to solve a problem, and coordinating activities with others, where
appropriate. Resources may be located in the social, physical or digital environment.

o

Evaluating operators with respect to how well they satisfy problem constraints.

The metacognitive processes associated with searching for a solution involve evaluating
resources with respect to whether they can be executed. In the artificial problem-solving context of
an assessment, this evaluation process is difficult to distinguish from the cognitive processes, as
listed above, and therefore the expert group specified that items that tapped this process should
be coded for analysis as requiring both cognitive and metacognitive processes.
•

Applying a solution:
In this third stage of adaptive problem solving, the primary cognitive process requires
implementing the selected operator(s) to solve the problem.
As part of the metacognitive processes associated with applying a solution, problem solvers must
evaluate whether they are making progress towards the goal and take actions if they are not. This
involves monitoring progress, regulating the application of operators and, finally, reflection.

Task dimensions
The APS expert group identified five task dimensions that are core dimensions for adaptive problem
solving. Each is briefly defined below.
•

Problem configuration – This refers to the initial problem setup and goal state(s). The problem
configuration includes the elements presented in the problem, the relationships among those
elements (e.g. whether they interact with each other or are independent) and the resources or
operators that are available to the problem solver.

•

Dynamics of the situation – The dynamics of the situation or task focuses on the change (or
absence of change) in the problem situation and the problem constraints across time and how this

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

76 
affects the problem configuration. It is the dynamism of the problem that requires respondents to
demonstrate adaptive problem-solving skills.3
•

Features of the environment – This dimension refers to various features that are characteristic of
the environment and the information and resources that are available.

•

Information environment – Various resources may be available to solve the problem. The APS
framework identifies three types of information sources:

•

o

Physical resources are hands on and can be manipulated. In real life these might include
resources available for driving a car or operating machinery by pressing buttons and pulling
levers.

o

Social resources are those that require the problem solver to engage in interpersonal and social
interactions. These include planning an activity with friends or leading a group discussion.

o

Digital resources are those that require the problem solver to make use of digital knowledge
and skills to interact with digital features or devices. Examples include using digital tools to sort
a table, send an email or format text.

Problem contexts – This dimension refers to the situation the problem is embedded in, and includes
personal life, work, or social and community contexts.

Factors that impact difficulty for adaptive problem-solving tasks
The APS expert group identified difficulty drivers for three of the identified task dimensions: problem
configuration, dynamics of the situation and features of the environment. The expert group noted that the
last two task dimensions – the information environment and problem context – affect the quality of the
context in which the problem is set but do not drive the difficulty of the problem.
•

The four difficulty drivers associated with problem configuration include: the number of elements,
relations and operations; the salience and accessibility of operators; the interactions between
problem elements; and the number of parallel tasks and goals. The expert group further explained
that the initial problem setup, or problem configuration, may have more or fewer elements and
these elements may interact with each other or be relatively independent. The elements may be
easily accessible or not, and may be more or less salient. Lastly, the problem may involve the
accomplishment of just one or several goals.

•

The difficulty drivers associated with the dynamics of the situation were identified as: the number
of features that change and their relevance for attaining the goal; the salience of the change; the
frequency of change; and the degree of impasse (if any) that the change may present.

•

Features of the environment that may impact difficulty include: the amount of information that is
present and the extent to which that information is relevant or irrelevant to solving the problem; the
structure of the environment, or lack thereof; and the number of sources of information.

Developing the cognitive instruments
The cognitive instruments included three sections:
•

the locator test, which consisted of easy literacy and numeracy items, was designed to both collect
information about participants with limited skills (screening out those without sufficient skills to go
on and complete the assessment) and to route participants via the adaptive testing algorithms to
the set of cognitive assessments that best matched their skills

•

the assessments of literacy and numeracy components

•

the direct assessment of the literacy, numeracy and APS domains.

For each of the three cognitive domains, test developers worked closely with the associated expert group
to ensure that the instruments reflected the frameworks. All items were also submitted for country review
to receive input on cultural and linguistic appropriateness as well as item content. The following groups
and organisations had responsibility for each of the domains: ETS was responsible for the development of
the literacy items, members of the numeracy expert group developed the numeracy and numeracy
components items, and a team of developers from the University of Luxembourg, with expertise in problem
solving was responsible for the APS items. ETS test developers also reviewed all numeracy and APS items
to ensure consistency in instructions, response modes and presentation across domains.
Several core requirements for the Cycle 2 assessment had important implications for the development of
the cognitive instruments. First, so that PIAAC can measure changes over time, the Cycle 2 literacy and
numeracy assessments needed to be linked psychometrically to the Cycle 1 assessments. Therefore, a
subset of Cycle 1 items was required to be included in the second cycle. These trend items were selected
to fulfil the number and types of items specified in the assessment design and to reflect the frameworks in
each of the two domains. A second requirement was that all items be capable of automatic scoring. This
was a necessary feature for implementing adaptive testing in PIAAC. Finally, because Cycle 2 was
delivered on tablets, items needed to utilise response modes optimised for that platform. This would also
help ensure that only basic digital skills would be required to navigate through the assessment and for
inputting responses, to reduce the computer-based assessment refusal rates encountered in Cycle 1.

Screen design and interface
The screen design for Cycle 2 was based on the design used in the first cycle, with a few changes
implemented to reflect the current interfaces that would be most familiar to respondents. As was the case
in Cycle 1, an important goal was to use a design that allowed a consistent display and interface across
the cognitive domains. A vertically split screen was used, with the stimulus material presented on the right
and the question or task information on the left. 4 This vertical split allowed a display area for stimulus
materials that was taller than it was wide, making it possible to format text with more natural line lengths in
order to improve readability. An additional consideration was the comparability of the display across
languages. The selected design accommodated “longer” languages, such as French and German as well
as languages with character sets that require more vertical space such as Korean and Japanese. The goal
was to avoid a situation where scrolling was required in some languages but not others. Such display
differences would require some respondents to hold the location of specific information in memory,
potentially making tasks more difficult in some languages than others and thus introducing construct
irrelevant variance. Finally, the proposed screen design considered future cycles of PIAAC, given that
displays have increasingly moved toward wide-screen formats.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

78 
In Cycle 1, the interface included Back, Forward and Help icons that were located in the lower left portion
of the screen. As shown in Figure 3.2, this layout was revised for Cycle 2, where those icons were moved
to the top right of the screen. This location is more consistent with the location of navigation icons used on
most web pages and with what users would be familiar with in applications such as Word and Excel, where
ribbons are at the top of the screen.
The user instructions for each test question both identified the stimulus and provided information about the
required response mode; for example, “Look at the brochure about public transportation. Tap on the
brochure to answer the question below.” The question or task description is displayed in a box below the
instructions.

Figure 3.2. Testing screens in Cycles 1 and 2
Cycle 1

Cycle 2

Items in all domains were grouped into units. Each unit focused on a single topic and included one or more
stimuli. In literacy and numeracy, respondents were able to move back and forth between items within a
unit. They were not, however, able to move back and forth between units. Once respondents tapped on
the NEXT arrow on the final item in a unit, a dialogue box displayed a warning that they were about to
move on to the next unit and it would not be possible to return to previous items. At this point, they could
either confirm that they wanted to go on or cancel the action and remain in the unit on which they had been
working.
Navigation in the APS domain was different. Due to the nature of how problems within a unit evolved, with
new information or impasses appearing, respondents were not allowed to return to earlier items in a unit.
Therefore, the BACK arrow was not available in these units. Respondents were informed of these
constraints in the introduction prior to the first APS unit and the interface was designed to help prevent
them from mistakenly going forward before they were ready. In APS, when respondents tapped on the
NEXT arrow, they were asked to tap a second time to confirm they were ready to advance.
In addition to navigation within and across units, in some literacy and APS units, respondents needed to
navigate among multiple stimuli. Respondents were able to move back and forth between those materials
using tabs, as shown in Figure 3.3. In cases where the stimulus consisted of a website with multiple pages,
respondents could tap on each page name to view that page, as shown.

Tablet response modes
Given that the delivery platform changed from laptop to tablet in Cycle 2, developers reviewed response
modes for the linking items and introduced several response modes for new items to take advantage of
the tablet presentation. Developers focused on modes that could be automatically scored across
languages for each of the cognitive domains and for both linking and new items in the assessment. The
critical goal was to use experience from previous assessments and development work to ensure that the
interface and response modes were as simple and intuitive as possible, while meeting measurement goals.
All of the item formats used in Cycle 1 were based on three response modes: selecting, numeric entry and
highlighting. These same formats could be supported in a tablet touch-screen environment and were
expected to be familiar to respondents who use a tablet or smartphone, and to be accessible to
respondents with limited ICT skills. It should be noted that each of these response modes was introduced
and demonstrated in the tablet skills introduction to the assessment.
•

Tapping – This response mode allowed respondents to tap on the screen to select graphical
elements, cells in a table, links on a web page, sentences in a text, and radio buttons or check
boxes to answer. Both single- and multiple-selection items were supported. This response mode
had an advantage in that, in general, selection areas could remain consistent across languages.
Therefore, scoring did not require much adaptation across different national versions of the items.

•

Highlighting – Highlighting was used in Cycle 1 for a set of literacy items that originated as paperbased items in IALS and ALL and some new items that were developed as part of Cycle 1. These
items allowed respondents to highlight single words, phrases or complete sentences in a text. The
highlighting rules in Cycle 1 maintained the kinds of scoring rules used in IALS and ALL, where
respondents sometimes underlined or circled responses rather than writing them on the provided
answer lines. A subset of these items was also included in Cycle 2. In Cycle 1, highlighting required
using a mouse, which can be a complicated skill for those with limited computer skills. In Cycle 2,
a stylus was provided that worked just like a highlighter that one might use on a sheet of paper. In
Cycle 1, developers defined a minimum correct response, as well as a maximum correct response,
for each highlighting item. This same scoring approach was implemented for Cycle 2.
It must be noted that, from a development perspective, translating the minimum and maximum
correct responses across languages was a particularly challenging task in Cycle 1. Countries spent
considerable time implementing and testing the minimum/maximum rules for their national versions

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

80 
of the highlighting items and contractors needed to check the implementation of these rules for
each language version. The highlighting response mode was critical in Cycle 1 to link back to
previous paper-based adult literacy assessments where test takers were able to underline
responses in a stimulus. This response mode was thus needed for a subset of PIAAC trend items.
However, given the challenges it presented, alternative text-selection options that were less
language dependent, such as tapping on one or more sentences in a text, were used for the new
items developed for Cycle 2.
•

Drag and drop – Some items required respondents to select and drag information on the tablet
touch screen. Examples include items where respondents were asked to sequence a set of
presented choices or drag a bar on a slider.

•

Numeric entry – In Cycle 1, respondents used the laptop keyboard to enter a numeric response. A
different response mode was needed for Cycle 2, where no keyboard was available to respondents.
Therefore, in the tablet environment, respondents answered by tapping on a numeric keypad that
appeared when the response box was tapped. Numeric entry items were scored automatically
based on the definition of correct numeric response(s) included in the scoring rules.

Because an important goal for the second cycle of PIAAC was to have more respondents agree to take
the digital assessment, the new response modes were designed to be simple and intuitive. Usability testing
was conducted early in the development phase with a limited number of individuals who represented the
range of ages and computer experience expected in the testing population. This testing informed item
development by providing evidence that new formats would not impact respondent performance. The
usability testing also informed the development of the tutorial presented to all respondents before the
assessment.
