Trend item selection
The assessment design for PIAAC Cycle 2 specified that about 30 trend items be included in both literacy
and numeracy. ETS made a preliminary selection of trend items based on the following factors:
•

Item quality – Only items that demonstrated strong psychometric performance in Cycle 1 were
considered for inclusion in Cycle 2. That is, developers looked for items with good item parameters
and no history of differential item functioning or translation problems.

•

Distribution according to the dimensions of the frameworks – Trend items were reviewed and
reclassified according to the Cycle 2 PIAAC frameworks by the expert groups and, to the extent
possible, selected to reflect the distributions recommended in the frameworks.

•

Distribution across levels of difficulty – The difficulty of items was also taken into consideration to
ensure items spanned the five proficiency levels used to report results from Cycle 1.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 81
In the case of numeracy, the NEG chair reviewed the proposed selections and made a few
recommendations for alternate items to consider. For both numeracy and literacy, the pool of trend items
was approved at the first meetings of the expert groups (in March and April of 2018, respectively). The
experts agreed that, as a follow-up to their meetings, they would review and revise the existing
classifications of the trend items with respect to the new Cycle 2 frameworks. The proposed pool of trend
items, with their updated classifications, was shared with the BPC and countries for approval.
All the approved trend items were reauthored into the HTML5-based platform used for Cycle 2. For
countries that participated in Cycle 1, the only changes to trend items included corrections to previously
unidentified errors or updates that were required due to changing circumstances, such as the introduction
of a new currency.
Two sets of changes were required for all returning Cycle 1 countries: updates to user instructions so they
would align with the tablet delivery (e.g. changing “Click” to “Tap”), and the addition of the keypad for
numeric entry items. Such revisions were implemented by the Consortium, and then countries reviewed
and approved the instruments. New countries translated trend items following the processes used for new
assessment items.

New item development
New items were developed to reflect the PIAAC Cycle 2 frameworks and take advantage of the tabletbased delivery. These items were based both on materials submitted by countries and materials developed
by the contractors. The development period extended from March 2018, with the first meeting of the expert
groups, to October 2018, when the expert groups finalised the selection of the field trial item pool.
For each of the three domains, stimulus materials were selected based on specifications provided in the
frameworks and included real-world materials such as newspaper and magazine articles, advertisements,
books, forms and web pages that adults aged 16-65 would typically encounter in a range of everyday life
contexts. Given the international context of the assessment, care was taken to select materials appropriate
across cultures and languages. Soliciting materials from participating countries and having all countries
review the stimulus materials were important steps to ensure diversity.
It was also important to avoid stimulus materials that might become easily dated. Those that contained
dates or references to contemporary individuals or events – particularly if such information was central to
completing tasks associated with those materials – could become dated by the time the assessment was
administered or problematic in future testing cycles if used as trend items.
Part of the development process included defining scoring rubrics, classifying items based on the domain
frameworks, and estimating the difficulty level for each new item. The estimated difficulty was based on
factors that were expected to impact difficulty, as noted in the frameworks, and experience with previous
large-scale surveys of adult skills. The difficulty estimates were used to assign items to clusters for the
field trial.
The platform collected a number of standard variables for each item for easy retrieval. These included the
scored response, raw response, number of actions taken, time to first action and total time. Beyond these,
additional information is captured and stored in log files for each item.

Reading and numeracy components items
The reading components assessment was designed to provide information about the component, or
foundational, reading skills of very low performers – i.e. individuals who were unable to complete many, or
any, literacy tasks. The assessment included two sets of tasks – sentence comprehension and passage
comprehension – both of which were administered in Cycle 1. The first set focused on the ability to process
meaning at the sentence level. Respondents were shown a series of sentences, which increased in

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

82 
complexity, and asked to identify if the sentence made sense in terms of its internal logic (e.g. “The red
car had a flat tyre.”) or properties of the real world (e.g. “Airplanes are made of dogs.”). Twenty-two items
were taken from Cycle 1. To enlarge the item pool without additional test development demands, an
additional 22 items were taken from PISA, for a total of 44 sentence comprehension items in the field trial.
The second set of reading component tasks focused on passage comprehension. For these tasks,
respondents were asked to read passages where, at certain points in a sentence, they were presented
with two words and had to select the word that made sense. Four passages used in Cycle 1 were included
in the Cycle 2 field trial.
The assessment of numeracy components, which was new in Cycle 2, focused on number sense. The first
set of items posed the question “How many?” and asked respondents to identify the number of real-world
objects displayed in an image. The number ranges included objects in groups of 5 to 9, 10 to 15 or 15 to
20, and the visual presentation of the items included rectangular and non-rectangular arrays, pairing and
random displays. Eighteen “how many” items were developed for the field trial.
The second set of numeracy component items asked respondents to compare unordered sets of numbers
to identify the biggest number. The sets of numbers included natural numbers, decimal numbers, fractions
or percentages in different combinations. Twenty-four “which is biggest” items were developed for the field
trial.
The reading and numeracy component items were administered only on the tablet for both the field trial
and the main study. This made it possible to automatically record both accuracy and response times. The
accuracy data served as indicators of the mastery of basic skills. The response times served as an indicator
of fluency, allowing researchers to explore its potential contribution to the mastery of the more complex
tasks in the PIAAC assessment.

National submissions
Countries were invited to participate in the process of developing new items for PIAAC. As is the case with
any large-scale international survey, the pool of tasks for PIAAC needed to reflect the range of contexts
and experiences of respondents across participating countries. One way to better ensure this was to solicit
national submissions once countries had been introduced to the PIAAC frameworks.
To support National Centres interested in item development, a narrated PowerPoint presentation was
provided that included an overview of the frameworks and sample items illustrating available item types.
The Consortium developed submission guidelines as well as PowerPoint templates that national teams
could use to mock up items. In preparing materials for submission, national teams were asked to provide
the following information about each item:
•

information about the source of the item (original, or from a book or other source)

•

information about any copyright considerations for the stimulus materials (who holds the copyright,
who had been contacted to seek permission to use the material, and copyright permission when it
was obtained)

•

the classifications of each item according to the core dimensions in the relevant domain framework.

Countries were also encouraged to submit stimulus materials without associated items. Wherever possible,
the Consortium developed items based on these stimuli to ensure a mix of materials that reflected the
cultural diversity of participating countries. National teams had three months to develop and submit items,
with a deadline of 31 July 2018.
Literacy submissions were received from Japan and Spain. In numeracy, submissions were received from
Japan, Germany, Spain and Sweden. Submissions received from countries were reviewed and evaluated
in terms of their fit to the PIAAC frameworks and contribution to the item pool.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 83
In addition, item writing workshops were conducted for both literacy and numeracy. A two-day numeracy
workshop was conducted by the chair of the numeracy expert group at the OECD offices in Paris on 12
and 13 June 2018. A literacy workshop was conducted by the lead ETS test developers in Princeton, USA
on 9 and 10 July 2018. Representatives from five countries participated in the literacy workshop and from
ten countries in the numeracy workshop.
Because APS was a new domain with complex development demands, the Consortium did not expect
countries to submit fully drafted APS tasks. Instead, countries were asked to submit ideas for problem
contexts. Submissions were received from Israel, Korea, the Netherlands and Switzerland.

Item reviews
Several types of item reviews were conducted during the test development phase. These included reviews
of draft APS contexts prepared by test developers by national teams, reviews of all cognitive items by
national teams, cognitive labs using several APS units, a translatability review of all items by cApStAn and
GESIS, and optional reviews of the tablet tutorial and domain orientations by national teams. Each of the
subject-matter expert groups met in October 2018 to review the proposed field trial item pool and
recommend the final selection of items. From October through December 2018, the Consortium revised
selected items based on input from the reviews and discussions among the experts, comments received
from countries, and wording recommendations based on the translatability assessment. These reviews are
described in more detail below.

APS context reviews
Given the complexity of this innovative domain for Cycle 2, test developers were interested in receiving
feedback from national teams about proposed units before they were fully developed and programmed.
Thus, descriptions of potential contexts for 26 units were released to national teams in June 2018 so that
they could identify if each context was acceptable as described, acceptable with modifications, or
unacceptable. For the latter two categories, national teams were asked to suggest modifications to help
test developers consider ways in which a context might be revised and/or to explain why a context was
judged to be unacceptable so that the test development team could better judge proposed contexts for
other APS units.

Country reviews
As an additional step, to better ensure that the new items reflected the range of contexts and experiences
of respondents across participating countries, and to obtain input about item content, all participating
countries reviewed the PIAAC item pool at several stages. A review form was developed for each set of
items and national teams were asked to provide ratings and comments regarding the following:
•

The overall appropriateness of each item. Items were to be classified into one of three categories:
acceptable as is, acceptable with modifications, or unacceptable. For the second category,
countries were asked to specify revisions that would make the item acceptable. For the third
category, they were asked to specify the reason(s) why they rated an item as unacceptable.

•

cultural concerns

•

translation concerns

•

any additional comments or suggestions.

Once the tablet tutorial and domain orientations were drafted, national teams were given the opportunity
to provide optional feedback to inform the final field trial versions. This review period was in early
April 2019. Revisions were made based on those comments and these materials were released to
countries in May for translation.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

84 
APS cognitive labs
During the development cycle, a team at the University of Luxembourg conducted a usability study focused
on the response modes (tap, highlight, drag and drop and numeric entry). Fifteen adults aged 18-62 who
reported either using a tablet less than once a month or never were asked to complete a representative
set of items. Participants received no training prior to using the tablet. Overall, the participants found the
response modes intuitive. However, they identified a few issues, such as the need to increase and highlight
the size and visibility of the tappable area for multiple-choice items, to provide more information about how
to clear previously highlighted text or how to change a drag-and-drop response. The developers used this
feedback to adjust the layout and interface, and the identified issues were addressed in the tablet tutorials
so that respondents could learn about and practice using the different response modes.

Translatability assessment
The translatability assessment was a new step added to the test development process for Cycle 2. This
review aimed to identify and correct wording in the English source that might present translation difficulties
in some languages. The review was also used to identify important aspects of the source that should be
highlighted in the translation guidelines.
As explained in more detail in Chapter 7, each segment of the English source for all assessment materials
was reviewed by linguists at cApStAn and classified in terms of its expected ease of translation. Where
appropriate, a senior linguist provided recommendations for alternate wording for text, and for the
translation guidelines. Test developers, and staff at GESIS who had agreed to provide feedback, then
reviewed those comments and either accepted the suggestions or proposed alternative wording. After
consultation among all parties, wording and translation guidelines were finalised.

Additional supporting materials
A set of interactive tutorials was developed to introduce respondents to the PIAAC instruments. These
were included to better ensure that all participants approached the survey with the same information about
how to navigate through the assessment and provide their responses. These materials were developed in
the spring of 2019.
The three types of introductory materials provided to respondents at select points in the assessment
workflow, included: a tablet skills orientation and practice, a more general tablet tutorial and domainspecific orientations.
•

The tablet skills tutorial was the first set of tasks presented to respondents. Here, respondents
were introduced to the skills required to complete the assessment on the tablet: tap, highlight, drag
and drop, and numeric entry. Respondents could watch an animation demonstrating each skill
and/or practice each as needed.

•

Next, respondents viewed the tablet tutorial, which provided a general orientation to the testing
screen and types of questions in the assessment (e.g. tap on a choice, tap on a sentence, and use
the numeric keypad).

•

Before beginning each of the cognitive sections of the assessment, a brief domain-specific
orientation was provided with information relevant to items in that section. For example, before the
literacy section, respondents were introduced to the paging interface used for multiple-source
stimuli and the scrolling interface used for longer stimulus materials.

 85

Items were authored into the platform from December 2018 through March 2019 to create the international,
English master version. During that period, test developers worked with the psychometric team to organise
units into clusters based on the design developed for the field trial. As explained in more detail in Chapter 1,
respondents were randomly assigned to take either literacy, numeracy or APS in the field trial. The clusters
for each domain were assembled so that each cluster was paired with every other cluster, and clusters
appeared in both the first and second positions in the administration to control for order effects.
In literacy and numeracy, both locator and main assessment clusters were assembled. Locator items were
assigned to one of four clusters, with each cluster consisting of four literacy or four numeracy items. Each
respondent received two clusters of locator items, or eight items in all. For the main assessment, each
cluster was designed to take about 25 minutes and each respondent took two clusters. Judgments about
total testing time were based on experience with previous adult assessments and evaluations of the
complexity of each unit. In total, five literacy and five numeracy clusters were assembled. Each literacy
cluster included 16 or 17 items and the numeracy clusters consisted of 16 items each.
In APS, each cluster was also designed to take about 25 minutes and included 13 or 14 items. As was the
case for the other domains, respondents received two clusters.
The component items were also organised into clusters assembled using a rotated design. For reading
components, sentence comprehension items were organised into four clusters. Clusters were balanced in
terms of the number of words in each sentence, a difficulty ranking based on professional judgment and
previous item performance, and the number of sentences which did not make sense (based on evidence
that these tended to be more difficult). Each respondent received two clusters of sentences and one
passage using a rotated design. For numeracy components, four “how many” clusters, each containing
four or five items, and four “which is biggest” clusters, each containing six items, were assembled. Again,
clusters were balanced in terms of estimated difficulty. Each respondent received four clusters in total: two
“how many” and two “which is biggest” clusters.
Once the international master was completed and released, countries engaged in a number of steps to
create their national versions of the field trial instrument. As described in more detail in Chapter 7, these
steps included: conducting reviews of the trend materials (for returning Cycle 1 countries), defining and
checking the scoring for highlighting items, translation of new items and supporting materials (e.g. tutorials
and orientations), and conducting final checks of both content and layout.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

86 
Scoring testing
In addition to implementing and testing the scoring for the literacy highlighting items, countries were asked
to perform additional scoring testing in October 2019. The scope of this testing was limited to those items
that might have had country-specific scoring rules. It included 7 items where currency amounts needed to
be provided as a response and 21 sentence-selection items. The currency items required testing to ensure
that any national adaptations (e.g. multiplying by 100 or 1 000 to more accurately reflect national costs)
were correctly implemented into the automatic scoring rules. The sentence-selection items were included
as a precaution to be sure that no sentences were inadvertently split or combined during translation, which
would render the automatic scoring incorrect.
A scoring testing file was created by the development team that listed each of the items to be tested. For
each item, countries were asked to input responses in several ways, including: (1) leaving the item blank,
(2) entering the correct response, as listed in the worksheet, and (3) entering one or more incorrect
responses. For the sentence-selection items, a fourth step was required: for each unit, teams were asked
to tap on each sentence in the text to make sure it could be selected. This step made it possible to confirm
that the selectable sentences in each translated version of the stimulus matched the source.

Moving from the field trial to main study instruments
The PIAAC Cycle 2 field trial was originally scheduled to be conducted from April through December 2020.
That schedule was, however, pushed back by about one year due to the Covid-19 pandemic. Field trial
results were analysed in the fall of 2021 and selections were made to create the main study cognitive
instruments from December 2021 through January 2022.

Selection and finalisation process
The process for selecting and finalising the main study items was based on a number of steps conducted
by the data analysts, psychometricians, platform specialists and test developers. These included:

Review of item performance
First, members of the data analysis and psychometric teams, in collaboration with the platform specialists
and test developers, reviewed the field trial data to identify the set of trend and new items that could go
forward to the main study. Items that did not perform as expected across participating countries were
dropped. Where items did not perform well in one or several countries, the team worked to identify potential
problems (such as errors in translation or adaptation) and consulted with countries to confirm if corrections
were needed.

Test development review of new items
All the trend literacy and numeracy items performed well enough to be considered for the main study item
pool so these did not require further review. However, the test development team conducted an in-depth
review of all new literacy, numeracy and APS items, focusing on the following aspects:
•

Items that were much harder or easier than anticipated were reviewed to identify possible problems
with wording, stimulus presentation, response options, etc.

•

Items that did not discriminate well or that had very high rates of omission were also reviewed.

•

For items that required multiple responses, the data for each selection were reviewed.

When a problem or concern was identified, the issue was discussed with the domain expert group and
removed from the proposed main study item pool.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 87
Selection of locator items (literacy and numeracy only)
As previously discussed, the locator was used for the following two purposes: (1) to screen out respondents
who did not have sufficient skills to take the main assessment and route them directly to the components
assessment, or (2) to inform the initial routing decisions in the adaptive design. In the main study, each
respondent began the assessment by taking the same set of eight literacy and eight numeracy locator
items. The locator items were intended to be generally easy, with most items at Below Level 1 and Level 1
and a couple items at Level 2 and the lower end of Level 3. Test developers also tried to ensure parallel
distributions of difficulty across the literacy and numeracy locator items.

Selection of the main assessment items (literacy, numeracy and APS)
Several criteria drove item selection for these items:
•

The items must provide good measurement.

•

The items must reflect the construct as defined in the frameworks.

•

Literacy and numeracy trend items must be retained for the main study wherever possible to
maintain the link between PIAAC Cycles 1 and 2.

•

The selected item pool must work within the adaptive design for literacy and numeracy and within
the cluster design for APS (see Chapter 1 for a detailed explanation of the assessment designs for
the three cognitive domains).

The test development team completed its proposed selection of items for the main study and presented
those proposals to the literacy, numeracy and APS expert groups for their review and approval in January
2022. At each of the expert group meetings, those selections, along with scoring rules and data capture,
were discussed. A summary of the issues discussed for each domain is given below.
•

Literacy – The literacy expert group reviewed 11 items that employed partial credit scoring in the
field trial. In all cases, these were items where a full credit response required two, three or four
correct answers. The experts requested that test developers review these items again following
the main study to decide if updated scoring rules would be supported based on that data. If so,
revised scoring rules could be implemented using an ad hoc scoring procedure.

•

Numeracy – The numeracy expert group reviewed six items selected for the main study that had a
partial credit scoring definition. For most items with partial credit, the field trial data showed that
respondents very infrequently selected responses captured by partial credit and, therefore, no
information was gained regarding these partial credit definitions. Following a careful review of the
scoring rules for these items, the expert group decided that three items should retain polytomous
scoring (full and partial credit) and the remaining three should be redefined as dichotomous (either
full or no credit). These updated scoring rules were then implemented for the main study.

•

APS – The APS expert group reviewed a set of issues around scoring rules, including the use of
partial credit scoring and the possible inclusion of navigation actions into such rules. A number of
units that employed partial credit scoring were reviewed. The expert group agreed that partial credit
should be dropped in cases where the frequency of such responses was so low (e.g. less than 1%)
that the inclusion of such scoring did not add to measurement or interpretation of results. In items
where partial credit responses were more frequently seen, the expert group recommended that
partial credit not be assigned to responses that reflected an incomplete problem solution (i.e. only
one of two required sets of actions were taken) but felt that it was appropriate in cases where
different sequences of the same actions or extra actions were taken. Test developers agreed to
explore partial credit scoring definitions that differentiated correct solutions that include extraneous
or less efficient steps from solutions that do not. Analyses would be conducted using the main

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

88 
study data, and after exploring the impacts on scoring, these new partial credit definitions could be
applied to man study scoring using an ad hoc rescoring procedure.
For items where the number of actions is relevant as a measure of problem-solving efficiency, the expert
group advised that test developers explore the extent to which combining the number of actions with the
existing item scoring rules would add to the interpretability of performance and differentiate respondents
performing at different levels. As mentioned above, it was agreed that these analyses would be undertaken
using the main study data and, if appropriate, applied ad hoc to the main study scoring.
Finally, a number of APS units contained multiple sources of information and respondents were able to
move between them when working on an item. As previously noted, special, additional variables were
defined in these cases to capture the sources a respondent viewed for items within such units. The experts
reviewed several items where, in the judgment of test developers, the information presented in a source
was required in order to answer a question correctly without guessing. The issue presented for discussion
was whether viewing these critical sources should be considered in scoring, i.e. a correct score should not
be assigned unless the appropriate source had been selected. The experts recommended that, in the five
cases where it was clear such information was required, scoring should be based on both the response
and source(s) viewed. Where it was possible that a respondent might recall key information from previous
items, scoring should be based solely on the provided response. As was the case for some instances of
partial credit, the impact on scoring was to be explored prior to making final scoring decisions for the main
study and applied using an ad hoc rescoring procedure.
Once the scoring and data capture rules were finalised, and the expert groups approved the main study
item pool, the proposed items were shared with the BPC and the national teams for final approval. The
number of trend and new items included in the main study, as approved by the expert groups, the BPC
and participating countries is shown in Table 3.4.

The results of the selection process are summarised below for each of the cognitive domains.

Literacy
The final literacy item pool for the main study, as shown in Table 3.5 below, consisted of 80 items: 28 trend

which called for eight literacy locator items and 72 items for the main assessment. The results of the

Main study item pool
The field trial literacy items demonstrated very high measurement quality. The 30 trend items generally
worked well. One item was easier than in Cycle 1 but was kept in order to be re-evaluated based on the
main study data. A scoring issue was identified for a second trend item but, because that could be fixed
for the main study, that item was retained as well. Two other trend items were not included in the proposed
main study pool based upon judgments made by the test development team: one was quite outdated,
having been originally developed for the IALS assessment in the mid-1990s, and another was not needed
as a locator task and was omitted to limit the number of highlighting items. As a result, the number of trend
items was reduced from 30 in the field trial to 28 in the main study.
Based on the reduction in the number of trend items selected for the main study, just 15 new items needed
to be dropped from the main assessment to meet the design requirements for the main study. It should be
noted that no full units were dropped following the field trial but, rather, selected items within units were
omitted. However, items were only dropped if the sequence of tasks within the unit maintained a logical
flow. Only two of the new items developed for Cycle 2 had to be omitted because they failed to meet the
psychometric criteria for inclusion and therefore could not be scaled. One item was dropped because it
was not needed in the locator and was judged to have basic numeracy demands that were not appropriate
for the literacy assessment. Six items were dropped based on the test development review. These items
were generally much more difficult than intended, and in several cases, were found to have unclear correct
responses. An additional six items were dropped based on considerations related to the adaptive design.
These items were omitted to reduce the number of items in a particular unit or to make the average difficulty
of the unit easier or harder, to facilitate incorporating the unit into the adaptive design.
More specific information about the distribution of the dropped and selected items across the locator and
main assessment is included below.

Locator items
Of the 16 items included in the field trial locator, only one was dropped from consideration for the main
study due to poor performance. That item was exceptionally difficult with only 6% of respondents, on
average, selecting the intended response. Upon further review by the test developers and experts, the
correct answer was judged to be insufficiently clear. The remaining selection process focused on
identifying items that would best support the intended difficulty distribution for the locator items.
A total of six items that had been used in the field trial locator were selected for the main study locator.
One unit with two items was moved from the main assessment into the locator for the main study in order
to include a low Level 3 item, and six of the new items that had been used in the field trial locator were
moved to the main assessment for the main study. The final main study locator included three Below
Level 1 items and three Level 1 items, as well as one Level 2 and one Level 3 item (based on the field trial
data).

Main study assessment items
Of the 80 items remaining under consideration following the development of the main study locator,
72 were needed for the two stages of the adaptive design in the main assessment. Eight additional items
that functioned well in the field trial and were of high quality were identified as items that could be excluded.
One challenge for assembling the adaptive stages for the literacy assessment was the larger numbers of
items in some units (in particular, compared with numeracy) and, in some cases, a broad range of difficulty
across items within units. Therefore, some of the items targeted for omission, as noted previously, were
those that would reduce the number of items within a unit or make the mean difficulty of the unit either
easier or harder. Care was taken to make sure that the logical flow of a unit was not impacted when omitting

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

90 
any items and to ensure that the selected items were those that best represented the construct, balanced
the difficulty of the item pool and resulted in a selection that optimised the main study design.

Reading components
As noted above, the components assessment for literacy consisted of two types of items: sentence
comprehension and passage comprehension. One of the sentence comprehension items could not be
scaled in the field trial analyses and was dropped. In order to reduce the time required to complete the
sentence comprehension tasks, seven additional items were dropped from the field trial item pool, resulting
in a total of 36 items in the main study. Test developers prioritised keeping sentences from PIAAC Cycle 1
rather than the items borrowed from PISA, and also focused on balancing the final selection in terms of
sentence length and the number of “Yes” versus “No” responses (“No” responses are typically more
difficult). No changes were made to the passage comprehension tasks; the same four passages used in
the field trial were included in the main study, and each respondent received one passage.

Numeracy
A total of 96 numeracy items was included in the field trial: 32 trend items and 64 newly developed items.

the main study assessment design, which called for eight numeracy locator items and 72 items for the
main assessment. The results of the selection process for the overall item pool and the locator and main
assessment are described in more detail below.

Main study item pool
As was the case for the literacy, the trend numeracy items performed well in the field trial. No items were
flagged for IRT misfit and, therefore, all 32 trend items could be used in the main study. As a result, the
number of new items needed to be reduced from the 64 used in the field trial to 48 in order to meet the
requirement of having a total of 80 numeracy items in the main study. Of the 64 new items, only one item
was omitted because of psychometric concerns (i.e. it could not be scaled).
Nine items were proposed for dropping following the test development review. These items were either
much more difficult than intended or had high omit rates. In most cases, review of these items by the test
development team and chair of the numeracy expert group suggested that these findings were the result
of unclear or unfamiliar stimuli.
An additional six items were dropped to conform to the assessment design. Five Level 3 items were
dropped to improve the distribution of items by difficulty level as there were other Level 3 items that showed
better measurement characteristics, so those were prioritised. One item was dropped because it was the
only remaining item in a somewhat complex unit after others in that unit had been dropped due to poor
performance or because they performed at Level 3.
More specific information about the distribution of the dropped and selected items across the locator and
main assessment is included below.

Locator items
Of the 16 items included in the field trial locator, none were flagged for poor performance. The selection of
the eight required items focused on meeting the primary goals of the locator, which were to identify and
collect performance data about respondents with very low estimated proficiency and to inform subsequent
routing decisions in the assessment. The selected items included two Below Level 1 items, four at Level
1, one at Level 2 and one at Level 3. The proposed set included items that addressed all of the cognitive
processes, representations and content areas defined in the framework, as well as two out of the three
context areas of interest.

Main assessment items
Of the 78 items remaining under consideration following the development of the locator, 72 were needed
for the two stages of the adaptive design. Six additional items that functioned well in the field trial and were
of high quality were identified as items that could be excluded. When choices needed to be made between
two similar items, test developers selected those that best represented the construct, balanced the difficulty
of the item pool and resulted in a selection that optimised the main study design.

Numeracy components
As previously explained, the components assessment for numeracy consisted of two types of items: “how
many” and “which is biggest”. The experts reviewed the field trial outcomes for both types of items. There
was consensus that the “how many” items represent number sense, the skill targeted by the numeracy
components, both in terms of the estimated difficulty level (all falling in the Below Level 1 category) and in
the presentation. Two of the 18 items were dropped to align with the main study design and limit testing
time for this section. The experts recommended that the clusters of these items be balanced with respect
to whether a respondent needed to count the objects (e.g. the number of objects is greater than 4 or 5)
and whether or not the objects were organised in an array.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

94 
Based on the field trial data, the “which is biggest” items ranged in difficulty from Below Level 1 to Level 4.
Upon further review, the experts concluded that items containing fractions and percentages extended
beyond what they wanted to assess as a fluency measure of number sense. These items were also,
understandably, among the most difficult component items in the field trial. The experts recommended
retaining just the Below Level 1 and Level 1 items that focused on natural numbers and decimals. As a
result, 10 items were dropped, resulting in a total of 14 “which is biggest” items in the main study.

Adaptive problem solving
Fifteen adaptive problem-solving units, with a total of 65 items were developed for the field trial. All of these
items were retained for the main study because they all met the psychometric criteria for inclusion and
contributed to the preliminary scale. A few items were flagged because they performed differently in a few
countries. While this was not a major concern given the limited number of countries in which this occurred,
those items were identified as ones which would be reviewed based on the main study data.
The initial goal was to develop an adaptive design for this domain, but a primary characteristic of the
domain – adapting to dynamically changing situations – made this a challenging goal. The adaptive design
requires that units (rather than items) be classified as easy, medium or hard. However, in order to assess
the ability of respondents to adapt to changing problem-solving demands, APS units were developed
where features of the problem changed one or more times. This meant that adaptive elements were
introduced at specific points within units. Unlike in literacy or numeracy, where an item or two could be
dropped to make a unit easier or harder, the flow of the problem tasks within an APS unit meant that items
could not be dropped without compromising the integrity of the unit and the measurement of the construct.
As a result of these considerations, a linear design with rotated clusters was approved by the Technical
Advisory Group for the APS assessment and the APS expert group supported this decision.

Main study item pool
As noted, the main study item pool included all of the items used in the field trial. Of the 15 units, three
were designed as “static” units. These units contained 21 items in all and were designed to assess skills
at the lower end of the APS scale, and focus mainly on problem solving. The remaining 12 units, which
comprised 44 items, were classified as “dynamic”, because respondents were presented with changes in
the problem situation that required them to adapt their solution strategies.

how the proposed instrument meets the framework requirements.

Tablet tutorial and domain orientations
Based on the finding that the vast majority of respondents in the field trial were comfortable using the tablet
to complete the assessment, the decision was made to shorten both the tablet tutorial and orientations.
The redesign of these materials made some explanations and practice optional, reducing both assessment
time and response burden.
In the field trial version of the tablet tutorial, each of the response modes was introduced in turn and
respondents were asked to practice answering each individually. For the main study version, the four ways
to answer (tap on a choice, tap on one or more boxes, tap on a table and tap on a sentence) were
summarised on a single screen and respondents were provided with the option to simply read the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

96 
description, practice, or tap on a “Learn More” button to read more details and/or view an animated
demonstration. The introduction to the numeric entry keypad was similarly shortened, while the overview
of the testing screen remained unchanged from the field trial version of the tutorial.
The three domain orientations were reviewed following the field trial and shortened to focus only on the
most critical information. This allowed respondents to spend less time with those introductions and proceed
more quickly to the assessment if they did not need the full explanations and practice.

4. Proficiency scale construction
Laura Halderman, Usama Ali and Fred Robin, ETS

This chapter describes the development of proficiency scales for literacy,
numeracy and adaptive problem solving (APS). The process began with a
well-defined framework for each domain, ensuring cohesive item
development and task selection. A robust field trial (FT) yielded data for the
main study (MS) item selection and informed the final main study (MS)
assessment design. Despite adjustments made during the study, special
analyses confirmed minimal impact on data quality and overall data yield.
This process enabled the creation of high-quality proficiency scales for
each cognitive domain.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 99

Introduction
This chapter describes the development of the direct assessment scales for cognitive skills. The
development of a high-quality scale begins with an assessment framework that defines the domain,
identifies the core elements to be assessed to represent the domain, and outlines the distribution of those
elements across the item pool. This assessment framework creates a blueprint that shapes the
development of a cohesive set of tasks. A strong framework and well-structured task set lay the foundation
for scales that accurately measure adult proficiency, determine task difficulty and provide meaningful
interpretations of adult skills at different proficiency levels.
At the beginning of Cycle 2, experts in literacy, numeracy and APS developed frameworks that reflect the
societal changes shaping adults’ interaction with these domains since Cycle 1. Each framework can be
reviewed in the OECD’s report on the assessment frameworks (OECD, 2021). Chapter 3 of this technical
report extensively covers the core elements defined for each domain, the representation of the frameworks
within item pools and the selection process for the FT and, eventually, the MS. Chapter 1 provides
additional insights into the MS item selection to fulfil the direct assessment design requirements.
This chapter focuses on the processes involved in developing cohesive scales by ensuring item pools
represent the framework goals, analysing and using FT data to select the best item pools for the MS and
creating an assessment design that supports analysis and reporting goals.

Field trial
The FT was an integral part of developing the proficiency scales. Specifically, the FT was designed to yield
data for evaluating the quality of the instruments and the scaling and analytic procedures anticipated for
the MS. The FT provided initial estimates of item functioning for the new items, information on the stability
of the Cycle 1 trend item parameters and an overview of the comparability of all items across language
versions.
The FT item pools were selected to provide adequate construct coverage based on the distribution of
characteristics specified in each domain’s framework. The literacy and numeracy item pools included a
significant proportion of items from Cycle 1 to create the linking between the Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 scales
for trend reporting. Chapter 3 describes the item pool in detail, with the percentage of trend items shown
in Table 3.12. It also describes the reading and numeracy component measures.

Field trial design
The FT was designed as a tablet-only assessment with a sample size of 1 500 completed cases per
country/reporting language. The requirement of 1 500 completed cases would ensure that each item
received at least 200 responses for the IRT-based scaling analyses. Chapter 1 and Figure 1.1 describe
the FT goals and design.
Health and safety restrictions due to the Covid-19 pandemic impacted several national teams during the
FT data collection period. In some cases, national teams were prohibited from conducting data in the field
while in others, data collection occurred more slowly than expected. The Consortium offered more flexibility
for the number of completed cases required in recognition of these challenges. A variety of scenarios were
communicated to countries:
•

Between 75-100% of the target sample size (>=1 125 and <1 500 completed cases) ensured
approximately 150 responses per item. Countries were given classical item analysis statistics and
results based on item response theory (IRT).

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

100 
•

Between 50-75% of the target sample size (>=750 to <1 125 completed cases) ensured
approximately 100 responses per item. Countries were given classical item analyses statistics and
results based on item response theory (IRT) if an item had 100 responses.

•

Less than 50% of the target sample size (>=375 to <750 completed cases) ensured approximately
50 responses per item. Countries were given classical item analysis statistics only.

If national restrictions prevented household data collection, national teams could conduct a small,
operational FT using a volunteer and/or convenience sample to test the survey operations, data collection
systems, and data management procedures. The target sample size for an operational FT was 250. In
cases where restrictions were most severe, national teams could conduct a simulated FT. In this scenario,
national team staff created responses to the background questionnaire (BQ) to test routing and data
capture and to the direct assessment (DA) to test data capture. This allowed for some testing of data
collection systems and data management procedures.
After the data collection period ended, the total number of countries per scenario was as follows:
•

Nineteen countries achieved 75%-100% of the target sample size.

•

Five countries achieved 50%-75% of the target sample size.

•

Two countries achieved less than 50% of the target sample size.

•

One country conducted an operational FT.

•

Three countries conducted a synthetic FT.

•

One country did not conduct any FT data collection activities.

The data yield was sufficient to implement the full international FT analysis plan and draw conclusions
about the performance of items to inform the MS design.

Field trial analyses and main study item selection
The results of the IRT analyses showed a good fit across the language versions for each domain: trend
and new items for literacy and numeracy and new items for APS.

Figure 4.1 shows the distributions of the mean deviation (MD) and the root mean square deviation (RMSD)
statistics—measures of misfit—across countries for the literacy and numeracy trend items. For all but two
literacy items, the item fit distributions were narrow and well within the FT thresholds of ±0.20 (and even
within the narrower MS thresholds of ±0.15). The two trend literacy items were carefully reviewed to identify
why trend parameters did not fit.
In one case, the test development team discovered errors in the highlighting scoring definitions for some
language versions. These were corrected during the FT to MS preparation process. The other item was
easier in the Cycle 2 FT than in the Cycle 1 MS. No obvious explanation could be found, although the
observed item difficulty in the Cycle 2 FT aligned better with the test developer’s expectations of the item’s
difficulty. As expected, except for these two items, the proportions of misfits across the country-bylanguage groups were lower than observed for the new items.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 101

Figure 4.1. Distributions of MD and RMSD across countries for trend items

The item review process was collaborative and included data analysts, psychometricians and test
developers. New items were reviewed for difficulty, discrimination and omission rates. Items that were
much more difficult or easier than expected were carefully evaluated to check for alternative keys or other
reasons the item performed unexpectedly. If needed, these items were eliminated from the MS item pool.
Items with poor discrimination and high omission rates were also candidates for elimination.
The literacy and numeracy expert groups reviewed the items selected for omission based on poor or
unexpected performance (no APS items were omitted for the MS). Some items that functioned well were
eliminated to reduce the item pool size to fit the MS design. To achieve the correct number of items, the
expert groups made final selections to ensure the best representation of the construct possible. Selecting
the locator items was a critical part of this process. The MS design required eight literacy and eight
numeracy items that ranged from Below Level 1 to Level 3. Difficulty, framework classifications and item
types were all considered when making the final selection.
The reading component items performed as expected. Figure 4.2 shows that all items were estimated as
Below Level 1 items (blue squares represent items in the sentences task, while green squares represent
items in the passages task). The items within the numeracy component task, “how many”, performed as
expected. All items were estimated to be below Level 1. However, some of the items in the “which is
biggest” task were harder than expected (the blue squares represent items in the “how many” task, while
green squares represent items in the “which is biggest” task). The performance and characteristics of the
“which is biggest” items were reviewed by the Numeracy Expert Group. The Group decided to omit the
more difficult items from the MS item pool. The final set of items included a small number of “which is
biggest” items that extended throughout Level 1. Also, the direct assessment items in both literacy and
numeracy performed across various proficiency levels. In Figure 4.2, red circles represent the main literacy
or numeracy items, while red triangles represent the literacy or numeracy locator items.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

The collaborative approach to item selection, using expertise from data analysts, psychometricians, test
developers and subject matter experts, ensured the MS design was built upon strong item pools that
represented their construct and had the best performance characteristics.

Field trial to main study transition
The fit statistics and item parameter information for each language/country version were shared with
national teams. Misfit information helped national teams identify errors in the translation that may have
made an item easier or more difficult compared to an item’s international, common performance.
Translation and/or layout corrections were made on a case-by-case basis. All translation corrections were
reviewed, approved and implemented centrally by cApStAn verifiers, and all layout corrections were
implemented by ETS staff working on the delivery system.

Main study design
Chapter 1 and Figure 1.3 describe the MS goals and design. The MS Locator items were selected from
the FT Locator item pool, when possible. Items from the rest of the FT item pool were used as needed to
optimise the difficulty distribution of difficulty (below Level 1 to Level 3) and framework characteristics.
Units/items were assembled into testlets using an optimal test design method implemented by humanguided software. Testlet assemblies were collaboratively reviewed and revised by psychometricians and

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 103
test developers, ensuring the best balance of psychometric and framework characteristics within and
across all testlets.
Simulation studies tested the implementation of the MS design before finalising it for the delivery system.
The psychometricians created simulated groups representing seven Cycle 1 countries concerning the
means and standard deviations of their PIAAC numeracy proficiency (overall country score ranged from
206 to 288). Response patterns were created to mimic the range of ability within each represented country
to test the routing, reliability and item exposure. The simulation studies showed that, regardless of their
overall skill, each country would have respondents assigned to the main combinations of numeracy
testlets: low-low, low-medium, high-medium, and high-high. This confirmed the routing was working as
expected. The results also confirmed that each item would have adequate exposure, meaning an
opportunity to respond. This was a critical finding because each item must have enough responses within
each language version for each country. Lastly, the studies showed strong IRT reliability across all country
skill levels (0.88 and higher), indicating that this design would produce reliable scores for all PIAAC Cycle
2 countries.

Main study
The MS administration began for most countries in September 2022, following comprehensive national
delivery system testing, case management system integration, a thorough international survey operations
training (a train-the-trainer model) and national interviewer training. After approximately one month of data
collection, several national teams reported that the direct assessment portion of the interview was taking
longer than expected for some respondents. This was causing difficulties for interviewers because they
could not predict an accurate interview length when some respondents could finish everything within two
hours (a combined BQ length of 45 minutes and approximately 60 minutes for the DA), while some
respondents took more than two hours. PIAAC was not designed as a timed assessment, but the MS
design included modelling expected testing times based on item-level timing data from the FT. The
modelling results aligned with the expectation that most respondents would complete the direct
assessment in 60 minutes.
The beginning of data collection revealed another challenge that was not anticipated. Many national teams
could not hire the number of interviewers they had planned. Staffing challenges were further exacerbated
by difficulties retaining interviewers, with interviewers resigning after being fully trained and working for
only a few weeks. The longer and variable testing time added additional complexity to the staffing
challenges national teams faced at the start of data collection.
Investigations into the causes of the longer and variable testing time confirmed that some paths through
the direct assessment were, on average, longer than 60 minutes. Modelling of the testing time
underestimated the DA duration because it focused on item-timing rather than unit-timing. In many units,
introductory screens provided a purpose for the unit, interactions with the stimulus and/or updated
information if a new stimulus was introduced, etc. The timing for these screens was not included in timing
estimates when they were based on item timing alone. Analyses based on unit time showed APS had the
longest average completion times. Some APS units had more extensive introductory screens and/or
tutorials on how to use special digital tools. Therefore, when respondents were randomly assigned to a
domain pairing with APS and one or both of the linear clusters contained a longer APS unit, their average
completion times could range between 68 to 74 minutes. The literacy and numeracy completion times were
a little longer on average than expected, but the extreme completion times reported by interviewers were
likely due to APS.
National teams were already reporting interviewer retention issues and slower production rates, so it was
clear that design changes were needed to reduce the timing variability across respondents. Because the
data collection had already started, the design changes had to pose minimal implementation risks and
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

104 
maintain the required level of data quality. Changes to the Stage 3 testlets for literacy and numeracy were
safest because there were no routing decisions dependent on Stage 3. The balanced MS design made it
possible to keep all units/items in the design and only reduce the exposure of some units (please see
Chapter 1 of this technical report for a complete description of Designs A and B and how item sets
appeared in Stages 2 and 3). The last literacy unit and the last two numeracy units were removed from
Stage 3. Literacy units have more items on average, so removing two units from numeracy was necessary
to have the same timing reduction in both domains. APS required bigger changes to reduce the average
completion time. The linear cluster design made removing the last unit of cluster 1 and the first unit of
cluster 2 possible because clusters were assigned by a balanced incomplete block design rather than an
adaptive design. An additional reduction was made to the percentage of Path 3 respondents assigned
components – from 25% to 12.5%. Each of these changes presented minimal risk to the delivery system
and was pushed out to countries through the case management system after the Consortium and national
teams completed a round of testing. Simulation studies showed the revised design would produce enough
exposures for each item to yield the responses required to create high-quality IRT-based scales. These
studies also predicted adequate levels of reliability, only a small decrease compared to the original design.
Special MS analyses were planned to evaluate the impact of the change to the design mid-data collection.

Main study analysis
The impact of the design change was assessed by conducting classical and IRT analyses on three
datasets:
•

The data collected with the original DA design and then the shortened DA design, referred to as
the full data or baseline scaling data,

•

The full data reduced by removing the item responses collected under the original DA design based
on the items removed in the shortened DA design, referred to as the design 2 data, and

•

The full data reduced by removing some item responses equivalent to what was removed in the
design 2 data, but from the end of the original DA, effectively removing from the end of the second
domain referred to as the truncated data. The rationale for the analysis was that the effect of
fatigue or disengagement is likely to manifest mainly in the very last items of the assessment.

Some countries collected data using only the original DA design (design 1), while others administered only
the shortened DA design (design 2). However, most countries administered both designs. Sampledependent comparisons were impossible because the samples before and after the design change were
not equivalent.

Data yield and assessment time
On average, 23% of the data was collected based on the original design. The reduced design was
approximately 10 minutes (66 to 57 minutes), on average, shorter than the original. Long interviews (i.e.
interviews over 2.5 hours) were reduced by 7.5% (from 20.5% to 12%). Critically, all countries collected
enough data at the item level to estimate item-by-county interactions for all major language groups and to
estimate country-specific (unique) IRT item parameters when needed. Figure 4.3 shows the distribution of
respondent’s direct assessment time for the original DA design (design 1) and shortened DA design
(design 2). While there were differences in total DA time across countries, the extent of the reduction was
very similar.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 105

Figure 4.3. Distribution of participants’ total direct assessment time by country

Scaling
The ultimate test of comparability assessment results is based on the stability of item parameters across
the two designs. Special scaling analyses evaluated the international (common) and national (unique) item
parameters and country proficiency mean and standard deviation across the two designs. Because the
design 1 and design 2 datasets are not randomly equivalent, comparing outcomes from separate design
1 and design 2 scaling analyses would not be conclusive. Therefore, results from four separate sets of
scaling analyses were compared:
1. Scaling of the full data (baseline scaling) that followed the normal procedure – this includes all
the data, regardless of the design.
2. Scaling of the full data using design as an additional group factor (design scaling) to allow for
different item parameters than the baseline item parameters to be estimated if the international
parameters do not fit the design 1 or the design 2 data well enough or the national parameters do
not fit the country-by-design 1 or country-by-design 2 data well enough.
3. Scaling of the design 2 data (design 2 scaling) – this approach discards the data collected under
design 1 that would not have been collected with design 2.
4. Scaling of the truncated data (truncated scaling) – this approach removes responses collected
under design 1 at the end of the DA (i.e. the second cognitive domain). To approximate the
decrease in testing time created by the design revision, half of the items in the Stage 3 testlet of
the second domain were removed when the two domains assessed were literacy and numeracy.
In comparison, the entire Stage 3 testlet of the second domain was removed when APS was one
of the two domains assessed.
These analyses found only minimal differences between the international and national item parameters
estimated from the various scaling analyses. Figures 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6 show scatterplots of baseline item
parameters (x-axis) against those from the design, design 2 and truncated scaling methods (y-axis),
respectively. In each figure, the top scatterplots compare the item slopes (a parameter) for APS, literacy,
and numeracy, while the bottom scatterplots compare the item difficulties (b parameter) for the same
domains. These plots show trend items as blue dots and new items as red dots.

Conclusions
The proficiency scales for the cognitive domains in PIAAC Cycle 2 were built using the same cohesive
approach from Cycle 1. The process started with a well-defined blueprint in each domain’s framework,
guiding the item development process from start to finish. A robust FT served as a rehearsal for all data
collection and analysis aspects. The MS data yield and quality were sufficient for assessing the item
parameters’ stability of trend items and for estimating the new items’ parameters. This enabled the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

110 
psychometricians to finalise the MS design, establishing the routing decisions between the locator and
Stage 2 and Stages 2 and 3. Simulation studies predicted the design would yield enough responses per
item for all countries, a critical requirement for developing high-quality, IRT-based scales. Finally, despite
the need to alter the design after data collection started, the special analyses that investigated the potential
impacts of the design change showed minimal impacts due to the change. This enabled the finalisation of
all scaling procedures and the creation of proficiency estimates.
