SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

134 

Introduction
This chapter documents the Consortium’s work in developing, testing and refining the PIAAC Cycle 2
background questionnaire (BQ). It starts by describing the conceptual framework behind the BQ, which
outlines the main policy questions that the PIAAC project seeks to answer. The chapter provides the
theoretical concepts represented in the BQ that are needed to approach these policy questions. It then
deals with the development of the BQ, outlining the decision-making process for selecting questions for
the BQ, and summarising the mixed-method pretest and translatability assessment that were conducted.
The chapter then describes the validation of the BQ based on analyses of data from the field trial (FT).
This is followed by a brief outline of the content of the BQ, including an overview of its structure, a brief
description of the permissible national adaptations and extensions, as well as of the international options
that were added. The chapter ends with a brief explanation of the quality checks in the BQ, including
instructions given to interviewers, the available help buttons, and built-in consistency checks. Throughout
the chapter, attention is paid to how changes between Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 were handled.

The policy context of PIAAC
Addressing the main objectives of PIAAC
PIAAC Cycle 2 has three broad objectives (OECD, 2017[1]). First, it aims to track the stock of information
processing and other transversal skills needed for effective functioning in the labour market and society
across a wide range of countries. Second, it should contribute to the understanding of how these skills
relate to individual, institutional and social factors that can influence the development, maintenance and
loss of such skills over the lifecycle, as well as to important economic and social outcomes. Finally, it
provides an important tool for policy makers interested in finding optimal ways to enhance the development,
maintenance and productive deployment of these skills.
The BQ is designed to collect data to support these objectives. For example, when monitoring the stock of
key information-processing skills in a given country, basic descriptive statistics based on the population as
a whole, such as the average or median level of skills, are of limited use when interpreted on their own.
They are even less useful for cross-country comparisons given that countries differ markedly across
population demographics (e.g. some countries have more migrants or more young people than others).
Therefore, it is preferable to adjust those descriptive statistics by core demographic variables such as age,
sex or immigrant background. It is important to have a clear picture of where the available skills are most
concentrated or which subgroups have a higher risk of skill deficiencies. The BQ must provide data that
allow us to accurately identify such subgroups.
Additionally, the BQ includes established measures of social and emotional skills, such as the “Big Five”
model of personality. It goes beyond basic demographic and socio-economic background variables, to
better understand how cognitive, social and emotional skills are related to each other, to economic and
social outcomes, and to a wider range of experiences that may be related to their acquisition, maintenance
and decline. The BQ also requires well-validated measures of a broad range of economic outcomes to
allow for a better understanding of the processes that link skill levels to such things as employment
prospects, working hours, earnings, job security, occupational status, and the quality of the match between
education and work. The same principles apply for measuring outcomes in other life domains, such as
personal health, perceived political efficacy and social trust. With respect to experiences contributing to
skill acquisition, maintenance and decline, i.e. antecedents of skills, formal education remains a central
focus. In addition to the highest attained level, the specific pathways taken to achieve this level, and the
particular field of study chosen, may be related to current skill levels in the population. Participation in nonformal education (often measured by participation in training) is also thought to have a strong effect on

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 135
skills. Other activities undertaken during the course of work and/or everyday life (e.g. collaboration with
co-workers) can also have a strong effect on skill development and maintenance. As such, the BQ also
needs to capture determinants of skills in various domains.
In summary, although PIAAC is a survey of adult skills, the skill measures on their own are of little value in
the absence of additional information on the people possessing those skills across the participating
countries. In that respect, the direct assessment and the BQ together form an integrated whole in support
of the objectives of PIAAC.

The main policy questions
The following three broad policy questions are central in PIAAC (OECD, 2012[2]):
A. How are skills distributed in the population?
B. Why are skills important?
C. What factors are related to skill acquisition and decline?
The following sections discuss how the BQ contributes to answering these questions.

How are skills distributed in the population?
It is difficult to overstate the importance attached to skills in policy debates in today’s world (European
Union, 2016[3]; Martin, 2018[4]; OECD, 2017[1]). A major concern for countries is that they may be falling
behind in the race to provide their populations with the skills required to compete and function in the modern
economy. Within countries, there are concerns that certain subpopulations may be affected by low levels
of key cognitive skills. At the other end of the spectrum, there are also concerns if there are enough people
with high levels of information-processing skills, so that countries are prepared to adapt to new
technological and economic developments. In some countries, there appears to be an oversupply of high
levels of general skills, but shortages in medium and high levels of vocational skills.
Therefore, policymakers have an interest in monitoring the stock of human capital in their country to identify
the distribution of skill levels among relevant subgroups. The BQ of PIAAC Cycle 2 plays a crucial role in
this regard by equipping countries with data to answer questions like:
•

How do skill levels compare across demographic subgroups defined by sex and age across
countries?

•

How do countries compare in terms of socio-economic and migrant inequalities in skills?

•

How do skill levels compare across sectors of industry? How do the skill levels of these sectors
compare to those in other countries?

Why are skills important?
From a policy point of view, any investment in skills has to be justified by relevant economic and social
returns. There is robust evidence linking cognitive skills to both economic (e.g. income, social status) and
non-economic outcomes (e.g. health, political engagement). Beyond just cognitive skills, social and
emotional skills have also emerged as important determinants of the same economic and non-economic
outcomes. One of the key goals of the BQ is to provide indicators that can show if differences in education
and skills matter economically and socially.
By including measures of social and emotional skills in the BQ, PIAAC Cycle 2 provides more opportunities
for policy-relevant research on how cognitive and social and emotional skills co-shape life. It also shows
how their relative importance varies by the specific outcome under consideration, by socio-demographic
subgroup, and/or by country. The inclusion of both cognitive and social and emotional skills, economic and

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

136 
non-economic outcomes, as well as measures of formal and non-formal education in the BQ allows
countries to address questions such as:
•

To what extent do those with higher cognitive skills earn more and enjoy better career development
and working conditions than lower skilled individuals, when they hold the same level of
qualification? How do social and emotional skills add to these relationships? Do these relationships
vary across countries?

•

Are there groups with skill proficiency levels that are so low that these form a barrier to participation
in the labour force, political participation and social life? Are these groups demographically similar
across countries?

•

To what extent is the relationship between formal and non-formal education and economic
outcomes effected by varying skill levels? Can high cognitive skills or specific social and emotional
skills compensate for low educational qualifications? Does this differ across countries?

•

Is there a general relationship between skills and well-being, health or social and political
engagement? If so, to what extent is this mediated by economic outcomes? How does this differ
between subpopulations and across countries?

What factors are related to skill acquisition and decline?
From a policy perspective, it is vital to understand the factors related to skill development, because this
helps render policy more effective, as well as allows for a better understanding of why certain
subpopulations are exposed to a higher risk of having low skills. It is important to not only understand
factors that can be directly influenced by policy, like formal and non-formal education, but also factors that
are related to the person’s social and immigrant background. Similarly, we need to include other factors,
like the family setting during childhood, or willingness to try new things at work and in social life, and
learning through trial and error. Despite a vast amount of research since the middle of the last century,
much remains unknown about the exact contribution of education to skill levels relative to other learning
processes, and of the mechanisms through which learning is achieved.
Finally, we need to be aware that skills can also decline or be lost. Preventing skill decline, particularly in
the part of the labour force at later stages of their careers, is probably just as important as promoting skill
acquisition, but the underlying factors affecting these processes may be quite different (Levels and van der
Velden, 2023[5]), and it is important to have good insight into both processes. Therefore, the BQ captures
a broad range of measures of formal and non-formal education, as well as other determinants of skill
acquisition and decline (e.g. childhood conditions and working conditions). This enables countries to
answer questions like:
•

How are formal and non-formal education related to skill development? Do these relationships vary
across countries?

•

What differences exist between subpopulations in terms of skill use with respect to having a formal
or non-formal education? Are there indications that certain subpopulations appear to profit less
from the investment in formal and non-formal education?

•

How do patterns of skill acquisition and skill decline vary between subpopulations? Are the factors
that determine skill acquisition the same as those that mitigate skill decline?

Conceptual framework
In this section, we describe the main theoretical elements of the conceptual framework and, where relevant,
indicate the items in the BQ that address these elements. The purpose is to provide a solid theoretical
basis for the policy questions formulated in the previous section, and to serve as a guideline for identifying

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 137
the relevant concepts and the implementation of those concepts into specific questions in the BQ. This
framework also serves as a guideline for the analysis and interpretation of the data, both in the FT, where
it was used to derive predictions on how particular sets of variables are expected to behave, and in the
main survey (MS), where it is used to derive hypotheses pertaining to the policy questions outlined in the
previous section.
The presentation of the theoretical framework is divided into three parts, roughly corresponding to the three
policy questions previously described. First, is a brief overview of the literature on the nature and
distribution of key skills. Although the direct assessment (DA) falls outside the scope of development of
the BQ, the fundamental purpose of the BQ is to provide the context information needed for analysing and
interpreting the results of the DA. As a consequence, it is essential to not only understand how the BQ
allows for interpreting the distribution of key skills, but to also describe the skills actually being measured
in the DA (and, of equal importance, what skills are not being measured). Following this, a summary of the
literature pertaining to skill acquisition and decline is given, which is related to how these ideas are
measured in the BQ. The theoretical discussion concludes with a similar review of the literature on
economic and non-economic outcomes of skills, again linked to the measurement of these outcomes in
the BQ.

The nature and distribution of key skills
As previously noted, policymakers have a strong interest in knowing how skills are distributed across
countries, as well as across different subgroups within countries. Therefore, it is important to first look at
some of the literature on the so-called “key skills,” several of which form an important subset of the skills
measured in PIAAC.

The quest for key skills
The last few decades have seen an increased awareness of human capital as one of the driving forces of
economic development. Policymakers realise the importance of investing in formal and non-formal
education as a way of improving the stock of skills, which has resulted in the need to be able to monitor
and assess the stock of human capital. One finding that was revealed is that education alone is a poor
indicator of the stock of human capital (Massing and Schneider, 2017[6]). Individuals with the same nominal
level and type of education can differ markedly in their command of various skills. Likewise, across
countries with relatively comparable levels of educational attainment, substantial differences have been
observed in the level of skills that are acquired through education. This has been shown in studies like
Adult Literacy and Life Skills Study (ALL) and in studies using the PIAAC Cycle 1 data.
As the emphasis shifts from educational qualifications towards skill measurement, the question naturally
arises as to what skills should be measured. Even the most basic tasks require many discrete skills.
Determining which skills should be measured is a complex and difficult task, which is compounded by the
fact that people not only make use of generic skills, such as the ability to communicate or the ability to
learn, but also of a large number of highly specific skills pertaining to particular tasks, situations and
objects.
In order to introduce some order in the understanding of the diversity of human skills, many scholars have
engaged in a quest for so-called core skills or key competencies. A major project in this respect was the
DeSeCo (Definition and Selection of Competencies) project. This project was initiated by the OECD to
provide a framework for international skill assessments. Competencies are defined in this project as “the
ability to successfully meet complex demands in a particular context through the mobilisation of
psychosocial prerequisites (including both cognitive and noncognitive aspects)” (Rychen and Salganik,
2003, p. 43[7]). The basic difference between this view and earlier concepts of skills is the holistic nature of
the concept of competence. It refers not only to a range of cognitive, social and emotional, and other

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

138 
prerequisite skills necessary to perform tasks in a competent way, but also to the notion of “orchestration,”
which is defined as the ability to use these constituent elements in a meaningful and deliberately arranged
way. Although the theoretical framework provided by the DeSeCo project injects theoretical rigor into the
discussion of skills measurement, it does not provide explicit recommendations as to which competencies
should be measured. It serves as an overarching framework describing the main underlying competencies
that give skills their significance.
The choice of direct assessments in ALL was based on these theoretical ideas, as well as on practical
considerations such as designing an instrument that could be administered at the respondent's home.
PIAAC Cycle 1 built on the direct assessments of literacy and numeracy skills in ALL, extending these to
the area of problem solving in technology-rich environments. In PIAAC Cycle 2, this latter domain is
replaced by the broader domain of adaptive problem solving skills (Greiff et al., 2017[8]; OECD, 2021[9]).
These skills are relevant across the full range of life contexts, from education through work, to home and
social life, and in interactions with public authorities. People with high levels of these skills are well
positioned to take advantage of the opportunities afforded by the modern world. Those who lack the skills
to deal with the complexity of the modern world are at risk of losing out (Hango, 2014[10]; OECD, 2012[2];
Shomos, 2010[11]).
Moreover, the importance of key skills such as literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving skills, and
the role they play in people’s lives, and in the economy and society in general, is expected to be profoundly
affected by a number of major changes taking place in the world. The OECD has pointed to three so-called
“mega-trends” in particular: globalisation, technological change and demographic change (see also (Allen
and van der Velden, 2013[12]; OECD, 2017[1])). These changes could potentially result in the reduction and
even elimination of whole sectors of employment, and although it is generally expected that they will also
give rise to a large number of new jobs and occupations, the concern is that the workers who are being
displaced from old jobs will be deficient in the skills necessary to take advantage of these new opportunities
(Goos, Manning and Salomons, 2009[13]). The nature and extent of such shifts is still being hotly debated,
with scholars such as Autor (2015[14]) suggesting that they may be overstated, although, scholars also
concede that much is still unknown in terms of how these trends will ultimately affect our lives. Until
recently, the effects looked to be largely confined to areas of work that relied heavily on standardisation
and routinisation; however, computers and technology appear to be moving more into relatively complex
and even abstract non-routine types of work (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2018[15]; Berger and Frey, 2016[16]).
This underlines the increasing importance of recognising adaptive problem solving skills as a key skill set
just like literacy and numeracy.
In terms of skills that are not measured in the DA, a decision had to be made to target the skills aspects
that best lent themselves to being administered via tablet, but this does not diminish the value of the
information gathered. It is also important to keep in mind that it is a subset of the skills possessed by the
individuals participating in the survey that are being measured. Social and emotional skills are not included
in the DA, but these are covered by questions in the BQ. Arguably, the most conspicuous omission is in
the area of occupation- or industry-specific skills used by individuals in their chosen line of work. Despite
the fact that employers often list generic cognitive skills and social and emotional skills as the most
important skills required in the workplace, professional expertise is also an essential condition for success
in many occupations (Humburg and van der Velden, 2015[17]; 2017[18]). For example, no one would doubt
that in order to become a good medical doctor, architect or car mechanic, it is necessary to acquire the
domain-specific knowledge and skills required of these occupations.
There is a plethora of specific professional skills, so it is not possible to measure professional expertise
directly in the PIAAC assessment. This is because no common assessment instrument exists that
measures all possible types of professional skills in a meaningful way for large populations. Although no
direct assessment of occupation-specific skills is included in the PIAAC survey, measures of skill use in
some more generic work-related areas, as well as in the domains covered by the DA, have been included

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 139
in the BQ. The absence of direct measures of specific skills underscores the importance of obtaining
information on the occupation of working (or recently working) respondents, their work experience and
current level, as well as the type (general or vocational) and field of education that they obtained. The
differences in performance on the DA based on occupation are likely to be at least matched or possibly
eclipsed by differences in the level and type of specific skills. As such, the residual occupation-level
variance in economic outcomes should provide a rough indication of the economic importance of specific
skills relative to the generic skills measured.

Skill use
The DA in PIAAC is limited to relatively few, albeit crucial, skill domains. Yet other skills (e.g. the skills
needed to work within teams, to work on multiple or flexible tasks, and to work independently) have become
increasingly relevant in modern workplaces. Earlier skills surveys like the International Adult Literacy
Survey (IALS) and ALL were mainly limited to the supply side of skills, i.e. the stock of skills of the
population. Over time, it became necessary to also collect some information on the demand side for skills,
particularly on their utilisation in the workplace. Additionally, compared to IALS and ALL, as well as PIAAC
Cycle 1, new questions in the BQ of Cycle 2 of PIAAC can shed light on changing returns to skills in
different sectors and occupations. For example, there is evidence that points towards a growing earning
inequality associated with earning differences between digitalised and non-digitalised organisations,
across a broad range of sectors and occupations (de la Rica and Gortazar, 2016[19]). Therefore, data on
ICT use at work and in private life can help identify at risk subpopulations.
Scales were developed that measure the use of key skills both at work and in everyday life with respect to
the types of devices/technology commonly used at work and in everyday life. Questions are included for
two of the central domains covered by the DA (literacy and numeracy) as well as questions pertaining to
the use of ICT and digital technology at work and in everyday life. Furthermore, the BQ includes various
questions to capture the use of interaction/social skills (such as cooperation, influence, managerial, selfdirection, horizontal interaction and client interaction), and physical skills (stamina and manual skills) at
work.
The measures of the use of “job skills” obtained in the BQ will not be direct measures of the “own skill”
held by respondents. Discrepancies between job-holders’ skills and job requirements are possible. Some
individuals may have an excess supply of some skills and not be using them fully on the job; while others
may have insufficient skills for the job they are doing, which may lead to poor performance. However, these
discrepancies are dynamic: they can appear and disappear as both jobs and people change. In the
domains being directly assessed, it will be possible to generate indicators of mismatch, such as individuals
with high levels of own skill but who are in jobs where that skill is used at a low level, or vice versa. There
are also two general questions on self-perceived skill underutilisation.

Social and emotional skills
PIAAC Cycle 2 includes measures of social and emotional skills and the final section of the BQ (Section K)
is dedicated to self-reports of key social and emotional skills. Section K draws on a recent questionnaire
of skills based on the “Big Five” personality framework (BFI-2; (Soto and John, 2017[20])), by using a
shortened version of the “Big Five” questionnaire (BFI-2-S; (Soto and John, 2017[21])).1 The “Big Five”
model of personality is currently the most widely used and well-validated framework to measure social and
emotional skills. It distinguishes five broad skill domains: Conscientiousness characterises the tendency
to be organised, responsible, and productive. Emotional Stability refers to the disposition to remain calm,
anxiety-free, and in a generally good mood. Extraversion describes characteristics such as being outgoing,
sociable and assertive. Agreeableness denotes the ability to be compassionate and respectful, and to
cooperate with others. And finally, Open-Mindedness (traditionally labelled Openness (to Experience))

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

140 
describes characteristics such as curiosity, aesthetic sensitivity and creativity. Within each of these five
broad domains, narrower facets can be distinguished that allow for a more fine-grained level of analysis.
A growing body of evidence from economics and personality psychology attests to the predictive power of
social and emotional skills in terms of a broad range of important life outcomes, including academic
achievement and educational attainment, income, health and social participation (Heckman, Stixrud and
Urzua, 2006[22]); for a review, see (Lechner, Anger and Rammstedt, 2019[23]; Roberts et al., 2007[24]). The
evidence shows that social and emotional skills have incremental predictive validity over cognitive skills,
with effect sizes rivalling or even surpassing those of cognitive skills for some outcomes. Moreover, social
and emotional skills are only modestly related to cognitive skills (Heckman and Kautz, 2012[25]), including
those measured in PIAAC (Rammstedt, Danner and Lechner, 2017[26]). This modest association suggests
that social and emotional skills can be cultivated relatively independently of cognitive skills. There is also
some evidence that the returns on social and emotional skills have even been steadily increasing in past
decades as tertiary-sector-type professions increasingly require “soft skills” and employers put increasing
value on them (Edin et al., 2022[27]). Additionally, there is evidence that social and emotional skills can
evolve over the course of one’s life and in response to policy interventions (Deming, 2017[28]; Kankaraš,
2017[29]).
Thus, the inclusion of social and emotional skills in PIAAC promises considerable added value and
analytical potential. Understanding the complex relations between cognitive skills, social and emotional
skills, education and training systems, and economic and non-economic outcomes across countries and
population subgroups is of crucial importance in using the data from PIAAC to draw accurate and effective
conclusions to inform policymakers (Brunello and Schlotter, 2011[30]).

Reporting categories to examine the distribution of skills
In order to effectively address skill deficiencies in terms of social equity, it is important to have a clear
picture of where the deficiencies are most concentrated. For example, are there population subgroups that
appear to be underskilled? To answer this and other questions, we need to know how skills are distributed
among relevant subgroups, as defined in the BQ (e.g. sex, age, socio-economic status or migration
background). These so-called reporting categories are important from the point of view of equity and
efficiency: if skill gaps lead to social and/or economic exclusion, this is not only detrimental to the wellbeing of the groups involved, but also to the functioning of the economy and society. However, the reasons
for skill gaps are likely to be systematically different for different “at risk” groups, so the policy measures
undertaken are likely to be group-specific. Age is also important because skill acquisition and skill decline
are both related to age, leading to typical age profiles of skills and skill-related outcomes. Occupation,
sector of industry and firm size are needed to detect labour market areas in which skill gaps exist and to
assess the extent to which investments in non-formal education are taking place to reduce these gaps.
This and similar information form the basis for determining possible policy interventions for the groups
where help is most needed. An individual’s highest level of education is assumed to be one of the strongest
predictors of their skills (see below), but because this is differentially distributed across countries, a
breakdown of this variable is needed for even the most elementary understanding of the results. In addition,
it is important to know how access to the education system is distributed across different subgroups that
are “at risk” from the point of view of skills proficiencies.

Understanding differences in skill levels
From a policy perspective, it is paramount to have a better understanding of the factors that may be related
to skill development. It can guide implementation of policies to make formal and non-formal education
programmes more efficient, as well as foster better understanding of why certain subpopulations are more
at risk of having low skill levels. This applies to factors like education and training, which are relatively
amenable to influence through policy, and to factors that are less well-defined, such as those related to

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 141
how people were brought up, go about their daily lives, or are perceived by others. Some of these factors
are learned in formal settings, such as university or the workplace, but many are also learned in the
personal or private domains of people’s lives or in the social or recreational settings in which they spend
time.
While it might seem almost trivial to discuss the effects of education on skill formation in countries, the fact
is that much remains unknown about the exact contribution of education, and of the mechanisms through
which skill formation is achieved. As was the case for defining and measuring skills themselves, there are
several strands of research pertaining to how individuals acquire or lose skills over their lifetime. One
prominent strand is that of sociological research, which points to the social (especially familial) environment
affecting educational performance, school choice and educational attainment (e.g. (Boudon, 1974[31];
Bourdieu, 1984[32]; Dronkers, 1994[33])). The second strand is educational research, in which scholars have
tried to uncover those features of education that are particularly effective in promoting learning (Glaser,
1991[34]). A third strand is that of the economics of education. Since the pioneering work by scholars such
as Becker (1964[35]) and Schultz (1963[36]), economists have looked at education, training and other
activities undertaken by individuals to improve their level of knowledge and skills as investments in human
capital that are expected to yield returns in the labour market (Cunha and Heckman, 2007[37]). Fourth, a
conceptually related but empirically distinct area concentrates on how people continue to learn after leaving
formal education. An important focus of this strand of research is on non-formal education and training in
which employees participate (Blundell et al., 1999[38]; Desjardins, Rubenson and Milana, 2006[39]). Finally,
this focus on lifelong learning has led to increased attention to the fact that individuals not only acquire
skills over their lifetime, but are also confronted with skill loss and a general decline in the ability to acquire
and retain new knowledge and skills (Arthur Jr. et al., 1998[40]; Flisi et al., 2015[41]). In this section we will
look at each of these strands of research. A schematic representation of the key mechanisms around skill
acquisition and decline is presented in Figure 6.1.

Figure 6.1. Schematic representation of skill acquisition and decline

The social environment
The opportunities and constraints facing different social groups have been extensively studied by
sociologists looking at the social barriers to formal (and more recently, non-formal) education and training.
Inequality in access to education related to the family background, both in terms of socio-economic status
and immigrant background, which are often intertwined, is persistent. Part of this inequality stems from

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

142 
differences in school performance and learning abilities, the so-called primary effects of social stratification
in education (Boudon, 1974[31]). These may be caused by differences in innate abilities and by differences
in socialisation processes (as well as their interaction, as the field of epi-genetics increasingly shows).
There is a large and growing body of literature documenting the importance of formative experiences in
childhood on cognitive and social and emotional development later in life (Cunha and Heckman, 2007[37];
Skwarchuk, Sowinski and LeFevre, 2014[42]). This is an important insight for many reasons, in particular
showing that the brain undergoes cumulative neurological changes in the process of acquiring literacy and
numeracy skills at a younger age that cannot be acquired as easily at later ages (Hinton and Fischer,
2010[43]). Such effects can play out in many different ways.
Even with the same school performance, students from different family backgrounds, typically measured
via parental occupation and/or educational attainment, make systematically different choices in education
(the secondary effects of social stratification in education). When considered with the number of choices
that have to be made during the educational career, the cumulative effect of these choices may overwhelm
the effects resulting from socio-economic differences in performance (primary effects), especially in
countries with many educational transition points. The differences in choices relate to differences in social
cost-benefit analyses: the social costs and benefits involved as well as the risks perceived in obtaining
education are different for students from different social backgrounds. Following an educational career
different from the one that is common within the family induces social costs, while the social and economic
benefits may be lower. Effects can also be more indirect, for example through composition effects in terms
of social and ethnic background in schools (Belfi, Haelermans and De Fraine, 2016[44]; Bellin, Dunge and
Gunzenhauser, 2010[45]). Biedinger (2009[46]) found that social background and parental involvement
explained a large part (though not all) of effects of immigrant background on pre-school learning in
Germany. As another example, Vogtenhuber (2018[47]) found strong parental-education effects on
attainment of both educational credentials and skills. Such effects are not necessarily confined to early
ages. For example, Stegers-Jager et al. (2015[48]) found strong effects of social background on the clinical
performance of medical students, distinct from the effects of past performance (as measured by GPA).
Also, there is evidence that children from single-parent families are disadvantaged in their formal education
and skill development (amongst other important outcomes, see (Dronkers, 1994[33])), partly because of the
more strenuous economic situation of such families, so it is important to know if a person grew up in a
single- or dual-parent home. The cultural capital of the family (Bourdieu, 1984[32]), often measured with
proxies such as parental education and the number of books in the home, also provides a powerful
predictor of the school performance.
Finally, while gender inequality in initial education has vanished, and actually turned into an advantage for
girls in many Western countries, gender inequalities still persist in fields of study, occupational choices,
earnings and later access to non-formal education (for the latter, see (Massing and Gauly, 2017[49])). This
underscores that the sex of the respondent is a key reporting category for PIAAC.
Together, sex and social background effects on skills could point to potential inefficiencies in educational
systems. The BQ includes indicators of sex, cultural capital (parents’ education and books in the home),
socio-economic background (parents’ occupation), immigrant background, and language used in the
parental home. Additionally, given that conditions in the childhood home influence cognitive and social and
emotional development, including motivation, it is important to control for childhood conditions in order to
estimate corrected (net) effects of formal and non-formal education on skills. Also, given that these
concepts refer to the past, their interpretation in causal terms is much more straightforward than for many
other concepts measured in PIAAC, making them powerful control variables. Therefore, in the BQ of PIAAC
Cycle 2 a number of new indicators of the home environment while growing up are included, such as the
level of urbanisation of the place of residence during childhood, the household composition, the number of
siblings, and birth order to serve as exogenous control variables.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 143
Effective learning and instruction
Following a certain education path does not automatically imply that all students are likely to acquire the
same set of skills. Research has shown that there is considerable variation among educational systems,
schools, study programmes and teachers, all of which influence the amount of skills students acquire
through formal education. A large part of the effect of education on skill development is likely to be indirect,
as students are turned into more or less effective learners who may or may not actively engage with
learning situations. In other words, different characteristics of education may affect the direct acquisition
of skills as measured in the DA, as well as the ability to acquire further skills after leaving education.
Situated learning theories (Glaser, 1991[34]) emphasise that competencies and competence development
are context-specific. They stress the importance of coherence and context-relevance (e.g. real-life
experiments, simulation and practical work experience) in the design of the curricula in order to develop
expertise. Active learning theories reject the traditional notion of the teacher as the only active person in
the classroom; imparting his or her knowledge directly to the student. The development of generic
competencies like problem solving and metacognitive abilities are fostered through “powerful learning
environments” (De Corte, 1990[50]), that incorporate active instructional methods like problem-based
learning and project-oriented education . In addition to these innovative ways of learning, which are based
on theories of how individuals actually learn, educational research has traditionally stressed “time on task”
as one of the most important factors affecting student outcomes. That is, the actual time students spent on
education (within the classroom and through self-study) is also a good predictor of learning outcomes.
The highest level of education achieved is the most important factor affecting skill levels. More years of
education are expected to have a positive impact on the general skill proficiencies. The type of education
is also important: general secondary education programmes typically devote more time to learning, and
make higher use of, literacy and numeracy skills than (pre-)vocational programmes, so higher literacy and
numeracy skills can be expected amongst graduates of general programmes. However, this relationship
reflects selection effects since youth with higher cognitive skills, or from higher social backgrounds, also
tend to perform better in school, and are either selected into or choose to follow more (cognitively)
demanding educational programmes. Institutional contexts play a major role in determining which
educational pathways are available to individuals and how individuals are selected into the different
options. Some countries use between-school ability tracking at the lower secondary level, so that selection
and learning effects may accumulate more over the educational career. Other countries delay selection
until upper secondary education, which is expected to lower the effects of social and immigrant background
on educational attainment and skills. At the tertiary level, in many countries, higher education systems
have diversified into a system with an “applied” type of university (often called college rather than
university) being more oriented towards the labour market, and a “traditional” type of university that is more
theoretically and research-oriented. A few countries even offer vocational education at the bachelor’s and
master’s levels (OECD, 2022[51]) which requires completion of vocational rather than general upper
secondary education for entry. Selection into these kinds of programmes as well as the learning
environment, are likely to differ across different types of institutional settings, and be associated with
differential skill profiles.
It is also important to identify whether the highest educational qualification has been completed outside
the host country (in the case of migrants), in order to identify any negative effect on skills, to analyse
migration-related devaluation of qualifications, or if the interest is in the outputs of the national education
system only.
Next, the particular field of education chosen will also affect skill levels: graduates from certain fields may
have higher scores in the literacy domain, while others may have higher scores in the numeracy domain.
As with types of education, people also self-select into fields of study based on their social background
and skills (e.g. people with strong mathematical skills are more likely to choose math-oriented fields). As

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

144 
a result, this also makes field-of-study measures useful for capturing skills that are not measured in the
direct assessment.
Finally, information about educational pathways (qualifications completed before the highest qualification)
is important in order to analyse how background factors affect selection into certain education pathways,
and how the specific pathway taken through the educational system affects the highest qualification
eventually obtained. This also allows for analyses of effects on adult skills, participation in non-formal
education, and possibly labour market or other outcomes. This is especially relevant given the known pathdependencies in educational careers and life-course development, so that the actual cause for low skills
may not lie solely in low educational attainment, but rather in early educational transitions into programmes
that are less conducive to general skill development or enrolment in programmes without successful
completion.2

Education as an investment
In economics, education and learning are treated as an investment. In this view, people are expected to
invest in education and learning when the costs are smaller than the future benefits. Not everybody is
equally likely to invest in the same amount of education. People differ in the degree to which they enjoy
education or learning, and in the degree to which they value the potential benefits of education, which
affects their decisions to learn. Borghans et al. (2008[52]) provide a model for investments in education and
learning that capture a wide range of potential differences between individuals. First, people differ in their
capacity to acquire skills. The costs of education are lower for people who acquire skills more easily
because they learn faster. Second, people differ in preferences. They might differ in how they value
learning, working and leisure. They might differ in how much they value a high income or other potential
benefits of education, and they might differ in how they value future benefits compared to current benefits
(time preference, discount rate) and how they account for risks in outcomes (risk aversion). Third, people
might face constraints in their choices. Credit constraints can influence the decision to attend school, but
also a lack of facilities for education and less favourable family conditions can be treated as such
constraints (Carneiro and Heckman, 2002[53]). Finally, the decision to invest in education will depend on
information available at the time of investment (Jensen, 2010[54]). If people do not know about the benefits
of education, it is unlikely that they will invest.
The main reason it is important to take account of factors expected to influence the willingness to invest in
education is that these factors may have a direct impact on skill levels that is distinct from the indirect effect
via the increased level of investment in education. If such factors are not taken into account, estimates of
the effect of education on skill levels will be biased. The BQ covers some, but not all, of these factors. The
questionnaire contains no direct indicators of innate learning abilities. It does, however, include a number
of control variables that are related to this concept, in particular the family background in terms of parents’
education, which are exogenous in the sense that they are not the result of choices made by the
respondents. Also, the section on social and emotional skills (e.g. measures of conscientiousness and
openness to new experiences) may capture personality characteristics that are related to the capacity to
learn, and to investment strategies. A measure of patience is also included, which is an important addition
to Cycle 2 since it can affect investment decisions.
In addition to formal education, it is also possible to invest in other forms of learning, such as non-formal
education. In surveys, investment in non-formal education is often measured by participation in training
activities, such as foreign language or software courses, music lessons or job-related training. From a
policy viewpoint it is important to not only obtain an indication of the volume of investments, but in the case
of non-formal education, to have information on the financing of such investments. A large part of nonformal education efforts is paid for by employers. Since most training received by individuals also benefits
other employers (externalities of training) this typically leads to too little work-related training being
provided, because part of the returns are captured by outside parties (competing organisations and the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 145
individual). From a policy perspective, this could warrant some interventions in the training market to
balance out this potential source of underinvestment in training. In addition, knowledge on current
investments in training can contribute to the formation of policies designed to provide more equitable or
effective inducements to encourage participation among those most in need of further learning. This refers
both to differences across different skills levels – Are low-skilled individuals investing enough in their
human capital? – and across key reporting categories as specified below. The questionnaire contains
indicators of whether the training was followed in working hours (to assess the level of investment by
employers in training in terms of opportunity costs), who contributed to the costs of training (to assess the
level of direct investment in training by employees, employers and other actors), and (reasons for)
nonparticipation in training activities in which the respondent would have liked to engage.

Non-formal education and the working environment
While there is more to be learned about the effects and effectiveness of education systems as producers
of key skills, there is also much to be learned about other channels thought to be related to skill acquisition
(and decline). Much of current policy debates on skills focuses on effects of non-formal education (for
example, organised on-the-job training, (European Union, 2016[3])). As mentioned above, non-formal
education is often referred to as training that is complementary to formal education. Training often takes
place in the workplace but can also be non-work-related and driven by personal interests.
Non-formal education is a key factor both for employment and training policies. It is important to understand
how skills are gained or maintained, and how individuals can prepare themselves for changes in society,
such as digitalisation (OECD, 2013[55]). The investment in non-formal education is one of the key measures
policy makers use to increase skills and competencies in addition to formal education. Non-formal
education is one of the most important forms of adult learning, which is recognised now as an essential
enabler of economic growth and social development within the rapidly evolving knowledge-based society
and economy. Previous research shows that the investment in training has positive effects on individuals
in terms of higher employment stability, higher wages and seems to be portable in many cases (Blundell
et al., 1999[38]), and positive at the company level in terms of productivity and competitiveness (Bartel,
1995[56]; Blundell et al., 1999[38]). Blundell et al. (1999[38]) report that employer-provided training is related
to higher wage returns than off-the job training and its effects are also the most long-lasting. Training may
have similar positive effects for those who are not employed, and in various countries training is an
important component of active labour market policies.
Regardless of the issue of direct causality, information on correlations between training, skills and
outcomes can be highly valuable from a policy perspective. There are strong indications of a so-called
“Matthew effect” (Kilpi-Jakonen, Vono de Vilhena and Blossfeld, 2015[57]), whereby training investments
fall most heavily on those who already have the greatest endowment of formal education and skills. At
least part of this effect may be driven by the wish for the greatest returns on investments in personnel: the
most skilled workers are given the most demanding tasks, which drives them to increase their skills even
further through training (Allen and de Grip, 2012[58]). In this context, understanding barriers to training is
important. Previous research shows that cost issues, lack of time and finding appropriate courses are
reported as the most common barriers (Desjardins, Rubenson and Milana, 2006[39]; Rubenson and
Desjardins, 2009[59]). Human resources practices and job characteristics are the major factors that
determine the opportunities for workers to attend training and to learn in an informal way. Although these
opportunities are often necessary for actual training participation, a workplace characterised by these
training opportunities might not be sufficient. Workers’ characteristics will probably determine whether the
learning opportunities at work are fully exploited. Personal characteristics, such as age, gender, family
responsibilities and level of education are found to be important determinants of training participation
(Bassanini et al., 2007[60]; Massing and Gauly, 2017[49]).

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

146 
Participation in non-formal education in the 12-month period preceding the survey is used as an indicator
of whether one ever participated in training, but the BQ also contains questions on recent investments in
non-formal education. This is measured by capturing information on participation in recent training,
including the main reason for participating, which is crucial for analysing the effects of the training, and
work autonomy.
Next to non-formal education, experiences at work can have an influence on skill acquisition and skill use.
As these are not only dependent on total work experience, but also on the specific way in which this
experience has been acquired. In addition to total work experience, the number and timing of changes of
employer and/or career breaks is therefore also important. There is likely a certain minimum time one
would need to remain with a given employer to have a reasonable chance of learning new things, and the
returns on tenure in most jobs are likely to remain positive for at least a few years (although probably not
in very low-level routine jobs). However, because the new experiences one can expect to be exposed to
when working long-term for the same employer are likely to diminish over time, it is expected that a certain
number of job changes over a person’s career will have a positive effect on learning. Lengthy career breaks
comprise periods during which the exposure to (work-relevant) experiences is likely to be limited.
In addition to these direct effects of work experience on learning, there may be indirect effects when work
history is interpreted by potential employers as a signal of productivity and learning potential. In that case,
a career characterised by frequent changes and/or lengthy interruptions might affect the willingness of
potential employers to hire an individual and to invest in his or her human capital. Lengthy periods of
unemployment – that is, seeking work without success – may have a negative effect on an individual’s
motivation and could lead to so-called “scarring effects,” where unemployment periods are a negative
signal to potential future employers.
The questionnaire contains a number of questions related to the above-mentioned aspects of employment
history, such as information on the total number of years of work experience, information on being out of
work in the last five years, and information on the number of different employers worked for in the last five
years.

Skill loss
The focus on lifelong learning and population ageing in recent years has led to increased attention to the
fact that individuals not only acquire skills throughout their lifetime, but are also confronted with skill loss
and a general decline in the ability to acquire and retain new knowledge and skills. An important finding of
IALS and ALL was that skill loss was sufficient to offset all of the expected gains from increasing
educational quality and quantity. Until now, only a few studies on different aspects of skills obsolescence
have been published. Most of these studies were published in periods in which unemployment was high.
This increased the focus on the adverse impact of skills obsolescence for the workers involved. It is
interesting that in the recent policy debates on skills obsolescence and “lifelong learning,” the main focus
has been on the waste of valuable human resources and on the non-optimal performance of workers with
inadequate skills. This brings skills obsolescence to the heart of the economic challenge the Western
economies face: transforming into a knowledge-based society with an ageing population.
On a population level, most cognitive abilities such as memory function, information processing speed and
attentional capacity tend to decline with advancing age. Adequate preservation of cognitive abilities is of
primary importance to older people, as cognitive decline can result in a loss of productivity among those
still working, and a loss of independence and autonomy for retired people. Large individual differences
exist in the offset and rate of decline of specific cognitive functions. The theoretical distinction drawn in
psychological research between “fluid” and “crystallised” abilities helps to understand these differences.
The former refers to functions that involve controlled and effortful processing of novel information (cognitive
mechanics), and the latter to the representation of learned skills and access to knowledge (cognitive
pragmatics). Fluid abilities are far more sensitive to ageing and both cognitive domains show different

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 147
developmental patterns across the life span. Fluid abilities typically start declining in the mid-20s, while
crystallised skills may improve up to and even beyond the age of 70. The distinction between the two is
important because the direct assessments in PIAAC will differ in the extent to which they relate to
crystallised or fluid abilities. One may hypothesise that numeracy and literacy skills relate more strongly to
crystallised abilities, while adaptive problem solving will relate more to fluid abilities. For adults, the decline
in fluid abilities is more likely to strongly hamper their working and everyday life than the decline in
crystallised abilities.
Recent advances in cognitive neuroscience have convincingly demonstrated that healthy brains show
considerable capacity to compensate for reduced integrity of functional networks or to reorganise existing
networks to adapt to changing task demands. The importance of adequate and continued exposure to
environmental stimuli during the lifetime is now considered pivotal for optimal conservation of cognitive
abilities in old age (conceptualised in the “use it or lose it” paradigm). Arthur et al. (1998[40]) conclude, on
the basis of a meta-analysis from the psychological literature on skill decay and retention, that there is
substantial skills obsolescence when they are not practiced or used. De Grip et al. (2007[61]) show that jobworker mismatches induce cognitive decline with respect to immediate and delayed recall abilities,
cognitive flexibility and verbal fluency. Also, as a result of specialisation, certain knowledge and skills
acquired during initial education may get lost. An important question within the broader research domain
of lifelong learning and adult education is whether training can help slow down the process of cognitive
decline among older populations. Here as well, the findings are mixed. For example, Canduela et al.
(2012[62]) found that training opportunities decreased with age, but that improved access to training (active
ageing policies) was a good way to keep older workers engaged in the labour market. However, Flisi et al.
(2015[41]) found little impact of lifelong learning on cognitive decline among older cohorts.
The BQ enables insight into some of the possible causes of skills obsolescence, such as age, health,
unemployment, participation in training, working below one’s level, long tenure and sector of industry.

Institutional factors
Scholars using the Cycle 2 BQ to analyse the nature and importance of key skills will benefit greatly from
the large-scale comparative nature of the survey, which allows the potential to exploit institutional variation,
to distinguish between country-specific and general patterns, to analyse potential heterogeneity of effects
across different settings, and to gain more control over selection issues through better identification
strategies using system-level characteristics (Flisi et al., 2015[41]; Hanushek and Woessmann, 2011[63]).
For example, Hanushek and Woessmann (2011[63]) showed that differences in institutional structures and
teaching quality could account for a significant portion of international differences in student achievement.
Massing and Schneider (2017[6]) demonstrated that there are cross-national differences in the association
between educational qualifications and skills. Related to that, Barone and van de Werfhorst (2011[64])
showed that a large proportion of the effects of education on earnings could be explained by cognitive
skills, but that this effect varied widely across countries. Levels et al. (2014[65]) showed that the extent to
which educational mismatches are explained by skill mismatches varied across countries as a function of
an institutional characteristic like employment-protection legislation. In a similar way, there is a need to
study whether policy and institutions can affect the process of cognitive decline. It is well established that
early retirement decisions are largely driven by institutions. Gruber and Wise (2003[66]), for example, show
there is a very strong cross-country relationship between retirement rates and government policy. If
keeping workers active can postpone cognitive decline, there is an important role for policies that increase
labour market participation of older workers. Although institutional factors are not measured directly in the
BQ, researchers can combine the information from the BQ with a wide range of external sources to
examine the role of institutions. Examples of strategies that can be used to achieve this are given below
in the section on ‘Limitations of the BQ’.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

148 
Understanding the relation between skills and outcomes
Ultimately, the importance of skills lies in their relation to relevant outcomes. In addition to economic
outcomes such as employment opportunities and rewards in the labour market, it is important to take
account of outcomes of societal importance in other areas that may also be influenced by skills, such as
health status, voluntary work, and political engagement. A schematic representation of the key
relationships between skills and outcomes is presented in Figure 6.2. Additionally, when estimating effects
of education and skills on outcomes, it is important to control for background characteristics (e.g. socioeconomic background, migration background, and cultural capital).

Figure 6.2. Schematic Representation of the Relationships between Skills and Economic and Social
Outcomes

Labour market outcomes
Cognitive skills are a key determinant of an individual’s productivity, and therefore it is not surprising that
cognitive skills are related to economic success. There is a large body of evidence showing that, at any
given level of education, higher cognitive skills are associated with better labour market outcomes (e.g.
Heckman et al., 2006). However, effects vary across outcomes, which may also be differentially amenable
to policy interventions. The BQ, therefore, needs to cover a considerable number of measures relating to
wages, labour market participation and status, and job characteristics.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 149
For those currently or recently in work, several important labour market outcomes are included in the
questionnaire, including working hours, individual earnings, job security, occupational status, and the
quality of the match between education and work.
One of the interesting questions in this respect concerns the precise role of education and skills in
producing these outcomes. There are contradictory hypotheses on this point. Very often the strong relation
between education and labour market outcomes is explained in terms of human capital theory (Becker,
1964[35]), which claims that people with more years of schooling earn more because the competencies they
acquired in education have made them more productive. While this is probably true to some extent, at least
in the aggregate, it tells only part of the story. Scholars such as Spence (1973[67]) and Arrow (1973[68]) have
pointed out that the selection, allocation, and rewarding of individual employees takes place on the basis
of signals such as formal qualifications as well as on the basis of productivity. This is usually explained in
terms of incomplete information and bounded rationality. The signals form a solution to this problem, as
they are assumed to indicate the average productive capacities of the group to which they refer. The labour
queue theory (Thurow, 1975[69])adds an interesting twist, pointing out that many relevant competencies
are not even learned in education, but picked up through work experience on the job. According to this
theory, education is an indicator of low training costs rather than high productivity. Finally, some scholars
have questioned whether education has any effect at all on graduates’ ability to perform, pointing out that
this relationship is in fact weaker than that between education and reward (Bills, 2003[70]). Credentialists
such as Collins (Collins, 1979[71]) have for a long time claimed that higher education does not lead to
superior competencies but is used by “gatekeepers” to legitimise the rationing of access to high-status,
highly paid jobs.
In reality, there is probably an element of truth in all these theories. The crucial point then comes down to
specifying the contexts under which one or the other mechanism prevails. Many studies have focused on
identifying “sheepskin” effects, so called because the effects are thought to be partially, if not wholly,
attributable to the possession of diplomas (which used to be written on sheepskin). Barrett (2011[72]) found
that only a third of the return from an extra year of education in Australia could be attributed to cognitive
skills (however, the skill gap significantly accounted for half of the wage disadvantage of migrants from
non-English speaking countries). Flisi et al. (2015[41]) found that educational attainment has generally
stronger effects on labour market outcomes than skills, although in some countries the opposite appears
to be true. Levels et al. (2014[65]) show that only part of the effects of required education on wages can be
attributed to differences in skill proficiency, but the extent to which skills mediate this effect differs with
institutional characteristics: it is smallest in countries with a high level of employment-protection legislation.
Similarly, Vogtenhuber (2018[47]) found that workers’ occupational status was strongly associated with the
highest educational qualification obtained, and to a lesser extent on worker skills. Olfindo (2018[73]) found
similar sheepskin effects for tertiary-educated workers in the Philippines. Lancee and Bol (2017[74]) found
that, although foreign education is associated with significant wage penalties, only a third of this effect is
explained by skills. In interpreting the results of all of these studies, it is important to keep in mind that
education aims to impart a broader range of skills than just those measured in surveys such as PIAAC.
Nonetheless, the evidence seems to point to varying degrees of credentialism in labour markets.
There are also indicators for strong direct effects of skills on economic outcomes. Shomos (2010[11]) found
good prospects for enhancing the Australian working-aged population’s employment chances and wages
by improving literacy and numeracy knowledge. Van der Velden and Bijlsma (2018[75]) show that the effects
of skill mismatch on wages are almost as large as the effects of educational mismatch.
For policy makers it is crucial to be able to distinguish between ‘true’ effects of skills from effects that result
from credentialism. Many of the control variables that are needed to get unbiased estimates of the effects
of skills on economic and social outcomes, are comparable to the ones discussed above on the effect of
education and training on skills development. However, education and training will now be treated as
control variables instead of as predictors of interest. As indicated above, the highest level attained in formal

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

150 
education is one of the strongest predictors of skills. This is not only interesting in its own right, as a skill
predictor or reporting category, but will likely be a confounding variable for many of the issues that
policymakers are trying to understand in the context of PIAAC. Level of education is also a strong predictor
of economic and social outcomes, and although this is often assumed to reflect differences in skill levels
between levels of education, the precise causal mechanism is still somewhat controversial (are the effects
all directly attributable to human capital, or do theories of signalling and credentialism also tell part of the
story?), and the residual effects of the level of education are a combination of sheepskin and unmeasured
skills (e.g. Heckman & LaFontaine (2006[76])). For example, school completion is probably used by
employers as a proxy for social and emotional skills. In this respect it is not only important to register
highest formal level and type, but also qualifications that may have been attained before the highest
qualification as well as uncompleted schooling. Even more important for getting unbiased estimates of
skills on potential outcomes is to identify exogenous sources of variation that might affect the level and
type of education. Variables that have been identified in the literature relate to family characteristics that
induce exogenous variation in the resources that are available, like birth order, number of siblings, and
geographical location when growing up (Angrist and Evans, 1998[77]; Bertoni and Brunello, 2016[78];
Brunello and De Paola, 2013[79]; Conley and Glauber, 2006[80]). Such variables have been successfully
applied to identify the effects of education.
In addition to level of education, labour market studies show large and robust differences in economic
outcomes between types of education as well as fields of study in secondary and tertiary vocational
education. Fields like arts and humanities and social sciences often perform poorly, while science,
business, and engineering often do better than average. From a policy point of view, it is important to
establish whether these differences are due to differences in the supply of and/or the demand for the skills
of the graduates of these programmes, signalling or credentialism, individual preferences, or other factors.
The variables related to training are not only relevant in predicting skills, but also in predicting economic
outcomes (when controlling for skills). Some studies suggest that the purported effects of training may be
overstated due to design issues. For example, Fahr et al. (2017[81]) found a strong wage effect of training
participation, which however vanished completely after the control group was restricted to employees who
were offered training but ultimately declined to participate. Ehlert (2017[82]) found patterns of effects of
training that strongly emphasised the importance of labour market structure, and which were more
consistent with job competition and credentialist models than with the human capital model of skills
production through training. Blundell et al. (1999[38]) report that employer-provided training is related to
higher returns than off-the job training. As indicated above for education, the precise causal mechanism
for this is not known, and the estimates of the returns from training are biased by heterogeneous selection
into training. For example, some people might seek training because they are expecting to be promoted
instead of the other way around. Good control variables, like firm size, are needed to control for this
unobserved heterogeneity. Most of these control variables, such as employee/self-employed status,
supervisory status, and job tenure, are the same as the ones we discussed above.

Non-economic outcomes
Skills are not only important for economic outcomes, but also for other outcomes such as well-being,
health, and civic participation. As noted by the OECD’s Working group on non-economic outcomes (OECD,
2016[83]), there has been a push from researchers and policy makers in recent decades for more direct
measures of societal and individual well-being. For this reason, the Cycle 2 BQ has added a question on
general life satisfaction, which, in addition to the existing measures of political efficacy, social trust,
voluntary work and general subjective health already contained in Cycle 1, helps to provide a more
complete picture of the wide range of economic and non-economic outcomes that are related to skills.
There are already a range of interesting studies available, relating education and/or skills to a wide range
of outcomes, such as obesity (Benson, von Hippel and Lynch, 2018[84]) and health (Cai, 2010[85]). The
extended set of non-economic outcome measures in Cycle 2 creates unique opportunities for enriching
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 151
and deepening analyses of such questions, as well as opening up potential new avenues of research. For
example, it will make it possible to examine the role of specific cognitive and social and emotional skills on
well-being, how well-being may affect the link between education and health, and through which potential
mechanisms well-being can affect labour market outcomes.

Limitations of the BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2 and how to deal with them
As outlined above, the BQ is of crucial value in making PIAAC Cycle 2 a unique data set for the analysis
of the distribution, determinants and outcomes of skills across countries. However, it is equally important
to acknowledge the limitations of the BQ (and the PIAAC design more generally), and to highlight strategies
for dealing with these limitations.
Most importantly, PIAAC uses a cross-sectional design, which limits the potential for causal analysis
compared to data sources that rely on panel designs. Additionally, to keep participation in the study
manageable for respondents, the average time needed to complete the whole BQ cannot exceed 50
minutes. As a result, although the BQ covers detailed measurements of a wide range of concepts across
multiple domains, other concepts that could have also been of interest (e.g. the last educational
qualification obtained if this is not the highest one, or additional economic and non-economic outcomes of
skills) could not be included. Finally, there are restrictions to the types of questions that could be included
in the BQ. For example, asking more detailed questions on parental behaviour during childhood would be
difficult because responses would be affected by recall bias. Given the cross-national focus of PIAAC, the
BQ is limited to questions which are appropriate across the participating countries, which means that
questions which could have been relevant for some countries are not included in the international BQ.
Nonetheless, despite these limitations, PIAAC Cycle 2 is still expected to be extremely valuable in further
advancing policy and research on skills. PIAAC Cycle 1, which faced similar limitations, has already
generated an overwhelming array of insights. This was partly a result of the innovative and creative
strategies that were employed to overcome the limitations of PIAAC. Most importantly, research using
PIAAC Cycle 1 has shown that the strengths of PIAAC can be further leveraged effectively by using the
data in conjunction with other data sources.
A first and relatively straightforward way to achieve this is to match PIAAC data with existing data sources
at the macro or meso level. For example, data on respondents’ professions and occupational sectors can
be combined with contextual data at the level of sectors or occupations. This is facilitated by the availability
of detailed information on professions and occupational sectors in the public use file of PIAAC. As such,
further characteristics of professions and occupational sectors can be brought into analyses of the PIAAC
data. Similarly, through existing data sources for country-level information (e.g. from the OECD and
Eurostat), factors at the national level (e.g. institutional characteristics of educational systems and labour
markets) can be used to complement the individual-level data in PIAAC.
Secondly, it is possible to create synthetic cohorts by combining similar data that were collected at different
points in time. This approach has already been applied successfully in analyses of the Trends in
International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMMS) and PISA data (Hanushek and Woessmann,
2011[63]). Similar comparisons of cohorts over time could be constructed with the PIAAC data from Cycles 1
and 2, potentially combined with the IALS and ALL data (for more information on trend derived variables,
see Chapter 11).
Finally, the strengths of the PIAAC data can be further enhanced by complementing the data with other
individual-level data sources within countries. As a key example, in Scandinavian countries and the
Netherlands, the PIAAC data can be matched with register data, which opens up unique opportunities for
adding a longitudinal component by using information on respondents that was gathered before and after
their participation in PIAAC. Related to this, in several countries it is possible to combine the PIAAC data
with information on respondents’ place or region of residence. This information can also be used to facilitate

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

152 
causal analyses based on the PIAAC data. For example, Falck et al. (2021[86]) have used information on
regional differences in the introduction of broadband connections to estimate the effects of ICT skills on
wages. Finally, in Cycle 1, some countries chose to turn the PIAAC data collection to a first wave of a
national panel data collection.

Outline of the BQ
The concepts described in this chapter are covered in the PIAAC Cycle 2 BQ in different sections. The BQ
is organised into 11 sections, each of which covers one or several substantive domains:
•

A. Personal characteristics

•

B. Education and training

•

C. Current status and work history

•

D. Current work (if currently working)

•

E. Last job (if not currently working)

•

F. Literacy, numeracy, and ICT practices at work

•

G. Literacy, numeracy, and ICT practices in everyday life

•

H. The working environment

•

I. Non-economic outcomes

•

J. Background

•

K. Social and emotional skills

In addition to the core BQ, containing all questions to be administered by all countries, countries were
allowed to add a maximum of five minutes of country-specific questions to the BQ as national extensions.
Countries could also include International Options A and/or B in their BQ. International Option A contains
the 30-item version of the Big Five scales to measure social and emotional skills (BFI-2-S instead of BFI2-XS3) in Section K. International Option B contains additional questions on the working environment in
Section H.
The development and validation of the specific content for each of these sections is discussed in the next
section.

The development of the BQ
The process of questionnaire development
The selection of the item pool for the MS BQ was the end point of an elaborate process that was already
initiated after the completion of PIAAC Cycle 1.
First, several working groups (i.e. on education and training, skill use and mismatch, non-economic
outcomes, and social and emotional skills) reviewed the PIAAC Cycle 1 BQ, and presented proposals for
dropping questions, for improving the measurement of existing concepts, and for introducing new concepts
and questions. The proposals from the working groups were then discussed by the Board of Participating
Countries (BPC) and the Background Questionnaire Expert Group (BQEG).
The BQEG consisted of the following members:
•

Prof. Dr. Guido Schwerdt (chair), University of Konstanz and research professor at the Ifo Centre
for the Economics of Education and Innovation.

•

Prof. Dr. Giorgio Brunello, University of Padova.
