Prof. Dr. Nathalie Greenan, Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers.

•

Prof. Dr. Corinna Kleinert, University of Bamberg and Deputy Director at the Leibniz Institute for
Educational Trajectories (LIfBi).

•

Prof. Dr. Sandra McNally, University of Surrey, Director of the Centre for Vocational Education
Research and Director of the Education and Skills Programme at the Centre for Economic
Performance.

•

Prof. Dr. Michele Pellizzari, University of Geneva.

•

Prof. Dr. Heike Solga, Free University Berlin and Director of the Research Unit “Skill Formation
and Labor Markets” at WZB Berlin Social Science Centre.

•

Prof. Dr. Simon Wiederhold, Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt, ifo Research Professor, CoDirector of the KU Research Institute for Business and Economics in Service of Humanity (BESH).

There were four meetings held with the BQEG:
•

5-6 April 2018, Paris

•

4-5 June 2018, Paris

•

19-20 October 2018, Paris

•

10-11 January 2022, Virtual

Based on the discussions in 2018, the Consortium prepared a draft version of the BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2
in which these proposals were incorporated. The BQ for PIAAC Cycle 1 was the obvious starting point for
developing the BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2. Most constructs covered in PIAAC Cycle 1 continue to be relevant
for the broad policy questions addressed in PIAAC. Additionally, maintaining measurements in the same
(or comparable) form offers the opportunity to directly compare results across PIAAC cycles and examine
trends. However, societies have changed since PIAAC Cycle 1 (e.g. considering the use of digital
technology at work and in everyday life), and these changes also need to be reflected in the BQ. Also,
some relevant concepts (e.g. social and emotional skills, types of formal education or educational
pathways) were not sufficiently covered in PIAAC Cycle 1.
Therefore, in developing the BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2, it was important to achieve a good balance between
continuity and change. Furthermore, PIAAC Cycle 2 offered the opportunity to refine concepts and improve
measurements that appeared to have limitations in PIAAC Cycle 1. As such, this meant that when
developing the BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2 it was important to (a) maintain a majority of questionnaire items in
the same form as in PIAAC Cycle 1 (labelled “strict trend items”); (b) improve the measurement of concepts
that were already included in PIAAC Cycle 1 (“soft trend items”); (c) add a limited number of new
questionnaire items, mostly capturing concepts that were not covered in PIAAC Cycle 1 (“new items”,
largely derived from existing data sources); and (d) drop questionnaire items that were included in PIAAC
Cycle 1, but that appeared to be lacking in usefulness or quality.
Since PIAAC Cycle 1 had been in the field, the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)
had been revised. ISCED is widely used by international official statistics as well as the OECD for making
data about formal education comparable across countries. For PIAAC Cycle 2, it was critical to switch from
ISCED 1997 (UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2006[87]) to ISCED 2011 (UNESCO-UIS, 2012[88]) while still
allowing a comparison with PIAAC Cycle 1. Furthermore, research has shown some weaknesses of the
national and international education measures implemented in PIAAC Cycle 1 (Schneider, 2018[89]).
Therefore, a coding scheme was developed that allows for deriving official ISCED 2011 and PIAAC Cycle
1 education categories, which provides more detailed information when there are reasons to believe this
will be helpful for predicting skills and/or labour market outcomes. This coding scheme is presented in
more detail in Chapter 11 on derived variables.
In the area of formal education, there was interest in measuring educational pathways in addition to highest
education, current education and incomplete education, in order to gain evidence on whether the pathway
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

154 
taken through the education system makes a difference – beyond educational attainment – regarding skill
development, educational and skill inequalities, as well as various outcomes of education. As such, a new
measure was developed, asking which (other) qualifications the respondent has obtained before the
highest qualification just reported. Respondents with less than upper secondary education are not asked
about their educational pathway.
In the area of non-formal education, the questionnaire was changed substantially compared to PIAAC
Cycle 1 to facilitate understanding of the questions and gather more reliable and policy-relevant
information. As mentioned previously, in PIAAC, training is used as an empirical indicator for the concept
of non-formal education. This led to a battery of mostly new (rather than strict or soft trend) questionnaire
items which still cover some similar concepts as in PIAAC Cycle 1 such as recent training volume, whether
training was job-related, training costs, motivation for and barriers to training. New concepts covered relate
to training content for one training activity (including a question on whether the training improved dealing
with workplace digitisation), whether a certificate was obtained for this training activity, as well as mode of
training (in-person or via distance learning methods).
Several of the newly introduced questionnaire items were included in a mixed-methods pretest as well as
in a translatability assessment to assess their functioning. After this, the draft BQ and the results of the
pretest were shared for feedback with national teams and the BQEG. The draft BQ was given a final round
of revisions, mostly by dropping questionnaire items that were of insufficient quality or priority. This resulted
in the BQ for use in the PIAAC Cycle 2 FT that was approved by the BPC in November 2018.
As the BPC has already expressed a strong priority for maximising the amount of trend information that is
available to compare with PIAAC Cycle 1, changes in the content of the MS BQ were expected to be
marginal and affect mostly new questionnaire items. In January 2021, the OECD shared a proposal for
dropping questionnaire items with the BPC. In this proposal, a number of questionnaire items were
presented as candidates to drop based on their analytical value, the estimated time needed to administer
the item, and expectations about the functioning of the questionnaire items. However, close examination
of the FT data was needed to reveal whether these assumptions held.
The results of the analyses on the FT BQ data that the PIAAC Consortium conducted, and the Consortium’s
recommendations for the MS BQ based on these analyses were discussed with the BQEG on 10-11
January 2022, after which the BPC was asked to make a final decision on the content of the MS BQ by 25
January 2022.

Ensuring cross-cultural applicability: Mixed-method pretest and translatability
assessment
Throughout the process of developing new questionnaire items or modifying trend items, care was taken
to also consider aspects of cultural relevance and translatability. Feedback by experts in questionnaire
translation and comparative measurement as well as by multicultural and multilingual Consortium
members was provided in various meetings and review rounds. Moreover, the following two methods – a
mixed-method pretest as well as a translatability assessment – were implemented to systematically
address cross-cultural issues in the preparation stage of the BQ.

Mixed-method online pretest
In August 2018, a 5-country mixed-method online pretest was conducted by GESIS to evaluate potentially
problematic questionnaire items in the BQ (old, modified or new items). The web survey combined the
questionnaire items that were selected for the pretest, together with open-ended and closed-ended
cognitive probes that aimed at testing validity and comparability. To the extent possible, existing
translations from PIAAC cycle 1 were re-used. New questionnaire items and cognitive probes were

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 155
translated using a double translation and reconciliation approach. The translation task was split among
GESIS (for German) and cApStAn (for all other languages).
For each country, a sample size of approximately 500 respondents was targeted. The five countries
included France (n = 528), Germany (n = 525), Japan (n = 521), Poland (n = 509), and the United States
(n = 501). The sample was drawn from online access panels (lead panel was respondi [now: bilendi]).
Quotas were set to ensure adequate and comparable representation according to age strata (16-30, 3150, 51-65), education (low, medium, high), and sex (female, male). Furthermore, respondents had to be
employed or self-employed, and 80% of respondents in each country were expected to have taken part in
at least one training event (either for professional or for personal reasons). Challenges in reaching the
quotas during fieldwork made it necessary to relax the sample specifications to some extent. This applied
in particular to the quota of low-educated respondents in Poland and the Unites States as well as to the
expected number of self-employed persons and those with experience in a training activity across all
countries. Nevertheless, the achieved sample allowed meaningful analyses both for quantitative and
qualitative testing.
During the quantitative analyses, response distributions, item non-response, and timing were examined
for different subgroups. The results of split-ballot experiments were also analysed. During qualitative
analysis, open-ended probe answers were analysed according to themes (content analysis), out-of-scope
answers, and any signs of response difficulty. In total, 16 questionnaire items were tested. If problems
were identified during analysis, appropriate improvements were proposed. For instance, the item “During
the last 12 months, have you participated in any training activity?”, a key question from the BQ training
module, was tested to assess to what extent respondents also included ongoing training activities when
responding. Results of the mixed-method pretest showed that ongoing activities were not consistently
reported by respondents. Thus, the item wording itself was amended to include an instruction clarifying
that ongoing activities were to be included. An internal pretesting report was produced with detailed
presentations of results and recommendations (Meitinger et al., 2018[90]).

Translatability Assessment
For all new questionnaire items in PIAAC Cycle 2, cApStAn performed a Translatability Assessment (TA)
with the goals to make the source material amenable for translation and to raise awareness of potential
hurdles for the adaptation of specific questions into certain languages or cultural contexts.
For PIAAC Cycle 2, seven TA linguists were selected to cover the PIAAC language pool in as broad a way
as possible. They all evaluated a subset of the new questionnaire items so that each item was evaluated
by at least three linguists. The seven languages selected were: Russian, Hebrew, Arabic, Hungarian,
Spanish, Japanese and Swedish.
Within the scope of TA, the linguists’ brief was to:
•

classify these potential issues using a set of 13 intervention categories, and

•

describe any translation, adaptation or cultural hurdles that may arise from the current form of new
questionnaire items in the English master version. As an aid in the process of identifying potential
issues, the linguists produced draft translations of the questionnaire items in the target language.
These draft translations were part of the deliverable, but not intended for any further use.

Once all the linguists had delivered their contributions, a senior linguist at cApStAn consolidated the
comments for the item developers’ consideration. The feedback from the TA resulted in various outcomes.
Often, the English master was revised either as suggested in the TA report, or in an alternate way that
addressed the issue. The TA feedback also resulted in translation notes to either explain the intended
meaning of the item/term or draw attention to certain aspects of the source wording that are important to
represent in the translation. In some cases, the TA feedback contributed to restructuring or dropping an
item from the questionnaire altogether.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

156 

The validation of the BQ
Analysis of Field Trial data
Based on the results of the mixed-methods pretest, the draft FT BQ was, in consultation with the BQEG,
given a final round of revisions. This resulted in the BQ which was used in the FT. The purpose of the FT
was to provide data that could be used to inform the evaluation of all key aspects of PIAAC, including the
BQ.
The analysis of the FT BQ data served three primary purposes. The first was to evaluate the operational
procedures specified in the Technical Standards and Guidelines 4 concerning the administration of the BQ.
The second was to assess the quality of the questionnaire items to ensure that respondents understood
the questions, and that the information collected through the BQ provided comparable data across
countries. The third was to provide the empirical information, including administration time, so the BPC
could make a final decision about the content of the MS BQ.
In order to achieve these goals, the following analyses were conducted:
•

analyses at the level of single questionnaire items, testing the functioning (including routing) and
the timing of the questionnaire items, overall and per country

•

analyses at the level of multi-item scales, testing the functioning and the cross-national
comparability of the hypothesised scales included in the BQ, overall and per country

•

correlational and multiple-regression analyses testing the validity of the measured constructs,
overall.

All FT analyses reported here are based on the PIAAC Cycle 2 FT data, which were collected in 2021.
Due to the repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic on fieldwork in numerous countries, the FT data was,
unlike initially planned, delivered to the Consortium in four batches. Data submitted by the Batch 1 deadline
was used in all the international FT analyses. Batch 2 data was only used in some of the analyses (i.e. for
the social and emotional skills scaling analyses and timing analyses).
For most of the international FT analyses, FT data were able to be used from 24 of the 31 countries that
are participating in PIAAC Cycle 2. These countries were Austria (AUT), Belgium (BEL), Switzerland
(CHE), the Czech Republic (CZE), Germany (DEU), Denmark (DNK), Spain (ESP), Estonia (EST), Finland
(FIN), France (FRA), Croatia (HRV), Hungary (HUN), Italy (ITA), Japan (JPN), Korea (KOR), Lithuania
(LTU), Netherlands (NLD), Norway (NOR), New Zealand (NZL), Poland (POL), Singapore (SGP), Slovakia
(SVK), Sweden (SWE), and United States (USA). For eight of these countries (BEL, CZE, EST, FRA, HUN,
NLD, POL, and SWE), only a partial data set was available in time for inclusion in the analyses presented
here (these countries delivered some of their data to the Consortium as a part of Batch 1 and the rest of
their data as part of Batch 2).
Across countries, a total of N = 32 532 interviews were included in most of the analyses. For most of the
analyses of the FT BQ data, only completed interviews and interviews that were broken-off before
completion (i.e. partial completes), were taken into account. For individual item functioning, routing checks,
multi-item scales in Section K, multivariate analyses and timing analyses, only completed cases were
included. Break-offs were excluded because they would have complicated or distorted the computations
for missing data and the overall length of the BQ – particularly for the minimum values. While there were
concerns that the COVID-19 pandemic could negatively affect the data yield, in the end, most countries
delivered sample sizes that were close to the original target of 1 500 cases, so that the data yield was
sufficient to carry out all the planned international analyses for the BQ.
Apart from an international FT report, all countries also received national reports in which country-specific
results were shown in detail, and in which any issues that require the attention of the national teams were
highlighted.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 157
Assessment of the questionnaire length
The length of the BQ is crucial in PIAAC not only as an important determinant of the quality of the
questionnaire data itself, but also because of the potential impact on the cognitive assessment following
the BQ. It is therefore important to minimise respondent fatigue so they have enough cognitive resources
to apply themselves to the DA.
The target length for the main study BQ for employed respondents – to whom the highest number of
questions is directed to – was 45 minutes. In addition, there was also a maximum of 5 minutes for national
extensions and international options, thus resulting in a target length of about 50 minutes. As a
consequence, one of the central aims of the FT analyses was to examine the length of the PIAAC BQ as
it was administered in the FT. The results of the timing analyses allowed the Consortium to assess the
extent to which the length of the BQ needed to be reduced in order to achieve the target length for the MS.
Item timings were crucial for determining possible candidates for deletion.
Timing analyses were carried out to determine the time required to complete (a) the core BQ by
employment status, (b) the full BQ by employment status, (c) the national extensions and international
options for employed respondents, (d) the different scenarios for the BFI in Section K, (e) each section of
the BQ, and (f) individual questionnaire items.
In this chapter, international results for (a)-(d) will be presented at the international level.

Data
In the PIAAC questionnaire administration software, questionnaire items or a battery of several items are
usually displayed on a separate screen. The timing data captures the total response time per screen,
starting from the moment the interviewer navigates to a new screen, and lasting until the interviewer
navigates to the next screen. All visits to a screen are counted, including time the screen is left open while
taking a short break.
Outliers were treated for the timing analyses using the same approach as in PIAAC Cycle 1. Extremely
long response times (i.e. response times exceeding four times the country median) for a specific screen
were capped at four times the median for that screen. Interviews with a total BQ response time of less than
10 minutes were considered unrealistic. As no timing data was available for the introductory text at the
beginning of the BQ; this was accounted for by adding, 30 seconds to all results at the BQ level.

Results
Length of the core BQ
The results of the analysis show that the international average length of the FT core BQ was 37:50 minutes
for all respondents, 40:07 minutes for employed and 30:50 minutes for not employed respondents. As the
average core BQ timing in Croatia (HRV) was extremely short (more than two standard deviations lower
than the international average), the international average was calculated without HRV. The somewhat
higher international average length of the FT BQ after excluding HRV was used as a reference point for
decision-making for the length of the BQ for the MS. That is, 38:28 minutes for all respondents, 40:44
minutes for employed respondents, and 31:23 minutes for not employed respondents. These results
supported that the core BQ did not need to be shortened solely because of timing reasons.
