Conclusions
The timing analyses showed that the international average length of the core FT BQ for employed
respondents was below the maximum target duration of 45 minutes, so no questionnaire items had to be
deleted for the MS for timing reasons. Therefore, recommendations for deletions could focus exclusively
on the validation results of the full FT BQ analyses (item non-response, construct validation, etc.).
However, as some countries exceeded the target of 45 minutes, they were encouraged to re-think the
inclusion of optional questionnaire items (national extensions and international options), but also to find
out reasons for their longer than average administration times. Issues that could have had an impact were
complex national adaptations in Section B regarding the measurement of formal education, the use of
register information requiring additional adaptations, the implementation of look-up lists, or whether
translations were longer for linguistic reasons. Longer response times could also have resulted from
difficulties in item comprehension. Thus, countries were encouraged to re-check their translations and see
if appropriate non-intrusive adjustments could be found for the MS.

Individual item functioning
Regarding individual item functioning, the focus was on item non-response data, response distributions
and summary statistics.

Item non-response data
The most relevant type of missing data is item non-response. For most of the questionnaire items, and
across all countries, item non-response was very low (1% or less per question for > 250 items). However,
certain questionnaire items showed higher non-response rates, especially the open questions on earnings.
Thanks to the follow-up questions offering respondents the possibility to report their earnings in broad
categories, earnings information could be gathered for most respondents who were unwilling to provide a
detailed response. This strategy was maintained for the MS.
Occupation and industry variables showed high levels of item non-response data as well, which was largely
driven by high amounts of item non-response in individual countries. These countries were urged to
increase their data collection and coding efforts with respect to these variables. Parental education was
another difficult question and not all respondents knew their parents’ level of education. This reinforces the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

160 
decision to obtain additional information on social background by adding questions on parental occupation
for Cycle 2.
In addition to item non-response, the number of valid skips in each item was analysed in order to identify
questionnaire items with reduced relevance that could be considered as candidates to be dropped. Several
new questionnaire items were identified that may not carry essential information and had a high number
of valid skips. First, item E2_Q10c (“Last job – Requirements – Educational level to do this job
satisfactorily”, with 98.0% valid skips), and item D2_Q12c in Section D (“Current work - Requirements Educational level to do this job satisfactorily”, with 90.7% valid skips). These items were only administered
to the small number of respondents who reported that the qualification needed to get their job
(D2_Q12a/E2_Q10a) was not the same qualification as the one needed to do their job. Second, item
H2_Q19b (“Current work - Skills in relation to what is required”, 92.1% valid skips) was not relevant for
many respondents. Respondents who were not currently or were recently employed (28%) were not asked
about perceived skill mismatch. Of those who were asked about perceived skill mismatch, 89% do not
report to feel underskilled. Thus, only a small number of respondents actually needed to report the type of
mismatched skills.

Distributions and summary statistics
Overall, the item response distributions were found to be plausible and to capture an appropriate degree
of variation. Only minor issues were identified. We found an underreporting of other educational
qualifications in items B2_Q02a and B2_Q02b. Therefore, the filter question B2_Q02a was dropped and
wording of B2_Q02b amended for the MS, to clarify that all qualifications obtained before the highest
qualification should be reported.
Some questionnaire items showed low variation, with individual response options used by either very few
respondents (sparsity) or many respondents (lumping). For ordinal scales, lumping often takes the shape
of floor and ceiling effects. This was the case for several questionnaire items having 5-point scales in
Sections F, G and H.
For the questionnaire items on social and emotional skills in Section K, a number of items showed high
means, skewness, and small standard deviations, resulting from lumping in category 4 of the 5-point scale
(for positively worded items). Closer inspection of the BFI-2-S items and feedback from the interviewer
debriefings suggested that social desirability and potential translation issues may have driven these issues.
The mode of administration (face-to-face) may have contributed to social desirability. Given that these
questionnaire items are part of an established scale, no changes were undertaken for the MS.
For nominal and ordinal variables, no out-of-range responses were found. For metric variables, a few outof-range values for various age and year variables were identified in a small number of countries. This
information was provided in the national reports and countries were able to fix this for the MS.
Outlier analyses for open numeric questions suggested that the cutoffs to top code variables to be derived
from these questionnaire items in preparation of the public use file were useful.

Routing
In order to investigate the flow of questions and overall functionality of the BQ, various routing checks were
conducted. The routing in a questionnaire ensures that respondents receive questions that are relevant for
them. We tested whether respondents received the questions they were intended to receive as defined by
the BQ design, and no other questions. These routing checks focused on crucial filters and branching rules
in the BQ. Two types of routings were checked: a) within-section routings, and b) between-section routings.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 161
For routings within sections, which often take the shape of simple filter questions, a few minor issues were
found that countries were asked to check for the MS. For routings across sections no systematic issues
were observed.
It is important to note that these routing checks were not exhaustive. For the preparation of the MS BQ,
countries were instructed to test the routing of their BQs, especially in areas where national BQs had been
modified for the MS.

Multi-item functioning
Sections F, G, H and K of the BQ contain item sets that can be regarded as multiple indicators of the same
construct. These were evaluated to establish whether developing a scale for these concepts is appropriate
and internationally comparable. The analysis was divided into two parts: analyses that focused on the
scales related to the use of reading, writing, numeracy, information and communications technology (ICT),
and work-related skills in Sections F, G and H, and then analyses of the new social and emotional skills
scales in Section K.

Multi-item scales in Sections F, G, and H – Skill use scale
The background questionnaire included 12 scales to assess respondents’ use of literacy, numeracy, and
ICT skills at work (Section F) and at home (Section G), as well as additional skills used at work (Section
H). All 12 scales were developed for PIAAC Cycle 1, but some items were revised in Cycle 2 to better
reflect today’s environment (i.e. soft trend items), some items were used without any revisions (i.e. strict
trend items), and some items were newly included in the scales for the Cycle 2 FT. Updates to the Reading
and Writing scales were proposed by members of the Literacy Expert Group, while updates to the
Numeracy scales were proposed by the Numeracy Expert Group and finalised in collaboration with the
OECD. The OECD updated the items in the ICT scales. Respondents were administered all items in the
scales they were routed to, and all items were Likert-type items with five response categories.
All revised items and scales were included in the Cycle 2 FT and their psychometric and statistical
properties were examined, thereby providing information for the final item selection for the Cycle 2 MS.
Analyses included descriptive analyses of the item- and scale-level score distributions, scale reliability,
inter-scale correlations, item response theory (IRT) scaling, as well as misfit analyses. (Note that similar
analyses were conducted using the MS instruments and data. A detailed description of the MS results is
provided in Chapter 11.)
The skill use scales were constructed with IRT, using the same model and methods that were used in
Cycle 1 (refer to OECD (2019[91]), Chapter 20). For the soft trend and strict trend items, the item parameters
estimated in Cycle 1 were assumed to apply to the Cycle 2 FT, and therefore were fixed. For the new
items, the international parameters were estimated by constraining the item parameter estimates to be the
same across all groups. For countries with multiple language groups, each language group was treated as
a separate group (referred to as country-by-language groups) in the scaling. All respondents were
weighted equally, regardless of the size of the country-by-language group. For each respondent, a score
was estimated for each scale using weighted likelihood estimation (WLE), provided that the respondent
had responded to at least three items in the scale.
The root mean square deviation (RMSD) was examined for each item and country-by-language group to
detect possible item-by-group interactions, which are an indication of misfit. The RMSD quantifies the
absolute difference between the model-based item characteristic curve (ICC) and the empirical ICC from
the country-by-language group’s data. RMSD values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating larger
misfit compared to the model parameters. For the trend items, the model parameters were the item
parameters estimated in Cycle 1. Note that in Cycle 1, no country-by-language group received groupspecific parameters (i.e. only the international item parameters were estimated), so the RMSD indicated

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

162 
how much the country-by-language group’s empirical data deviated from the Cycle 1 international
parameters. For the new items, the model parameters were the international item parameters that had
been estimated with data pooled across all the country-by-language groups that participated in the Cycle
2 FT. Thus, the RMSD also indicated how much the country-by-language group’s empirical data deviated
from the international parameters for the Cycle 2 FT.
The mean reliability coefficient – in Cronbach’s alpha – across the country-by-language groups was above
0.60 for all scales except for the Writing at Home scale which had a mean reliability coefficient of 0.58.
This scale had only four items, one of which did not contribute to the scale (i.e. very low slope parameter
and item information). Scales with fewer items are more likely to have lower reliability using Cronbach’s
alpha. Except for the Writing at Home scale, the scales’ median reliability coefficients were above 0.60.
These results indicated that most of the scales had sufficient reliability in most country-by-language groups.
The correlations of respondents’ sum scores across all 12 scales were used to determine whether each
scale contributed unique information. The sum score correlation between the Reading at Work scale and
the Writing at Work scale exceeded 0.70, indicating that these two scales measured redundant information
about skills. The sum score correlation between the Reading at Home scale and the Writing at Home scale
was also high at 0.60. Note that strong links between reading and writing are expected. Since these scales
were administered and scaled separately in Cycle 1, these scales remained separate for the MS.
Lastly, the percent of country-by-language groups flagged for high RMSD values provided an overview of
the fit of the item parameters. The distribution of the RMSD values was examined for each item, item type
(i.e. new, soft trend, strict trend), and country-by-language group. A cut-off of 0.20 was used to detect
misfit. For all items, the 75th percentile of the RMSD values across the country-by-language groups was
well below 0.20, indicating there were no items with significant item-by-group or item-by-cycle interactions.
As for the item types (e.g. new, soft trend, strict trend), the 75th percentile of the RMSD values across all
item*groups was well below 0.20. This means that for both the strict trend and soft trend items, the item
parameters from Cycle 1 fit the empirical data well for most country-by-language groups. For the new
items, the international item parameters fit the empirical data well for most country-by-language groups.
These analyses showed that the Cycle 2 scales had good fit across all country-by-language groups and
item types.
Several changes to the FT scales or analysis approaches were implemented in response to the FT
analyses. First, the Cycle 2 Planning scale had only two items which was not enough to ensure stable
estimation of the IRT item parameters or respondents’ skill levels. Therefore, this scale was excluded from
the IRT scaling in the FT and MS analyses.
Item G2_Q02d (a new item in the Writing at Home scale about social media) had a slope parameter of
0.16 and, therefore, did not contribute much to its scale. This was the only item that met the criteria for
recommended exclusion. Three other items also had low slope parameters, including F2_Q05f (a soft trend
item in the ICT at Work scale) which had a slope parameter of 0.30, F2_Q03c (a new item in the Numeracy
at Work scale) which had a slope parameter of 0.31, and F2_Q05e (a new item in the ICT at Work scale)
which had a slope parameter of 0.32. These items contributed less information to their respective scales,
but they were retained for the MS to satisfy construct validity and to prevent a decrease in the reliability
coefficient to under 0.60.
Given that G2_Q02d, the Writing at Home item about social media, was the only item with such a low slope
parameter, the social media items in the Writing at Work, Reading at Work and Reading at Home scales
were closely reviewed. The social media item in the Reading at Home scale (G2_Q01g) and the Writing at
Work scale (F2_Q02d) had low slope parameters, .35 and .37, respectively. The Reading at Work social
media item performed better, with a slope parameter of 0.61. However, these items were dropped from
the MS because of their limited contributions to the scale and to keep the Work and Home scales relatively
parallel. Analyses were performed to investigate the impact of deleting these items on the reliability of the
scales, and it was found that the reliability was not significantly affected.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 163
Multi-item Scales in Section K
Section K comprises the short Big-Five-Inventory 2 (BFI-2-S) as an established measure of social and
emotional skills. BFI-2-S is an inventory that measures each Big Five domain (Open-Mindedness,
Conscientiousness, Agreeableness, Extraversion, and Emotional Stability) with six balanced-keyed items
per scale. We assessed the psychometric properties of these five BFI-2-S scales using data from the 21
countries that had selected international option A and administered the full 30-item BFI-2-S in the FT, and
delivered (non-simulated) FT data as part of Batch 1 or 2. As a potential alternative to the FT core BQ
(which covered only Open-Mindedness and Conscientiousness) for the MS, the 15-item extra-short version
of the inventory, BFI-2-XS, was tested. It consists of the first 15 items of the BFI-2-S.
The five scales of BFI-2-S measure a single factor each, which was confirmed in an analysis of the
dimensionality through three complementary statistical indices for almost all domains in nearly all
countries. This supports that each scale score can be interpreted as reflecting a single skill factor.
Though slightly lower than in previous BFI-2-S validation studies, the scale reliabilities (internal
consistencies) for the five scales were mostly modest to good (Cronbach’s alpha: Min = 0.45; Max = 0.81;
Median = 0.69) and sufficient for most countries and domains, especially in view of the fact that these are
short scales comprising only six items. As expected, by halving scale length, BFI-2-XS scale reliabilities
were lower than those of the BFI-2-S (Cronbach’s alpha: Min = 0.31; Max = 0.71; Median = 0.48). However,
this did not translate to commensurately lower predictive power.
Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) per Big Five domain and country showed mixed results. When six
single items per domain define the factors, the measurement models fall below conventional standards of
model fit for many country–domain combinations, which can be partially attributed to the lower-thanexpected inter-item correlations within each domain. Using three facet scores (items parcels formed by
averaging two items defining a facet) instead – which is often done in research using the BFI-2-S –
improved fit acceptably for most domains and countries. Facet scores correlated more highly with each
other and are more normally distributed than single questionnaire items.
Exploratory factor analyses (EFA/ESEM models) testing a joint measurement model for all five domains
revealed that, in most but not all countries, the 30 BFI-2-S items conform to the theorised Big Five structure,
as judged by the congruency between the empirical factor loadings and an idealised Big Five matrix. For
some countries and domains, the congruency with the theorised/idealised structure was insufficient, most
likely due to substantial cross-loadings on other factors in addition to loadings on their intended factor.
Due to the measurement models not fitting well when assessing each of the Big Five personality domains
individually with their six corresponding items, the comparability of the BFI-2-S items across countries was
hampered according to measurement invariance tests. The traditional procedure for testing the strict
parameter invariance of factor loadings, intercepts, and residual variances via fit indices (CFI, RMSEA,
SRMR) requires a well-fitting “configural model” as a starting point. This was not achieved for many
country–domain combinations. Therefore, specific items and countries that lack comparability were
identified via the alignment optimisation method. This procedure revealed that, despite some wiggle room
for model parameters, at least some items from the five scales had non-invariant loadings and intercepts,
as is often the case in cross-national studies involving multiple languages.
Overall, some psychometric properties of BFI-2-S in the FT were good, particularly unidimensionality and
reliability, whereas others such as CFA model fit and comparability were mixed. Plausible explanations for
this include the face-to-face mode of administration, respondent burden/fatigue given this is the final
section of the BQ, and potential translation issues. Several psychometric issues may be remedied by
switching to the 15-item extra-short version (BFI-2-XS) of the inventory. Moreover, it is reassuring that
despite these issues, the BFI-2-S (and -XS) perform well and as expected when it comes to predictive
validity.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

164 
Analyses of construct validity
This section summarises the results of bivariate and multivariate analyses that were used to assess the
construct validity of key concepts. The main aim of the multivariate analyses of the FT data was to verify
the functioning of the broader analytical concepts that the BQ seeks to measure (i.e. whether items or
scales measure what they are intended to measure). The analyses served to assess the validity of each
item, and were guided by the conceptual framework for the BQ. Validity was assessed by looking at
whether the different instruments correlate as expected, either with measures that should capture similar
constructs (convergent validity) or with outcomes that they should predict (predictive validity). These
analyses are based on the pooled cross-national sample. The remainder of this section is structured based
on the main topics covered in the BQ, with each subsection focusing on one or several BQ sections.

Social background (sections A and J)
Items in Section A (Personal Characteristics) were used as reporting categories in the multivariate
analyses that were leveraged to assess the construct validity of items across the other sections of the BQ.
The same holds for items on current household composition (J2_Q01), living with a partner (J2_Q02), and
children (J2_Q03) in Section J. Taken together, the results of multivariate analyses suggested that these
items, most of which were included in PIAAC Cycle 1 in exactly the same form, continue to work as
intended.
Section J included questions on parental education (J2_Q04c, J2_Q05c) and parents’ cultural capital
(“number of books in home”, J2_Q06) that were already part of the BQ for PIAAC Cycle 1, but that were
revised for PIAAC Cycle 2. For parental education, the most important change compared to PIAAC Cycle
1 was that these questions were in the FT BQ preceded by filter questions (J2_Q04a for the mother, and
J2_Q05a for the father) that establish whether a mother (or female guardian) and a father (or male
guardian) were present at the time when respondents were age 14. If respondents responded ‘No’ to these
filter questions, they were not asked the questions about the education and occupation of the
mother/female guardian or of the father/male guardian. Although the analyses showed that the filter
questions generally worked well, a downside of using these is that no information is collected on the
education and occupation of parents/guardians who were not present. Even if parents/guardians were not
present in respondents’ lives at that time, respondents may still be aware of their educational level and
occupation. Removing the filter questions for the MS allowed for capturing parental/guardian education
and occupation for a greater number of respondents. For parents’/guardians’ cultural capital, the only
change compared to PIAAC Cycle 1 was that the reference age was lowered from 16 to 14 to bring it more
in line with the other questions in Section J. The results of the multivariate analyses showed that these
questions are related as expected to parental/guardian occupation, educational attainment, cognitive skills,
and earnings. We concluded that these questions still work as intended and did not need to be changed.
Mother’s and father’s occupations (J2_Q04d-f, J2_Q05d-f) were measured with a set of new questions.
These were also included in the FT for PIAAC Cycle 1, but not included in the MS. First, respondents were
asked separately whether their mother/female guardian and the father/male guardian held paying jobs
when the respondent was 14 years old. If they responded ‘Yes’, they were given two open-ended followup questions asking what their parents’/guardians’ main jobs were at that time, and what their
parents/guardians mainly did in their jobs at that time. The responses to these questions were then coded
according to the ISCO-08 classification. In our analyses, we included the coded responses at the 1-digit
level of this classification. The questions on parental/guardian occupation did not add much to
parental/guardian education in terms of predictive power in models explaining key outcomes such as
educational attainment, occupational status, cognitive skills, and earnings, but the measures did perform
well in exposing patterns of intergenerational transmission that are not captured by measures of
parental/guardian education alone. Therefore, these questions still added value, especially for comparative
research involving educational inequalities and social mobility.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 165
Section J also included a new item measuring the place of residence while growing up (J2_Q07).
Relationships between this item and key variables in the BQ were in line with what could be expected. For
example, respondents whose parents worked in skilled agriculture and fishery occupations were much
more likely to grow up in a country village or in a farm or home in the countryside, and respondents whose
parents worked as plant or machine operators were most likely to grow up in towns or small cities.
Additionally, when adding parental education and occupation to the model, respondents who grew up in a
country village were significantly less likely to have a tertiary qualification. All in all, from the perspective of
construct validity, this new item performs well. However, there is one caveat: there were indications that
the item could also partly capture respondents’ current place of residence, given that generally
respondents may be more likely to reside in places that are similar to the place where they grew up.
Finally, this section included new questions measuring the household composition while growing up
(J2_Q08), which was identified as a candidate to drop, and the number of siblings and birth order
(J2_Q09a-c). In terms of construct validity, the results of the multivariate analyses suggested that these
questions worked as intended. For example, respondents growing up with a biological single mother were,
on average, lower educated than respondents from a biological two-parent household. Also, people who
already reported that no mother or father was present at age 14 (J2_Q04a and J2_Q05a) generally
indicated in response to J2_Q08 that they did not grow up with two biological parents. Concerning birth
order, we found that respondents who are the oldest (i.e. firstborn) within their family were more likely to
attend higher education than respondents who are the youngest or born in-between (in cases where
respondents have more than two siblings). Regarding the number of siblings, results suggested that having
more siblings is positively associated with lower levels of education. Also, birth order was related to
cognitive skills and earnings: firstborn respondents or respondents born in-between were found to earn
slightly more and to have better cognitive skills than the lastborn within the family. Regarding the number
of siblings, respondents with more siblings (especially those with more than one other sibling) appeared to
earn less and have lower cognitive skills.

Education and training
Section B consists of two parts, one focusing on formal education, and one aimed at capturing non-formal
education (called training in the BQ itself). From a validity perspective, the results of the multivariate
analyses suggested that the update and extension of the education coding framework has generally been
successful. Educational attainment (B2_Q01) and incomplete education (B2_Q06b) were related as
expected to a range of outcome measures, both in bivariate analyses and after adding control variables in
multivariate analyses. The same applied to the relationship between educational attainment and current
participation in formal education (B2_Q05b).
For the new item measuring educational pathways derived from the other qualifications that were reported
(B2_Q02b; labelled as dropping candidate for the MS BQ), the relationships with other questions in the BQ
were examined to check whether the information received was valid. Four indicator variables were
constructed: (1) having had vocational education at least once in the pathway, based on the detailed
ISCED 2011 categories of ’other qualifications’; (2) having completed a (pre-) vocational rather than
academic or comprehensive track in lower secondary education, based on an extension of ISCED 2011
categories specifically for the measurement of education pathways in PIAAC; (3) having completed a
qualification at ISCED level 4 in the pathway, for those who obtained a tertiary qualification; and (4) having
completed a traditional 'academic' pathway (i.e. gone through the most direct path from
general/academic/comprehensive ISCED2 to general/academic ISCED 3 with access to 5/6/7, and then
straight on to ISCED 6 or 7, and possibly 8, without any "detours" via vocational programmes or ISCED 4
or 5). The results of multivariate analyses including these four variables suggested that these derived
variables were indeed meaningfully related to other key variables.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

166 
Respondents’ field of study (B2_Q04a, B2_Q05c) was measured with soft trend items, in which the
categories were updated in comparison with PIAAC Cycle 1, partly based on the ISCED 2013 field of study
classification. The multivariate analyses revealed that the updated variables show the expected
relationships with other key variables in the BQ. Also, for those respondents who are currently enrolled in
formal education, there was a clear relationship between the field of study of their current qualification and
the field of study of their highest obtained qualification, with most respondents continuing their education
in fields of study that were similar to those of their highest qualification.
For the part of Section B that focuses on non-formal education, training participation was related as
expected to a range of key variables such as age, migration background, educational attainment,
employment status, occupation, cognitive skills, and earnings. For all questions focusing on specific
aspects of the last training activity, the relationships with other BQ items were in line with what would be
expected. The results indicated that all items had adequate convergent validity, as indicated by
interrelationships between items measuring various aspects of the last training activity. They also exhibited
predictive validity, as evidenced by relationships between aspects of the last training activity and
educational attainment. All in all, from a validity perspective, this suggested that the efforts to further
improve the measurement of non-formal education compared to PIAAC Cycle 1 by adding new items,
revising difficult items, and dropping items with limited relevance was successful.
This also applied to the items that were labelled as candidates for dropping. The results for the item
measuring whether people have participated in training at any point in their life (B2_Q09) showed that
more recent training was more strongly associated with earnings and employment status than training that
took place more than 5 years ago. This was especially important given that older respondents and people
with lower levels of education were more likely to have participated in their last training activity more than
5 years ago. As such, distinguishing the timing of the last training activity in the BQ appeared to be of
added value. For the motivation for training (B2_Q12), clear relationships were observed with key variables
such as age, educational attainment and employment status. For the item on recurring versus one-off
training sessions (B2_Q13d), relationships with training content are as expected. No clear relationships
with educational attainment and occupation were observed, but from a theoretical perspective, there was
no reason to expect such relationships for this item. Finally, for the item capturing whether in their last
training activity respondents learned how to better carry out their work tasks by using computerised
equipment or digitally supported processes (B2_Q16c), there were no clear relationships with educational
attainment and occupation. This may reflect the increased use of computerised equipment and digitally
supported processes across a wide range of occupations, which may have further increased during the
Covid-19 pandemic. There were meaningful interrelationships with other BQ items, showing that these
types of training activities were more commonly provided through distance education than through inperson training, and for respondents who indicated that there were changes related to ICT in their work
environment. All in all, from a validity perspective, there were no reasons to drop these items for the MS
BQ.

Labour market status and outcomes
Section C largely consists of a set of items that captures the current labour force status (C2_Q01 to
C2_Q06) and self-declared main status (C2_Q07). Most of these items are strict trend items, and the other
items are soft trend items that only changed marginally compared to PIAAC Cycle 1. The interrelationships
between the current labour force status and self-declared main status were as expected (e.g. employed
respondents are most likely to self-identify as either full-time employed or part-time employed). Also, the
expected relationships between these indicators and key variables such as sex, educational attainment,
training participation, cognitive skills and earnings were as expected. As a result, these items already
performed well in PIAAC Cycle 1, and the results of the multivariate analyses suggested that this is still
the case for PIAAC Cycle 2.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 167
This section also contains two new items to capture whether respondents have been out of work in the
past 5 years, and if so, for how long (C2_Q08a, b). These new items were mostly added to gather more
information about the recent employment history of respondents, and about their experiences being out of
work. The results of the multivariate analyses were very promising: the first item on having been out of
work was relevant for several key variables, and the second item on duration appeared to be relevant as
well. For example, even controlling for several other variables, having been out of work in the past 5 years
was associated with lower earnings, especially for those respondents who have been out of work 3 to 5
years. Section C also included a new item on receipt of benefits (C2_Q11), simply distinguishing
respondents who received benefits from those who did not, and this item behaved as expected in relation
to other items in the BQ.
Sections D (for the current job ) and E (for the last job) contain several items on occupation (D2_Q01 and
E2_Q01), economic sector (D2_Q02, E2_Q02, D2_Q03 and E2_Q03), status in employment
(employed/self-employed, D2_Q04 and E2_Q04), number of years worked for the current employer
(D2_Q05), organisation size (D2_Q07a), number of employees (D2_Q08), and supervisory status
(D2_Q09). These items are mostly strict trend items, although some are soft trend items with minor
changes compared to PIAAC Cycle 1. These items were used as key determinants, outcomes, and/or
control variables across a wide range of multivariate analyses that focused on assessing the validity of
other BQ items. The same applied to the items that capture job satisfaction (D2_Q13) and earnings
(D2_Q14 through D2_Q16), which are all strict trend items that were used as outcome variables in a
substantial number of multivariate analyses. Taken together, the results of these analyses suggested that
these items still perform well, and did not need to be changed. Items on the type of employment contract
(D2_Q10 and E2_Q08) were changed slightly compared to PIAAC Cycle 1, but the results of the
multivariate analyses show that these items still behave as intended in relation to earnings, training
participation, and job satisfaction.
In Section D, three new items were added on changes in their work role (D2_Q06a-c). One item (D2_Q06a)
focused on moving to a lower or higher position, one item (D2_Q06b) captures whether people experienced
changes in tasks and responsibilities, and one item (D2_Q06c) looked at whether respondents moved to
a different unit or department. The interrelationships between the three items were as expected: if people
experienced one type of change, they were also more likely to experience the other types of change
(however, overlap was far from perfect, which underlines the relevance of distinguishing all three types of
changes in role). Relationships with key variables were also as expected. From a construct validity
perspective, all three items appeared to work well. Also, in multivariate analyses in which all three items
were included, particularly the items on changes in role and changes in tasks and responsibilities,
independent relationships with multiple outcomes were observed.
Section D also contained items on changes in organisation size (D2_Q07b) and on whether organisations
also had other locations or branches (D2_Q07c). Both items are strict trend items, but were labelled as
dropping candidates because they were expected to have limited informational value. For D2_Q07b, there
were relationships with education, occupation and industry, although these were partly explained by control
variables in multivariate analyses. For D2_Q07c, there were also relationships with education, occupation
and industry, but in this case, these relationships held after controlling for other variables. Also, for this
item it should be noted that it could offer useful information about the ‘total firm size’ if combined with
information from D2_Q07a, which captures the number of employees in the respondent’s work
organisation). From a construct validity perspective, both items appeared to function adequately.
To determine the education-job match (D2_Q12a-c, E2_Q10a-c), a comparison was made between the
qualification that is needed for respondents’ jobs with the highest qualification they had actually obtained
(B2_Q01). In the FT BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2, respondents were asked what would be the qualification
needed to get their type of job, as was done in PIAAC Cycle 1, but they were also asked what qualification
they would need to satisfactorily do their type of job. In contrast to PIAAC Cycle 1, where the education-

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

168 
job match was only captured for the current job, in the FT BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2 the education-job match
for the last job was also measured. All in all, education-job match variables worked well in relation to other
key variables, such as educational attainment, earnings, cognitive skills and occupation for both the current
job (Section D) and the last job (Section E) qualification variables. From a construct validity perspective,
the results suggested that all items related to the education-job match perform well. However, findings
indicated that people generally report the same qualifications for these two questions: only around 15% of
respondents reported that the qualification needed to do their job satisfactorily is different from the
qualification needed to get the job. Also, there was almost a perfect overlap in the classification of mismatch
between the two versions. Taken together, this suggested that the new items focusing on qualifications
needed to do the job was of quite limited informational value when added to the existing items on
qualifications needed to get the job. Therefore, it was suggested to drop these items for the MS BQ.
Finally, in Section E, two new items were included that capture respondents’ reasons for leaving their last
job (E2_Q11a, b): one that distinguishes between voluntary versus involuntary reasons, and one that
focuses on specific reasons. Both items behaved as expected in relation to key variables in the BQ. For
example, people who left their job voluntarily were more likely to be pupils/students and people in (early)
retirement, whereas respondents who left their job involuntarily were more likely to be unemployed or
permanently disabled. Also, people reporting (early) retirement as the main reason to leave their job were
almost all retired, and a substantial share of people who quit their last job because of health reasons
identify as permanently disabled. All in all, the findings for these items suggested that they perform well
from a construct validity perspective.

Work environment
Section H is the result of extensive development work that was initiated by the Skill Use and Mismatch
working group, and includes a mix of strict trend, soft trend, and new items. First, several items were
already included in exactly the same form in PIAAC Cycle 1. This applied to items measuring cooperation
(H2_Q01), horizontal interaction (H2_Q03a), problem solving (H2_Q06a, b), and working physically for a
long period (H2_Q07a). Overall, the relationships between these items and key variables such as
educational attainment, occupation, earnings, job satisfaction, cognitive skills, firm size, and employment
contract type were in line with what was expected, so the conclusion was that these strict trend items still
perform well. The item measuring precision work (H2_Q07b) was revised for PIAAC Cycle 2, and now
measures how frequently respondents used their hands and fingers for precision work. The results
supported the construct validity of this soft trend item, and showed that this kind of work is most frequently
done by craft or other trade workers.
In this section, the BQ also included a limited number of new items relating to client interaction (H2_Q03d),
work intensity (H2_Q12), standardisation, as measured by doing short repetitive tasks (H2_Q17), changes
in the work environment (H2_Q18a, b), and skill rather than qualification mismatch (H2_Q19a,b). For these
items, the general conclusion was that the findings of the multivariate analyses supported the construct
validity of the measurements. For example, service workers and shop and market sales workers report the
highest frequency of client interaction. Also, as could be expected, extraversion and openness were
positively related to the frequency of client interaction. Legislators, senior officials, and managers and
people working in the armed forces reported the highest work intensity, whereas people working in
elementary occupations reported the lowest frequency of working to tight deadlines and at very high speed.
A higher work intensity was positively associated with earnings, but negatively associated with job
satisfaction and self-rated health, which may reflect the effects of working on tight deadlines or at very high
speeds on stress. Skilled agriculture and fishery workers were most likely to report that their job involves
short repetitive tasks, as were people working on temporary agency contracts and apprentice contracts.
Changes in the work environment were measured with a multiple-response item, which gave respondents
the opportunity to mention multiple types of change they experienced in their work environment. The results

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 169
showed that different groups of respondents mention different types of changes in the work environment,
which underlines the relevance of distinguishing multiple types of change in this item. For example, people
working in skilled agricultural and fishery, craft and related trades, and plant and machine operators were
much more likely to report changes in machinery than people in other occupations, whereas changes in
information and communication technologies were reported by half of all legislators, senior officials, and
managers, and much less by the lower occupational status groups. Relationships were observed between
key variables in the BQ and responses to the follow-up question on changes in the work environment,
which asked whether respondents received training to support these changes.
Skill mismatch was measured by asking respondents whether their skills are higher than required by their
job, are matched to what is required by their job, or some of their skills are lower than what is required by
their job and need to be further developed. Respondents who identified as underskilled also received a
follow-up multiple-response question asking them which skills they were thinking of when they answered
the first question. In relation to qualification mismatch, overqualified people are significantly more likely to
be overskilled, and undereducated people are more likely to be underskilled. This strongly supported the
construct validity of this item. Moreover, both underskilled and overskilled people report lower job
satisfaction compared to well-matched people. Overskilled people also report lower earnings than wellmatched people, while there was no significant difference in earnings between well-matched and
underskilled people. All this suggested that the item was working as intended. Also, similarly to the item
on changes in the working environment, results on the multiple-response item on types of skill mismatch
suggested that distinguishing multiple skill categories was helpful in revealing how different groups of
workers have different types of skills in mind if they identified as being underskilled.
Finally, as part of International Option B on the work environment, Section H also included various new
items to measure four concepts: teamwork (H2_Q02a-e), knowledge sharing (H2_Q10), social support
(H2_Q13a-c), and participation (H2_Q14a, b). For teamwork, there are different items designed to capture
distinct aspects of working in teams. Additionally, relationships with key variables in the BQ were as
expected. For example, members of teams that can influence their own work targets report higher earnings
and job satisfaction. This also applies to the item on knowledge sharing, for which there were clear
relationships with educational attainment, occupation, training participation, job satisfaction, extraversion
and openness. For the items on social support, the item on the need for assistance (H2_Q13a) was
particularly relevant in relation to key variables in the BQ. For the other items on specific sources of support
(i.e. supervisors and co-workers), relationships with other variables were generally weaker, which may be
explained by the fact that these two items were only asked for respondents who indicated a need for
assistance. Although the results did not challenge the construct validity of these two follow-up items, the
informational value of these two items was slightly lower.
For participation in the work environment, there were clear relationships with educational attainment,
occupation, training participation, earnings, job satisfaction, cognitive skills, extraversion and openness
that are all in line with what would be expected. This led to the conclusion that the new items in International
Option B also performed as intended.

Non-economic outcomes
The FT BQ included six items related to non-economic outcomes. Apart from assessing the construct
validity of these items, they were also included as outcome measures in various multivariate analyses to
assess the construct validity of items in other BQ sections. Overall, from a construct validity perspective,
the results suggested that all items in this section performed well. Political efficacy (I2_Q01a) and social
trust (I2_Q01b) were already included in PIAAC Cycle 1, but the measurement was changed to bring the
items more in line with other surveys such as the European Social Survey. Both items generally showed
the expected relationships with key variables in the BQ such as educational attainment, employment
status, cognitive skills, and age. For political efficacy, it was slightly surprising that the difference between

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

170 
unemployed and employed respondents was not statistically significant. However, although unemployment
has been associated with lower political efficacy in the literature, there are also examples of null findings.
The conclusion was that the findings support the construct validity of these two soft trend items.
This section also included an item measuring whether and how often people do voluntary work (I2_Q02).
This is a strict trend item that was already included in the same form in PIAAC Cycle 1, but was labelled
as a candidate to drop because of the potentially limited informational value of the item. From a construct
validity perspective, there was no reason to question the performance of the item: the expected
relationships were observed with other key variables in the BQ such as educational attainment and
employment status, both before and after controlling for other variables. Self-rated health (I2_Q03) was
also measured with a strict trend item, and for this item there were no surprises in terms of relationships
with key variables such as educational attainment, employment status, cognitive skills, age, and sex,
either.
Additionally, Section I included a new item to capture patience (I2_Q04). This was measured by asking
respondents how willing they are to give up something that is beneficial for them today in order to benefit
more from that in the future. The findings generally supported the construct validity of this item: the
relationships with key variables in the BQ, such as educational attainment, were as expected. However,
since the item was conceptually close to social and emotional skills (and because this item was therefore
labelled as a potential candidate to drop), relationships between this item and the dimensions of the Big
Five domains were also assessed. Patience was observed to be positively and significantly related to
agreeableness, emotional stability, open-mindedness, extraversion, and conscientiousness. Additionally,
the extent to which patience is significantly related to earnings, if social and emotional skills are included
in the model, was examined. Patience was found to be positively related with earnings, even when
accounting for the five social and emotional skill scales. This suggested that although patience is
conceptually related to social and emotional skills, it had an independent association with key economic
outcome measures in the BQ. This implied that the item measuring patience was not redundant when the
social and emotional skill measures were also included in the MS BQ.
Finally, this section included a new item to measure life satisfaction (I2_Q05), based on similar items in
other surveys such as the European Social Survey. The results of the bivariate and multivariate analyses
supported the construct validity of the item. Clear relationships were found with key variables such as
educational attainment and employment status, and the results indicated that this new item worked as
intended.

Social and emotional skills
For the items on social and emotional skills in Section K, the aim of the multivariate analyses was twofold:
(1) to examine relationships between social and emotional skills scales and key outcome measures to
assess the predictive validity of the scales; and (2) to compare different versions of the social and emotional
skills scales with regard to the relationships with key outcome measures, and with regard to the explanatory
power of the different versions of the scales in predicting these outcome measures.
More specifically, four versions of the social and emotional skills scales were compared: (1) the full 30item version for all Big Five domains (i.e. BFI-2-S), which was used as International Option A in the FT
BQ; (2) a shorter 15-item version for all Big Five domains (i.e. BFI-2-XS); (3) the two dimensions that were
included in the core FT BQ (i.e. Conscientiousness and Open-Mindedness from the BFI-2-S); and (4) a
facet model using the full 30-item BFI-2-S version, which breaks each Big Five domain down into three
narrower facets (each measured by two items). For each of the four versions, the scale scores represent
unit-weighted sum scores, rescaled through the percentage of maximum possible (POMP) transformation
to a 0–100 range. Sum scores are the most widely used type of score for the BFI-2-S and similar
inventories. For the analyses, nested regression models were used to systematically compare the
performance of the four versions of the social and emotional skills scales in relation to multiple economic

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 171
and non-economic outcomes such as earnings, job satisfaction, employment status, training participation,
self-rated health, social trust, voluntary work, and life satisfaction. Differences were examined in the
adjusted R2 (or pseudo-R2 for categorical outcome measures) to assess differences in explanatory power
between the four versions of the social and emotional skills scales in predicting these outcomes.
All in all, the results suggested that the various versions of the social and emotional skills scales generally
showed the expected relationships, in line with previous research and the conceptual framework for the
BQ, with the economic and non-economic outcome measures. This suggested that the scales are
adequate in terms of predictive validity. Moreover, in terms of explanatory power, the 30-item BFI-2-S
version did not add much to the 15-item BFI-2-XS version for any of the outcomes. The results were
consistent in this respect across all outcome measures. For most outcomes, using only the two dimensions
that were part of the core FT BQ, the 12 BFI-2-S items measuring Open-Mindedness and
Conscientiousness, was suboptimal either in terms of explanatory power, or in terms of leading to different
estimates of the direction of the relationships between Conscientiousness and Open-Mindedness and the
predicted outcomes. Also, using a 15-item BFI-2-XS scale means an addition of only three items to the
core BQ, but makes it possible to capture all five dimensions, rather than the two dimensions included in
the core FT BQ. Taken together, adopting the 15-item BFI-2-XS version as part of the MS core BQ
significantly enhances the validity and explanatory power of the measurement of social and emotional skills
in the BQ compared to the two dimensions included in the core FT BQ.
It was noted that for some outcomes, the facet model offers additional explanatory power over the 15- and
30-item versions condensing the items into five domains each. Since the facet model can only be
constructed based on the 30-item version, using the 15-item version would mean that this option would be
lost. The findings suggested that this would mostly apply to self-rated health and life satisfaction, and less
to other outcome measures. Offering the other items of the full 30-item version as an International Option
would allow countries to still distinguish the different facets within the five dimensions. However, the FT
analysis showed that some items from both the 30-item BFI-2-S and 15-item BFI-2-XS suffer from
comparability issues, such as lack of measurement invariance across countries.
Additional analyses in which items with comparability issues were replaced by conceptually similar items
without comparability issues did not lead to different conclusions about relationships between social and
emotional skills and the outcome measures. This suggested that the comparability issues reported for
some items were not problematic in terms of the construct validity of the scales, and were unlikely to affect
future multivariate analyses in which the BFI-2-XS was used to measure social and emotional skills.
In conclusion, both the 15-item BFI-2-XS and the 30-item BFI-2-S versions of the social and emotional
skills scales were adequate in terms of predictive validity and generally sufficient in terms of reliability.
Moreover, in terms of explanatory power, the short 30-item version did not add much to the extra-short 15item version for any of the outcomes. Using only the two dimensions that were part of the core FT BQ (i.e.
the 12 items measuring Open-Mindedness and Conscientiousness) was suboptimal in terms of
explanatory power and predictive validity. Including the 15-item scale in the core MS BQ means an addition
of only three items, but makes it possible to capture all five dimensions, rather than the two dimensions
that were included in the FT BQ. Taken together, adopting the 15-item version for the core BQ significantly
enhanced the validity and explanatory power of the measurement of social and emotional skills in the BQ
compared to the two dimensions included in the core BQ. Offering the other items from the full 30-item
version as an international option allows countries to distinguish the different facets within the five
dimensions.

Summary and conclusions
The main goal of the analyses of the BQ FT results was to help finalise the instruments to be used in the
MS. The analyses have shown that, as in PIAAC Cycle 1, the FT BQ to a very large extent succeeded in
collecting the necessary information on respondents across the participating countries. The BQ FT items
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

172 
performed well in terms of item quality and construct validity, and this applies to new items as well as to
strict trend items and soft trend items that were already included in PIAAC Cycle 1. This reflected the
extensive development work on the new items (e.g. in the mixed-methods pretest and in the preparatory
work of several working groups and the international Consortium), and the fact that most new items were
based on items that had already been used in other surveys. Very few issues with routing were identified,
suggesting that the flow of the questionnaire within and between the sections worked as intended. Finally,
the duration of the FT BQ ended up being shorter than expected: employed respondents require on
average across countries less than 45 minutes to complete the BQ.
The duration of the core FT BQ was shorter than the maximum target duration of 45 minutes for employed
respondents, which indicated that it was not necessary to shorten the BQ for the MS from a timing
perspective. However, it was still advisable to drop or revise some items based on the analyses of item
quality, scaling, and construct validity, which showed that some items are either problematic or of very
limited added value. For each of the BQ sections, the consideration to drop or change items was based
on the findings of the FT analysis.
Based on the FT analysis, the following recommendations were given for each section:
•

For Sections A and J (Social background), the recommendation was to drop the filter questions on
whether a mother or female guardian and a father or male guardian were present when the
respondent was age 14 (J2_Q04a, J2_Q05a). All other items in Sections A and J in the MS BQ
were included without any changes.

•

For Section B (Education and training), the recommendation was to drop the filter item on whether
respondents have obtained any other qualifications (B2_Q02a), and to revise the wording of the
item asking about which other qualifications respondents have obtained, to only ask about those
obtained before the highest qualification (B2_Q02b). All other items in Section B in the MS BQ
were included without changes.

•

For Sections C, D, and E (Labour market status and outcomes), the recommendation was to drop
the items on the qualification needed for respondents to do their current and last job (D2_Q12b, c
and E2_Q10b, c).All other items in Sections C, D and E in the MS BQ were included without
changes.

•

For Sections F and G (Literacy, numeracy and ICT practices at work and in everyday life), the
recommendation was to drop four items (F2_Q01g, G2_Q01g, F2_Q02d, G2_Q02d) that are
related to reading and writing on social media. ,All other items in Sections F and G in the MS BQ
were included without any changes.

•

For Section H (Work environment), the recommendation was to include all items in Section H in
the MS BQ without any changes, and to offer International Option B, also unchanged, for the main
study.

•

For Section I (Non-economic outcomes), the recommendation was to include all items in Section I
in the MS BQ without any changes.

•

For Section K (Social and emotional skills), the recommendation was to include the 15-item BFI-2XS version of all five dimensions of the Big Five index to measure social and emotional skills as
part of the core BQ for the MS, and offer the other 15 items from the 30-item BFI-2-S as
International Option A. The core BQ would include questions K2_Q01a-e, K2_Q02a-e, and
K2_Q03a-e and International Option A would include K2_Q04a-e, K2_Q05a-e, and K2_Q06a-e.

Dropping items resulted in an average time savings of 1 minutes and 24 seconds, but the increase in the
total number of items to assess social and emotional skills (covering all the five dimensions) added 37
seconds. Therefore, the overall effect from adopting these recommendations was to reduce the expected
length of the core BQ for an employed respondent by an average approximately 47 seconds.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 173
Additional quality checks of MS data on formal education
In the FT, several countries did not collect data from real respondents, but rather used a simulated or
operational FT. Some countries also submitted their data too late to be included in the international FT
analyses report or had small samples. Therefore, the MS data on formal education, especially B2_Q01
(educational attainment), needed to be checked for those countries 5 to ensure high measurement quality
and potentially allow for final adjustments before the data are published. Furthermore, as previously
discussed, the measurement of educational pathways (B2_Q02) changed between the FT and MS as a
result of clear underreporting indications in the FT data. As a consequence, the PIAAC MS data on
educational pathways needed another evaluation, using data from all countries. The four derived variables
(DVs) that were constructed based on the pathway item in the FT were further developed between the FT
and MS, resulting in the construction of a fifth DV pertaining to the type of education completed in upper
secondary education (EP_TISC3).
A close inspection of educational attainment (B2_Q01) and educational pathway (B2_Q02b) variables in
PIAAC MS data showed that educational attainment is also well measured in those countries that had little
or no FT data to check at the time. The measurement of educational pathways improved considerably
following the deletion of the filter question B2_Q02a after the FT. Under- and over-reporting was still visible
to some degree in the data; some of which is due to measurement error in B2_Q01 rather than B2_Q02b.
The construct validation analyses showed that these potential measurement errors do not lead to invalid
DVs. On the contrary: the DVs reflecting the type of education completed at ISCED 2, and especially
ISCED 3, regardless of whether the educational pathway included the general qualifications preparing for
higher education, or whether it included vocational education, have substantial and statistically significant
effects on educational attainment, as well as on whether the highest attainment is of the vocational type.
More importantly, these variables have substantial and significant effects on cognitive skills. Most of the
variables also have substantial and significant effects on earnings beyond only educational attainment.
These DVs, as well as the pathway indicator variables from which data users can further derive variables
specific to their research, substantially increase the analysis potential of PIAAC data pertaining to the
antecedents of educational attainment, skills, and labour market outcomes.

The content of the Main Study BQ
BQ Main Study
As indicated above, based on the analyses of the FT data, a final MS BQ for PIAAC Cycle 2 was developed.
The BPC accepted the Consortium's final recommendations and approved the content of the MS BQ in
January 2022. The basic structure of the MS BQ is relatively straightforward, although some sections
involve somewhat complex routing depending on, among other things, the educational and labour market
status of the respondent. The BQ consists of a total of 11 sections. Six sections are completed by all
respondents. These are Section A: Personal characteristics, Section C: Current status and work history,
Section G: Literacy, numeracy and ICT practices in everyday life, Section I: Non-economic outcomes,
Section J: Background, and Section K: Social and emotional skills. The part on formal education in Section
B is also completed by all respondents, while young people (aged 16 to 19 and still in compulsory
education) skip the latter part on training. All respondents who are currently working complete Section D:
Current work, and respondents who are currently not working but had paid work in the past 5 years go to
Section E: Last job. Sections F: Literacy, numeracy, and ICT practices at work and H: The working
environment are completed by all respondents currently working or with paid work in past 12 months,
except students who work less than 9 hours a week. In addition to the core content of Sections H and K,
these sections also included International Options.

two sections.

National adaptations
Some questions or categories in the BQ had to be adapted to reflect different national contexts. All national
adaptations were negotiated and approved by the Consortium. The major adaptations countries were
required to perform for the main study BQ were the following:
•

All questions relating to formal education, such as highest qualification, educational pathway to the
highest qualification, current education and incomplete education in Section B, and education
required to get current or last job in Sections D and E, had to be adapted to the national education
system. Like in PIAAC Cycle 1, it was not feasible to use a standard international classification
directly in order to ascertain the level of education a respondent is currently following or has
followed in the past. In order to be comprehensible to respondents, all questions pertaining to
formal education needed to be framed in terms of the educational programmes and qualifications
currently or formerly available in that country. This was achieved following an elaborate
consultation process between countries and the Consortium: first, the Consortium transformed the
PIAAC Cycle 1 country-specific education categories to match the PIAAC Cycle 2 coding scheme,
applying the official ISCED mappings (UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2018[92]), for EU countries:
(Eurostat, 2022[93]) and including information on required years of education for each education

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

178 
category. Countries reviewed the results of this mapping, responded to Consortium questions, and
indicated further ways for improvement, which were checked, and if agreed to, implemented by the
Consortium. This process was continued until country and Consortium agreed on the final
education correspondence table. From this correspondence table, the Consortium derived lists of
formal education categories for the different BQ items related to formal education (e.g. deleting
outdated qualifications from the item on qualification currently being pursued). Subsequently, these
lists were integrated in the national BQs as response options for the respective questions by
countries, and the results again reviewed by the Consortium.
•

Country and language lists: Several questions in the BQ referred to countries or languages. These
questions have a two-stage structure – first, a closed list comprising a limited number of
countries/languages that are considered most relevant in the country concerned, and second, an
open question for those respondents who wished to report a country/language not included in the
standard list. Because the relevant countries and languages differ greatly from country to country,
each country was required to adapt these items to national needs.

•

In Section C, a question was included that was designed to capture the respondent’s job search
behaviour. Because search channels can differ subtly among countries, countries were asked to
inspect the examples and, if necessary, adapt or add examples to correspond to the national
institutions that may be involved.

•

In Sections D and E, several questions were used to ascertain the (last) occupation and (last)
economic sector in which the respondent works or had worked in the past. Countries were required
to check and, if necessary, adapt these items to the national setting.

•

All income questions were asked in two forms: First, respondents were asked to report their income
directly in the national currency. For respondents who were unwilling or unable to report their
precise earnings, the option was made available to report in broad ranges. Countries were required
to adapt the amounts and the currency used in these broad ranges based on explicit instructions
how these should be derived from national statistics on recent population earnings distributions.

•

For several questions throughout the BQ, countries were required to check, and if necessary,
adapt, the wording of questions to correctly reflect the national setting.

•

Wherever adaptations involved some kind of structural change to the BQ – for example, splitting
of a single item into multiple items, or the addition or deletion of one or more response categories
– countries were required to make any necessary adaptations to routings, derived variables and
so forth that make reference to the original items.

•

The use of registry information to pre-fill responses or the use of national look-up lists to facilitate
response process in the background questionnaire was restricted to questions pertaining to highest
educational qualification (B2_Q01), occupations (D2_Q01a/b, E2_Q01a/b), sectors of industry
(D2_Q02a/b, E2_Q02a/b), country of birth (A2_Q03b) and country in which the highest educational
qualification was obtained (B2_Q03b). Any pre-filled response needed to be confirmed by the
respondent in a follow-up question. In case registry information was used to pre-fill responses for
questions about job title or industry sector, which would be used to code into ISCO/ISIC
classifications, the standard open-ended questions (D2_Q01a/b, E2_Q01a/b, D2_Q02a/b,
E2_Q02a/b) about actual tasks of the respondent/the firm still needed to be presented to the
respondent.

National extensions
All countries were allowed to include a limited number of country-specific questions, known as national
extensions, that they required for their own policy purposes. In order to avoid undue burden on respondents
that could negatively affect the data quality, a strict rule was imposed that the total additional time added
to the questionnaire from extensions was not to exceed five minutes. The time estimates used to enforce

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 179
this restriction took into account the number and type of proposed items to be added by a country. All
proposals for national extensions had to be discussed and agreed upon with the Consortium.
In the period between the FT and MS, some countries requested adding national extensions to their BQ
related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The Consortium and the OECD created rules for the implementation of
these new questions. The additional national extensions relating to Covid-19 had to fit within the five
minutes allowed for national extensions, and preferably, these questions should be added to an additional
module. Again, these questions were reviewed and approved by the Consortium. Two countries (HRV and
NZL) have added these Covid-related national extensions.

International options
Countries were given the option to include one or two International Options. International Option A contains
the full five-dimensional 30-item version of the Big Five scales to measure social and emotional skills (BFI2-S instead of BFI-2-XS) in Section K. International Option B contains additional items on the working
environment in Section H. The total maximum time for both international options and national extensions
is five minutes. Fourteen countries chose to include International Option A in their MS BQ. Two countries
(USA and JPN) opted out of Section K entirely. Twenty countries have chosen International Option B.

Doorstep interview
The doorstep interview is a short version of the BQ designed to obtain key information on characteristics
of respondents who had been classified as literacy-related nonrespondents in PIAAC Cycle 1. Since these
individuals are essential to the population model for the estimation of proficiencies, it was decided that key
information should be collected about these persons in PIAAC Cycle 2. The doorstep interview contains a
total of six questions on gender, age group, years of education (in broad categories), subjective status,
whether the respondent was born in the country and, if not, time lived in country of interview. Except for
the question about education, the doorstep interview questions were designed to allow direct comparison
with those who responded to the BQ. This is because doorstep interview respondents typically would not
have been educated in the country in which they were interviewed, and therefore national adaptations of
doorstep questions were not possible. The doorstep interview was available in all PIAAC languages and
eight additional languages.

Quality check in the BQs
Countries implemented their national BQ with an authoring tool provided by the Consortium. The
Consortium checked the changes and compared it with the master BQ version using this authoring tool.
Test scenarios were developed by the Consortium with hypothetical respondents to test the routing and
flow of the questionnaire. Countries had to adapt these scenarios to their national BQ, after which these
test scenarios were tested in the tool. In addition, the national BQ was tested with the same scenarios after
translation to further ensure that translations were appearing correctly and that the functionality did not
change. The BQ also contained a number of features designed to assist the interviewers and ensure it was
administered in a standardised way across all countries. These features were:
•

Instructions given to interviewers: These instructions were designed to provide the interviewer with
any relevant information that might be needed in order to pose the question in the correct manner,
to indicate when to hand over and take back show cards, to provide support to respondents, and
so on.

•

Help buttons: In addition to these interviewer instructions, which were always visible to the
interviewer but not read out to the respondent, the BQ contained a number of help buttons that the
interviewer could consult if needed. These contained such things as additional information that

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

180 
could be provided to the respondent if needed, additional background information on the meaning
or intent of questions, and so on.
•

Consistency checks: For some items, there were consistency checks built into the BQ that were
triggered when a respondent gave an answer to a question that might be considered implausible.
Examples include the age at which a respondent has reported a given event or status or the
earnings reported by the respondent.
