7. Translation, adaptation and
verification of test and survey
materials
Laura Wayrynen (cApStAn), Dorothée Behr (GESIS), Anouk Zabal (GESIS)

This chapter outlines the processes for translating, adapting and verifying
the background questionnaire and cognitive instruments. It emphasises the
importance of maintaining comparability across different languages and
cultures while ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of translations.
The chapter describes the decentralised model used, where National
Centres are responsible for the localisation and translation, with guidance
and quality control provided by the PIAAC Consortium. Key tools and
procedures, such as double translation and reconciliation, verification
follow-up forms, training and workshops, are detailed to demonstrate how
the Consortium ensured high-quality translations across all participating
countries.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 189

Introduction
This chapter describes various aspects of translation, adaptation and verification of test and survey
materials for PIAAC Cycle 2.
The PIAAC assessment instruments comprise cognitive instruments and a background questionnaire
(BQ). They were originally developed in English but were then administered to samples of adults in the
countries’ national language(s) and, in some cases, other language(s) spoken by large proportions of the
population. The successful localisation of assessment instruments is an important component of the
project. Some definitions of terms used throughout this chapter are as follows:
•

Localisation can be defined, in general terms, as the process of adapting a product or service to a
particular language and culture. A successfully localised product or service appears to have been
developed within the local culture. For international comparative assessment studies, like PIAAC,
the challenge is to localise test and questionnaire items while maintaining the comparability of
collected assessment results and individual background data across countries and languages.

•

The localisation process can be broken down into translation/adaptation and validation. The words
translation and adaptation are used jointly because the term translation is deemed too restrictive,
referring to a more literal translation rather than the process of culturally adjusting a test or
questionnaire so that the meaning or cognitive demands posed by the test or questionnaire remain
unchanged. An adaptation may entail changing the picture of a stimulus, changing the combination
of July/summer to July/winter (or January/summer) for the Southern hemisphere, etc. It may, for
example, involve a change of wording, register, context, currency, measurement unit or form of
address. Validation refers to quality control steps, which will be defined later.

As in other major international assessment studies, the localisation process in PIAAC Cycle 2 mostly
followed a decentralised model:
•

The National Centres in the participating countries were each responsible for localising assessment
materials for use in their respective countries.

•

The PIAAC Consortium guided and assisted the National Centres throughout the process, in
particular by developing and conducting linguistic quality assurance (LQA) and linguistic quality
control (LQC) processes.

In PIAAC Cycle 2, the LQA processes implemented by cApStAn in cooperation with GESIS and other
Consortium members included:
•

Early resolution of potential localisation issues, via preliminary scrutiny of source assessment and
questionnaire materials to anticipate adaptation issues, ambiguities, cultural issues or item
translatability problems.

•

Definition of the localisation design, originally based on the OECD PISA (Programme for
International Student Assessment) design, and applied in PIAAC Cycle 1. The strong
recommendation endorsed by the Consortium included a double translation and reconciliation
design, making use of professional staff, and attending the training sessions organised by the
Consortium. The key quality control steps included in the design were the verification of initial
submissions from National Centres by verifiers who were appointed, trained and monitored by
cApStAn, a final check of instruments after post-verification revision by National Centres, layout
corrections by Consortium technical staff, and the documentation of all steps leading to the finalised
localised instruments.

•

Preparation of general translation and adaptation guidelines, separately for the BQ and the
assessment materials. These key documents set out requirements and roles, translation traps,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

190 
pointers on linguistic difficulty, psychometric traps, cultural adaptations, etc. They are further
described in later sections of this chapter.
•

Online user guides targeting specific groups (e.g. reconcilers) or topics (e.g. dealing with different
types of trend items). These online guides not only summarised key points and procedures from
the guidelines but also included links to the PIAAC Portal and information on how to use the Portal,
pointers for installing and using translation tools, and frequently updated FAQs.

•

Preparation of centralised tools for documenting and monitoring the successive translation,
adaptation and verification activities: for the cognitive items, the Verification Follow-up Forms (VFF)
used in the field trial and the Item Feedback Forms (IFF) used in the main study; for the BQ, the
Background Questionnaire Adaptation Spreadsheet (BQAS) used both for the field trial and the
main study. These tools included detailed item-specific translation and adaptation guidelines such
as specifications of adaptations that were mandatory, desirable or not allowed; advice on
terminology problems and idiomatic expressions; references to literal or synonymous matches that
needed to be echoed between stimuli and items; patterns in response options to be echoed;
formatting issues; and so on. Figure 7.1 shows an example of a VFF with item-specific guidelines.

•

Provision of training sessions for countries’ translation teams or their trainers of translators. A
general session was provided at a meeting in Rome, Italy, in November 2018, and modular
workshops (for the various types of materials) were provided at a Prague, Czechia, meeting in
March 2019.

•

Provision of a translation training kit so that the international training sessions could be replicated
in countries. The kit included a customisable PowerPoint presentation, materials for hands-on
exercises, confidentiality forms, and so on.

•

Continued assistance to National Centres throughout the localisation process.

Figure 7.1. Example of a VFF

In PIAAC, the implemented LQC processes included:
•

Verification by the Consortium of target versions of the instruments submitted by National Centres
against the source versions, with reporting of residual errors and undocumented deviations and
expert advice where corrective action was needed:
o

For field trial instruments newly developed for PIAAC Cycle 2: full verification of all national
materials.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 191
o

For field trial trend instruments: focused verification of changes requested by National Centres.

o

For trend literacy units: verification of the scoring rules in literacy items using the “highlight in
stimulus” response mode. In addition, countries were asked to test the scoring of these items
formally through a workflow.

o

For main study instruments: focused verification of changes requested by countries to their
finalised field trial national materials (whether to echo changes made to the source version or
at the initiative of the National Centres), and extra global checks for issues impacting item
functioning that were identified in one or more national versions and were considered likely to
appear in additional translations.

•

A final check procedure after National Centres carried out their post-verification revision of
instruments and Consortium technical staff made layout corrections, again with reporting and
follow-up of residual errors and/or unresolved issues.

•

The scope of verification included all translated instruments viewed by respondents: test units, help
and orientations, the entire background questionnaire including interviewer instructions and help
information, the doorstep interview, as well as language-dependent automated scoring rules (for
the “highlight in stimulus” response mode), and the “CAPI workflow” file used by interviewers to
conduct the questionnaire and assessment sessions.

Participation in the development of the source version
Early resolution of potential localisation issues via preliminary scrutiny of source assessment and
questionnaire materials is an upstream LQA process which aims to reduce the difficulties and workload
encountered later downstream. In the context of this so-called translatability assessment, cApStAn
reviewed the first drafts of new cognitive materials and of new BQ items with an eye toward anticipating
adaptation issues, ambiguities, cultural issues or item translatability problems, with suggestions for either
rewording or adding item-specific translation/adaptation guidelines. For the BQ, GESIS experts on
questionnaire translation were involved in the design of new items, providing additional input in terms of
translatability and cross-cultural design. Moreover, a five-country mixed-method online pretest conducted
by GESIS on a set of pre-final items helped to refine items in terms of cross-cultural comparability and
translatability (Meitinger et al., 2018[1]). Feedback from these “early” translation activities was fed back into
the design process.
Throughout the localisation process, cApStAn took care of an errata management process, whereby errors
in the source identified by National Centres or verifiers were tracked in an Excel file that was updated
throughout the instrument preparation process whenever new errata were identified and confirmed by the
item developers. The latest updated list of errata was made available to National Centres and verifiers at
every step of the process. When the first country signed off on their field trial instruments, the errata list
was ‘frozen’ so that any new errata from that point on was left to be corrected at the main study stage. This
ensured that the same errata were corrected in the field trial instruments of all national versions, regardless
of the timing of their finalisation.

Testing languages and translation/adaptation procedures, including double
translation design
Testing languages and translation/adaptation procedures for the BQs
The bulk of the translation occurred in preparation for the field trial. Therefore, the focus in the following
section will be on translation activities prior to the field trial rather than in preparation for the main study.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

192 

languages. These languages include the BQ instruments adapted into different localised versions of

Question types in the BQ and their respective translation needs
Strict trend, soft trend and new questions
With PIAAC being a cross-sectional survey repeated every ten years, the background questionnaire for
PIAAC Cycle 2 included questions used in the PIAAC Cycle 1 BQ, either as is (strict trend) or with some
minor adjustments (soft trend), to support trend analyses and comparability while ensuring the questions
were current. In addition, numerous new questions were developed to broaden the scope of measurement
and add innovative features.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 193
For the translation process, this set-up meant that countries that participated in PIAAC Cycle 1 had to (a)
review – and potentially correct – translations of strict trend questions, b) modify translations for soft trend
questions, and c) develop translations for new questions.

Items assessing social and emotional skills
A somewhat different translation approach was adopted for the new BQ module assessing social and
emotional skills. For these questions, the Consortium centrally provided the translations to the country
teams. In other words, if validated translations for these items already existed, they were adopted for the
PIAAC BQ. Alternatively, cApStAn produced translations, following a double translation and reconciliation
approach. These translations were, whenever possible, reviewed in each language by a domain expert
and native speaker identified by GESIS. During the translation process, countries were asked to review
the translations – a process similar to that implemented for the strict trend translations – and request
changes in case problems were identified. This approach was chosen because it proved to be successful
in a pilot OECD study on social and emotional skills items.

National adaptations and national extensions
Two additional question types need to be differentiated: national adaptations and national extensions.
Adaptations in PIAAC were foreseen for items that, although measuring the same underlying concept,
were in themselves substantively different from country to country and, hence, required country-specific
wording and/or structure (e.g. questions on education, occupation or income). Furthermore, countries were
allowed to include a restricted number of country-specific questions reflecting specific national interests.
All adaptations and extensions were subject to approval by the Consortium.

PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 countries
PIAAC Cycle 1 countries were to re-use their existing translations, adaptations and extensions from the
previous cycle and were to check whether these required any revision. Countries new to PIAAC in Cycle
2 needed to start the process of translation, adaptation and specification of national extensions from the
beginning.

The technological translation environment
Upon finalisation of the international source version of the BQ in the Questionnaire Authoring Tool (QAT),
countries implemented their respective adaptations and extensions using the QAT tool. This process
resulted in country-specific English-language source questionnaires. The Consortium then extracted, per
country, an XML Localisation Interchange File Format (XLIFF) file from the QAT. This file was fed by
countries into the customised OmegaT translation software and formed the basis for the translation
process.

Materials and support provided for and during the translation process
Country teams received an array of material for BQ translation. Apart from the international source BQ in
English, three key translation documents will be presented here: a) the Background Questionnaire
Adaptation Spreadsheet (BQAS), b) the “PIAAC Cycle 2: General Translation Guidelines for the
Background Questionnaire,” and c) the “PIAAC Cycle 2: Field Trial Background Questionnaire Translation
Workflow Overview.”
For each country, the BQAS not only included the common set of international BQ questions but also all
approved country-specific adaptations and extensions. The XLIFF file that each country received for BQ
translation mirrored the content of the BQAS. In the BQAS, a column entitled “Translation Notes” provided

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

194 
colour-coded information on whether items were strict trend, soft trend or new, and further instructions for
the translations (Behr and Scholz, 2011[2]), such as the meaning of a term or phrase or important
characteristics of response categories (see Figure 7.2). The need for these clarifications had been
identified by expert reviews focusing on potential translation problems, translatability assessments and
results of the multi-country mixed-method online pretests (Meitinger et al., 2018[1]).
The BQAS was not the environment for translation; it rather served both as a documentation tool and as
the vehicle of communication between countries and the Consortium during all phases of adaptation,
translation and verification.

Figure 7.2. Extract from the BQAS, including Translation Notes

Because the comparability of survey materials is essential to any meaningful use of cross-national survey
data, countries received a General Translation Guidelines document laying down a quality framework for
BQ translation. This document addressed both the general translation process as well as specific issues
to consider in the actual translation.
The General Translation Guidelines for the BQ outlined the required translation/review approaches
separately for the different types of questions. For the new questions, the guidelines strongly
recommended a translation approach consisting of double translation by two independent translators,
followed by team reconciliation. Double translation allows the identification of misinterpretations or
ambiguities, idiosyncratic wording or simply translator oversights; moreover, it offers stylistic variants from
which to produce a fluent translation. It has established itself as a state-of-the-art approach in questionnaire
translation. For reconciliation, a team approach was strongly recommended as a very efficient method.
Team reconciliation brings together a unique mix of competencies: translators and linguistic experts,
experts in the various domains of the questionnaire (education, labour, etc.), as well as experts in
questionnaire design and survey methodology. This broad range of expertise (translation, domain, design)
is regarded as essential for producing high-quality questionnaire translations (Behr and Shishido, 2016[3];

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 195
Harkness, 2003[4]; Harkness, Edwards and Villar, 2010[5]). Alternatively, as a minimum, a single reconciler
was required, ideally with input from a panel of experts in survey methodology and the various domains
covered by the BQ. Translators were to be skilled practitioners who translated materials into their mother
tongue and were experienced or trained in questionnaire translation. Reconcilers were to have strong
language skills in both source and target languages and be knowledgeable about questionnaire translation,
questionnaire design and the content domains covered by the BQ.
Countries translating into the same language (e.g. German for Austria, Germany and Switzerland) were
encouraged to collaborate by exchanging draft translations or discussing versions; ultimately, however,
they needed to ensure that their translations fit their national contexts and terminologies in particular for
highly specific questions such as the work sections and education sections. Some items were taken or
modified from other surveys or the PIAAC Cycle 1 field trial. Countries could use existing translations for
these as a starting point, but they were asked to carefully vet these and ultimately ensure adherence to
the PIAAC Cycle 2 BQ.
The soft trend questions included changes to the PIAAC Cycle 1 questions to different degrees, such as
mere changes in showcard numbering, textual adjustments to reflect societal or terminological change,
corrections of errors or wording improvements. Often, the existing translations could easily be amended
by country teams. Sometimes, a translation from scratch was necessary (as for the new items). Countries
were equipped with information on changes between PIAAC Cycle 1 and PIAAC Cycle 2 in the BQAS
Translation Notes as well as in separate documents detailing the changes. Changes could directly be
implemented in the translation tool OmegaT.
The translations of the strict trend questions were displayed and locked in the translation tool OmegaT for
PIAAC Cycle 1 countries. Countries could review these translations but not change them on their own.
Every change requested needed to be clearly defined, including documentation of the rationale for the
change, and submitted to the Consortium for approval. This procedure was chosen to ensure that trend
translations were only modified where absolutely necessary, and that preferential changes did not
endanger the measurement of trends. The BQAS served as the medium of documentation and
communication related to these change requests.
The BQ workflow required requests for adaptations to be documented by countries and submitted to the
Consortium for approval prior to the translation process. Many of these adaptations applied to all countries
in the same manner (e.g. all countries had to implement their own education measures). However, some
additional adaptation needs – beyond those that had already been agreed on – were only captured during
the translation phase, so that their approval process took place further downstream. The BQAS also served
as the medium of documentation and communication related to such additional adaptation needs.
The translation guidelines also provided advice to countries on issues to consider during the translation
itself. The translation objective was to produce a questionnaire that maintains the measurement properties
and the meaning of the source questionnaire while being as fluent and understandable as possible in the
target language. The overall task was to strike the right balance between faithfulness and fluency. In
addition, the importance of translation documentation was emphasised, e.g. the documentation of
particular translation decisions or challenges (Behr and Zabal, 2021[6]). The guidelines also presented the
concept of dynamic text, i.e. text segments that are automatically filled in during the interview situation
depending on answers given earlier in the interview. Dynamic text is part of survey programming; it may
not fit in the same manner as all languages (Behr, 2022[7]). Hence, countries were informed on how
dynamic text works and what they should do if they identify problems with their language. For instance,
the translation for “using your hands or fingers for precision work” was supposed to fit into both a present
tense question stem (“How often does your current job usually involve…”) and a past tense question stem
(“How often did your last job usually involve ...”). New items for PIAAC Cycle 2 avoided dynamic text to the
extent possible in order to prevent translation problems.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

196 
The document PIAAC Cycle 2: Field Trial Background Questionnaire Translation Workflow Overview laid
out the overall workflow for the translation and verification of the BQ with a view on facilitating countries’
coordination of their national translations. The document specified that the BQ translation workflow would
be launched upon completion of the BQ harmonisation workflow and follow the Translation Verification
Schedule (country-specific schedule, as negotiated with the Consortium). The document described the
translation elements (e.g. nationally-adapted BQ, BQ interface, doorstep interview questions and
materials), the role distribution and feedback loops, referred to all relevant files and documents, and
described all translation workflow steps. These steps were the following:
•

double translation (countries)

•

reconciliation (countries)

•

verification and review of trend updates (Consortium)

•

post-verification review (countries)

•

layout updates (Consortium)

•

final check (Consortium)

•

final review and testing (countries)

•

final review (Consortium).

Besides these three documents, country teams could draw on additional material for the BQ translation
process, such as: the PIAAC Cycle 2 BQ Draft Conceptual Framework; PIAAC Cycle 1 BQs;
documentation of international changes to PIAAC Cycle 1 items for PIAAC Cycle 2; BQ routing flowcharts;
WIKI user guides targeted at particular roles in the translation process (e.g. translator, reviewer and
verifier); translation schedules set up by the Consortium; instructions and training material for the
translation tool OmegaT.
Furthermore, a translation workshop was held at the NPM meeting in Prague in March 2019 for NPMs and
national staff responsible for the translation process. Translators were welcome to attend this meeting, but
most participated in subsequent national translation trainings. This international translation workshop
offered an introduction to the specificities of the translation of the BQ and covered: different documents,
guidelines and reference material pertaining to BQ translation; BQ translation and adaptation workflow and
timeline; introduction to the BQAS; introduction to the technical environment of the BQ translation;
documentation needs; translation exercises and discussion. The workshop material was made available
to national teams and allowed them to replicate the translation training in their countries with their chosen
personnel.
During the translation and reconciliation process itself, countries were given the opportunity to ask queries
about any problems they encountered (regarding meaning, technical issues, etc.).

Verification
After reconciliation and translation were finalised by the countries, the BQ translations were submitted to
the Consortium along with any documentation on special translation decisions, desired additional
adaptations or changes to strict trend items. The BQ translations then underwent verification procedures,
which are described in subsequent parts of this chapter.

Other instruments
Since PIAAC is a household survey, the selected respondents might have been unable to respond to the
BQ and the assessments because they did not speak the language of administration. To collect some
information from these potential respondents, a set of six background questions was developed and then
translated into the PIAAC languages and into 15 additional languages commonly spoken in the PIAAC

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 197
countries. These six questions were referred to as the doorstep interview. The translations for the doorstep
interview were provided by the PIAAC countries in the case of the PIAAC languages and by cApStAn in
the case of the additional languages listed in Table 7.2.

The technological translation environment
The translation environment for the cognitive instruments was the same as for the BQ translation: the
OmegaT translation software used for XLIFF files exchanged via the PIAAC Portal.
The National Centres were instructed on the principles and mechanics of translation/adaptation of PIAAC
cognitive materials at the Prague NPM Meeting in March 2019. Shortly after the NPM meeting, they
received a ‘translation kit’ that included general guidelines for translating and adapting PIAAC cognitive
materials, as well as a training module with PowerPoint presentations explaining these guidelines and how
they apply to the cognitive domains. It was assembled in a way that allowed countries to replicate
translation training locally. A training webinar for defining the highlight scoring text blocks was organised
separately in June 2019.

Trend and new items and their respective translation needs
As was the case for the BQ, the cognitive instruments in PIAAC Cycle 2 included test items taken from
PIAAC Cycle 1. This meant two different translation and adaptation workflows for those countries that had
participated in Cycle 1.

Trend items
It should be noted that there was a significant platform change, and the items from PIAAC Cycle 1 were
not available in a format that would have been directly usable in PIAAC Cycle 2; therefore, the materials
had to be transferred to the PIAAC Cycle 2 format and platform first. This was done centrally by the
Consortium. The National Centres were then asked to review the trend items using the PIAAC Portal
previews and document their change requests in the VFF designed for this process. The National Centres
were asked to only request changes in the case of outright errors such as:

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 199
•

Layout or technical issues: text overlapping borders, boldface, italics, or underlining missing, or
not matching the source, sentence repeated, spaces missing, etc.

•

Outdated adaptations: prices are no longer realistic; recommendations for time/date notations
have changed since PIAAC Cycle 1, etc.

•

Outright and serious linguistic errors: mistranslation, (relevant) part of the translation missing,
etc.

Once the review and subsequent verification processes were fully completed, the National Centres were
asked to test the scoring rules in the literacy items with highlight scoring mode using the facility available
in PIAAC Portal preview mode.

Materials and support provided for and during the translation process
Similarly to the general guidelines document for the BQ, its counterpart for cognitive materials stressed
the need for very high-quality translation in order to collect internationally comparable data – with the
additional challenge for cognitive materials to “retain the cognitive demand equivalence of tasks as much
as possible.”
The general guidelines included the recommended procedure of double translation by two independent
translators, followed by reconciliation by a third person. The team reconciliation approach, more suitable
for questionnaires, was not recommended, but a review of the reconciled version by national domain
experts was recommended as an additional quality-enhancing procedure.
The general guidelines laid down requirements for translators and reconcilers, addressed
security/confidentiality aspects, issues specific to assessment and questionnaire translation to pay
attention to, the general principles for cultural adaptations (and detailed instructions for the adaptation of
items dealing with currency), and explained the LQC processes that would follow the initial submission by
National Centres of translated materials.
Countries were also given item-specific translation guidelines (also referred to as “translation and
adaptation rules” or “item-by-item notes”) in the VFF used to document the translation/adaptation and
verification process. These guidelines were intended to draw the translators’ attention to possible
terminology problems, translation traps and issues for which adaptations were recommended, desirable
or ruled out.
At the NPM meeting in Prague in March 2019, the National Centres were given workshops on the
specificities of translating the cognitive items. The focus of these workshops was to familiarise translators
with the guidelines for translating and adapting tasks. That is, in addition to stressing the importance of
accurate translations, the workshops were used to emphasise the key role the construct plays in helping
to develop the adaptation guidelines. In order to accomplish these goals, these workshops were used to
provide a brief overview of the construct, demonstrate sets of specific items, and share and discuss specific
guidelines for the proposed items.
Throughout the localisation process (from initial double translations to reconciliation, then post-verification
review, layout adaptation and final check), the National Centres were assisted via email, as well as a
ticketing system dedicated specifically to queries related to OmegaT.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

200 

International verification of the national versions – Field trial
Assignment specification, verifier training
The following was the key “mission statement” for successful localisation taken from the PIAAC Translation
and Adaptation Guidelines:
In order to collect internationally comparable data in the study, the equivalence of all national versions is an
essential requirement, which means that the translation of materials must be of extremely high quality in each
of the national versions used by participating countries. Within the assessment context, an additional goal is to
retain the cognitive equivalence of tasks as much as possible so that each item examines the same skills and
invokes the same cognitive processes as the original version while being culturally appropriate within the target
country.
Essentially, verification is the LQC process put in place to check to what extent National Centres were
successful in accomplishing the above objective and correcting errors as needed. Thus, the verifiers’
mission statement was to:
•

ensure linguistic correctness and cross-country equivalence of the different language versions of
the PIAAC instruments

•

achieve the best possible balance between faithfulness to source and fluency in target versions

•

document interventions for both National Centres and the Consortium.

The verifiers were native speakers of each of the target languages, highly proficient in English as the
source language and as the working language to document their findings. They were trained to assess
whether translation and adaptation guidelines were followed, document possible deviations, insert
corrections as needed, and provide expert linguistic advice. They were knowledgeable about equivalence
issues, translation traps and meaning shifts that were likely to affect response patterns in achievement
tests. They also had experience in assessing the relevance of cultural adaptations in data collection
instruments. They were all familiar with the use of “verifier intervention categories” and verifier comments
in a standardised form.
Verifiers attended a two-day training seminar in Brussels, Belgium, in June 2019, organised by cApStAn.
They were instructed about the PIAAC Portal, the OmegaT software, the particularities of the different
instruments to be verified (BQ, literacy units, numeracy units, adaptive problem-solving units, reading
components), as well as the subtleties of verifying changes to trend items and scoring definitions for the
‘highlight in stimulus’ response mode. The training seminar included presentations and hands-on
exercises.

Overview of verification procedures
The National Centres submitted reconciled XLIFF files for verification via the PIAAC Portal, together with
the appropriate filled-in monitoring instruments (VFF for cognitive units, BQAS for the BQ).
Verifiers were instructed to compare each sentence of the target version of the instruments with the
corresponding sentence in the English source version and:
•

Examine whether the content of the items was equivalent across the two languages, with only
appropriate and needed adaptations (this involved checking compliance with each item-specific
guideline listed in the VFF or the BQAS).

•

Examine whether the target language was linguistically correct and struck the right balance
between faithfulness to source and fluency in the target language.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 201
•

When necessary, propose corrective action in the target language and document these
interventions in English in the monitoring instrument. Documentation involved selecting an
intervention category to identify the type of issue and writing an explanatory comment (see below
for details).

•

Check national versions against the latest PIAAC errata list, which was maintained and regularly
updated by cApStAn.

•

Check that the scoring rules were correctly applied to the trend literacy items using the highlight
scoring mode. None of the new items used this scoring mode.

Verifiers were assisted by cApStAn staff, who also reviewed verified materials, liaising as needed with ETS
on content and/or technical issues before materials were made available to countries.
The verified materials were made available to the countries via the PIAAC Portal. They were advised via
email when a batch of materials was ready for post-verification review and guided to the appropriate online
user guide explaining in detail how to process the feedback further.

Verification and post-verification process – BQ
Verification outcomes and how they were documented
The verifier compared each segment of the national target version with the national source version, taking
into account both general and item-by-item guidelines as well as the comments from the National Centre.
The verifiers’ suggested corrections were documented in columns “3.2 to 3.4 - Verification of the BQAS”,
using the same framework of intervention categories as for the cognitive units. Figure 7.3 shows an
example of a BQAS with a verifier’s intervention.

Figure 7.3. Example of BQAS showing a verifier’s intervention

The verifiers’ suggested corrections were mostly implemented in the materials. (In some cases, verifiers
made suggestions that were left to the country’s initiative. Such exceptions were explicitly stated in the
BQAS because, by default, verifiers’ entries in the BQAS described problems that they had corrected.)

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

202 
XLIFF files were verified using OmegaT, which does not offer “track changes” mode. Instead, to show
where verifiers intervened, the National Centres received automatically created difference reports showing
segment by segment what had been changed. Figure 7.4 shows an excerpt of a DIF report.

Figure 7.4. Example of a verifier intervention in a BQ DIF report

For strict trend items, the process was different: the National Centres had been asked to document their
change requests in the BQAS. Such trend segments were ‘locked’ in the OmegaT project, so the National
Centres were not able to make such changes therefore, the verifier was asked to a) first evaluate if the
change was acceptable: linguistically correct, in line with the rest of the BQ, a correction to an actual error
rather than a purely preferential change; and then 2) if the change was considered acceptable, implement
it in the OmegaT project, first unlocking the segment.

Processing verification feedback – Step 1: Consortium review
Once the verification step was completed, the files were made available to the BQ translation expert at
GESIS, who would then consult with the question developers at ROA or further GESIS experts on
education, training and social and emotional skills, as needed. The BQ translation expert would review all
issues flagged for their attention in the BQAS and provide their recommendation for the issue at hand in
the column ‘Post-verification comment (GESIS)’. Figure 7.5 shows an example of a Consortium comment.

Figure 7.5. Example of a Consortium comment in the BQAS

For changes in strict trend items, the Consortium member would either approve or reject the change by
selecting the corresponding status marker in column ‘Status’, see Figure 7.6 below.

Figure 7.6. Example of an approved change in a trend item in the BQAS

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 203
If the Consortium member rejected a change that the verifier had accepted (and implemented), the change
would be undone during the final check step.

Processing verification feedback – Step 2: Post-verification review by the National Centre
National Reviewers were advised to keep three different files open during the post-verification review:
•

the OmegaT project

•

the BQAS (one tab per BQ section)

•

the DIF report.

Additionally, they were asked to preview the programmed version of the BQ.

Consulting/annotating the BQAS
The National Reviewer was asked to review all verifier feedback in the BQAS, consulting the DIF report,
the XLIFF file within the OmegaT package and the PIAAC Portal preview as needed. If the National
Reviewer agreed with the change made, they were asked to confirm this by adding ‘OK’ in the column
‘National Centre Post-verification comment’. If the National Reviewer disagreed with the change, they were
asked to add a comment. If the change they wished to reject (or modify) was one labelled as “requires
follow-up”, they were also requested to explain their rationale for rejecting the change. If the change did
not have this label, a justification for rejecting the change was not a requirement.

Finalising XLIFF files
The verifier addressed most of the issues identified during verification, and the corrections/suggestions
were not “provisional” (not in “track changes” mode). Therefore, verified XLIFF files only needed to be
edited if the National Reviewer wished to undo or further modify a correction – or to implement a suggestion
listed in the BQAS but not actually implemented by the verifier. As a reminder (see previous section), in
case of undoing or further modification with regard to a change requiring follow-up, the National Reviewer
had to enter an explanation in the BQAS.

Returning the annotated BQAS and updated OmegaT package
After completing the above steps, the National Reviewer had to return the OmegaT package containing
the XLIFF files as well as the BQAS with the ‘National Centre Post-verification comment’ column filled in.
Figure 7.7 shows an example of a BQAS returned by a National Centre, showing where the National
Reviewer has commented on the verifier proposal.

Processing verification feedback – Step 3: Layout adaptation
Once the National Centre had completed the post-verification review, the files were moved to the ‘layout
adaptation’ step. In this step, the layout adaptation team at ETS addressed all layout issues raised by the
National Centre and by the verifier. An example of a layout comment is available below in Figure 7.8.

Figure 7.8. Example of a layout comment in the BQAS

For the BQ, the nature of ‘layout issues’ was a little different from the cognitive units. An issue corrected
at this point could, for example, be an update in the national source version rather than an actual layout

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 205
correction. But it could also be a layout issue in a more traditional sense: widening column width or adding
space where text did not fit properly.

Processing verification feedback – Step 4: Final check by cApStAn
In the course of the final check procedure, the following issues were checked:
•

All changes labelled as ‘requiring follow-up’ were double-checked for correct implementation.

•

All trend changes were checked for the (rare) cases where the verifier’s decision and the
Consortium’s decision were not in line: either to undo a change accepted and implemented by the
verifier, if the Consortium felt the requested change should not be made; or to make a change, if a
change request previously rejected by the verifier was deemed acceptable by the Consortium. All
additional post-verification changes made by the National Centre were verified.

•

The latest errata were checked and corrected in the national version.

Processing verification feedback – Step 5: Final review and testing by the National Centre
Once the final check was completed and files were released for final review on the PIAAC Portal, the
National Centre was asked to review all pending issues in the BQAS. If there were no further issues, they
were asked to proceed to the testing step.
The QAT was used to test the fully translated BQ. The QAT could be launched in a run-time mode using
the final translated XLIFF, which allowed national team members to complete the BQ with the full
functionality of a real testing session. The Consortium created a set of testing scenarios which consisted
of specific responses that would test the major routing branches of the questionnaire. National team
members completed all scenarios, documented the outcomes and exported the results of the test runs
from the QAT. These materials were submitted to the Consortium for their review.
The QAT team at ETS performed a final review of each national BQ. The final check was a technical review
to make sure nothing was missing before data collection (e.g. checking that the translated interface was
integrated correctly and that the national team completed testing).

International verification of the national versions – Main study
The guiding principle of PIAAC main study translation/adaptation and verification activities was to control
and limit the changes made by National Centres to their finalised field trial instruments and carry out a
verification focused on just these changes.
The MS instrument preparation process followed after the analysis of the field trial data. It focused on
identifying and correcting errors in the PIAAC instrumentation based on analysis of the field trial data and/or
experiences from the fieldwork. A number of cognitive and BQ items that did not work well in the field trial
for a majority of countries were dropped. In addition, National Centres were asked to review more closely
those items that functioned well overall but had differential item behaviour in their country. Countries were
asked to document the possible source of error and propose solutions in the MS BQAS for the Background
Questionnaire or an IFF for cognitive units. National Centres did not have editing access to any of the
instruments during this process; they reviewed the materials on the PIAAC Portal, and the verifiers
implemented all changes approved by the verifiers and the Consortium.
The rest of this chapter will describe the verification processes for the requested field trial-to-main study
changes per instrument. Countries were instructed on procedures at the virtual NPM meeting in January
2022.

Main study verification of the BQ
In the main study, the principle was to verify only changes made to the BQ since the field trial. The
environment and process were similar to the process for the cognitive units: The National Centres could
not edit the BQ; instead, they reviewed the MS BQ on the PIAAC Portal and used the BQAS created for
the main study to document their change requests. Unlike cognitive units, the items that showed differential
item functioning were not flagged within the BQAS. Instead, the Consortium provided each country with a
PIAAC Field Trial Report that covered different types of analyses, identified issues to consider for the main
study, and, if appropriate, offered some recommendations.
Countries were provided with instructions explaining how to record their change requests in the BQAS and,
what requests would be accepted and corrected or not. Types of corrections that would be accepted
included:
•

mistranslations (translation does not correctly reflect the meaning of the source)

•

incorrect adaptations

•

correcting substantial inconsistencies

•

deleting national extension questions

•

retaining deleted international questions as national extension questions for the MS

•

typos/misspellings

•

punctuation issues when they impact understanding

•

serious layout issues (i.e. text not fully visible on the screen).

Change requests in the following categories would be rejected by default:
•

editorial changes (i.e. changes for better fluency or other improvements when the original
translation was correct)

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

210 
•

renegotiating adaptations

•

minor punctuation changes or capitalisation issues

•

minor spelling or punctuation inconsistencies (e.g. adding/removing the final period at the end of
response options)

•

cosmetic layout changes

•

adding new questions not included in the FT.

Figure 7.14 shows an example of an MS BQAS documenting the main study verification process of a
change requested by the National Centre.

Figure 7.14. Example of MS BQAS with a change request from the National Centre and verifier
feedback

The proposed corrections were, in a first step, reviewed by the questionnaire developers at ROA, including
consultation with GESIS (on education, training and social and emotional skills) as needed. Corrections
could receive the status “approved”, “approved pending verification”, “additional questions” or “declined”.
In the verification step, verifiers centrally implemented the approved translation changes and further
consulted with GESIS/ROA as needed. In the final review and testing stage, the National Centres signed
off on the final version of the main study after having checked the changes implemented by the Consortium
and having completed a set of testing scenarios on their BQ.
Unlike in the field trial verification workflow, the post-verification review was not followed by a final check
whereby the verifier would systematically check the BQAS for any pending issues. Instead, it was passed
on to ETS for a final review. If there were remaining linguistic issues that needed to be corrected at this
point, ETS would pass the files on to cApStAn outside the PIAAC Portal workflow.

Main study verification of cognitive units
The starting point of the process was the IFF. One single IFF, one tab per each of the six batches (Trend
Literacy, Trend Numeracy, New Literacy, New Numeracy, Adaptive Problem Solving, Helps and
orientations) was prepared and made available to National Centres with instructions to document the
revisions they wished to make in the field trial instruments. The Consortium gave a strong recommendation
to limit these to corrections of errors, avoiding cosmetic or stylistic changes. The Consortium flagged items
in the IFF that demonstrated differential item behaviour in the field trial analyses so that the National
Centres could pay more attention to identifying potential linguistic issues in these items.
Countries were provided with instructions explaining how to record their change requests in the IFF and
what requests would be accepted and what requests would not. Types of corrections that would be
accepted included:
•

mistranslations (translation does not correctly reflect the meaning of the source)

•

incorrect adaptations (e.g. incorrectly adapted currency in a numeracy item)

•

text appearing untranslated (i.e. in the source language)

•

literal/synonymous match not kept
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 211
•

typos/misspellings

•

punctuation issues when they impact understanding

•

serious layout issues (i.e. text not fully visible).

While change requests in the following categories would be rejected by default:
•

editorial changes (i.e. changes for better fluency or other improvements when the original
translation was correct)

•

punctuation changes when the understanding was not impacted

•

minor spelling or punctuation inconsistencies (e.g. adding/removing the final period at the end of
response options)

•

cosmetic layout changes

•

changes that would make the item easier/more difficult than in the source language

•

changes that would bring two national versions of a country closer to each other, while both were
already correct.

Figure 7.15 shows an example of an IFF documenting the main study verification process of cognitive
units.

Figure 7.15. Example of IFF with a change request from the National Centre and verifier feedback

After this pass by countries, the materials moved to the verification phase.
Verifiers evaluated the requests in terms of linguistic correctness, equivalency to source, and consistency
across materials as well as provided an opinion on whether the request was to correct an error, make an
improvement or a preferential edit. Based on these aspects, the verifier either implemented the change as
requested by the National Centre, implemented it with further edits, or, if considered unacceptable, did not
implement it. There was also an option for “follow-up required” if the verifier needed further clarification
from the National Centre before agreeing to a change.
After the verification of the changes from the field trial to the main study was completed, the IFF was
passed on to the Test Developers for comments and to the Layout Adaptation team for correcting residual
layout issues, after which the IFF, as well as the updated Portal previews, were made available to the
National Centres. In this post-verification review, the National Centres were asked to check that their
requested changes had been correctly implemented. Or for changes rejected by the verifier, whether the
National Centres accepted the rationale for rejection or wished to provide additional justification for insisting
on the change.
As in the field trial verification workflow, the post-verification review was followed by a final check whereby
the verifier checked the IFF for any pending issues, corrected them and passed the results to the National
Centre for final review and testing. If further issues were identified, the IFF was returned to the final check
step as many times as needed until the National Centre was ready to sign off on their main study units,
which completed the instrument preparation workflow.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

212 
Main study verification of the help screens and orientations
The process for the main study verification for the tablet tutorial, helps and orientation modules was
essentially the same as that for cognitive units. National Centres were asked to review their field trial
screens and request changes, if needed, in the IFF. However, unlike in the cognitive units, in the tutorial,
help and orientation modules, substantial changes were introduced in the source after the change request
process had already been launched and IFFs made available to the countries. When the National Centre
submitted the files for verification, the initial files were replaced with the updated main study files, and the
original tab in the IFF was replaced with an updated one that listed all the edits made in the source. The
verifiers were then asked to implement these changes while verifying the National Centre’s change
requests. It was then the National Centre’s task to review the update made by the verifier. Figure 7.16
shows an edit like this and the subsequent documentation by the verifier and the National Centre.

8. Survey weighting and variance
estimation
Wendy Van de Kerckhove, Laura Alvarez-Rojas, Tom Krenzke, and Leyla Mohadjer, Westat

This chapter outlines the methods used to compute sampling weights and
estimate variances using replicate weights. It explains the purpose of
calculating sampling weights, which is to enable survey estimates to
represent the target population by compensating for non-response and
coverage bias. The chapter details the steps involved in the weighting
process, including adjustments for non-response and calibration to control
totals. Additionally, it describes the replication approach and multiple
imputation approach used for variance estimation to account for the
complex survey design and measurement errors.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 215

Introduction
This chapter describes the methods used to compute sampling weights and estimate variances using
replicate weights. The purpose of calculating sampling weights for PIAAC is to permit inferences from
sampled persons to the population from which they were drawn and to have the tabulations reflect
unbiased estimates of the population totals. Sampling weights can be considered as estimated measures
of the number of units in the target population that a sampled case represents. Weighting incorporates
several features of the survey, including the probabilities of selection of units in the sample and adjustments
for non-response and any known differences between the selected sample and the total target population.
Differences between the sample and the population may arise because of sampling variability, differential
response rates or coverage rates among subgroups of the population, and other types of response errors,
such as misclassification or measurement error.
In PIAAC, survey weighting was performed to accomplish the following objectives:
•

to permit unbiased estimates by compensating for possible disproportionate sampling of various
subgroups in the sample

•

to minimise biases arising from differences between respondents and non-respondents

•

to compensate for non-coverage in the sample due to inadequacies in the sampling frame or other
reasons for non-coverage

•

to bring data up to the dimensions of the population totals

•

to reduce sampling errors by using auxiliary data on population characteristics that are known with
a high degree of accuracy

•

to facilitate the estimation of variances using the replication approach.

Survey weighting
Weighting involves designing adjustment factors to account for variable probabilities of selection, and to
reduce potential non-response bias, deficiencies in the sampling frame and other complications that may
arise during the sample selection process. This section describes the standard weighting steps employed
in PIAAC. Countries were required to follow the weighting process outlined in the PIAAC Weighting and
Variance Estimation Plan produced by the Consortium, which followed the standards and guidelines in
Section 14 of the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines.1 This plan described the weighting process,
including the weighting steps, treatment of different disposition codes, calculation of weighting adjustment
factors, assignment of variance strata and variance units, and creation of replicate weights. Using the
weighting approach described in the Weighting and Variance Estimation Plan for all countries ensured
comparable estimates of proficiency and their sampling error across countries.
A final weight is required for each sampled person with a completed background questionnaire (BQ) and
BQ literacy-related non-respondents (LRNRs) with completed doorstep interviews. There were a number
of steps in the development of the final weights intended for use in the estimation and analysis:
•

assignment of a household base weight to each sampled household to compensate for differential
probabilities of selection (for screener countries only) 2

•

household-level eligibility and non-response adjustments to reduce potential biases arising from
differences between respondents and non-respondents (for screener countries only)

•

assignment of a person base weight to each sampled person to compensate for differential
probabilities of selection

•

person-level eligibility adjustment (for registry countries only) and non-response adjustments3

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

216 
•

trimming to reduce the impact of large weights, if necessary

•

calibration of the person weights to independent control totals to compensate for non-coverage in
the sample due to deficiencies in the sampling frame.

The following sections describe each of the weighting steps in detail. A summary of the adjustment factors
and resulting weights at each weighting step is provided in Tables 8.1 and 8.2 for registry and screener
countries, respectively.

Preliminary steps in weighting
Countries were responsible for selecting the variables that were used in their non-response and calibration
weighting adjustments. Prior to weighting, countries were required to evaluate the variables being
considered for the weighting adjustments in their PIAAC sample.
For the non-response adjustment, variables needed to be available for all eligible units and be related to
proficiency and response propensity. The pool of potential non-response adjustment variables came from
the sampling frame (and/or the screener) or other external sources. A common source of non-response
adjustment variables for screener countries was a country census. For registry countries, the registry data
were highly beneficial during the non-response adjustment.
For the calibration adjustment, all variables selected by countries were required to have reliable control
totals and be available for all BQ respondents and LRNRs who completed the doorstep interview. The
quality of the data from the external sources had to exceed the quality of data from PIAAC (e.g. the mean
square errors of the external estimates needed to be smaller than those of the uncalibrated estimates from
the survey). The concepts, definitions and coverage of the data (counts) from the external sources needed
to be the same as those employed by PIAAC. Additionally, the year of the control totals needed to be as
close to the data collection period as possible, ideally covering the same time period as the field period.
Variables used for non-response adjustment and in calibration must have less than 5% missing data. If the
amount of missing data of the variables used in weighting adjustments did not exceed the 5% threshold,
countries were required to follow the weighting standards and guidelines on imputing for missing data.

Household-level weighting adjustments
This section outlines the weighting process at the household level for screener countries, which included
the creation of the household base weights that reflected the household selection probability and were
adjusted for unknown eligibility and non-response to the screener.

Household base weights
For screener countries, the household base weight was assigned to all sampled households and was
computed as the reciprocal of the household selection probability. For screener countries with a multistage
sample design, the household selection probability corresponded to the product of the conditional selection
probabilities at each stage. For example, if households were selected within primary sampling units
(PSUs), then the household base weight would be
𝑊𝑘 =

1
𝑃ℎ𝑖 𝑃𝑘|ℎ𝑖

,

where Phi is the probability of selecting PSU i in stratum h, and Pk|hi is the conditional probability of selecting
household k within PSU i of stratum h.
The household selection probability also reflected any duplicate records in the sampling frame or any
changes to the subsampling procedures.

Household unknown eligibility adjustment
Before any household-level non-response adjustment was applied, an adjustment for unknown eligibility
was performed if the eligibility status of some households could not be determined. In this step, a portion
of the weights of the households with unknown eligibility status (i.e. whether they contained a person aged
16 to 65) was distributed to ineligible cases. An adjustment factor was computed as the proportion eligible
among those with known eligibility status to down-weight the cases with unknown eligibility status
(accounting for an estimated proportion that was ineligible). The down-weighted unknown eligibility cases

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 219
were then treated as eligible non-respondents. This adjustment was done within weighting cells defined
for the unknown eligibility adjustment (see Table 8.4).

Household non-response adjustment
For the screener non-response adjustment, the non-respondents were divided into two categories. The
first consisted of cases involving non-literacy-related non-response. Examples of this category included
refusals and non-response due to speech impairment. Non-literacy-related non-respondents were likely to
be similar to respondents with respect to proficiency scores. The second category was literacy-related nonresponse. Language problem was the only type of literacy-related non-response at the screener level.
Households with this type of non-response were presumed to differ from responding households with
respect to proficiency. Therefore, the weighting procedures adjusted the weights of the respondents to
represent the non-literacy-related non-respondents only. The weights of the LRNRs were not adjusted
during the screener-level non-response adjustment because their proficiency was expected to differ from
that of respondents. The contribution of the screener level literacy-related non-response to the total
population was accounted for by the literacy-related non-response adjustment carried out at the person
level (background questionnaire stage) involving the doorstep interview completes and assessment
LRNRs.
The next step in the weighting process was to adjust the unknown eligibility-adjusted weights to reduce
potential bias as a result of non-response to the screener. An adjustment was made to distribute the
screener unknown eligibility-adjusted weights of the non-literacy-related non-respondents to the screener
respondents. The non-response adjustment was performed within cells that were defined based on preselected weighting variables that were found to be related to proficiency and to response propensity (see
Table 8.4). Within each adjustment cell, the household unknown eligibility-adjusted weights of nonrespondents were redistributed over a relatively large pool of cases (approximately 30 or more
respondents). Additionally, the amount of variation in the non-response adjustment factors was kept to a
minimum by limiting the maximum allowable non-response adjustment factor, which was a function of the
achieved screener response rate.

Person-level weighting adjustments
This section describes the process of creating the person-level weights, including the computation of
person base weights; the person unknown eligibility adjustment that applied to registry countries only; the
non-response adjustment procedure designed to reduce potential non-response bias; the calibration of
weights to control totals; and the general trimming procedure used to reduce the impact of extreme weights.

Person base weights
For screener countries, the person base weights accounted for both non-response to the household
screener and differential within-household selection rates. The person base weights were computed as
the product of the household non-response-adjusted weight and the reciprocal of the within-household
person selection probability.
For registry countries, the base weight for each sampled person was computed as the reciprocal of the
person selection probability.

Person unknown eligibility adjustment
For registry countries, an adjustment for person unknown eligibility was performed if the eligibility status of
some sampled persons could not be determined due to the inability of the survey to locate and interview
these selected persons not residing at the address listed in the registry (see Chapter 19 for a discussion

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

220 
on inaccessible sampled persons). In the person unknown eligibility adjustment, a portion of the person
base weights of the sampled persons with unknown eligibility status was distributed to the ineligible cases.
An adjustment factor was computed as the proportion eligible among those with known eligibility status to
down-weight the cases with unknown eligibility status (accounting for an estimated proportion that was
ineligible). The down-weighted unknown eligibility cases were then treated as eligible non-respondents in
the non-response adjustment.

Person non-literacy-related non-response adjustment
For the non-response adjustment, the non-respondents were divided into two categories. The first category
consisted of non-literacy-related non-respondents (e.g. refusals and non-response due to speech
impairment). They were likely to be similar to respondents with respect to proficiency scores. The second
category was literacy-related non-response (LRNR). Types of literacy-related non-response include
language barrier, reading and writing difficulty, and learning-mental disability. Sampled persons with this
type of non-response were presumed to differ from respondents with respect to proficiency. Therefore,
LRNRs received a different treatment than non-literacy-related non-respondents.
As mentioned earlier, for screener countries, an adjustment was made to distribute the person base
weights of the non-literacy-related non-respondents and sampled persons with a disability to the
respondents’ weights.
For registry countries, excluded inaccessible sampled persons were treated as non-literacy-related nonrespondents in weighting. An adjustment was made to distribute the person unknown eligibility-adjusted
weights of the non-literacy-related non-respondents, sampled persons with a disability, and down-weighted
unknown eligibility cases to respondents.
The non-response adjustment was performed within cells that were defined based on pre-selected
weighting variables found to be related to proficiency and to response propensity (see Table 8.4). Within
each adjustment cell, the person base weights (for screener countries) or unknown eligibility-adjusted
weights (for registry countries) of non-respondents were redistributed over a relatively large pool of cases
(approximately 30 or more respondents). Additionally, the amount of variation in the non-response
adjustment factors was kept to a minimum by limiting the maximum allowable non-response adjustment
factor, which depended on the achieved BQ response rate.

Person literacy-related non-response adjustment
The weighting adjustment for LRNRs includes the screener LRNRs (if applicable), BQ LRNRs and the BQ
respondents who are assessment literacy-related non-respondents.
For screener countries, the weights of the BQ LRNRs with a doorstep interview completed and assessment
LRNRs were adjusted to account for the screener LRNRs and BQ LRNRs without a doorstep interview
completed. This adjustment assumed that the LRNRs to the screener, BQ and assessment were similar in
proficiency.
For registry countries, the weights of the BQ LRNRs with doorstep interview completed and assessment
LRNRs were adjusted to account for the weights of the BQ LRNRs without the doorstep interview
completed.
Involving the assessment LRNRs in the literacy-related non-response adjustment offered several
advantages. This approach (1) reduced the mean square error in the resulting estimates, (2) provided
stability in the weight adjustment and reduced the variations in the weights and in the estimates,
(3) reduced bias under the assumption that the assessment LRNRs were more similar to the BQ LRNRs
than the BQ non-literacy-related non-respondents, and 4) addressed the issue that sampled persons may

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 221
or may not have completed the BQ because of an arbitrary reason (e.g. unavailable bilingual interviewer
or interpreter).

Calibration
To address undercoverage bias, to reduce the mean square error of estimates and to create consistency
with statistics from other studies, the next weighting step was to adjust the survey weights to match
population control totals. At a minimum, weights were benchmarked to control totals for age and gender.
Respondents who completed the BQ and BQ LRNRs with the doorstep interview completed (because they
are part of the target population) received a final weight and were included in the calibration. If the
Consortium performed the weighting adjustments, one iteration of calibration, trimming (if necessary) and
recalibration was performed following the non-response adjustments. Not all countries that performed their
weighting included the initial calibration prior to trimming.
Three main calibration techniques employed by countries are post-stratification, raking and generalized
regression estimators (GREG). Post-stratification adjusts the survey weights of respondents so that the
weighted sample distribution is the same as some known population distribution (i.e., the sums of the
adjusted weights of the respondents are equal to known population totals for certain subgroups of the
population). The raking procedure uses an iterative procedure to adjust the survey estimates to the known
marginal totals of several categorical variables. The GREG estimator is a model-assisted approach that
can be used to adjust weights to exploit explicitly the relationship between a survey variable and auxiliary
variables.

Trimming the outliers
Even a carefully designed sample could not fully prevent the need for reducing extreme weights. Sample
designs that included the selection of dwelling units had more variability in the weights compared to directly
sampling persons from registries because of unequal household sizes. The use of non-response and
calibration adjustments also introduced variations in sampling weights. Weight trimming introduced some
bias into the sampling weights. However, the trimming adjustment, in most cases, reduced the sampling
error component of the overall mean square error more than it increased the bias as the adjustment was
applied to only a relatively small number of weights (Lee, 1995[3]).
The person weights were trimmed as necessary after the first calibration. Using a design-based procedure,
cells for trimming were formed from groups that were expected to be approximately self-weighting. In each
cell, weights above a cutoff value were trimmed down to the designated cutoff. To define the trimming cut
point, the Consortium examined the coefficient of variation (CV) based on the weights after raking (the cut
point was calculated separately by domain in case oversampling was used for some domains). The
Consortium trimmed the weights that were over 3.5 × √1 + 𝐶𝑉 2 times the median raked weight (within each
trimming cell if sampling rates varied by sampling domains). In a few instances, a review of the distribution
of the raked weights revealed that a different cut point was more appropriate, limiting the trimming to 2%
of the weighted total. Some countries that performed their own weighting used different criteria for trimming.
During trimming, the trimming factor was applied to each replicate weight. After trimming, the weights were
recalibrated back to the control totals.

Weighting quality control checks
Quality control (QC) checks were performed for both the full sample and replicate weights after each
adjustment in the weighting procedure to ensure proper implementation. The Consortium developed a
battery of QC checks to review the weighting process for adherence to the weighting standards and
guidelines and to check weight calculations for reasonableness and accuracy. Performing the weighting
QC checks was essential for verifying that the final weights produced for estimation are appropriate. The

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

222 
PIAAC schedule required the weighting QC checks to be conducted prior to the development of proficiency
scores. The quality standards for weighting were met for all countries; see Appendix 7 on adjudication
outcomes.

Summary of country-specific weighting implementation
This section presents the weighting steps performed for each country, variables used in weighting
adjustments and country-specific deviations from the weighting standards. All participating countries in
PIAAC were responsible for selecting potential weighting variables and preparing files for weighting. The
Consortium was responsible for deriving sampling weights for countries, unless a country chose to do so
themselves because of confidentiality restrictions or other considerations. Countries that opted to compute
their own weights were required to follow the standards and guidelines in Chapter 14 of the PIAAC
Technical Standards and Guidelines and the PIAAC Weighting and Variance Estimation Plan. The
weighting procedures described in the standards ensured that the estimates represent each country’s
target population and reduce the potential for bias due to non-response.

Weighting variables selected for countries
After data collection and data editing, countries were to identify proficiency-related variables for potential
use in the weighting adjustments. As part of the weighting process, the Consortium (or country) then
conducted an analysis to select variables for non-response adjustments that would be most effective in
reducing non-response bias. At a minimum, this analysis was to involve a classification tree or logistic
regression to evaluate the relationship of response status to potential weighting variables. The final set of
variables for unknown eligibility adjustments was based on an evaluation of the relationship of eligibility
status to potential weighting variables, or countries had the option of using the same variables as in the
non-response adjustment. Calibration variables were chosen by the country.
The list of weighting variables for each country is given in Table 8.4. All countries used age and gender in
calibration, as required in the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines. Region (or a geographic
variable) was also used in all countries except Singapore for either calibration or non-response adjustment.
In addition, most countries included in their weighting adjustments at least one variable related to
education, employment status or nationality, which have been shown to be correlated with proficiency.

Benchmark control totals used by countries
Control totals used in the benchmarking process were required to have the same definition and coverage
of the target population as PIAAC (non-institutionalised adults who are between age 16 and 65, including
citizens and non-citizens). If not, the counts from the external sources needed to be adjusted to make them
comparable to the survey estimates. All variables selected for benchmarking must have reliable control
totals available. The quality of data from external sources must have exceeded the quality of data from
PIAAC (e.g. the standard errors, or more generally, the mean square error of the external estimates needed
to be smaller than those of the non-benchmarked estimates from the survey). Table 8.5 presents the
control total variables used in calibration for each country, including its source and exclusions from the
target population.

national core sample and state supplemental samples were calibrated to population control totals and composited.
After compositing, initial trimming was done on the weights of doorstep interview respondents. Then the standard
rake-trim-rake procedure was applied to the combined sample.
