Variance estimation
Inferences will not be valid unless the corresponding variance estimators appropriately reflect all of the
complex features of the PIAAC sample design (e.g. stratification and clustering) and assessment design.
The replication approach is used for estimating variances for the international analyses of PIAAC data.
Under the replication approach, subsamples (also known as replicates) from the full sample are
systematically formed and statistics calculated with these subsamples are used to estimate the variance
of the full sample statistic. The replication approach, in conjunction with the multiple imputation approach
used to derive the plausible values, captures the variation due to the complex sampling and estimation
approaches, including:
•

sample design

•

selection

•

weighting adjustments

•

measurement error through the processing of multiple imputation of plausible values.

The replication approaches available for PIAAC were the following:
•

Delete-one jackknife

•

Paired jackknife

•

Balanced repeated replication (BRR)

•

BRR with Fay’s method.

As the primary tool for the analysis of PIAAC data, the PIAAC Data Explorer (described in Chapter 12) has
been adapted for handling the corresponding replication scheme for the country samples. For a detailed
description on replication methods for different sample designs, please refer to Morganstein (1998[4]).
The delete-one jackknife is also referred to as delete-a-group jackknife, random groups approach or JK1.
The paired jackknife is also referred to as JK2. The JK2 approach, with two variance units per stratum, is
appropriate for sample designs where PSUs are stratified or selected with systematic sampling from a
sorted list. The balanced repeated replication (BRR) approach is also commonly used when strata are
involved, and Fay’s method is a variant of the BRR approach.
Replication methods are applied to surveys by dividing the sample into specially designed replicate
subsamples that mirror the design of the full sample. To form the replicate subsamples, variance strata
and variance units are defined. Each subsample is reweighted to account for the subsampling that
occurred. An estimate is then calculated for the full sample and each of the replicate subsamples. The
variance of the full sample estimate is computed as the sum of squared deviations between each replicate
subsample estimate and the full sample estimate.
The general replication formula is:
𝑉𝑎𝑟(𝜃̂) = 𝑐 ∑𝑖 𝑓𝑖 (𝜃̂𝑖 − 𝜃̂0 )2 ,
where c takes any of the following values:
c = 1, for the paired jackknife (JK2),
c = (g-1)/g, for the random groups (delete-one) approach (JK1),
c = 1 / g, for the BRR approach, and
c = 1/[g(1-k)2]

for Fay’s method.

Other terms in the equation are defined as follows:
𝑓𝑖

A variety of sample designs were employed across the different countries participating in PIAAC.
Replication is adaptable to a wide variety of designs, including simple random sampling, systematic
sampling, stratified designs and multistage cluster designs. The BRR Fay’s approach was the preferred
approach for PIAAC Cycle 2. In general, the BRR method provides better performance for variance
estimation of quantiles, such as median, than the jackknife (JK) methods. BRR with Fay’s adjustment has
the additional advantage of eliminating the undesired consequence of undefined ratio statistics for small
domains by not eliminating any of the sampled units from the replicate estimates.

Creation of replicate weights
Participating countries followed the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines in providing the data
necessary for creating replicate weights. For PIAAC Cycle 2, Canada, Finland, Germany, Norway,
Sweden, Switzerland and the United States were responsible for defining variance strata and variance
units. For the rest of the participating countries, the Consortium defined the variance strata and variance
units. The specification of variance strata and variance units must conform to the design assumptions of a
replication method and should be determined by the type of sampling design that was used to collect the
data (e.g. whether stratification was used and how many PSUs were in each stratum). In addition, in some
cases the sampling strata and PSUs had to be grouped to reduce the number of replicates to fit the sample
design into a replication design that followed the PIAAC standards.
Once the variance strata and variance units were assigned, the Consortium/countries followed detailed
guidelines on how to form and create the replicate weights. First, replicate base weights were created. For
screener countries, the household base weights for the household were replicated. For registry countries,
the person base weights were replicated. Subsequently, all weight adjustments that were conducted for
the full sample were conducted on each replicate weight to capture the variation created, or reduced, by
the weight adjustments.

Summary of country-specific variance estimation implementation
Table 8.7 presents the replication approach employed by each country. For PIAAC Cycle 2, the
recommended variance estimation method was BRR with Fay’s adjustment and perturbation factor of 30%.
While this method was initially developed for designs that involve strata and two primary sampling units
(PSUs) per stratum, it may be extended to cases where many PSUs are sampled from a small number of
strata by creating pseudo-strata within the existing strata (or by using the selection sort order). It can also
be extended to cases where one PSU per stratum is selected by collapsing existing strata. All countries
but France used the FAY method. JK2 was used for France considering their special balanced sample
design. The allowed number of replicates ranged from a minimum of 15 to a maximum allowed of 80
replicate weights.

Recommendations for future cycles
Based on the field trial and main study experience of PIAAC Cycles 1 and 2, the Consortium is proposing
a series of recommendations for future rounds and cycles of PIAAC.
•

Countries should review the Weighting and Variance Estimation document during data collection
and develop the programs needed for the completion of the Sample Design International File
(SDIF).

•

For Cycles 1 and 2, the Consortium provided a programme for extensive quality checks so that
they could be implemented by countries before their submission of the SDIF. These checks were
also incorporated into the Data Management Expert software. A recommendation is that the
programme with these checks should be implemented periodically during data collection and start
doing data cleaning throughout data collection. Waiting to do the checks just before the final
submission of the file showed that this is not efficient, and it took extended periods of time to get a
final file for weighting.

•

Once the SDIF is submitted by countries after data cleaning, the Consortium will make a list of
changes to it and send them together with the updated file to countries for their approval. Once
there is an agreement with the changes implemented, the file will be made available for weighting.

•

The Consortium will compute sample weights for all countries to ensure consistency unless a
country has a reasonable justification (e.g. confidentiality issues) for weighting its own data. The
Consortium computed the weights for most countries in Cycle 2.

•

Countries should review the set of variables used in weighting by other countries (Tables 15.3a, b
and c in OECD (2019[5]) for Cycle 1, and Table 8.4 in this chapter for Cycle 2) to see if any variables
can be added to the weighting process for their country.

•

The same programs used for weight adjustments for the full sample weight must be used (or looped
through) for each of the replicate weights. If the replicate weights are out of alignment with the full
sample weights, it causes significant increase in the variances.

•

Countries need to ensure that the categories of the calibration variables, to be provided in the
SDIF, are the same (in terms of values and meaning) as given in the control totals.

9. Methodologies for scaling the direct
assessment
Usama Ali and Frederic Robin, ETS

International large-scale assessments rely on sampling designs to
efficiently collect data as well as on scaling methods to produce
comparable estimates of population proficiency. Тhis chapter describes the
analyses conducted to ensure that PIAAC data were of sufficiently high
quality, as well as the scaling methods implemented. The outcomes of such
scaling procedures will be presented and discussed in Chapter 10. The
chapter begins by describing the main study (MS) data yield for each
participating country and the analyses conducted to evaluate data quality.
Results indicated that respondents' routing through the multistage and
linear assessment designs, as well as domain position effects, aligned with
expectations. The data quality met PIAAC standards, and each country
collected sufficient data to ensure reliable, valid and comparable outcomes.
Subsequent sections detail the item response theory (IRT) and population
modelling methods used to scale the Cycle 2 data. These sections also
present the results of empirical analyses to validate the assumptions
underpinning the modelling and scaling processes. The final section
outlines the approach and methods used to estimate linking errors to report
trends between PIAAC cycles 1 and 2.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

242 

Introduction
The PIAAC Cycle 2 MS assessment design was developed to provide measurement across a broad range
of literacy and numeracy proficiency levels and to support the reporting of the evolution of literacy and
numeracy proficiency from Cycle 1 to Cycle 2. Major innovations implemented in Cycle 2 included:
•

The development of a tablet-based delivery platform as the single mode of delivery.

•

The development of new numeracy components that, along with the updated reading components,
contribute to the estimation of literacy and numeracy proficiency. The component measures
increase precision at the lower end of the two scales and allow to better characterise what adults
with low levels of proficiency are able to do.

•

The development of an abbreviated background questionnaire (BQ) known as the doorstep
interview (DI) to collect background information on six main background variables from
respondents unable to speak the assessment language.

•

The development of a new assessment of adaptive problem solving (APS).

•

In addition, important adaptive design innovations were developed to the efficiency of the
assessment, providing quality data for scaling despite larger item pools and a sample size that
remained constant.

Descriptive analyses of the test delivery, interviewer data, respondent data and missing data treatments
were implemented to prepare the data for scaling and to ensure that only data that met the PIAAC quality
standards were included in the analysis database. The final database used for scaling includes all valid
PIAAC cases (completed DI and BQ cases) with their final sampling weights.
Scaling analyses were conducted in three phases. In the first phase, IRT calibrations of the full data (from
all countries) were conducted separately by domain. For literacy and numeracy, item parameters were
estimated for the new items on the already established Cycle 1 scales provided by the trend items reused
from Cycle 1 (trend item parameters fixed to their Cycle 1 estimates, although in a very small number of
cases, Cycle 1 item parameters had to be re-estimated because their Cycle 1 parameters did not fit the
Cycle 2 data). For the new APS domain, item parameters were estimated for all the items as the Cycle 2
APS scale was newly established. The IRT calibrations produced common international parameters for all
the items as well as unique national item parameters to optimally fit the data of participating countries when
the international parameters did not fit. In the second phase, a population model 1 was estimated for each
country to establish the relationships between respondent characteristics collected in the BQ and
performance in the direct assessment, based on IRT parameters calibrated in the first phase. In the third
phase, each country’s population model was used to draw ten plausible values for each respondent.
Additionally, linking errors to account for the changes in the literacy and numeracy instruments used in
Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 were estimated.

Data yield and data quality
Examining interviewer-, test- and item-level data confirmed that the PIAAC Cycle 2 tablet platform
successfully delivered, captured and exported the log files, the process data and the item response data
as intended. Most respondents took the necessary time to respond to most, if not all, items in their assigned
forms. The proportions of missing data, including omitted responses (where respondents were presented
with an item but did not provide an answer) and not-reached items, were consistent with Cycle 1. Similarly,
domain position effects were comparable to those observed in Cycle 1.
The design updates made to the direct assessment portion of the cognitive instrument during the PIAAC
Cycle 2 data collection justified additional analyses to verify that the updated instruments functioned as
expected and that data quality remained unaffected. The reasons for this design change and its
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 243
implementation are described in Chapter 4, while the impact of these updates on each country’s outcomes
is detailed in Chapter 10 on Scaling Outcomes.
The following sections describe the data yield and quality analyses conducted and report results obtained.

Data yield
Thirty-one countries participated in PIAAC Cycle 2. Interviewers administered the BQ, followed by the
tablet tutorial, the locator, components (where applicable), and the direct assessment. The MS assessment
design is explained in detail in Chapter 1.
Table 9.1 presents the target and actual sample sizes for each country, including the total country sample
and a breakdown by language (where applicable). It also includes the number of respondents (and their
weighted percentage) who did not take the direct assessment (for whatever reason) but completed the DI
or the full BQ. The direct assessment was offered in 43 country-by-language versions across the
participating countries, as indicated in Table 9.1. The total PIAAC sample across countries included
161 052 respondents. Of these, 158 356 (98.33%) completed the BQ, while 2 696 respondents (1.67%)
took the doorstep interview (as language-related barriers prevented them from completing the full BQ).
Among those who completed the BQ, 4 639 respondents (2.88%) did not answer any items from the direct
assessment. The table further shows the proportion of data collected using the original direct assessment
instruments.
Most countries achieved or came close to their target sample sizes. For countries that fell short, a sufficient
number of cases were collected for the full scaling analyses, including evaluating item interactions (with a
slightly lower minimum item-level sample size judged acceptable). However, in these cases the smaller
sample sizes resulted in larger standard errors associated with their item and proficiency estimates and
fewer subgroups with enough data to be separately reported.

Routing through the cognitive assessment
After completing the background questionnaire, respondents proceeded to the direct assessment, which
consisted of three main sections: the locator, components, and main assessment. Respondents who
scored up to two correct responses in both the literacy and numeracy sections of the locator were routed
to Path 1. These individuals were then only assigned the reading and numeracy components and did not
proceed to the main assessment. Those who passed the locator but demonstrated relatively low
performance (meaning a literacy locator score of 3–6 and a numeracy locator score of 3–5) were routed
to Path 2, took the components and then moved on to the main assessment. Respondents, who
demonstrated stronger performance in the locator (meaning a literacy locator score of 7 or higher and a
numeracy locator score of 6 or higher) were routed to Path 3. A random portion of Path 3 respondents was
assigned to the components followed by the main assessment, while the remaining skipped the
components section and proceeded directly to the main assessment. In all cases, respondents who took
the main assessments were only administered two of the three assessment domains (randomly assigned).
Details about the routing decisions for Paths 1, 2, and 3 are provided in Chapter 1, Table 1.7.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 245
Figure 9.1 illustrates the distribution of respondents across the three paths in each country. As expected,
at the international level, only a small proportion of respondents – less than 2% - failed the locator and
proceeded along Path 1. Approximately 12% of respondents were routed to Path 2, while the majority,
86%, was routed to Path 3.
Only a small proportion of Path 3 respondents – 15.8% across countries – were routed to the components.
The inclusion of respondents from all paths ensured that sufficient data across the full range of proficiency
levels were collected, allowing for the scaling of reading components onto the literacy scale and numeracy
components onto the numeracy scale.

Routing through literacy, numeracy and APS
Each respondent from either Paths 2 or 3 was randomly assigned to two of the three domains (literacy,
numeracy and APS) in the main assessment. Random assignments were expected to produce randomly
equivalent data samples for each domain when administered in the first or second position. The position
effect analyses confirmed similar sample sizes and equivalent samples across domains and positions.
The literacy and numeracy assessments were conducted using the balanced hybrid MST design described
in Chapter 1. Respondents were randomly assigned to either an adaptive path (75% probability) or a linear
path (25% probability). Respondents in the adaptive path were routed to an easier (Low) or more difficult
(High) Stage 2 testlet, based on their performance in the locator (Stage 1), and then to a Low, Medium, or
High Stage 3 testlet. Respondents in the linear path were randomly routed to Stage 2 and Stage 3 medium
difficult clusters.

Data quality
Because PIAAC is a household survey administered by interviewers, data quality analyses focussed on
the way the interviewers conducted the BQ interviews and supervised the cognitive assessment, as well
as data on the ways respondents interacted with the platform and the assessments themselves.
Administering assessments on digital devices makes it possible to collect data on how test takers interact
with and progress through the assessment. Such data (e.g. the time taken to respond to an item, or the
number of actions taken before submitting an answer) known as “process data” (extracted from log files)
provide relevant information for assessing the validity of the actual response data. For example, timing
data can be informative for evaluating the level of engagement over the testing period. Very little time spent
on the assessment usually indicates low effort. Too much time spent could indicate technical problems,
most often associated with the test delivery platform, although it could simply indicate a participant at the
lower or higher end of the proficiency scale. The availability of response times in PIAAC makes it possible
to evaluate administration problems, level of engagement, position effects, relationships of items with
proficiency and between-country differences. In interpreting this information, however, the reader should
keep in mind that PIAAC was not a timed assessment, and respondents had, in theory, the possibility of
spending as much time as they wished on the cognitive assessment without being penalised in the scoring
phase.

Quality of interviews
In PIAAC, as a household survey, interviewers play a crucial role in data collection, as their actions can
influence the quality of the data, including the potential to shorten the data collection period or replicate
responses. While no data was directly collected on interviewers’ behaviour, aggregating information on
respondents’ timing behaviour at the level of the interviewer can reveal anomalies that could be plausibly
attributed to interviewers’ behaviour.
The number of interviews conducted by each interviewer, the timing of each interview as well as indicators
of the interviewee’s response behaviour were analysed. The goal was to identify interviewers who might
have had an unusual proportion of atypical interviews. In such cases, further feedback from the country’s
national team was requested and the information was reviewed by the PIAAC Consortium and the PIAAC
Technical Advisory Group to decide whether some or all of the interviewer’s data was appropriate 2
(Yamamoto et al., 2025[1]).
The OECD Secretariat conducted additional quality checks on the data, expanding on the quality control
procedures set in the Technical Standards and Guidelines. 3 These analyses identified some unusual
response patterns, suggesting that some respondents may not have exerted a reasonable level of effort
in answering the literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving assessment. This may call into question
whether their responses accurately reflect their proficiency. To identify such cases, the OECD relied on
the following criteria: a very short time spent on the assessment, a high share of very rapid responses, a
high share of missing answers, and locator failure (i.e. failure to answer a set of easy questions) from
highly educated, native-born respondents. Anomalies were mostly found in the responses to the cognitive
assessment; the pattern of responses to the background questionnaire did not raise particular concerns.
Disengaged respondents will always exist in surveys, and it is difficult to establish objective criteria to
assess whether a reasonable level of effort was exerted. In some countries (Israel, Lithuania, New Zealand,
Poland, the Slovak Republic and Spain), it was found that many of these respondents were clustered
around a few interviewers, suggesting that the problem may stem from such interviewers not following the
PIAAC protocols. In particular, interviewers were identified for which a high share of their cases met at
least two of the criteria mentioned above. This casts doubts on the quality of all data collected by such
interviewers. The following notes describe in more detail the results of the analysis in these six countries,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

250 
and the actions undertaken by the OECD to improve, to the extent possible, the quality of the published
data.
In Lithuania, New Zealand, the Slovak Republic and Spain, all cases from the identified interviewers (406
in Lithuania, 301 in New Zealand, 356 in the Slovak Republic, and 385 in Spain) have been excluded from
the data used to estimate the population model, which establishes the relationship between the variables
from the background questionnaire and performance on the direct assessment to generate proficiency
estimates. This exclusion enhances the robustness of the model, by ensuring it is estimated based only
on the cases considered to be of sufficient quality. In the absence of definitive evidence of data falsification
or other forms of interviewer misconduct, the responses to the cognitive assessment items still contributed
to the estimation of plausible values for these respondents.
In Israel, six interviewers were identified as having a relatively large share of cases with unusual response
patterns, using the same criteria that led to the identification of cases in other countries. All data from these
interviewers (748 cases in total) have been excluded from the data used to estimate the population model,
which establishes the relationship between the variables from the background questionnaire and
performance on the direct assessment to generate proficiency estimates. This exclusion enhances the
robustness of the model, by ensuring it is estimated based only on the cases considered to be of sufficient
quality.
Moreover, stronger evidence was collected that three of these interviewers breached data collection
protocols throughout the survey or were implausibly productive (conducting a very large number of
interviews in a relatively short period). As this raised additional concerns about the quality of data, the
responses to the cognitive assessment items for all cases of these interviewers were excluded from the
database (572 in total). Plausible values for these cases were then estimated using only their responses
to the background questionnaire (for which no unusual patterns were detected) and the parameters
estimated by the population model.
In Poland, nine interviewers were identified as having a relatively large share of cases with unusual
response patterns of respondents, using the same criteria that led to the identification of cases in other
countries. All data from these interviewers (774 cases in total) have been excluded from the data used to
estimate the population model, which establishes the relationship between the variables from the
background questionnaire and performance on the direct assessment to generate proficiency estimates.
This exclusion enhances the robustness of the model, by ensuring it is estimated based only on the cases
considered to be of sufficient quality.
Moreover, stronger evidence was collected that six of these interviewers in Poland breached data
collection protocols throughout the survey. For instance, some of these interviewers were implausibly
productive, conducting many interviews on a single day. Others did not record interviews or obtain
respondents’ phone numbers, which made validation of interviews more difficult. Yet another interviewer
was found to have falsified seven cases during data collection (cases which were immediately removed
from the dataset as part of the quality control process and are not included in the 774 cases under
consideration in this note). Twenty-seven other cases collected from this interviewer were, however,
validated and remained in the dataset. Since these factors raise concerns about the quality of all cases
completed by these six interviewers, the responses to the cognitive assessment items for all cases of these
six interviewers were excluded from the database (559 in total). Plausible values for these cases were then
estimated using only their responses to the background questionnaire (for which no unusual patterns were
detected) and the parameters estimated by the population model.
In Poland, other cases with unusual response patterns that could suggest possible disengagement or lack
of a reasonable level of effort during the assessment were identified. As these cases were not clustered
within any particular interviewer, they were left in the dataset and treated as all other cases, given the
difficulty of establishing objective criteria to determine whether reasonable effort was exerted, and whether
the results of the assessment truly reflect the proficiency of respondents. While similar cases are present
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 251
in all countries, the number of such cases in Poland can potentially have a significant impact on the
estimated proficiency of the overall population. This should be kept in mind when interpreting Poland’s
results.

Respondents’ engagement
The tablet-based platform captured response time data for all tablet-based items delivered in the
participating countries. Timing data can be informative in evaluating respondent engagement and effort
over the assessment period. Very little time spent on the assessment may be interpreted as low effort,
while more time spent on the assessment (or parts of the assessment) than expected for most respondents
may be an indication of a technical issue. Response time information was compiled for the full assessment
by domain, cluster, or testlet. Domain time by position and by routing path for MST data were also
computed. Overall, the results of the analyses described in detail in the next sections indicate that most
respondents in all participating countries were engaged in the PIAAC Cycle 2 survey, providing the highquality survey data needed for the scaling and reporting of PIAAC cycle outcomes within and across
countries.4

Direct Assessment
Using the original cognitive instruments, Table 9.2 shows that, on average, respondents across countries
spent 65 minutes on the cognitive assessment after completing the BQ. Approximately 25% of respondents
took about 51 minutes (first quartile) to complete the direct assessment, while about 25% took more than
80 minutes (third quartile). After the design update (which modified only the Stage 3 literacy and numeracy
clusters and testlets, along with all APS clusters), respondents spent an average of 59 minutes on the
assessment, with 25% taking more than 72 minutes. As intended, the updated cognitive instruments
reduced the assessment time by seven to ten minutes for most respondents.
The time spent on the cognitive assessment included the tutorial, locator, components (if assigned), and
the two domains (literacy, numeracy and APS) assigned to each respondent. On average, respondents
spent less than ten minutes on the locator, six minutes on the components, and approximately 20 to 24
minutes on each of the two domains they were assigned (Table 9.2).

Locator
The locator test consisted of eight literacy and eight numeracy items, ranging in difficulty from low to
medium. Table 9.2 shows that, on average, across countries, respondents spent ten minutes on the
locator. Approximately 25% of respondents took less than seven minutes (first quartile) to complete the
locator, while about 25% took more than 11 minutes (third quartile).
Components
Each respondent assigned to the reading and numeracy components section was administered
approximately 44 items. All Path 1 and Path 2 respondents, in addition to a random sample of Path 3
respondents (about 12.5%), were randomly assigned to the components. Table 9.2. shows that, on
average, across countries, respondents spent 6.2 minutes on the components. Approximately 25% of
respondents took less than 4.6 minutes (first quartile) to complete the components, while about 25% took
more than 7.3 minutes (third quartile).
Literacy and Numeracy Linear Clusters or MST Testlets
Due to the hybrid MST design implemented for literacy and numeracy, respondents were assigned to
different literacy and/or numeracy paths, each varying in the average and range of item difficulty. As
expected and consistent with the findings from Cycle 1 MS and Cycle 2 FT analyses, the time spent on

the assessment varied by path as shown in Figure 9.7, Panel a) for literacy and Panel b) for numeracy,
illustrating this variation in time by path. For example, comparing across paths, we see that the 75th
percentile of High_High path respondents took close to 35 minutes to complete the literacy part, while the
75th percentile of Low_Low path respondents took close to 20 minutes to complete the literacy part.
When comparing literacy and numeracy, the results followed a similar pattern. The most difficult adaptive
path, a combination of more difficult testlets known as the High_High path, assigned to higher-performing
respondents, required the most time to complete. The less difficult adaptive paths (Low_Medium and
High_Medium), as well as the linear paths, took similar amounts of time, with most respondents (up to the
75th percentile) completing the assessments in just over 30 minutes across countries.

APS Clusters
Respondents assigned to APS were routed through clusters based on the APS linear design, which was
structured to ensure that the time spent would be similar across all cluster combinations. Table 9.2 shows
that, on average, respondents across countries spent 22 minutes on the APS assessment. Approximately
25% of respondents completed the instrument in less than 15 minutes (first quartile), while about 25% took
more than 28 minutes (third quartile).

Classical Item analysis
Classical item analysis (IA) results were provided to countries for final review and validation of item
translation and item scoring. IA and item-level response time analyses also contributed descriptive (nonmodel-based) information for the review of the IRT calibration and item interaction results and to decide
whether any poorly fitting item was to be removed from scaling.
Cluster or testlet position effects were evaluated using IA proportion correct. Results were similar to the
Cycle 1 results. They were small enough that they did not noticeably impact measurement reliability, and
the random balancing of the content domains across positions (assessed in first versus second position)
ensured that bias would be introduced.
Item Analysis
Classical IA included the following statistics:
•

item response category statistics, including frequency and criterion score mean, standard deviation
and biserial correlation

•

item difficulty (proportion or percent correct when expressed as a percentage)

•

item discrimination (biserial and polyserial correlations).

Item response categories included several types of nonresponse and item score categories. An item
response was coded as not reached when a respondent did not answer the item or any subsequent item
in a non-adaptive cluster or an MST path. An item response was coded as omitted when a respondent did
not answer the item but answered one or more of the subsequent items in a non-adaptive cluster or an
MST path. In the computation of the item statistics and the scaling analyses, the not-reached responses
were excluded (i.e. treated as missing or not-administered), and the omitted were treated as incorrect.
The mean score, standard deviation, biserial/polyserial correlation and point biserial/polyserial correlation
were based on the total cluster or MST path score where the item appeared. In literacy and numeracy, IA
was conducted and reported based on the total data as well as the linear data only. Due to adaptation, the
total statistics are not comparable across countries and cycles, and the usual IA statistics evaluation criteria
cannot be used as they are. Thus, reviews focussed mainly on the linear IA statistics.
Statistics for trend items were compared with the computer-based PIAAC Cycle 1 results. International
and country-level IA statistics were evaluated to flag items that worked poorly or differently across
assessment cycles and/or across countries. All the item results were reviewed, but particular attention was
paid to the flagged items by countries, content experts, and psychometricians to determine whether an
item was flawed due to content or translation issues not yet identified or whether the scoring rule was not
applied correctly. Given all the reviews and quality checks that occurred during the development, field trial
and preparations for the main study phases, an item and its data are rarely removed from the main study
analyses.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 257
Position Effects
Item position effects are a concern in large-scale assessments because substantial position effects, if
present, could increase measurement error and may introduce bias in parameter estimation. To mitigate
any potential item position effects, the PIAAC Cycle 2 main survey design balanced the order of the
domains. Table 9.3 shows the average percent correct by position, domain and the average position effects
across all countries. To compare across domains, results were computed based on the linear data for
literacy and numeracy. On average, position effects (expressed as the differences in percentage correct
for assessment domains across different positions) were relatively small: 2.52% in literacy, 1.2% in
numeracy, and 2.06% in APS. The magnitudes of these position effects were similar to what was observed
in Cycle 1 for literacy and numeracy.

Treatment of missing data
PIAAC relies on a complex matrix sampling design and samples of diverse groups of respondents who
have no direct stakes in the assessment and for which participation is fully voluntary. As a result, some
missing data is to be expected and appropriate data treatment, depending on the nature of the missing
data, is needed. Some of the missing data may be relevant to the estimation of respondents’ proficiencies
and some not. Therefore, it is important to appropriately decide which of the missing data is to be ignored
and which is to be treated in a way that reflects the underlying reason for the data to be missing. The
treatment of PIAAC Cycle 2 missing data prior to IRT scaling and population modelling followed the same
approach used in Cycle 1 and prior studies (ALL and IALS).
At the item-level, the following types of missing data and data treatments were applied.
1. Missing by design: items that were not presented to a respondent due to the matrix sampling design
used in PIAAC (see Chapter 1). These were ignored in scaling because they are by construction
unrelated to respondents’ literacy, numeracy and APS skills.
2. Omitted responses: A missing response to an item that was administered to a particular respondent
followed by a valid response (whether correct or incorrect) was defined as an omitted response.
Consistent with Cycle 1, the treatment of omitted responses was decided based on the amount of
time the item was presented and the number of actions the respondent engaged in:
a. If a respondent spent less than five seconds on an item and showed less than the minimum
number of actions necessary to be able to answer the item, the nonresponse was considered
a rapid disengaged response and thus treated as not attempted and ignored in scaling.
b. In all other cases, omitted responses were treated as incorrect and contributed to scaling.
3. Not-reached responses: missing item responses after the last item answered at the end of a cluster
or testlet were considered as not attempted and thus treated as not-reached and ignored in scaling.
At the respondent-level, the number of responses to direct assessment items was considered to decide
whether the respondent data would be included in population modelling. Irrespective of this, all valid PIAAC
respondents received plausible values.
Respondents who completed the background questionnaire may not have been able or were unwilling to
take the direct assessment. Reasons for not responding to the cognitive assessment were categorised by
the interviewer as follows:
1. Refusal to participate for a reason unrelated to literacy, numeracy and APS skills
2. Literacy-related nonresponse (LRNR) is when the respondent is unable to respond due to a
language barrier or a cognitive skill-related disability, thus indicating a deficiency of literacy,
numeracy and APS skills. The doorstep interview was especially designed to collect as much
information as possible on literacy-related non-respondents. However, it was possible that some
respondents completed the full BQ (for example with the assistance of a translator) but then did
not proceed to the direct assessment because of language or other literacy-related barriers. As a
consequence, two sub-categories were considered:
a. LRNR cases who took the DI
b. LRNR cases who did not take the DI.
3. Inability to provide a written response due to a physical disability
4. Other unspecified reasons
Except for the DI cases, once the population model was determined, it was applied to these cases as well
as all the others to draw their plausible values. A specific population model was developed for the DI cases,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 259
and plausible values were drawn from it (see Doorstep interview cases section for a description of the DI
population model).

IRT scaling
IRT scaling was conducted to produce the IRT parameters for the new literacy and numeracy items and
all APS items because it was a new domain on a newly created Cycle 2 APS scale. Trend literacy and
numeracy item parameters from Cycle 1 were used as linking items across cycles, and their fit with the
Cycle 2 data was assessed. As indicated in the introduction, this is the first of the three analyses phases
leading to the generation of each respondent’s plausible values.
The next two sections describe the IRT models and item fit statistics used in PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2.
The following section describes the specific IRT calibration and scaling approach implemented to estimate
and scale the international (common) and national (unique) item parameters that best fit the total and the
country-by-language data for literacy, numeracy and APS.

IRT models
As in PIAAC Cycle 1, the unidimensional multiple-group IRT model (Bock and Zimowski, 1997[2]; Von
Davier and Yamamoto, 2004[3]); based on the two-parameter logistic model (2PLM; (Birnbaum, 1968[4]))
for the binary item responses and the generalised partial credit model (GPCM; (Muraki, 1992[5])) for the
polytomous item responses were used for each domain. The 2PLM is a generalisation of the Rasch model
(Rasch Georg, 1980[6]), which assumes that the probability of a correct response to item i depends only on
the difference between the respondent v’s trait level  and the difficulty of the item bi. In addition, the 2PLM
postulates that for every item, the association between this difference and the response probability
depends on an additional item discrimination parameter ai:

Formula 9.1
𝑃(𝑥𝑣𝑖 = 1|𝜃𝑣 , 𝑏𝑖 , 𝑎𝑖 ) =

exp (1.7𝑎𝑖 (𝜃𝑣 − 𝑏𝑖 ))
.

The probability of a positive response (e.g. solving an item correctly) is strictly monotonic, increasing with
. The item discrimination parameter ai characterises how quickly the probability of solving the item
approaches 1.00 with increasing trait level  when compared to other items. In other words, the model
accounts for the possibility that responses to different items do not have the same weight in relation to the
latent trait. The discrimination parameter ai describes how well a certain item relates to the latent trait and,
therefore, discriminates between examinees with different trait levels compared to other items on the test.
One important special case of the model is when 𝑎𝑖 = 1 for all items, in which case, the model is equivalent
to a Rasch model.
The GPCM (Muraki, 1992[5]), like the 2PLM, is a mathematical model for the probability that an individual
will respond in a certain response category on a particular item. While the 2PLM is suitable for items with
only two response categories (dichotomous items), the GPCM can be used with items with more than two
response categories (polytomous items). The GPCM reduces to the 2PLM when applied to dichotomous
responses. For an item i with mi + 1 ordered categories, the probability of obtaining a score of k (0, 1, 2,
…, mi) under the GPCM can be written as:

exp{∑𝑘𝑟=0 1.7𝑎𝑖 (𝜃𝑣 − 𝑏𝑖 + 𝑑𝑖𝑟 )}

Critical assumptions of most IRT models, including the one used in PIAAC, are conditional independence
(sometimes referred to as local independence) and unidimensionality. Under conditional independence,
item response probabilities depend only on the latent trait and the specified item parameters. There is no
additional dependence on any demographic characteristics of the respondents, responses to any other
items presented in a test, or the survey administration conditions. Under the unidimensionality assumption,
a common single latent variable accounts for performance on the full set of items. Analyses of PIAAC
Cycle 1 data showed that these assumptions were appropriate and item parameters have been estimated
for each cognitive domain separately through unidimensional IRT models. These assumptions were also
evaluated to be appropriately met for each domain in which any new items are used (see Chapter 10 for
more details).
These assumptions allow to formulate the following joint probability of a particular response pattern 𝑥𝑣 =

When replacing the hypothetical response pattern with the scored observed data, the above function can
be viewed as a likelihood function that is to be maximised with respect to the item parameters. To do this,
it is assumed that respondents (indexed v=1, 2, …, N) provide their answers independently of one another

Typically, the item parameters that provide the best possible fit to a given data set are estimated by
maximising this function through a process called item calibration. The item parameters can then be used
in the subsequent analyses, such as in the estimation of individual plausible values and population
characteristics. However, it should be noted that IRT modelling does not provide an absolute scale since
any linear transformation of the item and latent trait parameters in the above formula leads to the same
likelihood function (this is often referred to as scale indeterminacy or non-identifiability). Therefore, as part
of the calibration process, a choice must be made for the IRT scale to be determined.
For further information regarding the IRT models discussed, see Fischer and Molenaar (1995[7]), van der
Linden and Hambleton (1997[8]; 2016[9]), or von Davier and Sinharay (2013[10]) for the use of these models
in the context of international comparative assessments.

Item fit statistics
All PIAAC instruments (cognitive assessment and background questionnaires) were adapted and
translated for each participating country into one or more languages. To account for potential cultural and
language differences, optimally scale the item parameters and proficiency estimates across countries, and
link the scales across cycles, a series of multi-group IRT calibrations were conducted separately for each
assessment domain.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 261
In the first run of the series of calibrations, the parameters for the new items were estimated to be the same
common or international parameters applied to all subgroups and the trend items parameters were fixed
to their common or group-specific values from Cycle 1 (further item calibration details are provided in the
next section). As part of the calibration process, the fit of the common item parameters to the data for each
pre-defined group was evaluated to identify item-by-group interactions – i.e. when the fit of the model to
the group data was found to be poor according to a predetermined threshold.
In the subsequent runs, new unique or group-specific item parameters were estimated in the group or
groups in which misfit was found, and the item fit threshold was gradually lowered until the ultimate target
threshold was reached, thus allowing additional group-specific item parameters to be estimated. Using this
stepwise procedure optimise both the model-data fit and the comparability across all groups – keeping
common item parameters for as many groups as possible or minimising the use of unique parameters.
By allowing unique item parameters for items that show item-by-group interactions – in contrast
to excluding such items or accepting poor common item parameter fit – the measurement error is reduced
without introducing bias. The research base for this approach can be found in Meredith (1993[11]), Reise et
al. (1993[12]), Glas and Verhelst (1995[13]), Yamamoto (1997[14]), Glas and Jehangir (2013[15]); Meredith and
Teresi (2006[16]) as well as Oliveri and von Davier (2011[17]; 2014[18]).
Group-level item-fit analyses are a critical part of the scaling analyses described above. Different types of
differential item functioning (DIF) statistics can be used to evaluate the extent to which the IRT model
applied to a group fits the response data collected from that group. In the context of the multi-groups IRT
models used in PIAAC, the extent to which the model-based item characteristic curve (ICC, computed
using Formulae 9.1 or 9.2 for the 2PLM or the GPCM) and the empirical ICC can differ was evaluated
based on the mean deviation (MD) and the root mean square deviation (RMSD) statistics:

where g = 1, … , G is a country-by-language group; 𝑝𝑔𝑜𝑏𝑠 (𝜃) is the empirical proportion of correct responses
𝑒𝑥𝑝
and 𝑝𝑔 (𝜃) is the expected or model-based probability of a correct response given proficiency 𝜃 for group
g; and 𝑓𝑔 (𝜃) is the group-specific density on the respondents’ ability scale (Khorramdel, Shin and von
Davier, 2019[19]; von Davier, 2005[20]). The empirical proportion correct is based on the pseudo counts from
the expectation-maximisation (EM) algorithm that is used to estimate the model (Bock and Aitkin, 1981[21]),
while the expected probability correct is based on the estimated item parameters. The moments of the
group-specific densities are also estimated for each country-by-language group (Xu and von Davier,
2008[22]).
The empirical ICC is obtained from the observed responses across respondents for each item, and the
expected ICC is computed based on the IRT model using the estimated item parameters. RMSD quantifies
the magnitude, and MD quantifies the magnitude and direction of deviations in the observed data from
the estimated common or group-specific ICCs for each single item. However, while MD is sensitive to the
difference in observed and model-based item difficulty represented by the b parameter in Formulae 9.1
and 9.2, RMSD is sensitive to the differences in both item difficulty and item discrimination represented by
the a (or discrimination) parameter in Formulae 9.1 and 9.2.
To demonstrate the use of item fit statistics (RMSD, MD), Figure 9.8 shows one example plot for a
dichotomously scored item estimated via the 2PLM. The figure illustrates how the common item

parameters fit the data from most groups except one. The solid black line is the model-based 2PLM item
response curve that corresponds to the common item parameters; the other lines are smoothed observed
proportions of correct responses along the proficiency scale (horizontal axis) for the data from each group.
The figure indicates that the IRT model-based curve conforms to the observed data, as proportions
of correct responses given the proficiency are quite similar for most countries. However, the data for one
country, indicated by the yellow line, shows a noticeable departure from the common item characteristic
curve and curves for other groups. This item is far more difficult in that particular country, conditional
on proficiency level. Thus, a unique set of parameters would be estimated for this item and group.

IRT calibration and scaling of the PIAAC Cycle 2 data
Using the models and items fit statistics just described, IRT scaling was conducted separately for each
domain through a series of iterative multi-group concurrent calibrations and item fit analyses that
converged to the estimation of common (international) and unique (national country-by-language) group
item parameters. For literacy and numeracy, the scaling of the item parameters was accomplished by fixing
the trend item parameters to their computer-based (CBA) Cycle 1 values. Such constraints for new and
trend items are evaluated in each calibration iteration using item fit statistics to keep its common
parameters or free the item to have its own unique group-specific parameters. For APS, the indeterminacy
of the scale was resolved during item parameter estimation by setting the mean of the slope parameters
to 1.0 and the mean of the difficulty (or location) parameters to 0.0 in each calibration iteration. The reason
for the iterative process is to optimise both the international comparability of the proficiency estimates,
which depends on each group being modelled with mostly common item parameters and each group
model-data fit, which depends on estimating unique parameters when needed to fit the data. This approach
is the same that was successfully used in PISA 2018 and 2022. As a result, all the items used in PIAAC
Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 were estimated and scaled onto common IRT scales. In the case of APS, since all
items were new, a new IRT scale was established. More details on how the iteration process was
implemented and its outcomes are provided in Chapter 10.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 263
As was the case in Cycle 1, a potential difficulty in implementing this approach was the adaptive data
collection for literacy and numeracy. The purpose of adaptive testing is to better match test difficulty with
respondent proficiency and avoid administering items that are either too easy or too difficult. Unlike linear
testing, adaptive testing leads to the respondent samples responding to each item not being representative
of the respondent population – or put in another way, it results in large amount of not-missing at random
data in the full data matrix. Using such data for IRT scaling could lead to bias in the item parameters and
the respondent proficiency estimates (Jewsbury and van Rijn, 2020[24]). To avoid this issue, many testing
programmes use a two-step data collection design that allows for item parameters to be pre-calibrated
through a non-adaptive data collection. Once calibrated, the items are then incorporated into the
operational item pool used in scoring (Glas, 2009[25]). However, in PIAAC (as well as in PISA), this
approach would have required a much larger field trial data collection. Instead, the MST in PIAAC was
designed to support both data collection for scaling and adaptation to improve measurement. This was
done in Cycle 1 by using a probability layer to ensure that each item’s responses were collected from
respondents covering a broad enough range of proficiencies. Results confirmed that adaptive data
collected in such a way could be scaled in the same way linear data are scaled and provide equally
accurate item parameter estimates (OECD, 2013[26]; OECD, 2019[27]).
In PIAAC Cycle 2, the MST design was enhanced to improve the efficiency of the data collection for the
purpose of scaling as well as the efficiency of the adaptation (see Chapter 1). Therefore, the same IRT
scaling procedure was implemented as applied in past PIAAC and PISA cycles regardless of linear or
linear adaptive designs. Then, taking advantage of randomly equivalent linear and adaptive data collected
in PIAAC Cycle 2, further model-fit evaluation adding a linear/adaptive design factor to the calibration
groups – i.e. country-by-language-by-design – was conducted confirming that test adaptation did not
introduce bias in IRT modelling.
Another potential issue to address was the use of the component measures as part of Cycle 2 literacy and
numeracy. In Cycle 1, only reading components were administered, and the measure did not contribute to
the estimation of literacy skills. To incorporate the components data into the scaling in Cycle 2 without
affecting the already established Cycle 1 literacy and numeracy scales, an additional set of calibration and
scaling iterations were conducted after the scaling of the direct assessment was completed. By calibrating
the components as an additional step, after the calibration of the regular literacy items, the component
data did not affect the scaling of the direct assessment items, while the component items were scaled onto
their respective PIAAC scales using the final direct assessment items as fixed. While this could affect the
comparability of estimates at the bottom of the distribution, this was necessary to be able to improve
measurement at the very low end of the PIAAC scales.

Population modelling and multiple imputations
This section describes the population modelling approach that is employed in the analyses of PIAAC data,
which combines the latent regression model for a large number of background variables with the IRT model
for cognitive item responses. It also explains the imputation methodology for obtaining plausible values
and for using them to estimate descriptive statistics for populations and subpopulations. This methodology
provides databases that can be used for secondary analyses of relationships between proficiency and
background variables.
The primary goal of PIAAC is to provide comparative data on the information-processing skills of adults
within and across countries and over cycles, reporting on group-level scores in the domains of literacy and
numeracy in both cycles 1 and 2, and in the domain of adaptive problem solving in Cycle 2 (see Chapter
1 of this report). For large-scale assessments like PIAAC, where the number of items administered to each
respondent is necessarily limited, and the focus is on population characteristics rather than individual
scores, relying on point estimates of individual proficiency could lead to biased estimates of population

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

264 
characteristics due to measurement error, limited item coverage and complex sampling designs. These
assessments differ substantially from individual-level assessments in both item sampling and respondent
sampling complexity. In contrast, the use of multiple imputation (plausible values) helps to mitigate these
biases by accounting for error sources and providing more accurate population estimates (Mislevy,
1991[28]; Thomas, 2002[29]; Von Davier, Gonzalez and Mislevy, 2009 [30]; Wingersky, Kaplan and Beaton,
1987[31]; von Davier et al., 2006[32]).
To provide easy-to-use databases that researchers can use to estimate accurate and unbiased population
statistics, the same general approach adopted in Cycle 1 was followed. This approach incorporates the
IRT scaling of the respondents’ direct assessment data from multiple domains and the respondents’
background data specified as covariates (e.g. gender, country of birth, academic and non-academic
activities, attitudes, etc.) through multivariate latent regression models (von Davier et al., 2006). Data from
multiple cognitive domains are modelled together to increase the accuracy of the population estimates in
each domain by borrowing information from the other cognitive domains. The plausible value methodology
uses the latent regression models estimated from each country's data to impute multiple proficiency values
(plausible values) for each respondent instead of a single point estimate in each domain. The imputation
draws the plausible values from the posterior distributions constructed through the multivariate latent
regression model and the respondent data. The multiple imputations from the posterior distributions can
then be used to appropriately account for measurement errors in the relations between (sub)population
proficiency distributions and characteristics in the background data.
IRT scaling, latent regression and multiple imputation are carried out through the following steps:
1. IRT scaling – estimates the item parameters for each domain to provide comparable scales cross
countries and cycles using the unidimensional IRT models described in Formula 9.1 and Formula
9.2 (see also section “IRT calibration and scaling”).
2. Latent regression – estimates the regression coefficients () and the residual variance-covariance
matrix (∑) using the estimated item parameters from step 1 as true values (Thomas, 1993[33]).
3. Multiple imputation – draws ten plausible values for each respondent on each domain from
posterior distributions of proficiency using estimated  and ∑ (Mislevy and Sheehan, 1987[34]; Von
Davier, Gonzalez and Mislevy, 2009[30]).
Because of the large number of background variables collected, a “divide-and-conquer” approach (Patz
and Junker, 1999[35]) is used to reduce the computational burden of step 2 (latent regression) and to avoid
over-parametrisation. First, all variables in the BQ are contrast-coded.6 Contrast coding allows for the
inclusion of missing responses and avoids the necessity of assuming a linear relationship between the
responses to any question and the outcome variable. Second, a principal components analysis (PCA) is
conducted to 1) remove collinearity among variables when present and 2) reduce a large number
of contrast-coded BQ variables into a smaller number of principal components that are sufficient to account
for a large proportion of the variation in the BQ variables without over-parameterisation. This process is
conducted country by country to accommodate both common BQ variables collected across all countries
and optional specific BQ variables only collected in some countries, and to allow for the estimation of
country-specific relationships between the BQ and the direct assessment data.
The country-specific multivariate latent regression expresses the respondent’s proficiency distributions on
the multi-dimensional scales as a function of covariates (y) in addition to the item responses (x). Based on
Bayes’ theorem, the posterior distribution of skills given the observed item responses and covariates (i.e.
contextual information) is constructed as follows:

Analysis of data with plausible values
If the multivariate latent proficiencies 𝜽𝑣 were known for all respondents, it would be possible to directly
compute any statistic 𝑡(𝜽, 𝒚), for example, subpopulation sample means, sample percentiles, or sample
regression coefficients, to estimate a corresponding population quantity T. However, 𝜽 are latent variables
(not observed) and estimated through measurement models. To overcome this problem, the approach
developed by Rubin (1987) is taken in which 𝜽 is treated as missing data.
Therefore, the value 𝑡(𝜽, 𝒚) is approximated by its expectation given the observed data (𝒙, 𝒚), as follows:

Formula 9.10
𝑡 ∗ (𝒙, 𝒚) = 𝐸[𝑡(𝜽, 𝒚)|𝒙, 𝒚] = ∫ 𝑡(𝜽, 𝒚)𝑝(𝜽|𝒙, 𝒚)𝑑𝜽.
It is possible to approximate t* using plausible values (also referred to as multiple imputations) instead
of the unobserved 𝜽 values. A replication approach (Johnson, 1989[39]; Johnson and Rust, 1992[40]; Rust,
2013[41]); Rust, 2014) is used to obtain a variance estimate for the statistics of interest and to estimate the
sampling variability as well as the imputation variance associated with the plausible values.
As described in the earlier section, plausible values are random draws from the posterior distribution of the
proficiencies given the item responses 𝒙𝑣 , background variables 𝒚𝑣 , and estimated model parameters.
For any respondent, the value of 𝜽𝒗 used in the computation of t is replaced by a randomly selected value
from the respondent’s posterior distribution. Rubin (1987) argued that this process should be repeated
several times so that the uncertainty associated with imputation can be quantified. For example,
the average of multiple estimates of t, each computed from a different set of plausible values, is a
numerical approximation of t* in the above Formula (9.10); the variance among them reflects uncertainty
due to not observing 𝜽𝒗 . It should be noted that this variance does not include any variability due
to sampling from the population.
It cannot be emphasised strongly enough that the plausible values are not a substitute for individual point
estimates (e.g. single test scores). Plausible values are appropriate for accurate group-level inferences,
but they should not be used to make any inferences about individuals. Plausible values are only
intermediary computations in the calculation of the expectations to estimate population characteristics
such as subgroup means and standard deviations. When the underlying model is correctly specified,
plausible values will provide consistent estimates of population characteristics, even though they are not
generally unbiased estimates of the individual proficiencies with whom they are associated (Marsman
et al., 2016[42]; Von Davier, Gonzalez and Mislevy, 2009[30]). Other ways exist to estimate proficiency of
single respondents (e.g. bias-corrected maximum likelihood estimates, which are consistent estimates of a
respondent’s proficiency, or Bayesian posterior mean estimates, which provide minimum mean squared
errors with respect to a reference population). Point estimates that are optimal for individual respondents
have distributions that can produce non-optimal and biased estimates of population characteristics (Little
and Rubin, 1983[43]). Plausible values, on the other hand, are constructed explicitly to provide consistent
estimates of population statistics. For a further discussion of plausible values, see Mislevy et al. (1992[36])
Once the plausible values for each respondent have been produced (in PIAAC U=10 plausible values are
produced for each respondent for each domain), they can be employed to estimate the value of a

2. Calculate the sampling variance of T1. Denote the result V(T1).

for u = 1,2,…,U.

Example for partitioning the estimated error variance
The standard errors of mean proficiencies, percentages and percentiles play an important role in
interpreting subpopulation results and in comparing the performances of two or more subpopulations. The
resampling standard errors reported by PIAAC are statistics whose quality depends on certain features of
the samples from which the estimates are obtained. In certain cases, primarily when the standard error is
based on a small number of respondents, the mean squared error associated with the estimated standard
errors may be quite large.
The following example illustrates the use of plausible values for partitioning the error variance. Tables 9.4
to 9.6 present data for nine subgroups of respondents with differing employment status (variable C_Q07:
1 = full-time employed or self-employed; 2 = part-time employed or self-employed; 3 = unemployed; 4 =
pupil or student; 5 = apprentice or internship; 6 = in retirement or early retirement; 7 = permanently
disabled; 9 = fulfilling domestic tasks of looking after family; 10 = other). Ten plausible values were
calculated for each respondent for each scale (domain). Each column in these tables presents the means
of these ten plausible values.
The error variance, or squared standard error, of the mean plausible values, differs greatly for the
subgroups. The error variance reflects a component of error with regard to the lack of precision of the
measurement instrument and a component of error with regard to sampling. The variance can be reduced
by either increasing the precision of the measurement instrument (for example, increasing the number of
items) or increasing the sample size. The resampling method was used to estimate the variance due to

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

268 
sampling using each set of imputed values. This component of variance is similar across the ten plausible
values; the size is influenced by the homogeneity of proficiencies among respondents in a subgroup but
not by the sample size or by the precision of the survey instruments. The sampling error is smaller when
the subgroup consists of respondents with similar proficiencies. The total error variance can be calculated
as the summation of “sampling error” and “imputation or measurement error.”

The last column presents the standard error of the subpopulation mean, which is equal to the square root
of the sum of the two components' variance. Pairwise differences can be evaluated using these standard
errors. However, multiple comparisons, such as the six possible pairwise comparisons of this example,
need to consider an adjustment of significance level, such as the Hochberg Stagewise Procedure (HSP),
described in Hochberg (1988[44]).

Population modelling of PIAAC Cycle 2 data
The population model described earlier was applied to the PIAAC Cycle 2 data. Fixing the item parameters
to their values obtained from the unidimensional IRT scaling, multivariate latent regression models were
fitted to the data at the country level, and ten plausible values per domain were generated for each
respondent. Plausible values for cognitive domains (literacy, numeracy and APS) were generated for all
respondents participating in the assessment, regardless of whether they were administered items in that
domain. That is, respondents received plausible values for each test domain administered in their country
according to the test design implemented, regardless of the specific forms they took. Respondents who
did not participate or did not have responses in a particular domain were assigned plausible values for that
domain based on their responses to the BQ as well as the cognitive responses in other domains.
Plausible values allow for the accounting of measurement errors in secondary analyses. The plausible
values for the domain(s) respondents did not take have larger uncertainty than the plausible values for the
other domains. By using repeated analysis with each of the ten plausible values, the measurement error
will readily be reflected in the analyses, and the final aggregation of results can be conducted in a way that
the variability across the ten analyses is properly reflected.
All covariates used in the population modelling come from the respondents' BQ responses—the same as
done in PIAAC Cycle 1 (see Annex 4). The following sections provide further information about how
the population model was applied to PIAAC Cycle 2 data, how plausible values were generated, and how
plausible values can be used in further analyses.

Main sample other than doorstep interview cases
The software called DGROUP (Educational Testing Service, 2012[45]) was used to estimate the multivariate
latent regression models and generate plausible values (von Davier et al., 2006[32]; von Davier and
Sinharay, 2013[10]). During the estimation, the item parameters for the cognitive items were fixed at the
values obtained from the multi-group IRT models described earlier in this chapter. As in PIAAC Cycle 1,
nearly all respondent BQ variables, as well as some contextual characteristics, were included.
All BQ variables were contrast-coded before they were processed further. The contrast coding scheme
is reproduced in Annex 4 of this report. Contrast coding allows for the inclusion of missing responses and
avoids the necessity of assuming a linear relationship between the responses to any question and the
outcome variable. Note that with the introduction of within-construct matrix sampling design, missing by
design and missing by omitting behaviour were distinguished, which increased the number of contrast
codes needed to represent the BQ variables. With the contrast-coded BQ variables, a PCA is conducted
to 1) remove collinearity among variables when present and 2) reduce a large number of contrast-coded
BQ variables into a smaller number of principal components that are sufficient to account for a large
proportion of the variation in the BQ variables without over-parameterisation. Because each country can
have unique associations among the BQ variables, a set of principal components was calculated for each
reporting group (only Canada and Israel had two separate reporting groups). As such, the extraction
of principal components was carried out separately by country. In PIAAC, the number of principal
components retained in each of the multivariate latent regression models was selected to be the number
of principal components needed to explain 80% of the BQ variance.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

270 
Doorstep interview cases
Among the enhancements in PIAAC Cycle 2 was the introduction of the doorstep interview (DI). It was
directed to a segment of the population that is unable to take the BQ in the delivered language(s). The aim
of developing a model that is suitable for estimating the proficiency and generating plausible values for this
special subpopulation of individuals who did not respond to the full BQ is to provide proficiency estimates
and include this segment of the population in reporting. In Cycle 1, there were no proficiency estimates of
those cases with language barriers, unless an interpreter or facilitator was available to assist the
respondent. In these cases, only age and gender were available or were estimated by the interviewer. In
Cycle 2, the DI included six main background variables: age, gender, education level, employment status,
country of birth and years in the country (if not native-born). The DI was available in 28 PIAAC BQ
languages and 15 additional minority languages. Each country decided on the number of DI language
versions to be used to help access such subpopulations. Contrary to the BQ (where an interviewer asked
the questions and recorded the answers), the DI was self-completed by the respondent, who answered
the questions on a tablet.
The respondents who completed the main BQ had more than 240 variables collected. The respondents
who qualified for the DI and agreed to respond provided answers only to the six variables included in the
DI. This created a series of issues when applying the population model normally used for a completed
case of those who completed the BQ.
Multiple population models were explored, their performances were compared, and the approach judged
most appropriate to estimate the proficiency of the DI cases was proposed and approved by the PIAAC
Technical Advisory Group (Ali, 2024[46]). This approach was implemented separately for each of the 29
countries, out of 31, that had doorstep cases (Singapore and Sweden did not have doorstep cases) 7. It
proceeded in two steps. First, item scores were imputed (single imputation) for all literacy and numeracy
locator items in a way that mimicked the responses provided by the Path 1 respondents within each
country. For each DI respondent, this was done by drawing a proficiency value from the Path 1 posterior
theta distribution (averaged over all of the existing Path 1 respondents posteriors) and drawing correct or
incorrect responses given the drawn theta and each item international IRT model). Second, the DI
population model was estimated using the full PIAAC sample, including both non-doorstep cases and
doorstep cases, to create principal components by turning off all BQ variables except for the six doorstep
background variables noted below:
1. Gender: GENDER_R
2. Age: ETSAGEG5_C
3. Educational level: EDU_BQDI
4. Employment status: SUBJSTATUS_BQDI
5. Country of birth: BIRTHCNTRY_BQDI
6. Number of years in the country if immigrant: IMYRS_BQDI not native-born: IMYRS_BQDI
For countries with multiple languages, an additional variable – DALANG, indicating the language of the
direct assessment – was introduced for the doorstep run. This variable helped further distinguish between
non-doorstep and doorstep cases. For example, in Estonia, the direct assessment was offered in two
languages (Estonian and Russian), with DALANG reflecting these two categories, and a third category
representing languages used specifically in doorstep interviews. Another distinction in the doorstep model
is that, for Canada and Israel, only a single model was used for doorstep respondents (while two separate
models were used for the different language groups within the main sample who answered the full BQ).
Due to the limited number of BQ variables in each of these special doorstep latent regression models, the
number of principal components retained was chosen to explain 90% of the variance in the BQ data. The
population modelling of the doorstep cases was used to estimate and report only the proficiencies of those
cases but not the other non-doorstep samples used in estimating this model.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 271
Plausible values
Plausible values for the domains evaluated were drawn from the normal approximations to the posterior
distributions estimated from the multivariate latent regression models.
The plausible value variables for the domains follow the naming convention PV<domain>1 through
PV<domain>10, where “<domain>” took on the following form:
•

LIT for literacy

•

NUM for numeracy

•

APS for adaptive problem solving.

Linking PIAAC Cycle 2 to Cycle 1 results
There are three measurable sources of error variance to account for in reporting and evaluating how
proficiency in literacy and numeracy evolved from PIAAC Cycle 1 to PIAAC Cycle 2, in each country that
participated in both cycles. These are errors due to respondent sampling (sampling errors), errors due to
the reliability of the assessment (measurement errors), and errors due to the linking of different instruments
across assessment cycles (linking error). The linking errors are the result of the changes that occurred
between the two cycles, including changes in the assessment framework, the item pools, the mode(s) of
delivery, the assessment design and other factors. Thus, rescaling the combined Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 data
will produce new Cycle 1 country population means, and the magnitude of these differences will provide an
estimate of the linking error (OECD, 2024[23]).
For PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2, as well as future PIAAC cycles, the definition of calibration differences
starts from the ability estimates of a respondent v from country g in a target cycle under two separate
calibrations (e.g. the original calibration of a PIAAC cycle and its recalibration), C1 and C2. We can write
for calibration C1:

Formula 9.13
𝜃̃𝑣,𝐶1,𝑔 = 𝜃𝑣,𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 + 𝑢̂𝐶1,𝑔 + 𝑒̃𝑣 ,
where ûC1,g denotes the estimated country-specific error term in C1 and 𝑒̃𝑣 is the respondent specific
measurement error; and for calibration C2 accordingly:

Formula 9.14
𝜃̃𝑣,𝐶2,𝑔 = 𝜃𝑣,𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 + 𝑢̂𝐶2,𝑔 + 𝑒̃𝑣 .
Defined in this way, there may be country-level differences in the expected values of respondents based
on the calibration. These are a source of uncertainty and can be viewed as adding variance to countrylevel estimates. Given the assumption of a country-level variability of estimates due to C1 and
C2 calibrations, for the differences between estimates, we find:

Formula 9.15
𝜃̃𝑣,𝐶1,𝑔 − 𝜃̃𝑣,𝐶2,𝑔 = 𝑢̂𝐶1,𝑔 − 𝑢̂𝐶2,𝑔 ,
and the expectation can be estimated by:

272 

Formula 9.16
𝐸(𝑢̂𝐶1,𝑔 − 𝑢̂𝐶2,𝑔 ) = 𝜇̃𝑔,𝐶1 − 𝜇̃𝑔,𝐶2 = ∆̂𝐶1,𝐶2,𝑔 .
Across countries, the expected differences in the country mean (𝜇̃) can be assumed to vanish since
the scales are transformed after calibrations to match distribution moments. That is, we may assume:

The variance of the differences of country means based on Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 calibrations can then
be considered the linking error of the trend comparing the Y2 cycle means that were used to obtain
calibration C2 estimates and the Y1 cycle estimates. The linking error can be written as:

Formula 9.18
𝐺
