The main characteristics of this approach can be summarised as follows:
•

Scale-level differences across countries from adjacent-cycle IRT calibrations C1 and C2 are
considered.

•

The effect of the variability of scale-level statistics between two calibrations is evaluated at the
country level.

•

Within-country sampling variability is not targeted.

•

Sampling variance and measurement error are two separate variance components that are
accounted for by plausible values and replicate weights-based variance estimation.

The variance calculated in the Formula (9.18) is a measure of uncertainty due to the re-estimation of the
model when using additional data from subsequent cycles, which is obtained with potentially different
assessment designs, estimation methods, and underlying databases. To avoid the possibility that some
data points (countries) have an excessive influence on the results, the robust Sn statistic was used, as has
been the case in PISA. The Sn statistic8 was proposed by Rousseeuw and Croux (1993[47]) as a more
efficient alternative to the scaled median absolute deviation from the median (1.4826*MAD) that
is commonly used as a robust estimator of standard deviation. It is defined as:

Formula 9.19
𝑆𝑛 = 1.1926 ∗ med𝑖 (med𝑗 (|𝑥𝑖 − 𝑥𝑗 |)).
The differences defined above are plugged into the formula, that is, 𝑥𝑖= ∆̂𝐶1,𝐶2,𝑖 are used to calculate
the linking error for comparisons of cycles Y1 and Y2 based on calibrations C1 (using only Y1 data) and
C2 (using Y2 data and additional data including Y1). The robust estimates of linking error between cycles
by domain are presented in the next chapter (Chapter 10).

The Technical Standards and Guidelines allowed for the background questionnaire to be completed with
the aid of a translator or interpreter. This could have been a family member or a staff of the survey
organisation. Sweden was the only country that made systematic use of interpreters in both cycles of the
survey. As a result, all respondents in Sweden, in both cycles, were able to complete the background
questionnaire, and no respondents were classified as literacy-related non-respondents (in the first cycle),
nor took the doorstep interview (in the second cycle). This improved the precision of the estimates of
proficiency for such respondents in Sweden because richer information is available for them. However, it
also introduced a small difference in survey operations between Sweden and other countries, as adults
who were not able to participate in the survey because of language barriers were treated slightly differently
in Sweden than in other countries. As such adults constitute a very small percentage of the population, the
threat to comparability remains low. However, some caution is warranted when comparing results between
Sweden and other countries for groups of adults that may include a larger share of adults with very low
language proficiency (for example, recent immigrants).

10. Outcomes of scaling the direct
assessment
Usama Ali and Frederic Robin, ETS

This chapter reports on the outcomes of the item response theory (IRT)based scaling and population modelling of the PIAAC Cycle 2 direct
assessment, as well as of the scales constructed on the basis of items
included in the background questionnaire (BQ). It presents the results of the
analyses of the invariance of the IRT item parameters within and across
countries and the final international and national item parameters used in
the estimation of the proficiency scores. The chapter then describes the
location of the items across the proficiency scale based on their common
international parameters and reports the measurement information and
efficiency of the multi-stage adaptive testing (MSAT) designs. In addition,
summary outcomes of each country’s population modelling and drawing of
plausible values are reported, including estimates of the reliability and
correlations across cognitive domains and selected scales from the BQ.
Finally, the chapter presents estimates of the linking errors for trends
between PIAAC Cycle 1 and PIAAC Cycle 2.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 279

IRT scaling outcomes
The outcomes of IRT scaling include the proportions of items that are invariant across countries and PIAAC
cycles, as reflected in both the international (common) and national (unique) item parameters, as well as
items that were excluded from scaling. The international item parameters, as well as country-by-language
groups that received unique national or group-specific item parameters, can be found in Annex 10. A of
the chapter. A high proportion of invariant item parameters was observed for each country across scales
and cycles, indicating strong comparability of proficiency scales across both countries and cycles. The
following section outlines the international characteristics of the item pool for each domain, the efficiency
of the MSAT designs, and the item maps that position the items on the reporting scales.

IRT scaling and invariance of item parameters
The calibration and scaling of all the items used in the assessment followed the procedure described in
Chapter 9, using the mdltm software (von Davier, 2015[1]).1 Scaling was implemented through a multigroup IRT concurrent calibration of the data from PIAAC Cycle 2. The groups used for the analysis were
country-by-language groups. Senate weights were used to ensure that each participating country
contributed equally to the international scaling. For literacy and numeracy, the trend linking items were
fixed to their PIAAC Cycle 1 parameters in order to report PIAAC Cycle 2 results onto the PIAAC Cycle 1
scales. For countries that participated in PIAAC Cycle 1, the fixed trend parameters included both common
and unique parameters, as determined in the context of PIAAC Cycle 1. For new participating countries,
the fixed trend parameters were the PIAAC Cycle 1 international parameters. For APS, since there were
no trend items, no parameters were initially fixed. The APS scale was determined by constraining the mean
of the slope parameters to be 1.0 and the mean of the difficulty (or location) parameters to be 0.0.
As indicated in Chapter 9, IRT scaling proceeded through an iterative calibration process of the data
locator, Stage 2 and Stage 3 data and then the component data. The initial calibration was conducted
fixing the trend parameters as previously described, and item-by-country-by-language interactions were
evaluated using the mean deviation (MD) and the root mean square deviation (RMSD) statistics. Each item
in each country-by-language group featured at least 250 responses. In most cases, the international item
parameters (fixed for the trend items and estimated for the new items) fit the data for all country-bylanguage groups. When an item was identified as misfitting in a country-by-language group, unique
parameters were estimated for that group in the next iteration of the calibration process. The initial RMSD
threshold was set to 0.25 and then lowered by 0.05 (i.e. 0.20 and 0.15) at each subsequent iteration of the
calibration process. Finally, a threshold of 0.12 was applied, a value that has been shown to optimise both
the comparability of the proficiency estimates across country-by-language groups and group model fit.
Items were excluded from national scaling if, at the final iteration, the RMSD could not be reduced to 0.15
or below, its slope parameter was below 0.10, or its difficulty parameter was larger than 5.0 in absolute
value.
The process for literacy and numeracy was repeated using all of the cognitive data, including the
components, once the IRT scaling of the locator, Stage 2 and Stage 3 items were finalised. However, the
parameters for the locator, Stage 2 and Stage 3 items remained fixed when estimating the item parameters
for the component items.
Estimating unique item parameters is critical to modelling data obtained from instruments with many
national versions. At the same time, it is important to verify that in each country a sufficient number of items
receive international (invariant) parameters, to ensure the comparability of proficiency estimates across
countries within a cycle as well as across cycles.
Table 10.1 shows the total number of item-by-country-by-language interactions that were evaluated, as
well as the percentages of interactions categorised as invariant (common), variant (unique), and dropped

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

280 
(excluded from national scaling because of the reasons mentioned above), averaged across countries.
The proportion of invariant items in total was large for all domains, ranging from 92.8% for the literacy items
to 96.1% for APS items. The proportion of invariant parameters across trend items was not as high as its
proportion across new items, but this was expected because trend item misfit was evaluated in PIAAC
Cycle 1 and then again with the Cycle 2 dataset, many years later. The proportion of invariant parameters
across components items was the highest. The proportions of items excluded from national scaling were
very small for all cognitive domains, ranging from 0.1 to 0.3%. Overall, these results confirmed that the
linking within and across cycles was very strong and that PIAAC proficiency estimates can be compared
across countries and cycles. The detailed results for each country, provided in Annex 10.2, show that the
level of invariance (trend and new item) was appropriate to report comparable proficiency estimates for all
PIAAC Cycle 2 participating countries.

Test information and evaluation of multi-stage adaptive test design
Matching respondents’ proficiencies with the difficulty of items administered maximises measurement
precision. For this reason, the PIAAC Cycle 1 multi-stage adaptive testing design for the computer-based
assessment was developed to better align with respondents’ background profiles and abilities, while
maintaining a degree of randomness in the assignment. This approach ensured broad domain coverage
across all proficiency levels and participating countries. Additionally, a probability-based misrouting layer
was included to control the exposure rates of all booklets throughout the various assessment stages.
The adaptive design in PIAAC Cycle 2 replaced the Cycle 1 probability layer with a linear component
assigned to approximately 25% of respondents, creating a combined linear and adaptive design that
supported accurate item calibration. This update aimed at streamlining the test-taking experience by
adhering to a consistent path – either linear or adaptive – without mixing the two approaches from Cycle 1.
The primary goal of adaptive testing remains to improve the efficiency, validity and accuracy of the
cognitive measurement. Furthermore, an adaptive design may enhance engagement and motivation as
respondents are less likely to encounter items that are either too difficult or too easy for them, thereby
reducing disengagement, non-response and random responses.
Figure 10.1 illustrates the efficiency of the PIAAC Cycle 2 multi-stage adaptive assessment (after the
locator) for literacy and numeracy compared to the corresponding non-adaptive linear assessment (after
the locator). Relative efficiency was measured as the ratio between the average test information from the
adaptive part of the MSAT instrument and the average test information from the linear part. The vertical
axis shows the test information ratio, while the horizontal axis represents the literacy or numeracy
proficiency scales. By design, linear test information tends to peak in the middle of the proficiency
distribution, while adaptive test information is more spread out due to the routing of respondents to testlets
optimised to provide more information within specific targeted proficiency levels.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 281
Figure 10.1 demonstrates that the adaptive test forms in the adaptive MSAT design were consistently more
efficient than the linear test forms. Near the score of 250 (the average score around which the literacy and
numeracy scales were calibrated in PIAAC Cycle 1), the relative efficiency was slightly above 1.0. For
literacy, efficiency increased for respondents with higher proficiency (e.g. scores greater than 275),
reaching 1.25, and was even higher for low performers (e.g. scores below 200), reaching 1.40. For
numeracy, efficiency grew rapidly outside the medium proficiency range, reaching 1.50. This offered
notable improvements in the measurement for respondents at both the low- and high-end of the proficiency
scale.
Another way to express the relative efficiency of the MSAT is to convert the information gained into the
equivalent number of test items that a linear design would need to achieve the same measurement
precision at a specific proficiency level. This increased efficiency means that adaptive tests provided the
same amount of test information as linear tests but required up to 20% fewer literacy items and 33% fewer
numeracy items. For example, at proficiency level of 300, the adaptive numeracy test form – consisting,
on average, of 24 items – provides as much information as a hypothetical linear test form containing 30
items.

Figure 10.1. Relative efficiency of the multi-stage adaptive assessment over linear assessment for
literacy and numeracy

Population modelling outcomes
Population modelling combines IRT and latent regression modelling of cognitive and background data.
First, the analyses were carried out for each country to estimate country-specific latent regression
parameters. Then, plausible values were generated. In addition to producing the plausible values reported
in PIAAC Cycle 2, population modelling analysis also provided estimates of each countries’ test reliability,
inter-domain correlations, correlations between cognitive proficiencies and key background variables and
scales (skill use), and population- and subgroup-level performance distributions.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

282 
Before providing a summary of these scaling outcomes, the following sections describe the final steps for
producing these outcomes on the reported PIAAC scales, for providing the item response probability
values needed to update the literacy and numeracy described proficiency scales, and for developing a
described proficiency scale for the new domain of APS.
The last two sections provide the standard errors associated with the country mean estimates and the
estimated linking error for evaluating and interpreting PIAAC trends.

Transforming the plausible values to the PIAAC reporting scales
The plausible values are first produced on the IRT scale determined by the fixed item parameters used as
input to population modelling. Therefore, an additional step is required to transform the initial PVs values
from the IRT theta scales to the PIAAC reporting scales chosen to have a mean of 250 and a standard
deviation of 50 based on data from Cycle 2 participating countries (including Canada English and Canada
French as two entries). This choice of mean and standard deviation ensures that nearly all scaled PVs will
have values between 100 to 500 – in rare cases when a PV is negative, its value is then truncated to 0.
For literacy and numeracy, this was done in Cycle 1, and because Cycle 2 IRT was linked to Cycle 1 and
thus scaled onto the Cycle 1 scale, the same linear transformations as used in Cycle 1 ( (OECD, 2019[2]);
see Table 10.2 below) still apply. For the new APS measure, new transformation constants 2 have been
established following a similar approach as in Cycle 1. The APS IRT-to-reporting-scale linear
transformation constants were established so that the total senate weighted mean of the Cycle 2
participating countries is 250 and the standard deviation 50 (Table 10.2).

Item maps
Once IRT scaling and population modelling were completed, item maps for each domain were produced
to show the difficulty of all the items used in each domain relative to the domain’s overall proficiency
distribution. As the main purpose of the item map was to support the development and the descriptors of
the proficiency levels, the item difficulty statistic used was the proficiency value a respondent must have
to have a correct response probability of 0.67 (RP67) – the value used in PIAAC Cycle 1.
Figure 10.2 illustrates how the choice of an RP value determines the classification of an item into a
proficiency level. In this figure, the item is of medium difficulty and high discrimination, meaning it
effectively distinguishes between respondents of different proficiency levels. A respondent with a
proficiency score of 225 can answer the item correctly with a probability of 20%. For the probability of
giving the correct answer to equal 67% (the RP value), a respondent must have a proficiency of 266,
corresponding to proficiency level 2 (which spans scores from 226 to 275). Note that the selection of the
RP value impacts the placement of a particular item on the proficiency scale – for instance, a lower RP
(e.g. RP50) might assign the item to a lower level, while a higher RP (e.g. RP80 that was used in previous
adult surveys) might push it to a higher level. However, this decision does not affect the overall proficiency
distribution or the percentage of respondents in each level as illustrated in Figure 10.2.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 283

Figure 10.2. Item response function and RP67

The RP67 item maps were provided to the content matter experts and psychometricians, who used them
to determine appropriate boundaries and descriptors for the proficiency levels.
Figure 10.3 presents the classification of items across various proficiency levels (item maps) for literacy,
numeracy and APS using the RP67 threshold. These item maps show that items in each domain spanned
all proficiency levels, confirming that the instruments and the descriptors worked well together to provide
high-quality (reliable) proficiency information at all the reported levels. As expected, all reading and
numeracy component items were categorized below proficiency level 1, reflecting their measurement of
foundational competencies. Notably, the literacy domain showed no items classified at proficiency level 5.
Chapter 5 provides a detailed definition of the content for each proficiency level within each cognitive
domain. In contrast, Figures 10.4 to 10.6 illustrate the percentage of respondents in each country at each
proficiency level for each cognitive domain.

In the research literature there is no generally agreed-upon rule for characterising items along a proficiency
scale. RP values of 0.62 have been used in PISA while values as high as 0.80 have been used in some
adult surveys, including the International Adult Literacy Survey (IALS) and the Adult Literacy and Life Skills
(ALL) survey. The U.S. National Academy of Sciences recommended that the National Assessment of
Adult Literacy survey (U.S. survey of adults, administered in 2003 and then discontinued when PIAAC
Cycle 1 was implemented in 2011/12) use an RP value more closely aligned with school-based surveys.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

286 
For PIAAC Cycle 1, the decision was made to use an RP value of 0.67, which was then kept in PIAAC
Cycle 2. As noted earlier, the selection of the RP value influences the placement of individual items on the
proficiency scale. Consequently, item maps generated using the IALS and ALL RP value of 0.80 will differ
from those created using the PIAAC RP value of 0.67, even for the same items. However, this choice does
not affect the overall proficiency distribution or the proportion of respondents within each proficiency level,
and results remain comparable across these surveys. It is also essential to recognise that the RP value
does not impact the precision of measurement along the proficiency scale. The same items define the
underlying scale regardless of the RP value selected. Importantly, the RP value does not decide on which
items measure specific proficiency levels—all items contribute to the measurement precision across all
levels of proficiency. The RP value simply represents a single point on the item response function graph
at which a certain probability (e.g. 0.67) is reached. Respondents with a proficiency below this point have
a lower (but still positive) probability of answering the item correctly, and respondents with a proficiency
above this point have a higher probability of doing so. That means that an item located in proficiency level
4 using an RP value of 0.67 will also provide information on respondents that are located in proficiency
levels 3 or 5. The location of an item at a certain level simply implies that, for the chosen RP value, this
item is most representative of that particular proficiency level.

Domain intercorrelations
The estimated correlations (corrected for attenuation) among the three PIAAC domains across countries
range from 0.82 to 0.92 (average 0.88) for literacy and numeracy, from 0.79 to 0.91 (average 0.87) for
literacy and APS, and from 0.77 to 0.90 (average 0.85) for numeracy and APS (see Table 10.5). These
correlations are medium to high, as expected, indicating a strong relationship between the domains.
However, they also suggest that each domain maintains distinct characteristics.

Linking error
To allow analysing how skills proficiency has evolved over time, results from PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2
are reported on the same proficiency scale. To determine whether an observed change in proficiency for
a country or subgroup is statistically significant, the standard error of the difference should be calculated.
However, because the two cycles involve linked but non-identical assessments, this standard error must
account for an additional source of uncertainty, referred to as the linking error.
For each domain, a country’s (or subgroup) change in performance between PIAAC Cycle 2 and
PIAAC Cycle 1 is calculated as follows:
𝛥𝐶2−𝐶1 = 𝑃𝐼𝐴𝐴𝐶𝐶2 − 𝑃𝐼𝐴𝐴𝐶𝐶1
where 𝛥𝐶2−𝐶1 is the difference in proficiency between PIAAC Cycle 2 (C2) and Cycle (C1).

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 293
The corresponding standard error of the change in proficiency 𝜎(𝛥𝐶2−𝐶1 ) is:
2
𝜎(𝛥𝐶2−𝐶1 ) = √σ2𝐶2 + σ2𝐶1 + error𝐶2,𝐶1
,

where 𝜎𝐶2 is the standard error observed for PIAAC Cycle 2, 𝜎𝐶1 is the standard error observed for PIAAC
Cycle 1 and error𝐶2,𝐶1 is the link error.

Procedure for estimating the linking error:
The procedure used in PIAAC to estimate the linking error involved the following steps:
1. Concurrent calibration:
PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 data were calibrated concurrently following an iterative multi-group
approach similar to the one described earlier. In this calibration, the groups were defined by cycleby-country-by-language (i.e. separate groups for each country-language combination within each
cycle).
To achieve the best possible fit to the combined data, all item parameters were freely estimated in
the initial iteration. In subsequent iterations, the root mean square deviation (RMSD) fit statistics
were used to guide the estimation of group-specific item parameters. This allowed for groupspecific adjustments:
•

Items unique to Cycle 1 were fit specifically to the Cycle 1 country-by-language data,

•

Items unique to Cycle 2 were fit to the Cycle 2 country-by-language data, and

•

Trend (linking) items were calibrated to fit both Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 country-by-language data.

2. Scaling of Cycle 1 proficiency estimates from the concurrent calibration to PIAAC scale:
Because the concurrent calibration used a combined Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 datasets distinct from
the original Cycle 1 calibration, and no item parameters were fixed to maintain the original scale,
the resulting item parameters and person proficiency estimates were on a different scale from that
of PIAAC Cycle 1. To estimate the linking error it was necessary to transform the Cycle 1 estimates
derived from the concurrent calibration back onto the PIAAC reporting scale used in Cycle 1. This
was achieved by identifying a linear transformation that aligned the mean and standard deviation
of the Cycle 1 country mean estimates from the concurrent calibration with those of the officially
reported Cycle 1 estimates.
3. Estimation of linking error:
Once the concurrent calibration estimates were transformed onto the PIAAC Cycle 1 scale, the
recalculated Cycle 1 country means from Step 2 were compared with the officially reported Cycle
1 proficiency means. The differences between these paired estimates captured the effects of
linking across cycles. Based on 36 countries reported in Cycle 1, a total of 36 such differences
were available for analysis. To estimate the linking error, the 𝑆𝑛 estimator (Rousseeuw and Croux,
1993[3]) was applied – a robust measure that is less sensitive to outliers than either the standard
deviation or the median absolute deviation. This provided a stable and reliable estimate of the
uncertainty introduced through cross-cycle comparisons.
The 𝑆𝑛 method is defined as:
𝑆𝑛 = 𝑐. median𝑖 (median𝑗 |𝑥𝑖 − 𝑥𝑗 |),
where 𝑥𝑖 and 𝑥𝑗 represent the differences between the recalculated and original Cycle 1 country
means and c ≈ 1.1926 is a scaling constant that makes the estimator consistent with the standard

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

294 
deviation under normality. This provided a robust estimate of the spread of linking differences and
served as the measure of linking error across cycles.
Following the computation of the 𝑆𝑛 statistic, the linking errors for PIAAC literacy and numeracy—
denoted as the linking error between Cycle 2 and Cycle 1, error𝐶2,𝐶1 —are reported in Table 10.8
to reflect the uncertainty introduced through the cross-cycle comparisons.

Tim Huijts, Babs Jacobs and Roy Meijer, ROA; Matthias Bluemke, Clemens Lechner, Natascha Massing,

and non-formal education. Subsequently, the chapter discusses the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

298 

Introduction
The complex structure of the PIAAC background questionnaire (BQ) enabled the collection of various
information from a diverse population of adults. However, not all questions were appropriate for all
respondents. For instance, some questions were specifically tailored for those currently in the workforce,
while others were relevant only for those participating in training activities. Additionally, respondents who
were recently unemployed received a distinct set of questions.
The need to adapt the BQ in order to provide appropriate sections for a diverse population can be best
understood by examining the following examples:
•

Current industry and occupation, as well as skill use at work and information on the work
environment could be meaningfully asked only of those who were either employed or self-employed
at the time of the interview because respondents who are out of the labour force or never had paid
work cannot reasonably be asked whether they use their literacy skills at work.

•

For ICT skill use, questions assessing the domain were not presented to those without any previous
contact with digital devices. In contrast, reading, writing and numeracy skills used at home were
assessed for all respondents, and the corresponding scales for skills used at work were applied to
those respondents who were part of the labour force and the recently (less than 12 months)
unemployed.

•

Earnings were only asked of those working. Questions on earnings do not provide meaningful
information if respondents are no longer part of the labour force or have never had paid work. The
same holds true for questions addressing those who were in education or training at the time.

At the same time, sets of other questions in sections addressing general domains are available for
practically all respondents who completed the BQ. This is the case for skills used at home, educational
attainment and history, questions about health, civil engagement and social and emotional skills, as well
as socio-demographic information, among other things. The computer-based routing of respondents to
sections relevant to their particular situation and experiences led to higher item-level response rates.
Due to the complexity of the BQ, careful consideration is, however, clearly needed when analysing these
data.

Overview of BQ trend variables
International assessments can provide significant added value when used to analyse trends over time
across countries. For that reason, the Consortium aimed to collect and derive variables that can be viewed
as comparable across four assessments of adult skills: the International Adult Literacy Survey (IALS), the
Adult Literacy and Life skills (ALL), and PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2. For an overview of trend variables
with large-scale assessments in IALS and ALL, refer to Chapter 20 of the Technical Report of PIAAC Cycle
1 (von Davier et al., 2019[1]). In the following tables, BQ trend variables between PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle
2 are presented.

BQ trend variables – PIAAC Cycle 1
A large portion of the BQ items in PIAAC Cycle 2 are so-called strict or soft trend items that are completely
or at least conceptually identical to the Cycle 1 measurement. Consequently, many derived variables
based on BQ information are trend to PIAAC Cycle 1. An overview of the domains with available trend
variables to Cycle 1 is provided in Table 11.1. Detailed information about matching variables in the BQ
between PIAAC Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 is given in Annex B.

Development of derived variables on education
The PIAAC BQ contains measures of both formal and non-formal education. The International Standard
Classification of Education (UNESCO-UIS, 2012[2]) defines “formal education” in detail. The main
characteristics of formal education are that it is hierarchically structured, is provided in schools, colleges,
universities or other educational institutions, and leads to a certification. “According to the ISCED definition,
formal education can be seen as a complex ladder of education where recognised completion of one level
gives access to another higher level of complexity” (Eurostat, 2016, p. 18[3]).
In contrast, non-formal education is defined as “education that is institutionalised, intentional and planned
by an education provider. The defining characteristic of non-formal education is that it is an addition,
alternative and/or complement to formal education within the process of lifelong learning of individuals. [...]
non-formal education mostly leads to qualifications that are not recognised as formal or equivalent to formal
qualifications by the relevant national or sub-national education authorities or to no qualifications at all.”
(Eurostat, 2016[3]).

Formal education
Section B of the PIAAC Cycle 2 BQ measures four concepts related to respondents’ formal education:
•

Educational attainment refers to the highest educational programme successfully completed by an
individual. “In formal education, successful completion usually results in a qualification that is
recognised by the relevant national education authorities” (UNESCO-UIS, 2012, p. 15[2]). It is the
most important predictor of cognitive skills after social background. Educational attainment is
measured by question B2_Q01.

•

Educational pathways refer to the sequence and timing of educational programmes attended or
completed by the respondent. Due to time constraints, PIAAC Cycle 2 only collected information
on qualifications obtained prior to the highest qualification completed without timing information.
Furthermore, it collected information on individual education pathways, which is especially
interesting in differentiated education systems. The educational pathway is measured by question
B2_Q02b, using a check-all-that-apply question. This results in one indicator variable for each
education category.

•

Current participation in formal education refers to the educational programme a respondent
currently attends. It is measured by asking which qualification the respondent is aiming to obtain.
There is no reference to successful completion. This is measured by question B2_Q05b, which is
preceded by filter question B2_Q05a.

•

Incomplete education (“dropout”) refers to educational qualifications pursued but not actually
obtained. Due to time constraints, PIAAC Cycle 2 only collected information on the last programme
the respondent dropped out of. This is measured by question B2_Q06b, which is preceded by filter
question B2_Q06a.

In addition, sections D (question D2_Q12a) and E (E2_Q10a) of the background questionnaire assess
the educational qualification required for respondents’ current or last job, respectively.
All formal education questions were nationally adapted, i.e. they used country-specific response options
(see Chapter 6 and Annex C). Some countries applied more complex adaptations, splitting the information
across several questions. The country-specific variables were harmonised after data collection according
to specifications developed prior to data collection (with few adjustments still occurring afterwards). They
were transformed into derived variables based on ISCED 2011 (UNESCO-UIS, 2012[2]).1 For some, the
corresponding years of formal education, which were also specified by each country, were additionally
derived from the self-reported qualification. For educational attainment, an indicator of whether the highest
qualification obtained was vocational was also constructed. Table 11.3 gives an overview of all concepts

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 301

1-digit ISCED 2011
The simplest coding scheme provided as a DV in PIAAC Cycle 2 data represents ISCED 2011 main levels,
i.e. the first digit of ISCED 2011, presented in Table 11.4. While ISCED 1997 had seven main levels
(0 to 6), the revised ISCED 2011 has nine main levels (0 to 8). The former first stage of tertiary education
(ISCED 5) was differentiated into three new levels: short cycle tertiary (new ISCED 5), bachelor’s or
equivalent level (new ISCED 6), and master’s or equivalent level (new ISCED 7). The former second stage
of tertiary (ISCED 6) has been relabeled to “doctoral or equivalent level” (new ISCED 8).

While mean cognitive skills are expected to be ordered according to these levels of education, they will
also be heterogeneous within levels. This is due to the wide range of different educational programmes
offered within some ISCED levels across countries as well as the distribution of people within countries
across these programmes. In particular, ISCED level 3 (upper secondary education) is large and
heterogeneous in many countries. Therefore, two more highly differentiated variables are also offered as
derived variables for more fine-grained analyses.

3-digit ISCED 2011
When ISCED was last revised, a 3-digit coding scheme was developed to standardise the implementation
of detailed ISCED categories across data sources. While main levels had always been numbered in
ISCED, complementary dimensions such as programme orientation (e.g. vocational or general) and
access to higher levels of education had not yet been assigned standard codes in ISCED 1997 ( (UNESCO
Institute for Statistics, 2006[4]). Furthermore, a differentiation between codes for the classification of
educational attainment and related qualifications (ISCED-A) and codes for the classification of educational
programmes and related enrolment (ISCED-P) was also introduced (see (UNESCO Institute for Statistics,
2006[4]), Annexes II and III) to better differentiate between these concepts at the somewhat complex
boundary between ISCED 2 (lower secondary education) and 3 (upper secondary education): Short ISCED
3 programmes do not lead to ISCED 3 but ISCED 2 attainment.
A few adjustments were made for PIAAC Cycle 2. First, any differentiation (e.g. “some primary education”)
within ISCED level 0 (less than primary education) was dropped. The corresponding categories are very
rare as the proportion of adults at ISCED level 0 is extremely small in many countries. Second, ISCED
level 2 (lower secondary education) is not differentiated according to orientation, level completion and
access to ISCED level 3 since most programmes in participating countries are general, leading to
qualifications at ISCED level 2 that give access to ISCED level 3 (upper secondary education). Instead,
ISCED level 2 is differentiated in the 4-digit PIAAC-ISCED variable in a way that better represents the
differentiations observed in a number of participating countries (see next section). Finally, in the absence
of agreed-upon definitions for orientation in tertiary education, ISCED levels 6 (bachelor’s level) to 8
(doctoral level) are not differentiated here. Again, the 4-digit PIAAC-ISCED variable offers a non-official
differentiation instead, presented in the next section. Table 11.5 shows the official ISCED-A and ISCED-P
2011 codes and labels used in PIAAC Cycle 2, complemented by short labels used in the data.

4-digit PIAAC ISCED 2011 (“PISCED”)
A detailed 4-digit coding scheme extending 3-digit ISCED 2011 was developed to fulfil the analysis
requirements for all formal education variables in PIAAC Cycle 2. The new concept of educational
pathways required introducing some differentiation within ISCED 2 (lower secondary education) to
adequately represent pathways in countries with stratified lower secondary education, which is normally
not visible in ISCED 2011. The scheme extends ISCED 2011 (UNESCO-UIS, 2012[2]) (Annexes II and III)
in the following ways:
•

The three-digit ISCED coding scheme was extended by adding a fourth digit at the front. This digit
directly represents the broad ISCED levels (1=low, 2=medium, 3=high), so this simplified variable
can be obtained by just truncating the 4-digit code to the first digit. The second digit thus represents
ISCED 2011 main levels.

•

The third and fourth digits represent the second and third digits of ISCED 2011. They were switched
so that the third digit represents sub-levels (level completion and access to higher level, only levels
2 to 4) and the fourth digit programme orientation. Within programme orientation (fourth digit),
codes were switched (vocational=4 and general=5). These changes aim to improve the ordering
of codes by expected mean general basic skills (as measured in PIAAC) while still allowing the
derivation of ISCED 2011 codes.

•

At ISCED 2, two non-official codes are introduced to allow the distinction of different types of lower
secondary education in countries with differentiated educational structures at this level. This is
especially meant for the analyses of educational pathways since earlier transitions may affect later
outcomes in terms of both attainment and skills. Code 1245 classifies academically selective
general lower secondary programmes designed to prepare students for general upper secondary
education, giving access to higher education early on. These programmes often even span ISCED
2 and 3. In contrast, code 1204 includes pre-vocational or non-selective general lower secondary
education, after which students more often enrol in vocational education at ISCED 3. Code 1200
is used for ‘comprehensive’ educational programmes in countries with differentiation in ISCED 2,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

304 
as well as all countries without any such differentiation (or those few that refused to implement the
required distinctions).
•

While there are no internationally accepted definitions for academic/theoretically oriented and
professionally/practically oriented education at ISCED levels 6 (bachelor’s level) to 8 (doctoral
level, see previous section), national distinctions were used to differentiate between different types
of tertiary education. Thereby, cross-national comparisons can be limited to
programmes/qualifications that are more highly comparable than the broader ‘tertiary’ category.
o

Degrees from traditional, research-oriented universities are coded 3605 and 3705,
respectively.

o

Degrees from non-traditional university higher education institutions (such as higher education
colleges, polytechnics or “universities of applied sciences”) are coded 3604 and 3704,
respectively.

o

Vocational qualifications classified at the bachelor’s and master’s levels are coded 3603 and
3703, respectively. These only exist in very few countries, e.g. master crafts qualifications in
Germany. Still, it is important to distinguish them from applied and traditional higher education
degrees, given that entry requirements and related skills may substantially differ.

o

Countries without such differentiations in their tertiary education systems use the “nfs” (not
further specified) categories (3500, 3600 and 3700).

While educational attainment, educational pathways and incomplete education are coded in terms of
attainment (PISCED-A), current participation in education is coded in terms of educational programmes
(PISCED-P), in accordance with the ISCED-A and ISCED-P coding schemes in ISCED 2011 (see
(UNESCO-UIS, 2012[2]) Annexes II and III). In the BQ, the categories of these schemes were consecutively
numbered from 0 to 30, leading to codes that do not carry any substantive meaning (the BQ codes also
cannot be interpreted as being ordinal).
Table 11.6 shows the categories of the most detailed PIAAC education coding scheme, PISCED, as well
as the corresponding categories in the original BQ variables. The detailed categories can be summarised
in more flexible ways than the 3- and 1-digit ISCED variables presented in the previous subsections,
enriching the data substantially.

Educational pathway-derived variables
Educational pathways were assessed with a check-all-that-apply question. The resulting indicator variables
are somewhat cumbersome to analyse. To simplify analyses, several derived variables were constructed
to aggregate the information from the 30 educational pathway indicator variables:
•

The type of general education (a prevocational, academic or comprehensive programme)
completed at ISCED level 2 (lower secondary education) before the highest educational
qualification (EP_TISC2). This variable aims to measure academic selectivity in lower secondary
education in countries with differentiated general lower secondary education. There is a specific
category for the academic type in lower secondary education that is part of a programme spanning
ISCED levels 2 and 3 (so that affected respondents often did not actually mention the respective
ISCED level 2 programme on their pathway, in which case it was inferred from their ISCED level 3
qualification). This type is common in several European countries and represents the most
selective academic programmes.2

•

The type of education completed in ISCED level 3 (upper secondary education) before the highest
qualification (EP_TISC3). This is a logical extension of EP_TISC2 because most countries only
offer different options starting at ISCED level 3. In some countries, qualifications resulting from
“short programmes” and programmes that only partially complete ISCED level 3 (which only give
access to other ISCED level 3 programmes) are part of the standard educational career to the
completion of ISCED level 3. Since the variable only records the highest of all ISCED level 3
qualifications taken before the highest qualification, these qualifications become even rarer on this
derived variable. Given that ISCED level 3 is highly differentiated and contains very small
categories, data users should exclude categories from the ISCED level 3 pathway or aggregate
the categories further, depending on the specific research goals.

•

Having completed a qualification at ISCED level 4 before the highest qualification for those who
obtained a tertiary qualification (EP_ISC4). In most educational systems, ISCED level 4 is a detour
from a more direct pathway to tertiary education. 3

•

Having had vocational education at least once in the educational pathway before the highest
educational qualification (EP_VET). ISCED level 2 is excluded because vocational lower

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

306 
secondary qualifications are extremely rare, especially on the educational pathway. Note that
having had vocational education on the educational pathway implies a higher level of education on
average since ISCED level 2 is almost exclusively general. The variable can be combined with
VETC2 (highest education is vocational) to identify vocationally qualified respondents, whether as
the highest qualification or via their educational pathway.
•

Having completed a traditional 'academic' pathway, i.e. an academically selective programme at
ISCED level 2 and a general ISCED level 3 programme with access to tertiary (in countries with
differentiation at ISCED level 2) or a comprehensive programme at ISCED level 2 and a general
programme at ISCED level 3 with access to tertiary education (in countries with comprehensive
ISCED 2), versus no academic pathway at ISCED levels 2 and 3 (EP_ACAD). Some adaptations
were made for countries that have an academic pathway diverging from this pattern, e.g. Singapore
and Québec in Canada (where gen ISCED level 4 access ISCED levels 5/6/7 is a necessary part
of the pathway to higher education).

The rationale was that these elements of the educational pathway may influence skill development and
later labour market outcomes, in addition to the highest qualification. The first three derived variables
aggregate information from three individual ISCED levels, while the latter two draw on information from
multiple ISCED levels.

Non-formal education
In PIAAC Cycle 2, the indicator for participation in non-formal education is participation in so-called training
activities. Respondents who were under 20 years old and currently attending formal education at ISECD
level 3 and below skipped the questions on non-formal education.
In the sub-section on non-formal education, PIAAC Cycle 2 collects information on whether respondents
participated in any training during the last 12 months and, if yes, how many training activities they
undertook. For respondents who participated in training, there were several questions covering important
aspects of training participation. These were related to financing, content, use of computerised equipment
or digitally supported processes, training intensity, job-relatedness, and the usefulness of the (last) training
activity. Non-participants received a question about whether they had ever participated in training.
Furthermore, barriers to training were assessed, asking respondents who would have liked to participate
in (further) activities on what deterred them from doing so.
In order to support the analysis of the non-formal education items, some derived variables were developed.
They are presented in Table 11.7.

Development of derived earnings variables
Reporting earnings
There are obstacles when asking about respondents’ earnings in surveys due to the sensitive nature of
this question (Gauly et al., 2019[5]; Kim and Tamborini, 2014[6]). Like in PIAAC Cycle 1, the BQ deployed
two key innovations designed to make it easier for respondents to report their earnings to improve the
quality of the earnings data and reduce item nonresponse. The first was for respondents in paid
employment to choose between reporting their gross earnings per hour, day, week, two weeks, month,
year or by piece rate. Removing the necessity for respondents to convert from their own preferred payment
period to a predetermined standard should remove potential barriers to response and improve data quality.
Furthermore, this approach automatically takes into account potential country differences in the payment
period.
The second key innovation was an additional option for those who were still unwilling or unable to report
their precise earnings. These respondents were invited to report their earnings in broad categories. Again,
in such situations, the categories were expressed per hour, per day, per week, per two weeks, per month
or per year, according to the respondents’ preferences. This option was expected to be attractive for
respondents who had only a rough idea of how much they earn per period and for those reluctant to reveal
their precise earnings due to concerns such as privacy.
In addition to these key innovations, earnings were asked separately for wage or salary earners and the
self-employed. There was also a separate question for wage or salary earners on annual bonuses.
Earnings of the self-employed were asked per year, unless respondents had been in their current business
for less than a year, in which case they were asked per month. For earnings of both wage and salary
earners and the self-employed, as well as for annual bonuses, the option to report in broad categories was
offered to those who were unwilling or unable to report directly.
Although the design of the set of questions was expected to yield significant advantages in terms of
interview flow, item response and data quality, these advantages come at a price – there is no direct
measure of earnings that ensues directly from the survey. It was necessary to devise an elaborate set of
conversion rules to go from earnings as reported by the respondent to the derived earnings variables
included in the database. The first step is a rather straightforward conversion of directly reported earnings
from the earnings period option chosen by the respondent into every available alternative (e.g. from hourly
to monthly, from yearly to daily, etc.). The second, and by far the most complex step, was the conversion
of earnings reported in broad categories into an equivalent direct amount (for both regular and additional
payments). A third step comprised the construction of a set of standard variables that formed the basis for
the earnings-derived variables to be included in the public data file. A fourth step involved a purchasing
power parity (PPP) correction so that all earnings variables were expressed in terms of real disposable
earnings in a fixed currency (in this case, given in US dollars). Finally, all earnings indicators were
converted into deciles.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

308 
Conversion of directly reported earnings into all possible reporting periods
As stated above, the conversion of directly reported earnings into all possible reporting periods was quite
straightforward. It involved using a set of fixed conversion rules from each reporting period into every other
reporting period. Earnings reported as a piece rate were first converted into an hourly rate based on an
additional question regarding the usual number of hours per piece as estimated by the respondent. The
transformation of the data based on the different time periods for which earnings could be reported into
standard earnings rates was primarily based on the following standard conversion rates:
•

annual earnings = monthly earnings * 12

•

monthly earnings = annual earnings /12

•

bi-weekly earnings = monthly earnings * 12 / 26

•

weekly earnings = monthly earnings * 12 /52

•

hourly earnings = monthly earnings / [(average number of hours worked per week) * 52/12)]

Most of these variables were not intended for inclusion in the final data, which only included earnings
expressed in hourly or monthly amounts. The reason for creating these variables is that they are needed
as input for the following step, which is the conversion of earnings reported in broad categories into an
equivalent direct amount.

Converting broad categories into equivalent direct amounts
Respondents who were unable or unwilling to report their earnings precisely were given the option of
reporting in broad categories. These categories were estimated for each participating country based on
their PIAAC Cycle 1 earnings distribution. Country-specific projected earnings bands for PIAAC Cycle 2
were calculated by the Consortium and made available to the countries. For countries that were new to
PIAAC, the earning bands were estimated based on the national earnings distribution provided by the
country. For regular earnings of wage and salary earners, six broad bands were used, with the bands
divided roughly along the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles of the national distribution, provided
separately per hour, day, week, two weeks, month or year. For self-employed, the same bands were
applied, but only per year or month, depending on whether the respondent had been in the current business
at the time of the survey for at least a year or less than a year. For annual bonuses, three broad bands
were used, with bands divided at roughly 5% and 10% of the median of national annual gross earnings.
Although this option might have been convenient for some respondents, it did not yield a unique earnings
amount that could be directly compared with the earnings reported by the majority of respondents. In
principle, this could have been achieved relatively simply by either assigning the respondents who reported
in broad bands an earnings value equal to the mean or median of those who reported direct earnings in
the same band or by reducing the directly reported earnings to the same six bands. In practice, neither of
these solutions would have been satisfactory, though. Assigning band means or medians creates an
unwanted “lumpiness” in the distribution of the earnings data that may have undesirable effects in
subsequent analyses, especially when certain subpopulations are overrepresented in some of the bands.
Conversely, reducing all the data to bands would result in a considerable loss of information and would
limit the potential for analyses. This latter objection is even more telling when considering that the bands
are country-specific and, therefore, not strictly comparable across countries. Leaving the data unconverted
– that is, allowing users of the data to make their own conversions as they see fit – was not considered
because it would essentially render the earnings data as included in the public data file for this group of
respondents unusable.
As a result, a more ambitious approach was followed by imputing precise earnings for those who reported
in broad categories. This allowed us to merge the data from the broad bands seamlessly with those
reported directly. The primary objection to using imputed data for these respondents – namely that it is

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 309
only an educated guess rather than an actual amount and therefore involves considerable measurement
error at the individual level – was removed at the outset by imposing the restriction that the imputed amount
had to lie within the earnings range corresponding to the reported salary interval. This restriction placed a
very strict limit on the size of the measurement error and ensured that, in the aggregate, the band averages
of the imputed data very closely approximated the bands of direct reports within the same band. And
because the imputation made (indirect) use of those covariates known to be most strongly related to
earnings, it was possible to ensure that the imputed data behaved in a manner that is unlikely to distort
bivariate or multivariate analyses.
More precisely, the imputation was conducted in the following manner:
•

Precise wage and salary earnings were converted into the same broad bands as used in the BQ.
Extreme values (zero earnings and top 1%) were (temporarily) removed from the continuous
earnings data to prevent these from distorting the results of the regression models. 4

•

Earnings regression models were estimated separately for each of the six time periods/rates, and,
within each period/rate, separately for low, medium and high earnings (respectively, the lowest two
broad bands, the middle two, and the highest two). Predictors were age, gender, working hours,
skill level, skill use, highest completed education, broad occupation, country of birth (home country
versus elsewhere) and job satisfaction, as well as the precise earnings band to which the
respondent belonged. In contrast to PIAAC Cycle 1, the skill level was measured using a weighted
likelihood estimator (WLEs) that captures the average score across all domains after item
calibration instead of the plausible values (PVs). 5 The regression models for additional payments
also included the following predictors: private sector, fixed versus permanent contract, organisation
size, supervisory status, work experience and cohabiting with spouse. Compared to PIAAC Cycle
1, where the model was chosen according to the best performance (R-squared) in the testing
phase, the additional payments are now automatically assigned according to the highest R-squared
in the imputation phase. Note that all the regression models utilised the full data of all respondents
within the specified earnings band, regardless of the time period/rate in which the earnings were
initially reported. For example, the models for hourly earnings were estimated not just for those
who reported their earnings directly per hour but also for those who reported per day, week, biweekly, etc., of course duly converted into hourly earnings according to the above-mentioned
conversion scheme.

•

Based on each of these regression models, predicted earnings were saved in the dataset for all
employed respondents in the data, including those who reported earnings in broad bands as
opposed to directly.

•

For each of the broad bands and each of the time periods/rates separately, the data was sorted by
predicted earnings. Those respondents who reported earnings in broad bands were then assigned
the actual earnings value of their nearest neighbour with directly reported earnings in the ranked
dataset. Note that since this imputation was performed separately for each of the broad bands, the
assigned earnings value always lies within the specified band, even if the predicted earnings lie
outside this band. In addition, although these imputed earnings are assigned in terms of the time
period/rate in which the respondent reported their earnings, the full data of all respondents within
the specified earnings band was used. In practical terms, this means that a respondent, for
example, who reported their earnings in broad hourly bands could be assigned the hourly earnings
of the nearest neighbour who directly reported monthly earnings (converted according to the
above-mentioned conversion scheme).

•

A comparable procedure was used to impute the additional payments of those who reported these
in broad bands. In this case, only three broad bands were distinguished, and all payments were
reported on a yearly basis.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

310 
•

The imputed data on earnings and additional payments was merged with the equivalent data of
those who reported earnings directly. The resulting data was then recoded and combined into
several earnings variables, which are discussed below.

•

A flag variable was created to indicate whether earnings were imputed or directly reported.

It was decided not to impute earnings for self-employed respondents who reported their earnings in broad
bands. The primary reason is the unusual earnings distribution for the self-employed, and in particular, the
fact that a significant proportion of the self-employed had zero or negative earnings (in both cases reported
as zero in the data). It was not possible to develop sufficiently reliable and robust regression models that
were able to account for the unusual composition of this category of the self-employed in terms of
education, skills and other predictors.

Construction of a set of standard earnings variables
The combined actual and imputed earnings for wage and salary earners (i.e. hourly and monthly earnings
as well as additional payments) and the direct monthly earnings measure for the self-employed were used
to construct a set of standard variables that formed the basis for the earnings-derived variables included
in the public data file. Two variables (''EARNHR'' and ''EARNMTH'') measure hourly and monthly earnings
of wage and salary earners, excluding bonuses. By adding additional payments to these variables (after
the necessary conversion into the payment period concerned), two variables comprising hourly and
monthly earnings of wage and salary earners, including bonuses, were constructed (''EARNHRBONUS''
and ''EARNMTHBONUS''). For the self-employed, monthly earnings are included in a separate derived
variable (''EARNMTHSELF''). An overall measure of the total monthly earnings of wage and salary earners
and self-employed (i.e. “EARNMTHALL”) was created by combining the monthly earnings of wage and
salary earners, including bonuses, with the monthly earnings of the self-employed.

Purchasing power parity (PPP) conversion
The next step involved a PPP correction so that all earnings variables were expressed in terms of real
disposable earnings in a fixed currency (in this case, US dollars). This is simply a multiplication by a
constant value per country, based on data on purchasing power parity per country from the OECD. This
conversion was applied in the following derived variables:
•

EARNHRBONUSPPP "Hourly earnings including bonuses - PPP corrected $US (wage and salary
earners)"

•

EARNMTHPPP "Monthly earnings excluding bonuses - PPP corrected $US (wage and salary
earners)"

•

EARNMTHBONUSPPP "Monthly earnings including bonuses - PPP corrected $US (wage and
salary earners)"

•

EARNMTHSELFPPP "Monthly earnings self-employed - PPP corrected $US".

•

EARNMTHALLPPP "Monthly earnings including bonuses - PPP corrected $US (wage and salary
earners and self-employed)".

Conversion into deciles
Finally, several earnings indicators were converted into deciles. This involved dividing the data for each
earnings variable into 10 equally sized groups per country, strictly based on the position in the distribution
of earnings according to that variable. In case multiple respondents were exactly at the cutoff points, these
respondents were assigned to the higher and lower earnings group in the numbers required to produce
groups of equal size, with individuals being randomly sorted into the higher and lower groups. This resulted
in the following three derived variables:
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 311
•

EARNHRDCL "Hourly earnings in deciles excluding bonuses (wage and salary earners)"

•

EARNHRBONUSDCL "Hourly earnings in deciles including bonuses (wage and salary earners)"

•

EARNMTHALLDCL "Monthly earned income in deciles including bonuses (wage and salary
earners and self-employed)".

Measures and derived variables on social and emotional skills
PIAAC Cycle 2 includes self-report measures of social and emotional skills in Section K of the background
questionnaire. Social and emotional skills can help predict many important life outcomes, including
academic achievement and attainment, income, health and social participation (Lechner, Anger and
Rammstedt, 2019[7]).
The conceptual framework for the measurement of social and emotional skills in PIAAC Cycle 2 is the Big
Five model of personality (John, Naumann and Soto, 2008[8]). The Big Five model distinguishes five broad
personality domains: Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and OpenMindedness. Conscientiousness characterises the tendency to be organised, responsible and productive.
Emotional Stability refers to the disposition to remain calm, anxiety-free and in a generally good mood.
Extraversion describes characteristics such as being outgoing, sociable and assertive. Agreeableness
denotes the ability to be compassionate and respectful and to cooperate with others. Finally, OpenMindedness describes characteristics such as curiosity, aesthetic sensitivity and creativity. Any of the Big
Five personality domains can also be subdivided into facets, which measure specific traits and provide
more predictive information for specific behaviour.
The following section describes the instruments used to measure social and emotional skills via the Big
Five personality domains in PIAAC Cycle 2. It then describes the available derived variables and provides
recommendations for analyses using these variables.

Measurement of the Big Five in PIAAC Cycle 2
In PIAAC Cycle 2, shortened versions of the Big Five personality Inventory (BFI-2-XS and BFI-2-S) were
field-tested in the background questionnaire in Section K on social and emotional skills. These short
versions were derived from the BFI-2 (Soto and John, 2017[9]; Soto and John, 2017[10]), a contemporary
revision of the BFI (John, Donahue and Kentle, n.d.[11]). Both instruments are suitable for measuring social
and emotional skills and their relation to external outcomes (Rammstedt, Lechner and Danner, 2021[12]).
The BFI-2 covers the five personality domains, as well as three facets within each domain. The BFI-2-XS
comprises 15 items, while the BFI-2-S comprises 30 items.
The shorter BFI-2-XS is a subset of the BFI-2-S, meaning that all 15 items of the BFI-2-XS are also present
in the 30 items of the BFI-2-S. Some countries field-tested the BFI-2-XS, and others the BFI-2-S. This
section starts with describing BFI-2-XS, followed by a description of what the BFI-2-S allows in addition to
what is possible with the BFI-2-XS. An overview of the instruments is presented in Table 11.8.

domain and facet abbreviation (e.g. EXTR_ASSE).

The BFI-2-XS measures each of the five domains with three items, one per facet. This means that the
domain scores derived from the BFI-2-XS retain the greatest possible breadth and content validity for that
scale length. However, since each facet is only measured with one item, no derived variables can be
provided on the facet level for the BFI-2-XS.
The BFI-2-S measures each domain with six items, two per facet. This structure has two additional benefits
compared to the BFI-2-XS. First, the even number of six items per domain means that the scale can be
counterbalanced with three positively keyed and three negatively keyed items. This means that scores
derived from the BFI-2-S are more resilient to an acquiescent response style (Soto and John, 2017a),
meaning that the tendency of some respondents to agree to items regardless of content is mitigated.
Second, the two items per facet mean that facet-level derived variables can be provided.
The BFI-2 scales were administered by interviewers who presented participants with a showcard including
the response options. Participants gave verbal responses to each of the items. These responses were
later numerically coded from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree).

BFI-2 versions fielded in PIAAC Cycle 2
In PIAAC Cycle 2, 29 out of 31 countries chose to include Section K on socio-emotional skills. Of these 29
countries, 13 took the longer BFI-2-S and 16 the shorter BFI-2-XS (see Table 11.9). Since the BFI-2-XS is
a subset of the BFI-2-S, this means BFI-2-XS data is available for all 29 countries. In cases where BFI-2S was administered, the first 15 items shown to participants comprised the BFI-2-XS, while the second set
of 15 items were the additional BFI-2-S items.

Translation of the BFI-2-S and BFI-2-XS
The cross-cultural research context of PIAAC required additional attention to the translation of BFI-2 items,
which were originally developed in English (Soto and John, 2017b). Translations were centrally managed
and produced by the PIAAC Consortium to ensure internationally comparable translations of the BFI-2.
First, the Consortium checked if there were existing translations for all languages. If no existing translation
was found, cApStAn followed the double translation and reconciliation approach to create an initial
translation. Next, experts on the measurement of socio-emotional skills from each participating countries
were identified and asked to review the translations. Finally, the national teams of participating countries
were asked to review the translations before and after the PIAAC Cycle 2 field trial. The full description of
the translation process of the BFI-2, as well as the final translations used in the PIAAC Cycle 2 main study,
can be found in Rammstedt et al. (2024[13]).

Derived variables on social and emotional skills
Depending on which version of the BFI-2 is field-tested, the following derived variables are provided per
country:
•

Scaled scores for the BFI-2-XS based on three items per domain are available for all 29 countries
(five variables, one for each domain).

•

Scaled scores for the BFI-2-S based on six items per domain (five variables) are available for 13
countries (five variables, one for each domain).

•

Scaled scores for the BFI-2-S facets based on two items per facet (15 variables) are available for
13 countries (15 variables; one for each of the three facets for each of the five domains).

Variable names of domain and facet-level derived variables can be found in Table 11.8.
Each derived variable is a within-country, z-standardised, unit-weighted scale score of the respective Big
Five domain or facet. The creation of unit-weighted scale scores was achieved by calculating the mean
response per respondent for a particular BFI-2 domain or facet. A small number of respondents with
missing responses were excluded and did not receive any scale scores. Then, the mean and standard
deviation of the unit-weighted scale scores were calculated within countries. Weights were used to obtain
weighted point estimates of mean and standard deviation within countries. Finally, respondents were
assigned z-scores based on the within-country weighted means and standard deviations for each DV. This
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

314 
makes mean-score comparisons between countries intentionally impossible and upholds an agreement
reached between the OECD and the Board of Participating Countries to create an index or derived variable
for social-emotional skills that could not be compared across countries.

Analysis recommendations
The derived variables are z-standardised scores per country and domain combination. This has the
following intended technical consequences:
•

Across countries, mean and variance comparisons are not possible, as all derived variables have
a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one.

•

Within countries, mean and variance comparisons between socio-demographic groups are
possible.

•

Within countries, correlations between derived variables and other variables are possible.

Beyond the technical consequences, researchers should keep in mind that short scales, like the BFI-2-S
and ultra-short scales, like the BFI-2-XS or BFI-2-S facet scores, trade some of their reliability and metric
invariance across countries for efficiency and reduced respondent burden. As a consequence, data users
should use caution when comparing the size of correlations between social-emotional skills and other
variables across countries. For example, authors should be very careful when making claims such as
“conscientiousness is more predictive of numeracy in one country than in another”. Note that calculating
interaction effects that involve countries is such a comparison of correlations. However, interpretations of
the effect direction (i.e. positive or negative correlations) can be made. For example, “conscientiousness
is predictive of numeracy in all covered countries”.
Note that for the 13 countries that field-tested the BFI-2-S, two sets of domain-level derived variables are
available: a set of five variables derived from three items, each in analogy to the BFI-2-XS, and a set of
five variables derived from the full set of six items, each from the full set items of the BFI-2-S. For analyses
involving countries beyond those 13, the BFI-2-XS variables should be used. However, for research
focusing only on countries that used the BFI-2-S, the BFI-2-S derived variables should be used to take
advantage of their higher reliability as well as their greater resilience against acquiescent responding.
Lastly, Annex 11.A of this chapter provides country-level reliability estimates (Cronbach’s α) of the BFI-2S and BFI-2-XS. Researchers can use the reliability estimates to correct correlations for attenuation due
to measurement error. Each reliability estimate corresponds to one derived variable, either of the BFI-2-S
or the BFI-2-XS. Correction for attenuation can be especially useful for the BFI-2-XS as it is bound to have
lower reliability than the BFI-2-S due to its shorter scale length. As mentioned above, shorter scales such
as the BFI-2-S and the BFI-2-XS are expected to have lower reliability than conventional-length scales.
However, they optimise for an efficient assessment while retaining conceptual breadth and criterion validity
(Rammstedt, Lechner and Danner, 2021[12]).

Development of derived variables on skill use, influencing, learning and task

which asks respondents to report on their use of skills both inside and outside of work. The frequency and
type of activities associated with reading, writing, numeracy and information technology were targeted in
the BQ using multiple items related to activities both in and out of work. In addition, other areas, particularly
those involving workplace intrapersonal, interpersonal and other generic “soft” skills not included in the
direct assessment, were also addressed through a set of self-reported questions. These scales are found

Scaling methodology
All of the items included in the skill use scales are Likert-type items with five levels (e.g. “never”, “less than
once a month”, “less than once a week but at least once a month”, “at least once a week but not every
day” and “every day”6) in addition to the response options “do not know” and “refuse to answer”. Prior to
scaling, the responses for all items were recoded so that the response corresponding to the lowest level
of the construct was coded as zero. Any missing responses (because an item was not administered), as
well as the “do not know” and “refusal” responses, were treated as ignorable missing data and were
excluded from the scaling.
As in Cycle 1, the scales were constructed using item response theory (IRT), specifically the generalised
partial credit model (GPCM) (Muraki, 1992[14]), which is explained in detail later in this chapter. The
software mdltm (version 1.965) (Shin et al., 2017[15]; von Davier, 2015[16]) was used for the scaling.

Groups used in the scaling
In the initial scaling run, item parameters were estimated using data from all individuals with available data
from all participating countries. Each country was included in the scaling using senate weights, which is a
linear transformation of the final full sample weight (SPFWT0) such that the sum of the senate weights for
each country adds up to 5 000. The purpose of using senate weights is to ensure that each country
contributes equally to the scaling and analyses. However, due to missing responses within each country
(some respondents did not receive or reach the skill use section of the survey), the sum of the senate
weights of the cases used to calibrate the item parameters for each scale may not add up to 5 000 for each
country.
Note that for Canada, the respondents who took the BQ in English and those who took it in French were
treated as separate groups in the scaling. For Israel, the respondents who took the BQ in Hebrew and
Arabic were treated as separate groups. For all other countries, all respondents in the country were treated

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

316 
as a single group, regardless of the language in which they took the BQ. For simplicity, the countries and
country-by-language groups used in the scaling process are called groups in the remainder of this chapter.

Generalised partial credit model (GPCM)
The GPCM (Muraki, 1992) is a mathematical model for the probability that an individual will select a certain
response category for an item with more than two response categories. For an item i with m + 1 ordered
categories, the probability of an individual 𝑣 selecting a certain response category k (0, 1, 2, …, m) under
the GPCM can be written as:
𝑃(𝑥𝑣𝑖 = 𝑘|𝜃𝑣 , 𝛽𝑖 , 𝛼𝑖 , 𝑑𝑖 ) =

exp{∑𝑘𝑟=0 𝐷𝛼𝑖 (𝜃𝑣 − 𝛽𝑖 + 𝑑𝑖𝑟 )}
𝑚

𝑖
∑𝑢=0
exp{∑𝑢𝑟=0 𝐷𝛼𝑖 (𝜃𝑣 − 𝛽𝑖 + 𝑑𝑖𝑟 )}

The overall item location parameter  can be regarded as the item’s general location on the latent
continuum of the construct being measured. Items with a higher  parameter require a higher latent trait
for a higher response category to be selected. The d parameter is the step parameter (of which there are
m for an item with m + 1 categories, with the step parameters for each item summing to 0), which
represents the deviation of the category intersection  from the general location  The category
intersection  is the intersection between two neighbouring category characteristic curves, in other words,
the point on the latent continuum  at which a higher response category is more likely to be selected (e.g.
the point on the latent continuum where the individual is more likely to select “to some extent” than “very
little”). Note that  and d can be used to calculate the category intersection  using the following formula:
𝛿𝑘 = 𝛽 − 𝑑𝑘
The discrimination parameter  scaled by a constant D = 1.7 signifies the slope of the category
characteristic curves. In other words, it indicates how well selecting a certain response category
discriminates between individuals on the latent continuum . To solve the indeterminacy of the IRT scale,
the average of the item discrimination parameters  across all the items in a scale was constrained to one.
For illustrative purposes, Figure 11.1 displays the category characteristic curves of a four-category item
(e.g. a Likert-type item with response categories “not at all”, “very little”, “to some extent” and “to a high
extent”), with the three item parameters used in the GPCM (i.e. ,  and d) represented in the figure. For
comparison, Figure 11.2 displays the category characteristic curves of an item for which only the 
parameter has been increased while the  and d parameters were kept the same as in Figure 11.1.
