Special handling of trend scales
Scales that had three or more trend items (i.e. INFLUENCEC2, READHOMEC2, READWORKC2 and
TASKDISCC2) were treated as a trend scale. For these trend scales, the scaling process began by fixing
the item parameters of the trend items to the international parameters that had been estimated in Cycle 1,
a procedure called fixed parameter linking. There were no group-specific item parameters in Cycle 1. For
trend scales that consisted of both trend items and new items, the item parameters for the trend items
were fixed at the beginning of the scaling process, and the item parameters for the new items were newly
estimated using data from Cycle 2. Note that all the items in the trend scales were evaluated for the
goodness-of-fit of the item parameters.
For the scales that had only two trend items (i.e. ICTHOMEC2, LEARNATWORKC2, NUMWORKC2,
WRITHOMEC2 and WRITWORKC2), the scaling process also began by fixing the item parameters of the
trend items to the international parameters that had been estimated in Cycle 1. However, these scales
were treated as new scales for all other processes, such as the transformation of the weighted likelihood
estimate (WLE) scores into scale scores and the categorisation of the scale scores into quintiles.
Therefore, these scales are not considered to be trend scales.

Releasing item parameters
The invariance of latent constructs across groups was evaluated using multiple-group concurrent calibration
with partial invariance constraints. In the initial scaling run, the item parameters were estimated using data
from all individuals with available data. The item parameters that were estimated in this initial scaling process
are called international parameters since they were estimated using responses from all participating
countries. After the initial scaling, the fit of the international parameters for each item was evaluated for each
group using the root mean square deviance (RMSD). The RMSD for group 𝑔 is defined as:
𝑒𝑥𝑝

2

𝑅𝑀𝑆𝐷𝑔 = √∫[𝑝𝑔𝑜𝑏𝑠 (𝜃) − 𝑝𝑔 (𝜃)] 𝑓𝑔 (𝜃)𝑑𝜃
It quantifies the difference between the observed item characteristic curve (ICC) for the group based on
the pseudo counts from the E-step of the Expectation-Maximisation (EM) algorithm, 𝑝𝑔𝑜𝑏𝑠 (𝜃), with the
𝑒𝑥𝑝
model-based ICC, 𝑝𝑔 (𝜃) (Shin et al., 2017). RMSD values range from zero to one, with values close to
zero indicating good item fit, meaning that the model-based item parameters fit the data for the group well.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

318 
Note that the RMSD statistic is sensitive to group-specific deviations of both the item location parameter 𝛽
and the item discrimination parameter 𝛼.
When the RMSD for an item*group exceeded a pre-defined cutoff of 0.25, it was considered that the modelbased item parameters did not fit the group’s data well. In this case, unique item parameters (also called
group-specific item parameters) were estimated for the group using data only from that group. Note that if
more than one group had similar response patterns for an item, data from those groups were pooled
together and the same unique parameters were estimated for those groups.
The process described above is called releasing item parameters. Item parameters were released, and
parameters were re-estimated until all item*groups had an RMSD value under 0.25. Note that in Cycle 1,
item parameters were not released, so none of the groups received unique item parameters.

Social media items
For the READHOMEC2, READWORKC2, WRITHOMEC2 and WRITWORKC2 scales, an additional item
on social media was administered in Czechia, Finland and Latvia. For these four scales, after the item
parameters for the non-social media items were calibrated, a final round of scaling was conducted to
calibrate the item parameters for the social media item (with the parameters for the non-social media items
fixed to the parameters from the previous run). For Czechia, Finland and Latvia, the WLE scores were
based on the non-social media items as well as the additional social media item. For the other countries,
the WLE scores were based only on non-social media items.

Scale scores
The scaling process described above produced WLE scores (Warm, 1989[17]) for each individual. An
individual who had fewer than three valid responses for a scale (whether due to non-administration, failure
to reach the section, gave a “do not know” response, or refused to respond) did not receive a WLE score,
and the scale score was set to missing. All other individuals received a scale score, even those who had
selected the lowest category for all items on the scale. This is in contrast to the procedure used in Cycle 1,
which recoded these scores as missing (von Davier et al., 2019[1]).
The practical implication of this is that, while comparing relationships between skills use scales and other
variables across PIAAC cycles does not pose issues, comparing average scores could be problematic,
because the population for which the scores are available could be different. Comparability can be restored
by either dropping Cycle 2 respondents who selected the lowest category for all items (mimicking how
those cases were treated in Cycle 1) or by replacing the Cycle 1 missing values with the same values
assigned to Cycle 2 respondents who selected the lowest category for all items.
For the seven new scales, the WLE scores were transformed into a reporting metric to have a mean of two
and a standard deviation of one across all cases with available data, weighted by the senate weights. The
transformation constants that were used to transform the WLE scores into the scale scores (scale score =
A*WLE score + B) are displayed in Table 11.11. Note that A was calculated as 1 / SDWLE , while B was
calculated as 2 – A*MWLE , using the WLE of all cases with available data, weighted by the senate weights.

12. International data and analysis tools
Tim Daniel and Darrell Gwaltney, IEA;
Eugenio Gonzalez, ETS

This chapter provides an overview of PIAAC’s public-use data and analysis
tools. It details the contents and structure of the public-use data files,
including the types of records and variables included, as well as those
excluded for various reasons. The chapter also describes the two main
software tools provided for data analysis: the PIAAC International Data
Explorer (IDE) from ETS and the IDB Analyzer from the International
Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA) and
highlights their functionalities and analytical capabilities. Additionally, it
addresses general considerations for analysing PIAAC data, emphasising
the importance of using sampling weights and accounting for the complex
survey design.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 331

Introduction
Designing, collecting, validating and analysing PIAAC data was a very complex, highly demanding and
collaborative process involving all Consortium partners, a broad range of external experts, all participating
countries and the OECD Secretariat. As such, PIAAC requires data products that reflect its design
complexities. To support and promote secondary analyses, the OECD prepares a public-use version of
each national database and this technical report, which are available to interested analysts and users in
the scientific community as well as the general public. The international public-use version of the PIAAC
data is made available in two different ways: the PIAAC International Data Explorer (IDE), a public-use
aggregate database underlying a web-based data analysis software, and a set of national public-use files
(PUF) that comprise person-level microdata from those countries that are permitted to release their
national data, limited to the specific variables they agree to release. Each version of the national publicuse data, either the IDE or the PUF, includes a reduced set of variables compared to the full national
database. Generally, but not always, more variables were suppressed in the national PUFs compared to
the data available in the IDE.
This chapter is intended to provide a basic introduction to the PIAAC public-use data and the software
tools capable of replicating the descriptive and inferential analysis presented in the publications of the
Survey of Adult Skills 2023 (OECD, 2024[1]). First, the chapter will discuss the contents of the public-use
data both at the record and the variable levels, the approach to identifying missing data under a complex,
multi-trajectory design, and the available database formats. Then, the chapter will describe general
analytical considerations, followed by the types of analyses supported by the two software tools provided
by the Consortium: the IDE and the IEA’s IDB Analyzer.
This chapter, however, does not intend to cover and illustrate the full range of possible analytical
techniques appropriate for PIAAC and, therefore, does not describe advanced modelling of data, such as
structural equation modelling. Nonetheless, analysts wishing to use the public-use microdata to undertake
advanced analyses not covered by the provided software or those wishing to use alternative statistical
software packages will find sufficient technical information on the structure of the database, the included
measures and the variance estimation approach to configure such software and statistical models
successfully.

Files in the database
As described in Chapter 20 on Data Management and Data Cleaning Procedures, a large number of raw
response data files and documentation were processed to form a series of files that jointly made up the full
national databases for PIAAC, that is, all variables collected or derived as part of PIAAC. These national
databases consisted of one main flat file holding respondent/household level information, an audit log file
holding interview process and timing data, and, for each respondent, a set of cognitive log files native to
the computer-based assessment (CBA) platform used in PIAAC. Of these files, only the main flat file is of
key analytical interest and thus forms the basis of the public-use data described in this chapter. Other parts
of the national database, such as the cognitive log data, are not part of the public-use data described here.
For naming the files, operational identifiers based on the ISO 3166/UN M49 standard were used for the
value labels identifying countries and subnational entities for available samples. Table 12.1 provides
details. Data files are named using the alpha-3 code of the national entity. Within databases, the variable
CNTRYID holds the numerical codes and labels of the national entity to which the data belongs. The
variable CNTRYID_E holds the numerical codes and labels of the subnational entity.
Except for two participants, national entities participated in the assessment; therefore, the codes and labels
for CNTRYID and CNTRYID_E are identical. Two entities participated at the subnational level: the Flemish

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

332 
Region of Belgium and England in the United Kingdom. Additionally, for Canada, the English- and Frenchspeaking parts are identified as subnational entities. Keeping this information in two separate variables
allows for analysis at the level of the national as well as subnational entities as appropriate.

Records in the public-use data
This section describes the records included in the public-use data. PIAAC used a highly complex
assessment design that resulted in several possible trajectories through the interview process. Therefore,
users must understand this design to make appropriate use of the data.

Records included in the public-use data
Each participant’s public-use data includes the records that were considered suitable for analysis. One
exception to this rule is discussed below. More specifically, each record corresponds to a validated

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 333
responding sampled person. Each record also conforms to the international target population definition,
which is adults aged 16 to 65. All records in the public-use data were adjudicated and weighted.
While the vast majority of records in each public-use data are “true completes,” that is, sampled
respondents that followed the intended interview workflow until the end, there are noteworthy exceptions.
Three main groups of respondents are included in the public-use data that have weights and replicate
weights but with partial records: language-related nonrespondents1 who completed the background
questionnaire (BQ) with assistance but not the assessment; respondents who discontinued the
assessment after it began; and respondents who completed a doorstep interview.
The inclusion of these three types of records directly relates to the PIAAC Cycle 2 Technical
Standard 4.3.3, which defines a completed case as one that contains at least the following: 2
•

responses to key background questions in the full background questionnaire (BQ), including age,
gender, highest level of schooling, employment status and country of birth (native/non-native)

•

the tablet tutorial section is attempted

•

the locator is attempted.

A limited number of Abbreviated Interview Cases (AICs) also counts as completed cases, where an AIC is
defined as having:
•

responses to key background questions in the full BQ, including age, gender, highest level of
schooling, employment status and country of birth (native/non-native)

•

the locator is not attempted for a literacy-related reason, i.e. language barrier, reading/ writing
barrier, or learning/mental disability

•

responses to key background questions in the full BQ, including age, gender, highest level of
schooling, employment status and country of birth (native/non-native)

•

the locator is not attempted due to lack of tablet skills

•

completed doorstep interview (see Chapter 9 for more information on the doorstep interview).

OR

OR

Records excluded from the public-use data
As part of the data collection, validation and weighting, certain cases in the original national databases
were excluded from the analysis and the public-use data. The excluded cases include, but are not limited
to, out-of-scope respondents; selected households with no sampled persons; non-interviews, meaning
sampled persons who were not interviewed due to refusal or other reasons; a small number of suspected
falsified cases detected as part of the validation and quality control; respondents with less than the
minimally required BQ or doorstep interview items (age, gender, highest level of education and
employment status); and cases with certain anomalies or unclear origin. These cases were flagged
accordingly, and no weights were computed.
In relation to this, it should be noted that seven countries targeted respondents outside the international
target population definition. In the case of Denmark and Singapore, this related to an oversample of
individuals who had participated in the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA).
In the case of Chile, an oversample targeted individuals at the age of 15. The Slovak Republic oversampled
teachers. Finally, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the United States included a sample of respondents
aged between 66 and 74/75 years. These groups of cases were excluded from the respective PUFs.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

334 

Variables in the public-use data
The PIAAC design is a highly complex one that integrates sophisticated sampling and weighting
approaches, a multistage adaptive assessment design, a rich BQ, a tablet-based assessment delivery
platform, innovative item formats, related process information, and a range of derived measures, indicators
and indices.
With that said, it is obvious that such rich data contains variables of varying analytical utility and priority.
For example, a large number of variables only include process-related information or temporary information
that is necessary for specific steps, such as during the computation of weights. This section describes the
types of variables included in each country’s public-use data. It also describes those excluded because
they carry no analytical utility for international comparisons or address identified and/or assumed
disclosure risks.

Variables included
The public-use data underlying the PUF and the IDE contain different sets of variables. The PUF includes
a comprehensive set of 2 483 variables. Of these, only about 750 are included in the data accessible
through the IDE. The majority of variables included only in the PUF relate to the individual cognitive item
scores and process information. Table 12.2 provides a breakdown of variables by type, name or naming
convention and whether the respective group is available in the IDE or the PUF.

Variables excluded, suppressed or coarsened for some or all countries
The public-use data includes a subset of the information available in the full, national databases. The
public-use data does not include any variables using national adaptations and extensions in the BQ. It only
includes variables that were derived across all countries. Further, a sizable number of variables were
excluded in consultation with the OECD because they have no or very little analytical utility, were intended
for internal or interim purposes only, relate to secure item material, or include personally identifiable data
or data that may increase the risk of unintended or indirect disclosure.
The groups of variables excluded from the public-use data are:
•

direct, indirect and operational identifiers for respondents and interviewers

•

interim sampling, disposition, data availability, demographic and weighting information

•

certain BQ or process variables that are available in coded or derived from (for example, country
and language), especially detailed write-ins

•

all national adaptations and extensions in the BQ

•

original scale score values (theta) before standardisation to an international metric.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

336 
National data from national adaptations or extensions is not of key interest in an international large-scale
assessment and comparison. However, national data might be available but only by directly contacting the
concerned PIAAC participant.
A particularly important issue is to preserve the confidentiality of individual respondents in the release of
the public-use aggregate (IDE) and microdata (PUF) in order to prevent unintended or indirect disclosure.
The risk of such disclosure is greatest in cases where the combined characteristics of a respondent in a
sample lead to a unique individual in the population. The higher the sampling fraction, the more likely a
unique record in the sample will also be unique in the population. As agreed by the Board of Participating
Countries (BPC), countries were given the possibility to either coarsen or suppress their data prior to
submission to the Consortium and the OECD and/or afterwards during the production of the public-use
data. PIAAC participants were asked to suppress information only when deemed absolutely necessary to
meet national legislative requirements to increase the usefulness and analytical power of their national
data. Differences in national laws resulted in a large degree of variance in the number of suppressions
across participating countries. The list of suppressed variables is available at the OECD PIAAC website. 3
Suppressed data are represented in the public-use data by missing codes. As with national data, more
detailed data might be available but only by directly contacting the concerned participant.
Database users should note that the most complete set of information was available to the Consortium for
analysis and the OECD for reporting and archiving. The IDE is based on a set of reduced national
databases that include fewer variables and less information as a function of suppressions. Finally, the
PUFs contain the most restricted data in PIAAC, containing the largest number of suppressions.
In many cases where more than one participant requested the suppression of a particular variable for the
IDE or PUF, a coarsened version of this variable (suffix “_C”) was created that includes the level of detail
deemed suitable for public release by the concerned countries (see group “BQ – Derived coarsened
information” in Table 12.2 above). Therefore, analysts are encouraged to use such a coarsened variable
if the aim of the analysis is to include the most complete set of countries, albeit with a reduced level of
detail.
As a result (and similar to other data collections), public users of the data in the IDE or PUF may be unable
to fully replicate particular tables, figures and other exhibits in the international reporting because such
reporting was based on the most complete set of confidential information, which is not available to the
general public.

Representing valid and missing data
As in all survey projects, missing data can occur for different reasons. PIAAC is no exception, and despite
the intention to collect complete or almost complete information, there are gaps in the data. In principle,
missing data in a survey may occur when there is no or almost no observed data, as well as no
administrative data for a respondent (unit non-response) or when some variables for a respondent are
unknown or cannot be known (item non-response).
To understand the missing data pattern in PIAAC, users are reminded of the complex assessment design.
Missing data in PIAAC can occur for a number of reasons:
•

Missing data by design (that is, it is known a priori that they will not be collected) for some or all
respondents because of the way the assessment is designed.
o

Respondents with literacy-related dispositions (see above) were not administered the
interview.

o

A small number of PIAAC participants did not participate in the international options.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 337

•

•

o

Certain sections in the BQ were intentionally presented to subpopulations (domains) only with
reference to responses given to prior questions (“valid skip”).

o

Domain item clusters were assigned based on random allocation and previous proficiency
information collected.

Missing data due to the response process.
o

Respondents may have broken off the interview after it was started as a function of, for
example, time, motivation, fatigue or sensitive questions being asked.

o

Respondents may have explicitly refused to respond to questions in the BQ, or they may not
have known the answer to a question with sufficient certainty. These were coded in the data
as “refused” or “don’t know”.

Missing data due to logistics, processing or analysis.
o

Data were captured, yet CBA result files were lost during the transfer.

o

Erroneous routing in national versions of the BQ collected fewer data items for particular
respondents than intended.

o

Certain data items (variables and/or a subset of values) were not provided or suppressed due
to regulations relating to the confidentiality of information.

o

Respondents with literacy-related dispositions were routed to the doorstep interview.

o

A small number of values were obvious outliers, otherwise useless, or erroneously coded in
the original national databases.

It should be noted that no imputation was done for missing item responses except for the imputation of
earnings from precise and/or broad categories and the multiple imputation of proficiency scale scores for
the literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving domains.
Table 12.3 below provides an overview of the main missing values and their type, scope and representation
in SAS and SPSS PUFs. The representation of missing values differs in these two statistical packages. In
SAS, the standard missing code (.) and other special missing values were used. In SPSS, a code that
depends on the length of the numeric variable was used. Variables of one digit use missing values 6, 7, 8
and 9; those with two digits use missing values 96, 97, 98 and 99; variables of three digits use 996, 997,
998, 999; and so on unless missing values conflicted with payload values, in which case the variable
lengths were increased.
The PIAAC public-use data includes a small number of coded variables that are defined as strings because
the respective coding schemes are defined as strings. For example, occupational codes may appear as
using a numerical scheme but need to be stored as strings because codes include leading zeroes would
be lost if converted to a number. The use of string variables and, therefore, string missing values relates
to ISCO codes for occupation, ISIC codes for industry, region codes, and language codes. In these cases,
number-based strings such as “9999” were used to represent missing data.

In addition to the general missing scheme described above, which applies to the largest set of variables,
the specifications of some derived variables included missing schemes specific to a particular variable or,
in some cases, a small set of variables. These missing values are fully documented in the SPSS files and
SAS format scripts. Given that the number space for missing values (or letters in case of SAS special
missing values) is limited, some of the per-variable missing schemes may use the same missing code, yet
the type of these codes may vary from one variable to the next. Data users are strongly encouraged to
review the coding of missing values in derived BQ variables carefully, using the information provided as
part of the SAS/SPSS files and earlier in this report prior to analysis.

Public-use file (PUF) formats
While the data underlying the IDE is not directly accessible to users, the PUFs are. They are available in
three standard formats – SPSS, SAS and CSV – allowing for data to be loaded and used in these and
many other standard packages.
SPSS data files are standard, Windows-based .sav files and encoded in Unicode (UTF-8). SPSS data files
include full dictionary information from the applicable metadata maintained in the codebooks: i) variable
types and formats, ii) variable labels, iii) value labels (including any missing value labels), iv) missing value
definitions, and v) variable measurement levels.
SAS formatted files are standard, compressed .sas7bdat data files for Windows environments and
encoded in Unicode (UTF-8). Variable types, widths, decimals and labels are assigned to all variables
according to the labels defined in the metadata. SAS does not provide a way to store value labels on the
file permanently. Therefore, each PUF file in SAS format is accompanied by an equivalently named .sas
file that includes syntax to assign formats (value labels). The SAS format syntax files include the relevant
LIBNAME, PROC FORMATS, DATA and FORMATS statements. These syntax files can be executed
against each individual SAS export file in order to display value labels in analytical procedures such as
PROC UNIVARIATE, PROC FREQ, etc.
The CSV files were created by the OECD Secretariat as a direct export of the SAS files.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 339

Data analysis and software tools
General considerations for data analysis using PIAAC data
For analysts familiar with population estimation using other large-scale educational survey databases such
as those produced by, for example, the OECD PISA or IEA studies, the analysis of PIAAC data will present
relatively few difficulties. For those unaccustomed to working with complex survey sample data, the
technical report, this chapter in particular, and the analytical tools provided by the Consortium, contain
sufficient technical information and references to support statistically correct analyses.
The three main analytical requirements that any analysis of PIAAC data needs to account for are the use
of sampling weights, the complex multistage cluster sample design that was implemented to balance the
research goals and cost-efficient operations, and the use of multiple-imputed proficiency estimates, the
so-called “plausible values.” The key challenge for analysing PIAAC data, especially when one or more of
the proficiency scales are involved, lies at the intersection of the uncertainty in estimating population
characteristics due to sampling and the uncertainty introduced when using multiple imputations. In addition,
another key challenge for PIAAC – in contrast to other international studies – is that there was no common
variance estimation procedure across all participating countries.
Standard analytical packages for the social sciences and educational research do not readily recognise or
support handling the complex sample and assessment designs. This gap is filled by the two software tools
made available by the Consortium (and the OECD’s tools in R and Stata) to assist data users in accessing
and analysing the PIAAC data and producing basic outputs: the IDE and the IEA’s IDB Analyzer. Each of
these software tools addresses a slightly different set of needs. While the IDE is a web-based application
that allows relatively easy and publication-ready access to basic estimates of means, totals and
proportions, the IDB Analyzer, used in conjunction with the PUFs, allows unit record access to the publicuse data and the opportunity to conduct analyses offline, derive additional variables, and produce various
estimates for further use and reporting.

The PIAAC International Data Explorer (IDE)
The IDE is a web-based application developed by ETS that allows the user to query the international
PIAAC data via a secure web browser. The IDE can be used to compute a diverse range of statistics
including, but not limited to, means, standard deviations, percentages by subgroup, percentages by levels,
linear regression and percentiles. All statistics are computed, taking into account the sampling and
assessment designs. In addition, the IDE can conduct significance testing between statistics from different
groups and display the results in graphical form. Results from the IDE can be directly exported and saved
in Microsoft Word, Microsoft Excel and HTML formats. The IDE is accessible from any computer connected
to the Internet from the following address: http://piaacdataexplorer.oecd.org/ide/idepiaac.

The IEA’s IDB Analyzer
The IEA’s International Database Analyzer (IEA, 2024[2]) is an application that can be used to combine and
analyse data from IEA’s large-scale assessments as well as analyse data from the OECD’s Teaching and
Learning International Survey (TALIS), PISA and PIAAC.
The IDB Analyzer creates SAS, SPSS and R syntax that can be used to analyse national PUFs. The syntax
generated and the referenced macros take into account information from the sampling design in the
computation of sampling variance. In addition, it handles plausible values. The resulting code can be used
to calculate estimates of achievement and their corresponding standard errors, combining sampling and
imputation variance. The code generated by the IEA’s IDB Analyzer enables the user to compute

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

340 
descriptive statistics and conduct statistical hypothesis testing among groups in the population without
having to write any programming code.
The IEA’s IDB Analyzer is licensed free of cost by the IEA and is for use only in accordance with the terms
of the licensing agreement. While users can use the software for free, they do not have any ownership of,
copyright or other intellectual property rights to the software itself or its components, including the
underlying macros. Users are only licensed to use the enclosed macros in combination with the IEA’s IDB
Analyzer unless explicitly authorised by the IEA.
The IEA’s IDB Analyzer is available from the following permanent URL: http://www.iea.nl/data.html. The
software license expires at the end of each calendar year, when users will again have to download and
reinstall the most current version of the software. Features are added on a continuous basis to support
additional surveys and databases or include additional types of analysis, options or outputs. Technical
support for the IEA IDB Analyzer can be obtained by contacting the IEA at idb-analyzer@iea-hamburg.de.
The IEA IDB Analyzer is fully self-documenting, and each version comes with a comprehensive help
manual as part of the installation (IEA, 2022[3]). Users of the PUFs are referred to this more detailed
documentation with respect to the use and interpretation of the IDB Analyzer’s features, options and
outputs.
The IDB Analyzer consists of three modules – the Convert Module, the Merge Module and the Analysis
Module – which are integrated in one common application window.

The Convert Module
The convert module is used to convert SPSS files to RData format.

The Merge Module
The Merge Module is used to combine data files from different study participants. The Merge Module also
allows the user to easily select individual or groups of variables to create a smaller and more manageable
dataset. When running the Merge Module, the IDB Analyzer creates syntax that merges and combines
files specified by the user, keeping only the selected variables yet automatically adding all the variables
required for correct variance estimation.
Merged data files created using the Merge Module can be processed either with the Analysis Module of
the IDB Analyzer or by any other analysis software that accepts SPSS files as input.

The Analysis Module
The Analysis Module of the IDB Analyzer provides procedures statistics for any variable of interest at the
country level and specific subgroups within a country. It also computes percentages of respondents in the
population that are within, at, or above benchmarks of performance or within user-defined cut points in the
proficiency distribution, percentiles based on the achievement scale, or any other continuous variable.
The Analysis Module can be used to analyse data files from PIAAC regardless of whether they have been
pre-processed with the IEA IDB Analyzer Merge Module. The Analysis Module can create code for several
analysis procedures. Like the Merge Module, the Analysis Module creates syntax that computes the
statistics specified by the user.
The following analyses can be performed with the Analysis Module:
•

Percentages and Means: Computes percentages, means and standard deviations for selected
variables by subgroups defined by the user. The percentage of missing responses is included in
the output.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 341
•

Percentages only: Computes percentages by subgroups defined by the user.

•

Linear Regression: Computes linear regression coefficients for selected variables predicting a
dependent variable by subgroups defined by the user. The IDB Analyzer can include plausible
values as dependent or independent variables in the linear regression equation. It also has the
capability of contrast coding categorical variables (dummy or effect) and including them in the linear
regression equation.

•

Logistic Regression: Computes logistic regression coefficients for selected variables predicting
a dependent dichotomous variable by subgroups defined by the user. The IDB Analyzer can
include plausible values as independent variables in the logistic regression equation. It also has
the capability of contrast coding categorical variables and including them in the logistic regression
equation.

•

Benchmarks: Computes the percentage of the population meeting a set of user-specified
performance or achievement benchmarks by subgroups defined by the user. It computes these
percentages in two modes: cumulative (percentage of the population at or above given points in
the distribution) or discrete (percentage of the population within given points of the distribution). It
can also compute the mean of an analysis variable for those at a particular achievement level when
the discrete option is selected.

•

Correlations: Computes correlation for selected variables by subgroups defined by the grouping
variable(s). The IDB Analyzer is capable of computing the correlation between sets of plausible
values.

•

Percentiles: Computes the score points that separate a given proportion of the distribution of
scores by subgroups defined by the grouping variable(s).

Prior to every analysis, the IEA’s IDB Analyzer calculates unweighted and weighted descriptive statistics
for the analysis variables (means, standard deviations, minimum and maximum) and frequencies by
analysis subgroups. In addition, except when computing percentiles, the estimate of the population size
for each of the subgroups processed (sum of the sampling weights), and the corresponding standard errors
are computed. Bar or line charts are drawn by default when computing percentages, percentages and
means and when calculating the percentages of the population within benchmarks with or without an
analysis variable.
When calculating these statistics, the IEA’s IDB Analyzer can use any continuous or categorical variable
in the database or scores in the form of plausible values. When using plausible values, the IEA’s IDB
Analyzer generates code that takes into account the multiple imputation methodology in the calculation of
the variance for statistics as it applies to the corresponding study.
All procedures offered within the Analysis Module of the IEA’s IDB Analyzer make use of appropriate
sampling weights and standard errors of the statistics that are computed according to the variance
estimation procedure required by the design as it applies to the corresponding study. In the case of PIAAC,
this functionality extends to the level of participants, as the variance estimate method (VEMETHOD), and
the number of replicate weights (VENREPS) are encoded in the respective PUF.
For a complete list of features, options, output fields, and parameters, users are referred to the help manual
that is part of every installation.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

342 

13. The PIAAC Portal
Mike Wagner and Paul Brost, ETS

The chapter covers the design and functionality of the PIAAC Portal, a webbased system developed to facilitate communication and collaboration
among the numerous contractors and participating countries involved in the
PIAAC project. The Portal served as a central repository for project-related
information, providing features such as document management, workflow
task management and translation previews. It supported the sharing of files,
organising project activities and the development of high-quality translations
of the assessment instruments. The technical implementation of the Portal
was based on WordPress, with custom functionalities to meet the project’s
specific needs.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 345

Introduction
A project as complex as PIAAC, with a large number of contractors and participating countries and
economies, requires a significant amount of communication and collaboration. The PIAAC Portal was
developed to support this work. This web-based system operated as the central repository for projectrelated information, as well as a single sign-on pathway to access a range of project-related subsystems.
The Portal supported sharing files, organising and tracking project work activities, previewing translated
instruments and other means for sharing information among the project participants.

Document Management
Sharing files was fundamental for sharing information throughout the PIAAC project. Files ranged from
documentation of project design and standards, presentations from meetings and webinars (both slide
decks and video recordings), tracking spreadsheets for translation reviews, and software packages with
the PIAAC Delivery System. All files needed to be available throughout the project, as people joined and
left the project, and access to the files, in many cases, needed to be closely managed. The PIAAC Portal
implemented a document repository to support this. The repository was a directory-based file store, which
was presented to the end users as a set of folders and files, similar to Windows Explorer. Figure 13.1
shows an example of the Document Manager home page.

Figure 13.1. PIAAC Portal Document Manager

File access was based on the user’s role on the project (e.g. contractor, NPM, team member). Access
could be limited at the country level, such that only users from a given country could access files in a
certain folder. Version control was another important feature of the document management function in the
Portal. Each version of a file that was loaded to the Portal was saved, along with the time it was uploaded
and the user who uploaded it. Users could easily review the file history and download all previous versions
of a file.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

346 

Workflow Task Management
Many of the project activities required collaboration among various parties, including between national
teams and contractors. The Portal supported these activities through Workflow Tasks. Workflow Tasks
specified the steps in an activity, the user role responsible for each step, the artefacts (files) involved in
each step and the schedule for the steps. The use of Workflow Tasks is best illustrated through an
example. Prior to the field trial, national teams reviewed country-specific scoring (e.g. currency items) in
trend computer-based assessment (CBA) items and requested corrections to errors (if any). Table 13.1
shows an example of the process followed for the Trend Scoring Review workflow on the task management
page.

Table 13.1. Workflow Task Management

The type of workflow applied to Trend Scoring Review had four steps. First, a task instance of this workflow
type was created for each country and each language version. Each task instance included two documents:
a log of the scoring test results and a form for requesting changes to the scoring of the CBA items. Second,
the user could take control of the task, if he/she had the Portal role associated with the active step for a
task instance (i.e. the Reconciler or NPM in the Scoring Review step). Third, the user was able to update
the files associated with the task, once he/she had control. Fourth, the user indicated the step was done
and moved the task to the next step once the work for that step was completed. Each step of the task
instance had an associated due date, and users could review their outstanding tasks and determine if any
were past due. A Tasks overview page was available for all users, with filters and sorting of the results
provided. Figure 13.2 shows an example of the Tasks overview page.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 347

Figure 13.2. Workflow Tasks Overview

Translation Previews
Translation and adaptation of the cognitive and background questionnaire instruments was an important
activity in the preparation of the PIAAC survey. While the translation process focused on translating the
text a sentence at a time, reviewing the translations in the context of the actual instruments was critical to
maintaining high quality and comparability. The PIAAC Portal provided a simple way for users to generate
live previews of their instrument translations, both as they were being updated and after they had been
submitted through the translation workflows. This functionality was presented as a separate “Translations”
tab in the Portal and is shown below in Figure 13.3.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

348 

Figure 13.3. Translations Preview Page

CBA Unit Previews
Previews of CBA units were supported in two different ways. One was the direct preview of XML
Localisation Interchange File Format (XLIFF) files that were being actively translated. These XLIFF files
were generated from within the OmegaT tool used during the translation process. 1 At the top of the
Translations tab in the Portal, users could upload one of these XLIFF files and generate a live, interactive
preview of the translated CBA unit in a separate web browser tab. The unit to preview and the language
of the translation were determined on the fly from the contents of the XLIFF file.
Alternatively, copies of the latest translations for all units in all languages were saved on the Portal. These
XLIFF files were generated at the end of each translation workflow step, so while the translations were in
progress during the translation process, they reached a level of stability that warranted moving ahead in
the workflow. The files could be browsed by selecting the country, language and domain (LIT, NUM, APS
or the miscellaneous XYZ materials which included transition screens, tutorials and orientations, etc.) from
menus on the Translations tab. This step produced a list of the XLIFF files that could be previewed. Clicking
on an entry in the list opened the preview in a new web browser tab. As when uploading an XLIFF file, the
preview was generated on the fly, not from a version that had already been imported. This ensured that
the latest translation was used.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 349
The CBA unit previews were also used to check the scoring of the items in the units. A checkbox was
available for a “Scoring Review Mode”. This mode presented users with functionality for answering the
questions on the screen and checking how the response would be scored (correct, incorrect or omitted).
Figure 13.4 below shows an example of the Scoring Review Mode page.

Figure 13.4. Scoring Review Mode

BQ Previews
The Portal also supported previews of the background questionnaire (BQ) translations. This functionality
was added for the main study, since translation changes were centralised in this phase of the project. In
the field trial, XLIFFs were uploaded through the Questionnaire Authoring Tool (QAT), a separate web
application, for generating previews. With the Portal, XLIFF files were generated automatically at the
completion of each BQ translation workflow step. Like the CBA units, these files could be accessed by
selecting the country and language to preview. For the BQ previews, it was also possible to generate a
PDF version of the translated questionnaire, as well as to download the testing data collected from the
previewed BQ.

Other Features
The PIAAC Portal provided other features and information sources used by project participants. These
included:
•

Contacts – A list of project contacts, including members of national teams, the OECD Secretariat,
and the PIAAC Consortium partner organisations. Contact information included the country and
organisation of the individual, as well as phone and email information. Contacts could be filtered
and sorted easily.

•

FAQs – A variety of frequently asked questions and answers could be easily browsed. The FAQs
were organised by subject area (Sample Design, Translation, Delivery System, etc.).

•

National Summary Information – This page was a custom database which documented information
about each country’s participation in the project. It included data about the languages which were

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

350 
used by each country for the BQ and direct assessment, options selected by the country (e.g. use
of section K in the BQ, whether the country would use their own CMS or the International CMS),
and sampling information such as the use of a screener or registry data for sampling and the target
number of completed cases in the field trial and main study.

Technical Overview
The PIAAC Portal was developed as a customisation of WordPress, the open-source content management
system.2 WordPress provides foundational services for managing and authenticating users, creating and
serving web pages and web postings, and a framework for implementing custom functionality. The PIAAC
Portal installation was implemented using PHP and MySQL and was deployed to an Ubuntu Linux server
that ran via Amazon Web Services.
The document management functionality within the Portal was built as a custom page type in WordPress.
The front-end code, which displayed the list of files and folders and provided an interface for uploading
and downloading files, was based on the open-source project jQuery File Upload. 3 On the back end,
custom PHP code was created to manage access control and handle file uploads and directory creation.
This back-end code used an SVN repository for version control of the file hierarchy.
The Workflow Tasks and Translation preview functionality were also implemented as custom page types
in WordPress. For the Workflow Tasks, one page displayed the list of tasks available to the user, using an
open-source data grid.4 The data grid supported the filtering and sorting of the task listing. Each task
instance was implemented as a separate page within WordPress. The task metadata, such as the
schedule, the current workflow step and the country and language for the task, were implemented as
custom page attributes on each of the task pages. The files associated with each task instance were
managed in the same way as the document repository. An instance of the document management widget
was embedded in each of the task instance pages, and the files themselves were stored in an SVN
repository with full version control functionality.

14. The PIAAC International Case
Management System
Mike Wagner and Paul Brost, ETS

The PIAAC International Case Management System (iCMS) was a critical
tool for managing the PIAAC survey in 20 participating countries. It
consisted of a standalone application for interviewers (the iCMS Client) to
manage cases and conduct interviews offline, and a web-based
administration system for field supervisors to oversee data collection
activities. The system enabled secure data synchronisation, detailed case
management activities and comprehensive reporting capabilities.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

352 
The Case Management System (CMS) for PIAAC was a critical component for the successful
implementation of the survey. It served a role in the implementation of the standards and guidelines for
both sampling and survey operations. In PIAAC Cycle 2, the PIAAC Consortium provided a standard
International Case Management System (iCMS) that 20 countries used for their data collection. Eleven
countries implemented their own national CMS customised to their needs. 1 This chapter focuses mainly
on the functionality and the implementation of the iCMS. However, the basic functionality of the iCMS will
be common to national CMS versions.
The iCMS comprises two unique components. The iCMS Client was a standalone application that ran
natively on each interviewer’s tablet. It was integrated with the PIAAC Delivery System (PDS) and
contained the functionality required by the interviewers in the data collection work. The iCMS Client could
run in a completely offline mode, with no Internet connection. Network connectivity was required when an
interviewer initially logged in to the system (to validate the account credentials) and when syncing data
with the iCMS Administration System (iCMA), the second component of the iCMS.
The iCMA was a web-based application, accessed via standard web browsers like Chrome or Firefox.
Administrators and survey operations managers used the iCMA to monitor and manage the data collection
activities of the interviewers. In addition, the application provided access to the collected data to the data
management expert (DME), both for further management and for downloading.

The iCMS Client
Interviewers typically completed most of their work through the iCMS Client application. Using the iCMS
Client, interviewers were able to:
•

review their list of assigned cases;

•

view status for a case as well as its individual interview components;

•

record the outcome of contacts with sampled dwelling units or sampled persons;

•

launch and conduct the PIAAC modules;

•

transmit data to the National Centre and receive new assignments when online.

The iCMS Client was used to conduct the interview and to launch all the PIAAC instruments, which could
include pre-interview questions, the curbside observations, the screener, the background questionnaire
(BQ), the doorstep interview, the direct assessment and the post-interview questions. Please note that not
all instruments were used in all countries.
The iCMS Client ran as a standalone application, integrated into the PIAAC Delivery System (PDS)
programme. After installation, the PDS was configured to start the standard PDS functionality, or, for
countries using the International Case Management System, to start the iCMS Client. When the Client
started, a login screen was presented to the user, as shown in Figure 14.1.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 353

Figure 14.1. iCMS Client Login Screen

After logging in, the interviewer was presented with the home screen of the iCMS Client (Figure 14.2). The
user could then access the different features of the iCMS Client through the navigation bar.

Figure 14.2. Client Home Screen of the iCMS

Data Synchronisation
The Sync functionality of the iCMS was used to securely synchronise the tablet data with the national
server. Because the system was designed to be used offline, case data was not automatically sent to or
retrieved from the national server. Instead, users determined when to manually initialise this process. By
default, the system only synchronised updated cases between the tablet and the national server to
minimise data transfer.

Figure 14.11. iCMS Client Synchronisation Launch Page

If a user was unable to sync the data to the national server in a timely fashion, the iCMS Client allowed the
user to generate a backup of the tablet data to prevent data loss. The backup consisted of a zip file
containing the encrypted tablet data, which could be used to restore a tablet if necessary.

Figure 14.12. iCMS Client Backup

The iCMS Administration System
The second main component of the iCMS was its Administration System (iCMA). The iCMA was a website
allowing administrators and survey operations managers to access case data from anywhere with Internet
access. The iCMA could be used to load cases into the system, review existing cases, manage both iCMS
and iCMA users, extract case data, or run a series of reports based on the latest case information. The
iCMA was designed to provide access to a limited set of functionalities or the entire system, depending on
users’ needs. Personally identifying information (PII) had a second layer of encryption added to ensure it
was only visible to authorised individuals.
When a user logged into the iCMA, they were presented with a list of functionalities appropriate for the
user access level. If a user was not permissioned for a specific feature, it was not displayed on the landing
page. The full list of features is shown in Figure 14.13.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

360 

Figure 14.13. iCMA Landing Page

Data Encryption
During synchronisation, the iCMS securely transmitted data between the iCMS client and the iCMA site
using encryption (HTTPS). Furthermore, personally identifying information (PII) was saved in the iCMA
using an additional level of encryption. When the national iCMA website was initialised, the national
administrator specified the national encryption key to protect case data PII. This key in encryption used
the AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) algorithm and was securely associated with each authorised
account. For each user on the national team who needed to access PII, a copy of the national key itself
was encrypted with the password of the user. When a user logged in, their password was used to decrypt
the stored copy of the national key. This was saved in memory for the user’s session and used when PII
needed to be retrieved and displayed or stored in the database. These encrypted copies of the national
key were stored both in the iCMS Administration System database, as well as on the interviewer tablets as
part of the iCMS Client database. Through this key management process, only authorised users within a
country had access to the keys to decrypt national Restricted Data. No consortium members had this
access to the keys.

User Permissions
Users created by the iCMA could be granted one of the following roles:
•

Site Administrator – This role granted the user full access to the iCMA.

•

Interviewer – The user was assigned an Interviewer ID and was able to log in to the tablets but
was prevented from accessing the iCMA.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 361
•

Report Viewer – This role allowed users to view the reports generated by the iCMA but did not
grant any permission to other sections of the site, such as user management, case management
or data exports.

•

DME – This role was created for the DME system, allowing it to make application programming
interface (API) calls for the extraction of case data directly into the DME application.

•

Case Manager – Users were granted access to the case management and reports. These users
could be further restricted to having read-only access to the cases and/or be limited to cases
belonging to specific regions.

Additionally, each user could be permitted access to case data considered to be Personally Identifying
Information. All interviewers, site administrators and case managers with write permissions had to be
granted this access. Without this access, PII could not be decrypted and was not visible on the site.

Case Management
Cases were loaded into the iCMA by uploading a Sample Control File (SCF), as defined by the Sampling
and Weighting File Layouts document. Once loaded, case administrators performed several actions on
cases, such as:
•

Searched for cases based on case metadata, such as the address, primary sampling unit (PSU),
assigned Interviewer, case status, address status or disposition codes (see Figure 14.14).

•

Assigned cases to interviewers.

•

Updated specific case data, such as the address, case status, or disposition codes associated with
an interviewee.

•

Reset a person, screener, curbside observation or a full case. This allowed supervisors to re-open
cases which they accidentally closed or with incorrect information.

•

Viewed the case log data to see historical changes for key metrics.

•

Downloaded completed PDS files.

Figure 14.14. iCMA Case Listings

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

362 
By clicking on a CaseID entry on the Case Listings page, the case information page loaded. This page,
shown in Figure 14.15, allowed supervisors to review the case details, drill into the data extracted from the
PDS for interviews, and update both case and person information.

Figure 14.15. iCMA Case Details

Reports
The iCMA provided several sets of reports that could be generated at any time during or after data
collection. These reports fell into three categories:
•

Production Reports – These reports displayed the status of the data collection. They were used to
determine the proportion of cases that had been completed for each section of the interview
(screener, if applicable, BQ, doorstep interview and assessment). Reports were grouped for the
entire data collection or limited to specific subsets, such as individual interviewers, regions, PSUs
or supplemental samples.

•

Sample Monitoring Reports – These reports assisted users in predicting the expected number of
completed cases as well as breaking the data out by a set of predefined metrics, such as regions,
gender, urban/rural and age groups. This information was critical to ensure teams were on track to
meet their data collection goals.

•

Quality Control Reports – These reports were used to ensure the integrity of the data being
collected. Quality Control Reports included data such as interviews that were conducted too
quickly, outside of expected time ranges, or summaries of interview validation results.

Quality Control and Validation
As part of the data collection quality control, countries were expected to monitor interviews and to validate
subsets after the interviews were conducted. The iCMA provided the user with the ability to review and
track these activities.
As shown in Figure 14.16, iCMA users could record the status of a case validation directly in the system,
including the method and outcome of the validation attempts. This information was immediately reflected
in the Quality Control reports available in the iCMA.

Data Extraction
From the iCMA, users could export the PIAAC data in several ways. Files such as the SCF and Sample
Design International File (SDIF) could be regenerated as needed. Additionally, the full set of data collected
by the iCMS and iCMA could be exported as a series of csv files, which could then be reviewed in Microsoft
Excel. This data contained the full set of case/person data, electronic records of contacts and case log
information, as shown in Figure 14.18. Additionally, several web methods were available for the DME to
connect directly to the iCMA over the Internet. Through these methods, the DME could query the SDIF,
case data and PDS files to be queried and extracted as needed.

15. The PIAAC Delivery System
Mike Wagner and Paul Brost, ETS

This chapter provides details on the PIAAC Delivery System (PDS), a
software application used to administer PIAAC instruments on interviewers’
tablets. The PDS managed the routing of respondents through various
interview steps, including the background questionnaire and the multistage
adaptive design of the direct assessment. It operated offline with local data
storage. It integrated with a case management system to launch the
interview and to manage and export collected data. The chapter also
covers the PDS’ architecture and technology, the workflow within the PDS
and its integration with the questionnaire authoring tool.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

366 

Introduction
The PIAAC Delivery System (PDS) was the software application that administered the PIAAC instruments
(background questionnaire, doorstep questionnaire, direct assessment) on the interviewers’ tablets. The
PDS implemented the PIAAC Testflow, which was the routing of respondents through the various steps in
the interview, including the multistage adaptive testing (MSAT) logic of the direct assessment. In addition,
it managed and exported the data collected through the instruments.
The PDS was installed as a standalone application on the interviewer’s tablet, which ran offline, with no
need for network connectivity. The entire content of the PIAAC instruments (assessment items and
questionnaires) was packaged on the application and could be managed locally on the tablet. The Case
Management System (whether the International Case Management System (iCMS) provided by the
Consortium or a nationally developed CMS (nCMS), see Chapter 14) was responsible for interacting with
the PDS to start or restart cases in the PDS and to take the data collected by the PDS and return it to the
national centre for further processing. A high-level overview of the interactions between external systems
such as sampling and data management, the case management system and the PDS is shown in Figure
15.1.

Figure 15.1. PIAAC Systems Overview

Users (interviewers and respondents) did not typically interact directly with the PDS. They interacted with
the instruments (questionnaires and assessment) as they were delivered. A simple, internal case
management system could be enabled to allow testing of the software and review of the instruments.

PDS Architecture and Technology
The PDS was fundamentally a classic three-tier web application. It leveraged a Model View Controller
(MVC) designed to structure the software.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 367

Figure 15.2. PDS MVC Architecture

The controller module within the PDS was called the Sequencer, and it managed the transitions from one
element of the interview to the next, as well as orchestrated data management (see Figure 15.2). The
structure of the interview was represented in the Test model. As the respondent moved through the
interview, the Sequencer updated the Test model to reflect this navigation and updated the Browser View
with the next content that should be displayed. Dynamic sections of the direct assessment (e.g. the MSAT
portions) were elaborated as they were encountered by invoking the Test Builder module. The Test Builder
module in turn implemented the routing decisions and expanded the selected testlets.
The display of individual questionnaires and assessment units was handled via separate subsystems
embedded within the PDS. These same subsystems were used online during the development and
translation of the instruments, which enhanced the equivalence of what the translators/reviewers and the
respondents saw.
The PDS was built using Node.js and the Electron framework.1 Electron supports building native desktop
applications that are rendered via an embedded web browser – Chromium, the open-source core of the
Google Chrome web browser.2 The Chromium browser implemented the view of the MVC architecture,
and the controller and model components were implemented as web services using Node.js that ran locally
within the Electron application. These web services were also exposed externally from the application for
PDS-CMS integration support.
Data was stored locally on the interviewer’s tablet using an internal, No-SQL database. The PDS used
NeDB, a JavaScript database which stored data as JSON objects and implemented a MongoDB like
interface for inserts, updates and queries. 3 The database ran locally and offline on the tablet. NeDB
employed a lightweight design. This was especially suited for a single instance application such as the
PDS, capable of handling the estimated few hundred cases or less typically saved on a single interviewer’s
tablet. Additionally, because the database supports an interface similar to MongoDB, it is possible to
transition to an online system in the future.

PIAAC Workflow
The sequence of instruments and the logic for routing among them was defined in the PIAAC Workflow. A
graphical view of the workflow is shown in Figure 15.3.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

368 

Figure 15.3. PIAAC Interview Workflow

The portion after the Case Initialisation and before the Post-Interview Questions was implemented within
the PDS, while the other steps were part of the Case Management System. All routing within the PDS
occurred automatically. The interviewer was not required to make any decisions or take any actions except
to move to the next assigned activity.
As illustrated in the workflow diagram, the questionnaires, both the standard background questionnaire
and the doorstep interview questionnaire, operated as a black box. Any routing within the questionnaire
was handled by the Questionnaire Runtime subsystem. However, for the direct assessment,
implementation of the test design routing happened in the PDS. When a test session started, a series of
random numbers was generated within the PDS, and these were used in making the routing decisions
among the domains and within the MSAT. These random numbers, along with scores on some
components (e.g. the locator), were used to determine which component to deliver next as the respondent
proceeded through the assessment. Annex 15.A of this chapter shows the PDS variables that store these

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 369
random numbers, as well as the variables used for recording the scores for the various assessment
components and the path through the direct assessment.

The PIAAC Questionnaires
The PIAAC questionnaires were authored through a multi-step process using a custom application, the
Questionnaire Authoring Tool (QAT). The QAT is used to create the questionnaires, adapt them to their
national context and preview and test them. The development of the PIAAC BQ was based on the following
process.
•

Master versions of the BQ were created in English in the QAT by Consortium staff.

•

The master BQ was copied to each country to create a national master version.

•

Countries adapted their national master version in the QAT, making modifications to the structure
of the questionnaire necessary to support their national context.

•

Consortium staff reviewed and approved the adaptations for each country.

•

Countries tested their adapted national master BQ to ensure that routing, derived variables and
other aspects operated correctly.

•

Consortium staff generated XLIFF files from the adapted national master. Countries translated to
their national languages, with Consortium verification.

The development of the doorstep interview questionnaire followed a different but similar process. No
national adaptations were required, and the translations were managed through a combination of central
translation by cApStAn and by national teams (see Chapter 7).
When users logged in to the QAT, they were taken to a home page, as shown in Figure 15.4. This page
gave users access to the many features of the tool.

Figure 15.4. Questionnaire Authoring Tool home page

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

370 
QAT Editor Tool
Consortium staff used the QAT Editor tool to create the master questionnaires. Likewise, national centres
used the same tool to implement their national adaptations. It is an online editor that allows a user to add,
delete or edit a question in the questionnaires. When users opened the QAT Editor, they were presented
with a view of the structure of an entire questionnaire. However, it is important to note that this was not a
What You See Is What You Get (WYSIWYG) view of what interviewers saw when they interacted with the
questionnaires. The view focused on the structure of the questions and used a forms-based presentation.
Figures 15.5 and 17.6 show the main view of the QAT Editor for a National Project Manager (NPM).

Depending on the mode, the access for modifying questionnaires in the Questionnaire Authoring Tool
