Questions Expanded View and Questions Preview
Figure 15.7 shows the information that was visible when an item was expanded.

Figure 15.7. The Expanded View information

The features available for users in the questionnaire item screens included:
A. Show/Hide Screen button could expand or collapse a specific questionnaire screen or rule header.
B. Screen Number label showed the ranking of the screen in the sequence of questionnaire items out of
the total number of questionnaire screens.
C. Screen ID displayed the technical identifier of the screen and rule headers.
D. Template label displayed the name of the template used for editing the questionnaire screen (see
section about questionnaire templates for additional information).
E. Lock/Unlock button made a questionnaire screen editable or not for a National Project Manager. This
button was not available to NPMs.
F. Preview button opened a preview of an item, giving the user a view that reflected the interviewer‘s view
of a questionnaire item.
G. Add Screen button inserted a new question or rule in the questionnaire just below the expanded item.
H. Delete Screen button removed the question or rule from the questionnaire. Users who clicked this
button received a notification asking for confirmation of deletion.
The QAT offered two preview options for reviewing and checking the quality of the questionnaire. The first
option was a question preview panel that could be accessed from within the Questionnaire Authoring Tool,
using the Preview button available in the expanded view of each question. In this preview mode, the
identifiers of response fields were visible to help facilitate questionnaire authoring. Also, for table-based
items, blue vertical bars were available to change the column widths of the table, allowing the user to
customise the item layout. This mode is shown in Figure 15.8.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 373

Figure 15.8. Preview of a question in the Questionnaire Authoring Tool

The second option was a full questionnaire preview that was available via the “Review and Test the
Questionnaire” link on the QAT homepage. This option allowed users to navigate through the entire
questionnaire in a test environment and offered the same conditions as those experienced by interviewers
during the field trial and main study.

Question templates
The Questionnaire Authoring Tool editor was a template-based authoring system that supports multiple
question types, the design of the rules-based routings driving the questionnaire flow, and the enforcement
of the quality of the answers via consistency checks.
The question types (i.e. Templates) that were available in the Questionnaire Authoring Tool Editor
included:
•

Exclusive Choice – A single list of response options allowing a single choice.

•

Multiple Choice – A single list of response options allowing one or more choices.

•

Drop Down – A single list of drop-down menu responses.

•

Drop Down (Table) – An array of one or more drop-down menu responses arranged in a table.

•

List of Text Inputs – A single list of short text inputs, with optional constraints on the type and range
of inputs.

•

Multiple List of Text Inputs (Table) – An array of short text inputs, with optional constraints on the
type and range of inputs.

•

Free Text Input – A long text input, supporting multiple lines of input.

•

List of Exclusive Choice (Table) – Multiple exclusive choice items arranged in a table. The options
for each item can be arranged horizontally or vertically.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

374 
•

List of Multiple Choice (Table) – Multiple non-exclusive choice items arranged in a table.

•

Scale Question Type – An item where the response is entered by manipulating a slider widget.

•

Information – An item that presents information to the respondent, with no response captured.

Additionally, there were three templates for defining rules that were used within the questionnaire:
•

Consistency Check Rule – A rule which validated the response to the previous item. If the rule was
not satisfied, an error message was displayed.

•

Routing Rule – A rule that allowed the automatic branching to one or more items based on previous
responses.

•

Derived Variable Rule – A rule that set the value of a hidden, derived variable that could be used
in subsequent rules. These variables could also be substituted into the question text of items to
implement dynamic texts, which adapted to previous responses.

The PIAAC Direct Assessment
The items for the PIAAC direct assessment were implemented using web-based technologies: HTML, CSS
and JavaScript®. Modern web browsers (such as the bundled Chromium browser) provided a suite of
features and functionalities that enabled attractive presentations and facilitated engaging interactivity. At
the beginning of the development work, an overall user interface was designed with a common set of
elements such as navigation, help and screen layout. Items were implemented in such a way that these
common elements were shared, so that the same elements were used across all items in each language
version.
PIAAC items or questions were generally grouped into units consisting of one or more common stimuli and
a set of items. Each unit was constructed independently; stimulus and question components were
developed in English and then translated into various national versions. The development was done by
experienced web UI developers using standard HTML and CSS for the onscreen display and adding
custom functionality via JavaScript. Each unit could be viewed on its own or grouped with other units into
a test form for delivery as part of the assessments.
In some cases, common functionalities were split out into shared programming libraries that could be
reused in multiple units. For example, in literacy, the management and display of multiple sources in tabs
were encapsulated into a shared library. The library also managed the recording of data and supported
the scoring of the respondent‘s performance based on unit-specific criteria.
The visual aspects of the PIAAC Cycle 2 items and the automated coding of respondent responses were
both implemented using JavaScript®. Shared libraries were created to implement this coding in a common
way. The libraries targeted the various response modes used within PIAAC:
•

Form – for all responses that used common web form elements such as radio buttons, checkboxes
and numeric keypad entries.

•

Drag and drop – for items that used drag and drop as the response mode.

•

Selection – for items where the response was given by clicking on an object or region of the screen.
This could be, for instance, clicking on part of an image, a cell in a table or a segment of text.

•

Ad hoc – A general catch all category that uses custom JavaScript® code to implement the coding.
This was used for unique situations, such as highlighting text in some literacy items.

In all cases except the ad hoc coding, the coding for a specific item was specified using rules composed
of conditional expressions and Boolean operators. Each library implemented appropriate conditional
expressions (e.g. a CONTAINS operator in the Drag and Drop library to test if a drop target held a particular
drag element). The Form scoring library implemented additional logic for interpreting numeric responses.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 375
Numbers could be compared as an exact match (i.e. the response must match the key exactly, character
for character) or as a numeric match (i.e. the response and key were numerically equivalent, such as 12.50
and 12.5). Exact matches were used for currency-based responses in numeracy, for example, €18.43 is
accepted, but €18.4300 is not. Besides numeric equivalence, the numeric matches also supported
alternate interpretations of number responses. For instance, alternate decimal point symbols (dot or
comma) were both accepted in a response.

Translation and Online Item Review
Given the need to support translations and adaptations for different national language versions of each
assessment unit and questionnaire, an automated process for the integration of these translation
adaptations was critical. This process commenced with the initial development of the materials. For the
assessment units, the HTML files that implemented the display of the unit contained only HTML markup
and the text to be shown on the screen. Layout and formatting specifications were stored separately in
CSS stylesheets. Graphics were designed so that they contained no text, no labels, etc., and were placed
on top of the graphic via HTML and CSS. For the questionnaires, the QAT saved the items in an XML
format so the text could be readily identified. The text of both types of items was then extracted from these
HTML and XML files and saved to a standard file format, XLIFF, used for computer-supported translation.4
National teams utilised an open-source tool, Omega-T, to perform the translation and adaptation process.5
Once a translation was completed, the XLIFF file was injected into the original source version of the unit
or questionnaire, resulting in files with the translated text replacing the source text.
One of the guiding principles of the platform development was that the quality of a translation was
enhanced when translators viewed their translation in the context of the stimulus and items they were
translating. Ideally, translators would work in a completely WYSIWYG mode, so that they entered their
translations directly within an interface that displays the items as they would be seen by the respondents.
However, this was not technically feasible with the current authoring method. Furthermore, the visual
aspects of the items, which are tightly controlled for comparability, could have distracted translators from
the text to be translated. A good compromise was to provide translators with an easy-to-use preview
feature to view their translations as functioning items from the PIAAC Portal and QAT. Users were able to
upload a locally prepared and saved XLIFF file, with either partial or complete translation, and in a matter
of seconds, preview the given unit or questionnaire in the same design and layout as a respondent would
view and interact with it within the delivery system. This was an important factor, particularly for the more
complex and interactive assessment units across the domains. This preview also allowed countries to test
and identify potential problems with their translated units before receiving the final versions packaged
within the software to be used by interviewers. Therefore, reported problems were fixed as early in the
schedule as possible.

PDS – CMS Integration Support
The PIAAC Delivery System (PDS) was started, controlled and terminated from the Case Management
System (CMS) via integration interfaces. These interfaces took two forms. One was an HTTP based REST
API, which ran locally on the tablet. The other was via command line scripts, which provided the same
functionality as the REST API.
The following integration methods were provided: basic or administrative methods.

Basic Methods
•

StartPDS – Started the PDS and optionally unlocked the content and started or resumed a case.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

376 
•

UnlockPDS – Unlocked the PDS using the key that encrypted the direct assessment’s content and
the results ZIP files exported from the PDS.

•

LockPDS – Locked the contents of the PDS, preventing any activity until the UnlockPDS function
was called.

•

StartCase – Started or resumed a case in the PDS. Parameters indicated the language to use
initially for the case, as well as the type of case (standard case with BQ and assessment or
doorstep interview).

•

GetCaseState – Got the current status of the case. Possible return values were:
o

running

o

paused

o

breakoff

o

finished

o

not found

•

GetCaseData – Returned meta data for the case, used by the CMS for reporting. This data included
basic demographic data for the respondent, disposition codes for the segments of the interview
and start and end times for each segment.

•

ExportResult – Generated a password-protected ZIP file with the results data that was collected
for the case.

•

StopPDS – Shut down the running PDS.

Administrative Methods
•

DropCase – Removed a case and all its data from the PDS.

•

DumpCase – Extracted the raw data for a case from the PDS in a format compatible with the
ImportCase function.

•

ImportCase – Imported a case dump (from the DumpCase function) into the PDS. Used for
transferring a case from one PDS to another.

•

DumpAllCases – Extracted all case data from the PDS.

•

RestoreAllCases – Imported a dump of all cases from another PDS, replacing any existing cases.

The PDS exposed a standard REST API via a port on the local host interface of the tablet. The port number
was dynamically assigned at start-up, and the value assigned could be found in the file “PORT.txt”, located
in the same directory as the PDS application. The system started searching for a free port at 3000 and
used the first open port it could find. This value was written to the PORT.txt file.
Methods in the REST API were available via both GET and POST interfaces. If file data had to be sent,
that data had to be posted via multipart form-data encoding. Resource methods communicated status
information via HTTP result status codes, plus additional JSON data. The PDS returned one of three
possible HTTP results codes:
•

200 – Success

•

400 – Bad request

•

500 – Internal PDS error

The command line scripts were called from the command line in a Windows environment, typically
programmatically. There was a command line script for each of the supported REST API methods. Some
of the scripts required one or more parameters matching the parameters used in REST API methods.
Every script displayed a small piece of information about its purpose and usage if the parameter value ‘-h’
was entered, e.g. ‘StartCase -h’.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 377

Data Management
As noted above, the PDS used an internal document database to store data that had been collected on
the tablet. Since the PDS ran offline, without Internet connectivity, it was important to export this data so it
could be transferred back to the national centre for data processing and analysis. The PDS-to-CMS
integration functions provided the means to do this. The primary function used was ExportResults, which
generated a ZIP file with the results for a given PERSID. The ZIP file was password protected using a
unique password assigned to each country. Each ZIP file contained some or all of the following:
•

A subdirectory with the results of the background questionnaire or doorstep interview, as
appropriate.

•

A series of “VAR” files contained the variables that were collected during the direct assessment.
These files were in JSON format with name/value pairs.

•

A “context” subdirectory with internal JSON files used for capturing results in the assessment units.

•

A “cookie” subdirectory with internal JSON files used for capturing status data for each assessment
unit.

•

A “trace” subdirectory with a JSON formatted file where process data was logged.

Some or all of these files and subdirectories could be missing if, for instance, the assessment had not been
started.
Besides results data, the PDS supported exporting the raw database contents for one case, or for all cases.
These files could be used by the CMS to transfer one or all cases from one tablet to another. This was
useful, for instance, when transferring a case that had been started from one interviewer to another.

16. The PIAAC Dashboard
Tim Daniel (IEA), Darrell Gwaltney (IEA), Nina Thornton (Westat), Tom Krenzke (Westat), Leyla Mohadjer
(Westat)

This chapter introduces the PIAAC dashboard, a tool designed for
managing and monitoring field operations. The dashboard consolidated
information from various datasets into a set of production and process
monitoring key performance indicators, enabling efficient tracking of data
collection status, sample yield, response rates and interviewer
performance, among others. Through frequent updates and graphical
overviews, the dashboard created efficient monitoring and supported early
detection of anomalies. This enabled timely corrective actions to ensure the
integrity of the survey data.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 381

Introduction
The PIAAC dashboard, an innovation introduced in PIAAC Cycle 2, was created for the management and
monitoring of field operations. Survey control charts and statistical graphs were arranged together to report
on the data collection status, sample yield and response rates, instrument timings, and outcomes of
interviewer fieldwork.
An important feature of the dashboard was the ability to extract the most significant key performance
indicators (KPI) from many datasets and activities and present them on one screen. This allowed users to
track and manage fieldwork based on the information presented as summary graphics of available
indicators. The dashboard also allowed study management staff to monitor field operations frequently to
improve interviewer efficiency and productivity. This contributed to reducing time and costs while
maintaining high quality in line with the total survey error (TSE) framework. The data that populated the
PIAAC dashboard came from a variety of sources, including the case management system (CMS), the
survey platform, the sampling data and the interviewers’ tablets.
Quality control of survey operations was a responsibility of national teams. Failure to monitor or infrequent
monitoring of the data collection process creates a significant risk that errors or falsifications remain
undetected or are discovered too late in the field period for timely corrections. The consequences of lowquality data were two-fold: 1) non-sampling errors result in PIAAC proficiency estimates that may be
misleading to the OECD and the public in general, and 2) the propagation of such errors culminates in the
decision to accept or reject the data during the adjudication process.
The advantages of using the PIAAC dashboard include frequent tracking of various production and quality
control metrics. Field staff could precisely track the number and times of contact attempts and actively
monitor the work of interviewers to enable early detection of cases with invalid data. Since the dashboard
provided consolidated graphical representation or snapshots of multiple production and paradata reporting
tools on a single page, supervisors and managers could rapidly identify anomalies or concerns. If an
anomaly was detected, further investigation was done using the reporting functionalities available in the
Case Management System (CMS). In addition, the use of the dashboard as the early alert system obviated
the need for field staff to review a series of separate reports from disparate sources on an ongoing basis
to detect issues that were of concern.

Key Performance Indicators
The PIAAC dashboard was populated with paradata variables and key variables from the interview and
assessment that directly related to data quality. The dashboard displayed fifteen KPIs, each in a separate
window on the screen. Indicators were grouped into KPIs used for production monitoring or process
monitoring. Six KPIs displayed information related to the status of production (performance indicators),
and nine KPIs provided information on quality control metrics (process monitoring indicators). A brief
description of each KPI within the two groups is provided below.

Production monitoring
The production monitoring indicators were the following:
•

P1 – Sample yield projections and progression of the ratio of actual sample yield to target sample
yield using disposition codes of cases worked by week. The production component of this KPI
allowed countries to track the pace of production, including the number of completed assessments.
The dashboard’s ability to filter by region allowed field managers to track and compare results
across regions and to provide feedback to supervisors in regions where production was lagging.
The sample yield projections component of this KPI also allowed managers and statisticians to

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

382 
project whether the released sample could yield the expected number of completed assessments
by the end of data collection, thus informing the decision as to whether a reserve sample should
be released. If a release was warranted, planning for the release in terms of staffing and work
strategies was completed in advance so that the cases could be worked soon after assignment to
field interviewers. Field management staff could also use information in this KPI to determine if
certain areas could benefit from a targeted approach of working pending cases, particularly those
cases lagging in non-response status.
•

P2 – Actual and target unweighted response rate for Screeners (if applicable), BQ, assessment
and overall. Information obtained from reviewing response rates allowed the allocation of resources
to areas where the response rate was lagging and redirected fieldwork away from areas where the
overall response rate was stagnant despite targeted efforts. It informed the use of strategies to
gain cooperation (for example, developing additional outreach materials and using interviewers
experienced with non-response conversion). Information in this KPI was also useful in detecting
downward trends early so that mitigating strategies could be implemented expeditiously for
maximum effect.

•

P3 – Progression of number of completed doorstep instruments and ratio of actual count versus
expected count, overall and by region. Since countries had estimates on the expected percentage
of literacy-related non-response, tracking completed doorstep interviews both at the national and
regional levels allowed comparison of actual versus expected numbers of completed interviews.
The number of doorstep interviews completed was not expected to be high across countries since
interviewers were trained to only offer the doorstep interview as a last resort to respondents with
language barriers. Therefore, interviewers who completed a higher number of doorstep interviews
than expected could be monitored closely to ensure they were following study protocols.

•

P4 – Count of cases by quality of contact protocol. The PIAAC Technical Standards and
Guidelines1 set the minimum number of contact attempts per case as six in-person contacts or
seven telephone contacts (Standard 10.3.2, Standard 10.3.3), with contact attempts occurring on
weekdays, weeknights and weekends. This KPI is designed to easily detect whether contact
attempts made by interviewers followed the standards and guidelines. The information from this
KPI allowed field management to help interviewers develop more efficient work strategies to reach
respondents and to ensure that cases were worked appropriately across all regions and all
interviewers. This KPI display included filters to check contact attempts on both finalised and not
finalised cases (excluding completes), thus ensuring that cases were worked fully in accordance
with the contact protocols.

•

P5 – Distribution of interim and final disposition codes by instrument. This KPI displayed the
distribution of interim and final disposition codes by instrument. Information on the status of pending
cases, including appointments and callbacks, helped determine the scope of viable cases at any
time during the field period. The number of interim refusals provided timely alerts, prompting nonresponse conversion efforts and helped direct refusal converters to be deployed in areas as
needed. The display of final disposition codes allowed tracking of the number of cases associated
with final codes for each instrument. The distributions of interim and final disposition codes also
provided insight into the calculation of response rates in KPI P2. This KPI was useful for ‘at-aglance’ reporting on the distribution of disposition codes to the Consortium for quality control
purposes.

•

P6 – Distributions of the number of actual completes versus projected completes (by region, age
group, gender, language, mode of assessment) by week. This KPI displayed the weekly number
of completed assessments in the field versus the projected number at any particular point in the
field period. The comparison of actual versus projected numbers helped field management staff in
implementing strategies to narrow the gap between actual and expected numbers. Moreover,
information available in the display also allowed tracking of actual completed assessments by

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 383
region, age group, gender and language and the actual number of completed BQs so that field
efforts could target increasing the completion rate for particular categories of concern.

Process monitoring
The process monitoring indicators were the following:
•

Q1 – Discrepancies in age and gender between instruments CI (registry countries) or screener
(screener countries) compared against BQ information. This KPI displayed discrepancies (by
interviewer) in the age and gender information recorded either in the CI or screener for sampled
persons versus the information self-reported by the respondent in the BQ. For registry countries,
discrepancies between the age and/or gender questions in the CI versus the BQ are displayed.
For screener countries, discrepancies in the reported age and/or gender for a sampled person
reported by the screener respondent versus what the respondent reported during the BQ were
flagged as anomalies. Such discrepancies may have resulted from misreporting by the respondent,
incorrect recording of information by the interviewer, or from the wrong case being accessed by
the interviewer. However, a discrepancy could also be an indication of an interviewer intentionally
submitting false data or data obtained from someone other than a sampled person. Being alerted
to such discrepancies at the interviewer level in real-time during data collection helped avoid the
costly and time-consuming validation of all cases completed by such an interviewer.

•

Q2 – ID of interviewers with two or more occurrences of an instrument started too early (i.e. before
8:30 am) or too late (i.e. after 9:00 pm). Field management could monitor instances of interviews
started too early in the day or too late in the evening. However, a respondent may have requested
an interview at an unusual time to accommodate their schedule. As a general rule, interviews do
not take place very early in the morning or late at night. Therefore, any assessment completed by
an interviewer before 8:30 am or after 9.00 pm was displayed on this KPI at the interviewer level
and flagged as a potential problem, thus enabling supervisors to determine whether the case was
valid after following up with the interviewer.

•

Q3 – ID of interviewers with two or more occurrences of a BQ and assessment completed on
different dates. Interviewers were trained to administer the BQ and assessment in one session to
avoid the risk of the respondent refusing a follow-up visit to complete the assessment and
streamline work efficiencies. Interviewers who routinely conducted the BQ and assessment on
different days were identified using this KPI since this pattern was a potential indicator of the
interviewer not following the study protocol.

•

Q4 – ID of interviewers with two or more occurrences of a BQ administered in less than 20 minutes
or more than 90 minutes. BQs of short duration are not typical unless the respondent, for example,
has limited or no work history. This KPI displays instances of interviewers who have administered
two or more BQs with short timing (less than 20 minutes). Monitoring this KPI helped field staff
determine when follow-up was needed to ensure that the short timings were not a result of the
interviewer shortcutting (e.g. omitting questions by entering Don’t Knows/Refusals) or providing
false information. Since this KPI also displayed instances of interviewers who spent more than 90
minutes to administer at least two BQs, field staff could improve work efficiency by providing
retraining to interviewers on administering the interview at a reasonable pace.

•

Q5 – Number of completes per month for each interviewer who ever met either criteria: 20
interviews or more in a month or 90% percentile of interviewers in terms of completes in a month.
This KPI allowed field management to monitor super-producers, interviewers who complete 20
interviews or more in a month, or those in the top 90% percentile of interviewers in terms of the
number of completed interviews in a month. Since additional validation efforts were warranted on
high-producing interviewers, being quickly alerted to extraordinary production saved resources,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

384 
time and effort in case the completed interviews were not conducted according to the study
protocol.
•

Q6 – Percentage of interviewers with no case either observed or audio recorded, one case either
observed or audio recorded, and two or more cases either observed or audio recorded. This KPI
displayed the progress of audio recordings in terms of the percentage of interviewers who did not
submit any audio recordings, submitted only one audio-recorded interview, or submitted the two
required recordings from completed interviews. Field management could also track the progress
of interviews that were observed in person. By monitoring the KPI, staff could stay informed on the
status of the recordings and/or observations and prompt interviewers to submit their recordings per
the requirement or observers to carry out the required number of observations.

•

Q7 – Percentage of interviewers who have at least x% of cases validated at select validation rate
level, where x= 7%, 9%, 10%, 90%, 100%, by month. Validation efforts are critical for ensuring the
validity of the data being collected. An early start with the implementation of validation efforts put
countries in a better position to deal with potential problems soon after these were detected. This
KPI displayed the percentage of interviewers who had a percentage of their finalised cases
validated. Therefore, this KPI helped inform management when validation efforts were lagging or
if validation efforts were on pace with finalised interviewer work.

•

Q8 – A summary of the duration of the BQ provides a table of counts for intervals in minutes and
the mean duration. The table displayed a row for the overall distribution of timings and a row for
each of the 25 interviewers with the shortest duration of BQ administration timings. Interviewers
who routinely completed BQ administration in atypically short times could thus be readily identified.

•

Q9 – A summary of the duration of the assessment provides a table of counts for intervals in
minutes and the mean duration. The table displayed a row for the overall distribution of timings and
a row for each of the 25 interviewers with the shortest duration of assessment timings. An optional
display was available showing a summary of timings based on the assessment route completed
by the respondent (i.e. RSLTLOC = 1, 2 and 3 combined, or RSLTLOC = 2, 3 combined). As in
KPI Q8, this table displayed information that was conducive to identifying any interviewers who
routinely completed interviews with short assessment timings, thus prompting further investigation
of interviewer behaviour and potential falsification.

weekend. Based on the Technical Standard 10.3.2, no further contact attempts were necessary for these

Technical aspects
The IEA developed individual dashboards for each country. The dashboards contained aggregated
information on mainly field operation tasks, following the insights and expert advice of Consortium
members. Dashboards were populated using data collected and captured in the CMS, survey control file
(SCF), sample monitoring parameters (SMP) and sample design information file (SDIF), or during the
interview. Countries first imported this data into the IEA Data Management Expert (DME) software. Then,
data was prepared for upload within the DME by calculating aggregated numbers that were uploaded to
the dashboards.
Data uploads for dashboards were done in update mode always to get the most recently completed status
for various process indicators. Upload data packages only contained aggregated, anonymised data and
countries were able to check the content of data packages prior to upload. Data packages were only
uploaded once the contents had been actively approved by countries. Uploads were logged with a
timestamp within the DME software and a summary report of the uploaded data was provided for each
individual upload. Data to populate the dashboards resided on a dedicated server hosted by the IEA
Hamburg. The database tables were populated and updated by regular uploads of new data packages
from the DME software. These uploads were triggered by staff in the national centre operating the DME
software on, at least, a weekly basis for maximum benefit in monitoring progress and quality.
The PIAAC dashboards were presented online on individual websites for each participating country. In
each country, access to the websites was restricted to registered users who had permission to view the
information displayed in the dashboards. Authorised Consortium staff were able to access and review
dashboard information individually by country.
The interface of the individual country PIAAC Dashboard was split into two sections: Performance and
Process. The Performance tab contained KPIs P1 through P6, and the Process Tab contained KPIs Q1
through Q9. Each country could also request individual KPIs to be toggled on or off. This would remove
the KPI in question from the Country Dashboard. Toggling off a KPI was used in the event of a KPI
containing sensitive information for a country, or if the KPI in question was not in use for a country.

Data flow and confidentiality
From the CMS, both SMP and SDIF data were used for the Dashboard KPI calculations. In addition,
information collected during the interview and loaded into DME was used as well as temporary disposition
codes and other workflow information. Table 16.1 summarises which variables were used for the
calculations within DME as well as the resulting variables that were eventually used for data upload to the
dashboard.

Use of the PIAAC Dashboard in countries and by the Consortium
Use in countries, general usage statistics and frequency of updates
Countries were first introduced to the PIAAC Dashboard during the field trial. This enabled national teams
to test the monitoring capabilities of the system. During the main study, 22 countries used the dashboard
on a regular basis. A convenient feature of the dashboard was that countries could opt to only upload the
data required for the KPIs that they selected to use for monitoring and management of fieldwork. Of the
nine countries that did not use the dashboard, reasons for not using the system included (1) countries’ use
of survey organisations that had their own dashboard, (2) language barriers that prevented the supervisory
staff from using the dashboard (provided in English only), and (3) data confidentiality restrictions.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

388 
Using the dashboard, national teams that had contracted survey organisations to conduct fieldwork had
the added advantage of independently tracking the progress of data collection without being reliant on
these organisations providing summary reports on the status of field production and the progress of
monitoring activities.

Dashboard use in international Quality Control Monitoring
The Consortium was successfully able to use the PIAAC dashboard to monitor the status of fieldwork during
the main study. The availability of information in the KPIs provided a convenient overview of the progress
countries were making toward achieving their target of completes as well as ‘at-a-glance’ high-level
summaries of work completed by interviewers and the progress made with meeting PIAAC quality control
requirements. This information supported follow-up discussions with team members during bimonthly Quality
Control calls, thus eliciting explanations on anomalies observed or prompting further investigation on issues
noted. Of the countries that reported interviewers who falsified data, some teams credited the ready
availability of process monitoring metrics, particularly aberrant instrument timings and age and gender
discrepancies, that alerted them to conduct additional scrutiny of completed work to uncover falsification.

17. PIAAC field operations
Nina Thornton, Tom Krenzke and Leyla Mohadjer (Westat)

This chapter provides details on several aspects of field operations
conducted by participating countries and economies during the PIAAC
Cycle 2 main study. A comprehensive programme of instruction for
interviewer training and best practices during the field period was provided
to national teams by the Consortium to achieve the goal of collecting high
quality data that are comparable across and within countries. Country
compliance with the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines that were
in place for field operations are described herein.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 391

Introduction
As with all aspects of PIAAC, countries were expected to comply with the PIAAC Cycle 2 Technical
Standards and Guidelines (TSG)1 in the planning and conduct of fieldwork, including data collection. These
standards are included in Chapters 2, 8, 9 and 10 of the TSG. The TSG included a quality assurance (QA)
and quality control (QC) programme to gather information about the design, plans and implementation of
PIAAC data collection in each country collected through the submission of forms and reports, as well as
online and in-person meetings.
This chapter presents information about the 31 countries and economies that completed the PIAAC
Cycle 2 main study data collection. These are, in alphabetical order: Austria, Canada, Chile, Croatia,
Czechia, Denmark, England (United Kingdom), Estonia, Finland, the Flemish Region (Belgium), France,
Germany, Hungary, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Korea, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, New Zealand,
Norway, Poland, Portugal, Singapore, the Slovak Republic, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United
States. The information presented in this chapter is based on data reported by countries.
The following sections highlight findings with respect to data collection timeline, fieldwork production, field
staff training, field management structure, including interviewer staffing, non-response reduction and
fieldwork quality control. At the end of data collection, interviewers submitted feedback related to the
national interviewer training and their field experience administering PIAAC, briefly described in the final
section.
Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the OECD and the Consortium delayed the start of the PIAAC Cycle 2
field trial from April 2020 to April 2021. The primary goals of the field trial were to test and refine all systems
and processes developed for the main study, including the data collection instruments, the tablet-based
delivery platform, and sampling and survey operations procedures. Countries were required to collect
1 500 completed cases for the main language or each reporting language. Since countries were facing
different challenges that could impact fieldwork, the OECD and the Consortium allowed flexibility to a
limited number of PIAAC standards in order to ensure that all countries could successfully conduct a field
trial to inform main study survey planning and implementation.
Countries unable to conduct a full field trial were permitted to submit a reduced number of completed cases
than originally planned. In these exceptional cases, countries were allowed to conduct an operational field
trial and complete 250 cases which facilitated the testing of sampling and survey operations procedures
prior to the main study. Countries unable to conduct face-to-face data collection were permitted to complete
a simulated field trial to test the data collection instruments.
Of the countries that participated in the main study, only two (Canada and Ireland) were limited to
conducting a simulated field trial. The United States completed an operational field trial and conducted
interviews with volunteer respondents at the commercial survey organisation offices. Two countries new
to PIAAC Cycle 2, Latvia and Portugal, were unable to finalise contracting with a survey organisation to
conduct a field trial within the planned timeline (April – June 2021). Both these countries conducted an
operational field trial immediately prior to the start of the main study.
All participating countries and economies were expected to fully adhere to the PIAAC TSG for the main
study. However, there were some deviations from the TSG with regard to data collection in a few countries.
Whenever the Consortium identified these deviations, whether during the planning or implementation
stages, countries were required to submit a derogation letter detailing the rationale for the deviation.
Derogation letters were reviewed by the Consortium and the OECD prior to granting approval. In general,
all countries complied and followed the PIAAC TSG during the main study.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

392 

Main study data collection timeline
After adjustments to the timelines due to the COVID-19 pandemic, countries were scheduled to begin data
collection for the main study on 1 September 2022 and complete fieldwork by 30 April 2023 (8 months or
242 days). Table 17.1 presents detailed information about each country’s adherence to the data collection
timeline.
Twenty-four countries began data collection by mid-September, and two countries began by the end of
September. Of the remaining five countries, three began data collection in October, and two countries
started data collection early in 2023.

Fieldwork progressed slower than projected in many countries due to unanticipated challenges such as
staffing shortages from the outset or due to interviewer attrition. Some countries also reported difficulties
reaching certain population subgroups (e.g. immigrants, younger respondents, etc.). After careful
consideration and close monitoring of the progress of data collection as well as projections for completed
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 393
cases across countries, the OECD and the Consortium allowed some countries to extend the data
collection period. Data submission was organised in three batches, as shown in Table 17.1. Twelve
countries that completed data collection close to or on the original timeline were grouped in Batch 1 (data
submission deadline of 16 June), eleven countries that completed data collection approximately a month
later were grouped in Batch 2 (data submission deadline of 19 July), and eight countries that completed
data collection in August 2023 were grouped in Batch 3 (data submission deadline of 31 August).
Only six countries completed data collection on or before 30 April, which was the original end date for data
collection in the main study. The actual length of the field period ranged from 60 days in Korea to 340 days
in New Zealand, with an average data collection period of 260 days.

Fieldwork production
This section presents data on each country’s data yield in terms of completed cases and completed
assessments. Based on their sample design, countries were required to complete between 4 000 and
5 000 cases that meet the definition of a complete case for each reporting language. As stated in
Standard 4.3.3, a completed case is one that meets the following minimum criteria: responses to key
background questions in the full BQ, including age, gender, highest level of schooling, employment status
and country of birth (native/non-native); the Tablet tutorial and Locator sections of the direct assessment
are attempted.
Details related to countries’ sample design are covered in Chapter 2 of this Technical Report. Countries
that oversampled special populations had specific requirements for target sample size and for the target
of completed cases. Table 17.2 includes the number of completed cases (as defined in Standard 4.3.3 of
the TSG) and completed assessments for the PIAAC main samples of adults aged 16-65. The number of
completed cases includes cases that were categorised as having a language barrier, reading/writing
barrier, learning/mental disability or technical problems. Some countries oversampled specific groups
within their main sample of adults aged 16-65. In addition, some countries selected supplemental samples
(e.g. adults aged 66-75 years old, prior PISA participants, etc.). The sample sizes reported below do not
include respondents from these supplemental samples or any other sample that is not part of the main
PIAAC sample.

a During data collection, the Consortium psychometricians approved a reduced target of 3 500 completed cases in French (the original target

Despite the significant challenges that several countries faced, such as staffing shortages, slow pace of
data collection and extension to the field period, which impacted project resources, 21 countries met or
exceeded the PIAAC standard minimum for completed cases.

Field staff training
Providing timely, adequate, and standardised training to interviewers is an important step in promoting the
collection of quality data. Interviewers are required to be familiar with the survey procedures, to administer
them consistently to all respondents and to produce data that is as error-free as possible. Familiarity with
survey procedures allows interviewers to focus on gaining and maintaining respondent engagement and
co-operation, which in turn helps with maximising response rates.
Chapter 9 of the TSG covers all aspects of requirements related to the training of PIAAC field staff, which
constitutes a successful training approach. Countries were, at a minimum, expected to:
•

Conduct interviewer training in person no more than two weeks prior to the start of data collection.

•

Train interviewers in small groups of 15-20.

•

Assemble a team of training staff, including a lead trainer, assistant trainer(s) and technical support
staff.

•

Offer adequate training on all aspects of conducting the PIAAC survey. Countries were expected
to conduct national training based on the international field trial training provided by the Consortium
(at NPM Meeting 5 held in February 2020, a virtual refresh of the training held in February 2021,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 395
and the main study training at NPM Meeting 7 in July 2022). The Consortium provided countries
with a comprehensive training guide, which included training scripts, exercises, role plays, and
home study content with suggested times for various training topics (see Table 17.5).
•

Provide sufficient in-person training on the background questionnaire, doorstep interview and direct
assessment administration using training scripts provided by the Consortium.

•

Provide adequate time during in-person training on gaining respondent co-operation in the form of
lectures, roundtable exercises and group discussions. These interactive sessions were designed
to facilitate an exchange of ideas between experienced and less experienced interviewers
regarding effective strategies for dealing with different types of concerns from respondents who
are reluctant to participate.

Training logistics
The Consortium recommended that countries conduct interviewer training no earlier than the week before
the start of data collection. The goal was to minimise learning loss, thus allowing interviewers to effectively
utilise the information gained and skills learned during training in the conduct of fieldwork.
Nine countries (29%) held interviewer training sessions three weeks or more prior to the start of data
collection (Canada, England (United Kingdom), Estonia, France, Japan, Latvia, the Slovak Republic,
Sweden, and Switzerland). Based on the training resources available as well as the number of trainees,
some countries held training sessions staggered in time so that only a fraction of interviewers received
their training just before beginning fieldwork; for the early groups of interviewers that were trained, there
was a considerable lag between training and data collection.
The total number of initial interviewer training sessions conducted by countries varied from one in
New Zealand, Singapore, Spain and the United States to 91 in France. The overall duration of the training
sessions varied with an average of 3.2 days of training conducted across all countries.
Twenty-one countries delivered training in person, while ten countries used a hybrid mode of training,
conducting both in-person and virtual training sessions. Two countries (Canada and Spain) conducted
several rounds of attrition training sessions and resorted to training interviewers virtually for resource and
cost efficiencies. All countries included home study materials that trainees completed as independent study
prior to attending training. Home study material included PIAAC-specific content and optional countryspecific content.
Twenty-five countries (81%) continued to train interviewers long after the start of data collection (more than
three months) to compensate for interviewer attrition and ensure coverage in understaffed regions.
There was considerable variation in the number of hours of training that supervisors received across
countries due to various factors, such as their experience with procedures at the survey institute,
participation during the field trial and attendance at the interviewer training sessions. Details related to
training hours for supervisors and interviewers are included in Table 17.3.

Training content
The Consortium recommended that countries implement an interviewer training programme of
approximately 18-22 hours covering the topics shown in Table 17.5. Since countries were allowed to adapt
the training scripts to be aligned with their nationally adapted BQ and to include content relevant to their
national context or survey institute requirements, there was variation in the duration of the training
programme across countries.
In general, topics that could be customised to country needs included training on contacting
respondents/households, distribution of incentives, and administrative topics. However, for topics such as
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

398 
administration of the PIAAC survey instruments and the use of disposition codes, countries were required
to use the Consortium training scripts to ensure that all interviewers across all participating countries
received the standardised training programme developed by the Consortium. Some countries conducted
training that was shorter for experienced interviewers than for interviewers who were new to interviewing
and/or to the project. Countries that retained interviewers who worked on the field trial generally exempted
interviewers from training modules covering administrative topics or the use of the case management
system. Newly hired interviewers received general interviewer training (GIT) aligned with the statistical
institute or survey organisation’s specific requirements on topics including gaining co-operation, refusal
conversion, ethics and administrative procedures, such as reporting time spent completing fieldwork.

The recommended total time for PIAAC training was approximately 20 hours, including training on screener
administration and the optional Curbside Observations module. Countries that did not use an address
sample or include the Curbside Observation module were able to conduct training of a shorter duration.
Details related to the training content administered by countries are included in Table 17.6. Twenty-three
countries (74%) met or exceeded the number of hours recommended for gaining co-operation training
(about 2.5 hours). Nineteen countries (61%) also included refusal conversion training as part of the general
interviewer training.
Twenty-four countries (77%) spent the recommended amount of time training interviewers on the
administration of the BQ, doorstep interview and direct assessment (6.0 hours or more). The time
recommended for administering the instruments was deemed necessary to allow interviewers to become
familiar with the BQ questions, become comfortable with launching the instruments, and master the
technical aspects of survey administration in order to focus on maintaining respondent co-operation and
engagement.

trainee’s ability to administer the PIAAC interview could be evaluated. Thirty countries (97%) included role
play or practice interviews as part of the training curriculum.

Staffing and field management
Hiring a sufficient number of staff (e.g. supervisors and interviewers), closely supervising interviewers
during data collection and monitoring production goals and response rates are the fundamentals of
successful fieldwork. Details related to staffing resources available to countries, as well as field
management, are included in the following sections.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

400 
Interviewer hiring and attrition
Each country was required to hire a sufficient number of interviewers to achieve its goal for data yield within
eight months (see Table 17.2 for production targets). Standard 8.3.1 of the TSG provided guidance for
countries when planning recruitment and hiring of field staff. National teams were also advised to use the
best information available from similar national surveys conducted in their country and to consider their
PIAAC field trial experience when estimating staffing needs.
Table 17.7 provides detailed information about staffing levels and attrition. Only two countries (Hungary
and Korea) had interviewers available to work full time (40 hours or more per week), while seven countries
(Estonia, Germany, Latvia, New Zealand, Poland, Portugal, the Slovak Republic and Sweden) had some
number of interviewers available to work full time. In general, across most countries, interviewers worked
part-time.

During the main study, as with the field trial, several countries continued to face significant challenges in
recruiting, hiring and retaining interviewers. Seventeen countries (55%) experienced substantial levels of
interviewer attrition (20% or more). Nine countries (29%) terminated interviewers; 11 countries (35%)
dismissed interviewers for quality control issues, while 13 countries (42%) dismissed interviewers due to
poor productivity. Interviewers who completed their assignments and left the project were not considered
to impact the attrition rate. Across countries, the number of interviewers added due to attrition ranged from
nine (Norway) to 245 (Canada). Five countries did not conduct attrition training during the field period as
they had adequate staff trained during the initial national training sessions to cover data collection
requirements.

Field management
All countries had adequate staff to oversee and manage the data collection effort (Standard 8.1.1).
Countries reported the number of management staff employed to oversee PIAAC data collection in the
National Survey Design and Planning Report (NSDPR). In addition, the numbers of supervisors and field
managers were also reported in the Data Collection Form. Table 17.8 shows details related to the
management structure and the experience profile of interviewers recruited and hired.
Countries reported that supervisory staff were available for timely interaction with the interviewers using a
variety of communication methods – supervisors were available via email and telephone (text messaging
and calls) and for in-person meetings when needed for issue resolution and guidance. Twenty-nine
countries (94%) had supervisors managing 30 or fewer interviewers as per the Consortium guideline. At a
minimum and across most countries, meetings with the field director, field managers and supervisors were
conducted on a weekly basis. In some countries, management staff were kept apprised daily of the
progress of fieldwork.
Almost all countries had some interviewers with prior PIAAC experience, either from the field trial or
Cycle 1, and this number ranged from two in the United States to 170 in France. Since Ireland conducted
a simulated field trial, interviewers with prior PIAAC experience were not available; Latvia and Portugal
also did not have interviewers with prior PIAAC experience, as these were countries new to PIAAC in
Cycle 2. Both countries conducted an operational field trial immediately preceding the main study. Due to
challenges faced by some countries with recruiting and hiring, further compounded by attrition, the number
of interviewers without prior survey experience (face-to-face data collection) ranged from four in the
Flemish Region of Belgium and Ireland to 317 in Canada. However, based on the number of interviewers
assigned to fieldwork, 21 countries had 50% or more of their interviewers with extensive face-to-face
survey experience.

Non-response reduction
Implementation of a comprehensive strategy to promote survey participation is a key element in obtaining
acceptable and/or high response rates. To this end, countries used a variety of outreach materials and
tools, reviewed information on contact attempts and non-response, and utilised strategies specifically
aimed at minimising non-response. The Consortium provided templates of non-response letters that could
be used in non-response follow-up efforts to target specific reasons for respondent refusals, such as being
too busy or concerns about the legitimacy of the study. Examples of endorsement letters and community
authorisation letters were also provided.

Use of introductory materials and outreach tools
Countries were required to develop a ‘best practices’ strategy to minimise non-response in accordance
with Standard 10.5.1. This included providing an introductory letter to sampled persons/households in
advance of the interviewer’s visit (Standard 10.2.1) and using a variety of tools to increase the visibility and
legitimacy of the study. Table 17.9 shows that 28 countries (90%) used an introductory letter and a study
brochure. All countries except Finland hosted a study telephone line for respondents, while all countries
except Latvia included a PIAAC study website.
Ten countries used endorsement letters, and 18 countries used newspaper articles and/or press releases.
Twenty-one countries disseminated study information through social media platforms such as Facebook
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 403
and YouTube, seven countries created PIAAC informational videos that were shared on various platforms,
and five countries placed ads on radio and television. Two countries also conducted press conferences
and gave interviews on television and radio.

Management and monitoring of contact attempts
Interviewers were required to attempt at least six in-person or seven telephone contact attempts with
sampled persons/households, with at least one attempt occurring on a weekday, weeknight and weekend
in keeping with Standard 10.3.2 and Standard 10.3.3.
The PIAAC TSG recommended initial in-person contact with sampled persons/households (Standard
10.2.1) since telephone contacts are more likely to lead to refusals. However, some countries have
established procedures for making initial contact by telephone. Table 17.10 shows that 15 countries (48%)
made initial in-person contact and 14 countries (45%) used a combination of telephone and in-person
contact modes, while two countries (Norway and Sweden) exclusively used telephone mode for initial
contact with sampled respondents.

 405
While PIAAC interview components, including the BQ and the direct assessment, are intended for inperson administration only (Standard 10.3.4), the Consortium allowed countries to incorporate multimode
approaches (web, telephone, paper) when completing the Screener instrument, if this approach had
already met with success in other national surveys conducted by the country. None of the countries opted
to use a web screener. Ireland and the United States used mail-in screener questionnaires after a required
number of unsuccessful in-person contact attempts with sampled households. Chile and Portugal deployed
an advance team of interviewers who used paper screeners to collect the required information prior to
dispatching field interviewers to complete the interview in households with eligible participants. Canada
was able to implement telephone screening as contact information was available for about 75% of the
sampled addresses; New Zealand and Portugal completed screening by telephone when respondents
provided this information in response to the introductory letter. Spain used telephone screening for cases
where access to rural households was difficult, when respondents were not home, and for refusal
conversion cases; telephone screeners were allowed in all cases after an in-person contact attempt was
made.
Another innovation in this cycle was the introduction of the doorstep interview, a new interview component
available for respondents who were unable to complete the BQ in the PIAAC language(s) of the country
due to language-related reasons. Although the doorstep interview was designed to be administered in
person, four countries (Denmark, Finland, Norway and the United States) submitted derogation requests
to complete the doorstep interview with respondents by telephone. Switzerland submitted a derogation
request to include online administration as well. The Consortium and the OECD approved these derogation
requests.

Documenting non-response
In order to facilitate the management of contacts with sampled persons or sampled households,
interviewers were required to document the results of contacts, including detailed information on each
contact attempt that resulted in non-response (Standard 10.3.8).
During PIAAC Cycle 2, countries had the option of using the international Case Management System
Administration (iCMA) site, which included an international Case Management System (iCMS) or their
national case management system. Countries using the iCMA system could manage various aspects of
the administration of data collection activities on a national level. One feature included in the iCMS was
the built-in capability for interviewers to document details of contact attempts when non-response occurred.
The system collected information related to the contact attempt day, date, time, contact mode, outcome
and any relevant comments to facilitate follow-up visits and allow non-response follow-up strategies to be
devised. Using the iCMS reporting functionality and the PIAAC dashboard (details included in Chapter 16),
management staff also had the ability to monitor how contact attempts were progressing during the data
collection. Twenty countries (65%) used the international case management system to manage various
aspects of fieldwork.
The remaining 11 countries used a national case management system to collect details on contact attempts
including information about the person who refused, their relationship to the respondent, the strength of
the refusal, the likelihood of conversion, problems encountered and any additional relevant information
that might facilitate future contact with the respondent. For countries using the iCMS, the system included
a non-response form that collected this information. Countries that used a national CMS collected these
details to varying extents, as shown in Table 17.11.

Countries also reported on the most frequently cited reasons respondents provided for refusing the BQ
(Table 17.12) or the direct assessment (Table 17.13). Countries tracked the reason for the refusal in their
CMS. For example, in the iCMS, once a respondent refused, the interviewer completed a refusal form to
help with subsequent refusal conversion attempts. Information gathered included the respondent’s reason
for refusing. The top three reasons for refusal were reported in the monthly Data Collection Form submitted
to the Consortium.
For non-response to the BQ, lack of interest and lack of time or ‘too busy’ were the most often cited reasons
in about 70% of the countries, followed by ‘too long’ (61% of countries). Additional reasons for refusal cited
by respondents included concerns about data privacy and confidentiality related to information gathered
in the BQ, and many respondents also mentioned the lack of an option to complete the survey online.

Non-response strategies
Countries were strongly advised to implement a comprehensive strategy to deal with non-response cases.
Table 17.14 presents the non-response strategies used by countries. Almost all countries implemented a
combination of strategies. The three most frequently used approaches by countries to address nonresponse were the reassignment of cases to other interviewers (27 countries, 87%), the use of tailored
letters and/or refusal conversion letters (19 countries, 61%), and the use of senior interviewers, supervisors
or travellers to follow up on non-response cases (20-22 countries, 65-71%). Some countries also provided
additional incentives for refusal conversion cases, as noted in Table 17.15.

Use of incentives
With the exception of Denmark and France, all countries provided incentives to the respondents. Details
regarding the nature of incentives distributed to respondents completing the survey instruments are
provided in Table 17.15.

Fieldwork quality control
Each country was required to implement a comprehensive fieldwork quality control plan. This plan
included:
•

an evaluation of interviewers during training and data collection

•

the implementation of timely validation to verify that the interviewer contacted and completed
interviews with the sampled person/sampled household

•

the review of survey and process data through the analysis of automated management reports and
by monitoring key indicators on the PIAAC dashboard.

Audio-recording/observation of interviews
Countries were required to review audio recordings of completed BQ interviews (Standard 10.9.5)
submitted by interviewers during the early stages of data collection and provide feedback. The

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

412 
Consortium’s recommendation was for interviewers to record the third and 10th completed interviews.
There were challenges in meeting this standard as some respondents across countries considered the
recordings to be intrusive and had concerns about data privacy. Furthermore, not all interviewers
completed two interviews either due to reassignment of cases or because they left the project before data
collection ended.

Monitoring was conducted by reviewing audio-recorded interviews, observing the interviews in person, or
a combination of both approaches. Twenty-one countries (68%) reviewed full BQ audio recordings, and
four countries (Canada, Japan, Korea and Sweden) only reviewed snippets of the recordings. Countries

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 413
also reviewed audio-recording snippets to ensure that the interview was conducted according to protocol
and to assuage any concerns related to interview administration when needed. Eleven countries monitored
in-person interviewers during the conduct of a field interview, and one country (Austria) only observed
interviewers completing a practice interview during training.
Table 17.16 shows the number of interviewers assigned to PIAAC and the number of interviews that were
audio-recorded or observed in each country. Some countries employed additional methods to confirm the
interview was conducted through geolocation (Israel, New Zealand, the Slovak Republic and the United
States) or video confirmation of the ongoing interview (Portugal).

Validation
Validation (back-checks) is critical to data validity; it is the most important quality control feature of
household data collection. As stated in the TSG (Standard 10.9.3), the validation requirement includes the
verification of 10% of an interviewer’s finalised work, including cases finalised as non-response. The
validation plan countries implemented had to ensure that:
•

cases for validation were selected randomly

•

at least 10 percent of each interviewer’s cases were validated

•

all finalised cases were eligible for selection to be validated, not just completed cases.

The requirement to validate each interviewer’s completed work at the 10% level was challenging for
countries: only seven countries did so, although 16 countries validated 10% of finalised work for 75% or
more of their interviewers. Eight countries met the lower threshold (7% of cases validated for 90% or more
interviewers).
Several reasons factored into countries being unable to validate the work of all interviewers who finalised
cases – (1) not all interviewers who received assignments finalised them because cases were reassigned
to other interviewers or they left the project early; (2) respondents were hard to contact by telephone or did
not respond to mailed validation letters; (3) when validation was attempted several months after the
interviewer’s visit, the respondents had difficulties recalling the interview; (4) some countries had
restrictions on recontacting cases that were finalised as refusals or respondents with disability; and (5)
some countries had insufficient resources to manage validation efforts early in the field period as resources
were diverted to recruiting and training interviewers due to attrition.
In addition to completed cases, 18 countries (58%) validated selected cases finalised as completed
doorstep interviews, refusals, ineligibles and noncontacts. Seven countries (Germany, Israel, Japan,
Norway, Portugal, Singapore and Sweden) conducted back-checks on 100% of completed cases.
Singapore purposefully selected all cases for validation, while Finland and Ireland only validated the
randomly pre-selected cases for validation.
Details related to the implementation of validation are presented in Table 17.17.

Fifteen countries (48%) uncovered instances of falsification. Falsification included instances of the
following:
•

underreporting the number of household members in the screener

•

conducting the interview at a non-sampled address

•

misusing the disposition codes

•

having a non-sampled person complete the BQ and/or assessment
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 415
•

helping the respondent complete the assessment

•

fabricating answers to the BQ and the assessment.

The potential for falsification underlines the critical importance of validation for in-person studies that
require interviewers to work independently in the field. A rigorous validation procedure is, therefore, critical
to substantiating data quality. Countries that reported falsification either reset and re-fielded cases when
possible or deleted falsified data. In addition, countries endeavoured to meet the PIAAC TSG requirement
of validating 100% of cases completed by any interviewer who falsified data (Standard 10.9.4).

Other quality control checks
In addition to validation by contacting the sampled household/sampled person, countries were advised to
use the PIAAC dashboard to monitor reports to track information on timing data as well as any other means
of detecting falsification available to them, such as geolocation of interviewers. Seventeen countries (55%)
used the PIAAC dashboard, and 26 countries (84%) used all available monitoring reports to track interview
administration length, interviews completed very early (before 8.30 a.m.) or too late (after 9.00 p.m.), the
time elapsed between interviews, and the number of interviews completed per day. Thirty countries (97%)
tracked overall interview and instrument duration.
Details related to the use of monitoring reports and other quality control checks implemented by the
countries are included in Table 17.18.

Countries were also advised to monitor the quality of data throughout the main study data collection. As
shown in Table 17.19, all countries conducted a range of checks on data quality. Twenty-seven countries
(87%) conducted checks on data frequencies; 26 countries (84%) monitored timing data of completed
instruments; 25 countries (81%) reviewed open-ended responses; 23 countries (74%) reviewed ‘don’t
know’ and ‘refused’ responses; and 19 countries (61%) reviewed ‘other specify’ responses. All countries
conducted age and gender discrepancy checks. Checks were implemented in registry countries by
comparing registry information to the respondent-provided information; in screener countries, checks
compared information obtained from the screener respondent to that provided by the sampled respondent.

Interviewer productivity
Unusually high interviewer productivity, as measured by the number of completed interviews during a time
period, can be an indication of falsification. Countries reported information on the minimum, maximum and
mean number of completes per interviewer on a monthly basis using the Data Collection Form. The
Consortium’s guidance was to increase the validation rate of high-producing interviewers, vigilantly monitor
the dashboard quality control indicators and automated quality control reports and implement checks on
the data quality of completed interviews.
Countries with high-producing interviewers were vigilant about monitoring their completed work and
conducting additional validation. Twenty-two countries (71%) implemented additional validation checks on
cases completed by high producers. Details related to interviewer productivity are provided in Table 17.20.
The number of completed interviews per interviewer varied across countries based on the total number of
interviewers and their case assignment. The mean number of completes per interviewer ranged from 13 in
France to 96 in Switzerland. The mean number of completes per interviewer was within the 20-60 range
for approximately two-thirds of the countries (65%). The maximum number of interviews completed by an
interviewer varied widely among countries and ranged from 46 in Denmark to 431 in Latvia.

Countries were required to administer a debriefing questionnaire and/or hold debriefing sessions with
interviewers to gain insights into their perspectives on all aspects of survey administration. The information
collected included interviewer feedback on the home study and training they received, their field experience
administering the PIAAC survey instruments, and suggestions for improving procedures for future cycles
of PIAAC. Countries were required to provide a report to the Consortium summarising the key findings. An
international debriefing summary was generated and provided to the Consortium and the OECD.
