18. Quality Control monitoring activities
Nina Thornton, Tom Krenzke and Leyla Mohadjer (Westat)

This chapter details the monitoring activities implemented by the
Consortium that ensured the data collected by participating countries and
economies during the main study were of high quality and reliable.
Participating countries and economies were required to submit forms to the
Consortium documenting the plans for fieldwork, as well as report on the
progress of interviewer training and data collection on a pre-arranged
schedule. National teams also participated in quality control calls with the
Consortium on a regular basis during data collection to discuss any
emergent issues and the status of fieldwork.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

420 

Introduction
This chapter presents the details of the survey operations’ quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC)
activities conducted by the Consortium as part of the main study during PIAAC Cycle 2.
This quality control and monitoring programme was designed to: (1) support the collection of data and
results that are valid, reliable and comparable across countries and over time, and satisfy accepted quality
assurance goals; (2) keep the OECD and the Consortium informed about the progress of data collection;
and (3) provide guidance to countries needing assistance. This programme was considered the best tradeoff of quality and cost within the constraints of the project.
In keeping with the goals of the QA and QC programme outlined above, national teams and the Consortium
worked together to ensure all aspects of survey operations were managed and monitored during data
collection by implementing the following:
•

Monitoring adherence to the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines (TSG) 1 during
preparation for and conduct of data collection to ensure standardised survey procedures were
followed across all countries.

•

Tracking the progress of data collection, identifying potential problems and implementing solutions
on a timely basis during the field period.

•

Identifying sources of non-sampling-related error to inform analysis.

The PIAAC QC process provided continuous support to countries in following the technical standards
before, during and after data collection. Furthermore, through the process, the OECD and the Consortium
stayed informed of the status of data collection in each country on a regular basis throughout the field
period. Overall, all countries co-operated with the requirements of this robust programme.
The process described in this chapter was followed for all aspects of the field operations described in
Chapter 17. The next section describes the QA and QC activities for survey operations, while the
subsequent section details the countries’ compliance with these activities. The chapter concludes with a
brief summary.

Quality assurance and quality control activities
Quality assurance (QA)
The QA process for survey operations consisted of the development of standards and guidelines, including
the QC process, a QC and management manual, and the training of national teams on QC activities.

Development of standards and guidelines for survey operations
The first step in the implementation of the PIAAC quality assurance programme was the specification of
standards and guidelines covering all aspects of the survey life cycle, from sample design and data
collection to data processing and analysis. Chapters 8 to 10 of the PIAAC TSG specifically address topics
related to survey operations, such as field staff recruitment, staff management and training, and field
management practices and requirements for data collection. The PIAAC standards are based on generally
agreed-upon policies or best practices for the conduct of the survey.

Development of the survey operations QC and management manual
The purpose of this manual was to: (1) provide national teams with details on important survey operations
standards, including practical suggestions on their implementation (e.g. field management reports,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 421
monitoring of interviewers during the field period, tools to increase respondent co-operation); and (2)
provide national teams with details on the logistics of the PIAAC quality control programme (e.g. forms to
be submitted, quality control call schedule).

International training on survey operations QC
The international training on survey operations QC took place prior to the field trial, during the international
PIAAC meeting held in February 2020 (NPM Meeting 5) and detailed the essential points covered in the
QC manual. As a result of the year-long delay to the field trial due to COVID-19, the QC content was
delivered again to national teams virtually in February 2021, prior to the start of the field trial scheduled in
April 2021. Key content was also presented during the survey operations workshop (NPM Meeting 7) held
prior to the main study data collection scheduled to begin in September 2022.

Quality control (QC)
The QC process was implemented through the review of country submissions of QC forms and summary
reports, conduct of QC calls, ad hoc meetings and email exchanges as needed. This section provides a
summary description of each activity.

National Survey Design and Planning Report (NSDPR) review
Each country was required to submit plans for survey implementation in the Main Study NSDPR by 13
May 2022, prior to the scheduled start of data collection on 1 September 2022. The Consortium reviewed
the plans submitted by each country and provided feedback. Country responses on issues noted were due
by 15 July 2022, after which the Consortium reviewed responses and approved the country submissions
in August 2022. Countries were expected to adhere to the standards specified in the survey operations
chapters of the TSG, covering content related to Ethics, Survey Planning, Field Management, Field Staff
Training and Data Collection (including 82 standards). When deviations from the standards were reported
in the NSDPR, countries were required to submit a derogation request to the Consortium and the OECD
for approval.

PIAAC dashboard monitoring
The Consortium and countries utilised the key performance indicators (KPIs) available on the PIAAC
Dashboard to monitor quality control metrics. However, not all countries used the PIAAC Dashboard during
the field period. Details related to the use of the PIAAC Dashboard are described in Chapter 16.

Quality control calls
The Consortium conducted QC calls with each participating country on a regular basis throughout the
critical field trial and main study data collection periods. The goals of the calls were to: (1) review and
discuss the information provided in the monthly data collection forms submitted by countries (see below);
(2) provide countries with the opportunity to ask questions in real time; and (3) discuss any emergent
issues impacting data collection that may have arisen in each country.
QC calls were held monthly with each country during field trial data collection and reduced to every other
month during the main study, except for countries that were unable to conduct a field trial. Countries new
to PIAAC in Cycle 2 that only conducted an operational field trial, participated in monthly calls throughout
the main study data collection. However, countries and the Consortium could request additional calls when
needed.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

422 
QC call participants varied somewhat from month to month, depending on the topics for discussion, but
generally included the country’s National Project Manager, National Sampling Manager and National Data
Manager, as well as key Commercial Survey Organisation (CSO) staff and key Westat survey operations
staff representing the Consortium.
QC calls followed a specific agenda guided by the data collection form and the summary notes from the
QC calls were documented in reports, which included the topics discussed, any decisions made and
pending action items. The Minutes Reports were posted on the PIAAC Portal and available to Consortium
partners and national team members.

Data collection form
Countries were required to complete the data collection forms on a monthly basis. These forms were used
to guide the discussion during the QC calls and focused on the topics covered in Chapters 2, 8, 9 and 10
of the PIAAC TSG. The form included 77 short answer questions.
The following topics were addressed in the form and during the calls:
•

timeline for national interviewer training and data collection

•

field staffing and management

•

plans for contacting households/respondents

•

respondent outreach materials/use of incentives

•

strategies for dealing with non-response

•

case management system

•

production numbers, including details on finalised cases and the disposition codes assigned to
instruments

•

projections on reaching the target (adaptive survey design)

•

field QC measures

•

ethics and confidentiality.

Countries posted the updated data collection forms on a monthly basis (according to the preset schedule)
to the PIAAC Portal, which was accessible to national team members and the Consortium. Countries were
also required to submit a Data Collection Form within a month after data collection ended and a final
version once data cleaning was completed.

Summary interviewer training reports
To ascertain adherence to the interviewer training programme designed by the Consortium, countries were
required to complete one summary training report at the end of the main national interviewer training (prior
to the start of data collection) and complete an additional report after the end of data collection documenting
details of attrition training sessions held during the field period. The report included details related to:
•

the number of training sessions

•

the dates when training was conducted

•

the number of trainees

•

the experience profile of the trainees

•

the training content by topics

•

the number of training hours

•

supervisor training details.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 423
In addition, countries evaluated the trainees during interviewer training and through in-person observation
of trainees conducting role plays or practice interviews.
The completed summary training reports were posted to the PIAAC Portal.

Interviewer debriefing questionnaire and summary report
Countries were required to administer a debriefing questionnaire to interviewers following the conclusion
of data collection in order to obtain interviewer feedback. The debriefing questionnaire included 36
questions covering:
•

interviewer training

•

administration of the instruments (screener, background questionnaire, doorstep interview, and the
direct assessment)

•

challenges encountered (gaining respondent co-operation, refusal conversion, health and safety
concerns)

•

the overall interview.

Each country was required to summarise interviewers’ feedback on the questionnaire and submit the
summary report to the Consortium. The national summary reports were posted to the PIAAC Portal.

was usually done with advance notice.

Summary interviewer debriefing report
Countries were required to debrief interviewers on their main study experience and provide a report to the
Consortium. All countries submitted the summary interviewer debriefing report. Based on the national

Conclusion
Overall, the PIAAC quality control programme implemented by the Consortium and national teams for all
aspects of survey operations met the intended goals of supporting and documenting the adherence to the
standards across all countries and providing timely information to implement corrections throughout the
process.

 427
Country compliance with the QA programme and conducting QC activities was high throughout the critical
months of fieldwork (see Annex G on adjudication outcomes). The programme facilitated the exchange of
information and novel fieldwork strategies used among countries, which in turn helped foster a sense of
co-operation and “shared experience”. National teams were also kept apprised of the overall progress of
data collection across countries through monthly webinars hosted by the Consortium. The experience
gained from the PIAAC QA and QC activities programme will serve countries and the OECD as they plan
for future rounds of PIAAC.

19. Indicators of the quality of the
sample data
Tom Krenzke, John Lopdell, Wendy Van de Kerckhove and Leyla Mohadjer, Westat

This chapter focuses on the quality assurance and quality control
procedures implemented to ensure that the PIAAC sampling and weighting
standards were met. It details key quality indicators for each country,
including coverage rates, response rates and results of non-response bias
analyses. The chapter also describes the development of technical
standards and guidelines, sampling and weighting activity toolkits, and the
adaptive survey design used to monitor and improve data quality. Overall, it
emphasizes the importance of rigorous quality control measures to produce
reliable and comparable survey data across countries.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 429

Introduction
The sampling and weighting procedures described in Chapters 2 and 8 were undertaken with the goal of
minimising total survey error and producing samples that are representative of the target population. This
chapter begins with a discussion of the quality assurance and quality control procedures that were
implemented to ensure the sampling and weighting standards were met. The remaining sections report
key quality indicators for each country. They provide coverage rates and response rates, describe the
results of non-response bias analyses (NRBA), and give sample sizes and design effects.

Quality assurance and quality control procedures
Quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) procedures were put in place to ensure the achievement
of high-quality data that are comparable between countries. In this section, we describe the samplingrelated QA process used by the Consortium to help achieve this goal and the QC procedures required of
countries to ensure that the quality goals related to sampling were met. Country compliance with the
sampling and weighting QC procedures are addressed in Chapters 2 and 8, respectively, while the nonresponse bias analysis QC procedures are addressed at the end of this chapter.

Quality assurance activities
The QA process for sampling activities involved the development of standards and guidelines, the
production of sampling documents, the creation of sampling and weighting activity toolkits, and
communication with countries. This section provides a summary description of each activity.

Technical Standards and Guidelines for sampling, weighting and non-response bias
reduction
For Chapters 4 and 14 of the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines1, the Consortium produced
standards, guidelines and recommendations for each of the following:
•

Target population: To ensure that the target population for PIAAC is clearly defined in each
country and is consistent across countries.

•

Sampling frame: To ensure that the sampling frame(s) is of high quality, provides acceptable
coverage of the target population, and meets the requirements for sampling, location of selected
population members and estimation.

•

Sample size: To establish minimum sample-size requirements for each country to meet the
analysis goals of PIAAC.

•

Sample design: To specify the PIAAC sample design that will produce a probability-based sample,
representative of the target population, in each participating country.

•

International and national sampling options: To describe potential country-specific
supplemental sampling options and their implications for sample size.

•

Sample selection: To specify procedures for selecting a probability-based sample from the PIAAC
target population following the sample design of PIAAC.

•

Indicators of survey quality – under-coverage bias, non-response bias and response rates:
To establish indicators to measure the quality of PIAAC survey data with respect to representation
of the target population and to provide standard procedures for measuring these indicators.

•

Respondent incentives: To increase response rates by offering sampled adults some incentive
for participating in PIAAC and for attempting the assessment.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

430 
•

Sample monitoring and adaptive survey design: To produce a plan for countries to use in
monitoring the sample during data collection to allow timely reaction to any developing shortfalls
or other potential for non-response bias in the outcome sample.

•

Weighting: To provide a standard weighting approach to reduce non-response bias and coverage
error and to facilitate the production of point estimates for the target population and their associated
sampling error estimates.

Sampling, weighting and NRBA documents
The Consortium created sampling, weighting and NRBA documents to provide further details on the quality
standards in Chapters 4 and 14 of the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines. The Sampling Plan
Part I document (Sample Design and Selection Plans) gave an overview of the PIAAC sample design and
a description of the information that countries should include in their sampling plan forms (described
below). The Sampling Plan Part II Weighting document (Weighting and Variance Estimation Plans)
described the weighting process, including the weighting steps, treatment of different disposition codes,
calculation of weighting adjustment factors, assignment of variance strata and variance units, and creation
of replicate weights. The Sampling Plan Part III NRBA document (PIAAC Response Rates and Nonresponse Bias Analysis Plans) described the goals for identifying and reducing non-response bias before,
during and after data collection. It also included requirements for the NRBA and examples of analyses
conducted for PIAAC Cycle 1. The Consortium also provided countries with a Sampling Activities
Guidebook, which discussed step-by-step chronology and mechanics for meeting the requirements for the
PIAAC sampling activities.

Sampling and Weighting Activity Toolkits
The Sampling and Weighting Activity Toolkits are a set of Consortium-developed programs and
worksheets to aid countries in various sampling- and weighting-related activities. The toolkits were optional
to countries but served countries that needed them and helped ensure consistent and high-quality results.
Types of toolkits included are as follows:
•

Sample size – Excel spreadsheets to calculate initial person and dwelling unit sample sizes.

•

Sample selection – Documentation to aid countries in selecting the probability samples, using
Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS).

•

Design effects (DEFF) – Excel spreadsheets to compute DEFF due to clustering as well as DEFF
due to differential sampling rates.

•

Within-household selection – Test input files for the algorithm to select one or two persons in a
household.

•

Response rates – Excel spreadsheets to calculate actual and projected response rates for each
data collection stage.

•

Variable selection – Programmes, documentation, examples and test files for the selection of
weighting variables.

•

Survey Control File (SCF) edit checks – Programmes (in SAS and R) and instructions for
conducting checks on the SCF variables prior to the submission of the final SCF.

•

Sample Design International File (SDIF) edit checks – Programmes (in SAS and R) and instructions
for conducting checks on the variables in both the preliminary and final SDIFs prior to submitting
them to the Data Management Expert (DME) system.

•

NRBA – R code and documentation for performing the seven non-response bias analyses. These
were made available to countries that conducted their own NRBA.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 431
Sampling workshops and other communications
Communication with countries is an essential part of the QA process. To this end, the Consortium
conducted a sampling workshop at the NPM meeting prior to the Field Trial. The workshop covered
information on sample design, sampling plan forms, Field Trial sampling requirements and sample sizes,
Field Trial QC forms for sample selection, sample monitoring and within-household selection. A second
sampling workshop was held prior to the Main Study. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, this workshop was
presented as a series of recordings that were made available to countries and covered information on the
Main Study sample design, sample selection, sample monitoring, adaptive survey design, sampling files,
weighting and variance estimation, non-response bias analysis and an overview of the schedule. Two live
virtual Q&A sessions were held shortly after the release of the workshop recordings and were offered at
different times to accommodate country schedules. Countries were asked to review the workshop
recordings prior to the Q&A session. One of the Q&A sessions was recorded for the benefit of any countries
that were unable to attend the live session. Countries were also offered the option of a virtual consultation
to discuss any questions they had that were not resolved through the workshop or Q&A sessions.
Given the importance of the SDIF as the key input file for the Main Study weighting process, the Consortium
presented the SDIF submission process at the December 2022 NPM webinar. This was followed by
another webinar in March 2023, following on from countries’ submissions of the preliminary SDIF. This
webinar focused on common issues found in the preliminary SDIFs, with the aim being to minimise the
number of issues encountered in the final SDIFs.
The Consortium communicated with countries through presentations on sampling and survey operations
requirements at NPM meetings. It also provided feedback through in-person consultation sessions (at NPM
meetings) or through emails or calls as needed.

Quality control activities
Sampling QC checks gathered the information necessary to monitor the countries’ sampling activities and
facilitated a series of validity checks conducted by the Consortium. They were implemented through a
series of electronic forms and data files for the Field Trial and Main Study. The QC process started with
the Consortium reviewing the materials and responding to the country with suggestions for changes or
recommendations for improvements. Each QC form or file had a submission schedule to ensure countries
met the timeline for various project activities. Real-time monitoring of all aspects of sampling was critical
in allowing the Consortium to uncover problems with sampling activities and for the countries to incorporate
changes if necessary. This section provides a summary description of each QC activity.

Sampling, weighting and NRBA plans
To reduce burden, the Consortium created a series of Sampling Plan Forms that contained all the
information needed to meet the requirements listed in Chapter 4 (sample design and selection) and
Chapter 14 (weighting/estimation) of the National Survey Design and Planning Report (NSDPR). Countries
were required to complete and return the forms at least six months prior to the start of the field trial data
collection. This deadline was set to ensure the field trial sample design and selection steps provided all
the necessary opportunities to test various aspects of the main study sample design and selection
activities. Countries then had the opportunity to update their main study plans after the field trial.
Sampling Plan Form Part 1 addressed the standards and guidelines related to sample design and
selection. It was to be completed separately for the Field Trial and Main Study. The form included questions
on country plans for each of the following:
•

country-specific supplemental samples

•

target population definition

•

background design information

•

sample design and sampling units

•

within-household selection rule (for countries with dwelling unit [DU] sampling)

•

sampling frame description

•

coverage rate of target population

•

sample selection methods for area units (if applicable)

•

sample selection methods for DU and within-household sampling (if applicable)

•

•

initial sample size worksheet

•

•

•

quality control.

Sampling Plan Forms Part 2 and Part 3 pertained to the main study only. Part 2 checked countries’ ability
to comply with the weighting chapter (Chapter 14) of the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines. It
included questions on potential variables for weighting adjustments, planned weighting procedures and
the intended variance estimation method. Part 3 addressed expected response rates and NRBA plans.

Sample selection quality control forms
The QC sample selection (SS) forms collected detailed information about the country sample selection
process and the results. Countries were to submit forms after each sample selection stage, allowing
adequate time for countries to respond to the Consortium comments and questions and to revise
procedures if necessary. The forms were important to verify that the selection of a probability sample
adhered to the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines.
The forms covered the following:
•

description of the sampling frame

•

definition of the sampling unit

•

variables used for stratification, sorting and measure-of-size calculations

•

list of certainty units, such as large primary sampling units (PSUs)

•

average, minimum and maximum cluster size

•

number of units on the frame, number of units sampled, weighted totals and target population
totals, by stratum

•

weighted population totals by characteristics of interest (such as region or age)

•

weight distributions, where the weight is the inverse of the selection probability

•

description of any oversampling

•

description of the reserve sample

•

formulae for selection probabilities

•

mapping of country disposition codes to Consortium codes

•

description of the Survey Control File, including the number of observations and variable names
and labels.

Sample monitoring quality control reports
The sample monitoring process was intended to help countries identify potential shortfalls in the sample,
problems in achieving the desired response rate and the potential for non-response bias in the collected
sample. Continuous monitoring was used to allow countries to employ procedures to address these
problems during data collection while there was still time to intervene, helping countries meet the goals
associated with sampling and data quality. Countries were required to complete QC sample monitoring
(SM) reports every month during data collection. In addition, every second month during data collection, a
meeting was scheduled between the Consortium and the National Centre to review progress and discuss
any survey operations and sampling issues. For countries using the international case management
system (iCMS), the sample monitoring reports were generated within the iCMS. Countries that used a
national CMS were required to prepare SM reports that contained, at a minimum, the same information
provided in the SM reports generated by the iCMS. The Consortium prepared materials to assist countries
with this, including table shells, mock examples of completed SM forms and a response rate toolkit. The
Consortium reviewed the SM reports and provided feedback to countries. The reports collected information
on the number of cases released for data collection, the numbers at different stages of data collection (not
yet worked, in progress, or finalised), and the number of cases completed, response rates and expected
yield by key subgroups. Countries were asked to monitor these figures by gender, age groups and
geography to help identify any shortfalls in yield or unusually low response rates.
The PIAAC dashboard is an innovation that was introduced in Cycle 2 to facilitate the management and
monitoring of field operations. An advantage of using the PIAAC dashboard is that it enabled timely tracking
of various production and quality control metrics. These included sample yield projections and progress
compared to the target sample yield, actual response rates compared to the targets for each sampling
stage (screener, BQ, assessment and overall), and weekly numbers of actual completes compared to
projected completes by region, age group, gender and language. Twenty-two countries used the
dashboard. For the nine countries that did not use it, reasons for not using the dashboard included (1)
countries’ use of survey organisations that had an existing dashboard, (2) language barriers that prevented
the supervisory staff from using the dashboard, and (3) data confidentiality restrictions. More details on the
PIAAC Dashboard are provided in Chapter 16.
Countries that used the iCMS were required to prepare a Sample Monitoring Parameter (SMP) file, which
contained key parameters for use in ongoing monitoring of the sample, including the expected proportions
by region, age group and gender, expected response rates, expected numbers of completed screeners,
BQs and assessments, and the expected proportion of completed cases for each interim disposition code.
This file was uploaded to the iCMS and the information was used in the monthly SM reports, the dashboard
and the adaptive survey design.

Adaptive survey design
In PIAAC Cycle 2, adaptive survey design was introduced as a standard (4.9.1), with the aim of helping
countries achieve the goals for the number of completed cases and reduce non-response bias. The two
components of adaptive survey design that countries were required to implement were completed case
projection and case prioritisation. Completed case projections were to be computed before data collection
and continuously updated during data collection to estimate how many completed cases were expected at
the end of data collection. The projections were intended to help inform whether additional sample releases
were needed during the data collection period. Case prioritisation was to be conducted to guide the field
management staff in helping interviewers focus on completing higher priority cases. Cases were to be
prioritised in two phases. In Phase 1, the first few priority groups were derived from whether cases had
met established contact attempt protocols (Standards 10.3.2 and 10.3.3). By fully meeting the contact
attempt protocols, the case prioritisation process indirectly reduced bias due to non-response. In Phase 2,

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

434 
for cases meeting the contact protocols, a statistical-based ordering was assigned to each case. The
objective of the statistical-based ordering was to reduce bias due to non-response.
The adaptive survey design components were incorporated into the iCMS. For countries using a national
CMS, a document was prepared that gave instructions for how to implement both adaptive survey design
components.

Sampling-related quality control data checks
The Consortium provided countries with suggested sampling-related QC checks that the countries could
run during data collection. These checks were intended to supplement the record consistency checks in
the Data Management Expert (DME) software and emphasised variables relating to the SCF and SDIF.
SCF and SDIF edit check toolkits were made available to countries for this purpose. These toolkits provided
detailed instructions, along with programs in SAS and R, for implementing QC checks on the extensive
range of variables on these two files. Having countries carry out these checks prior to submitting them to
the Consortium was intended to reduce the number of revisions required during the Consortium’s review
period. This was particularly important for the final SDIF, due to the tight schedule between the due date
for submission of the final SDIF and the beginning of the weighting process.

Survey Control Files, Sample Design International Files and Weighting International Files
The SCF was the central file containing the sample for data collection, along with sample design
information such as selection probabilities and sampling strata. This file was loaded into the CMS prior to
data collection. Before loading the SCF to the CMS, a quality control process was implemented on a partial
version of the file (i.e. a version with any personally identifiable information, such as address, removed) to
ensure that it was aligned with the expectations of the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines,
especially those related to sampling activities. This partial SCF process included edit checks provided by
Westat that were to be conducted by the country. Further checks were then conducted by Westat, including
comparisons with the sampling plans and sample selection forms. Once the file was approved, it could be
loaded into the CMS.
At the end of data collection, countries provided the Consortium with an SDIF that contained sample
selection data for each sampled unit, including sampling strata, probabilities of selection, ID variables,
disposition codes and auxiliary variables for weighting adjustments. The SDIF was the input file to the
weighting process. The Consortium performed QC checks on the file to verify that variable definitions and
formats were consistent with the specifications in the SDIF layout and that those fields reflected the
information provided by the countries in their sample selection forms and weighting plans.
Countries also provided Weighting International Files (WIFs) for Benchmark Control Totals to the
Consortium. The files contained the external control totals to be used in the benchmarking adjustments.
The benchmark WIFs were reviewed to check that the overall target population total was the same for
each variable used in the benchmarking adjustment and that there was a set of control totals for each
benchmarking variable included in the SDIF. Countries performing their weighting adjustments also
supplied a WIF for Quality Control Checks that was used to supplement the checks performed through the
weighting QC forms. The weighting QC forms are described below.
So as not to jeopardise the weighting schedule due to data reconciliation issues, countries were asked to
provide a preliminary version of the SDIF and benchmark WIF before the end of data collection and then
a final version after data collection.

Weighting quality control forms
The Consortium developed a set of QC checks to review the weighting process for adherence to the
weighting standards and guidelines and to check weight calculations for reasonableness and accuracy.
Prior to the weighting period, each country needed to complete and return a checklist on the PIAAC
Technical Standards and Guidelines related to weighting (Weighting QC Form W-0). They indicated
whether the standards and guidelines were consistent with their implementation and understanding and
indicated any deviations. They also needed to complete a W-1 form that contained checks on the
benchmark control totals, theoretical base weights and any imputation performed for weighting variables.
In general, the Consortium performed the weighting adjustments for countries in Cycle 2. However, some
countries opted to perform the weighting themselves, most commonly due to confidentiality restrictions.
During weighting, countries that formed their own weights were required to report on details of their
weighting adjustments and weight distributions through a series of QC forms. If the Consortium conducted
the weighting steps, the Consortium provided the forms to the countries for their review.
Form W-2 covered base weights and replicate weights, including the variance strata and variance unit
assignments. Form W-3 was on the basic NRBA before adjustments and consisted of one form for screener
non-response adjustments to be completed for screener countries and one form for BQ non-response
adjustments to be completed for both registry and screener countries. The W-3 forms described the
classification tree analyses and presented the results of these analyses. The objective of the analyses was
to identify subgroups/areas with low response rates and inform weighting adjustments. Form W-4 covered
the household-level weighting adjustments for screener countries, and Form W-5 dealt with the personlevel weighting adjustments. Form W-6 covered the final calibrated person weights. The forms included
the following checks:
•

descriptive statistics (including the counts of cases with missing and non-missing weights and sum,
mean, minimum, maximum and coefficient of variation (CV) of weights) on the full sample weights
across weighting stages for the full sample, and by region, age group and gender, respectively

•

the sum of replicate weights across weighting stages

•

descriptive statistics on selected replicate weights across weighting stages

•

unweighted and weighted counts by response status and weighting adjustment cells across
weighting stages

•

description of trimming procedures

•

listing of the largest weights

•

comparison of control totals to external totals and weighted PIAAC totals

•

design effect calculations

•

a list of the variables included in the classification tree analysis, a description of how these were
chosen, the method and weights used, how respondents and non-respondents were defined, the
results, and which variables would be used in the weighting adjustments.

Performing the weighting QC checks was essential for verifying that the final weights produced for
estimation were appropriate. If any issues with the weighting adjustments were identified by the weighting
QC forms, problems needed to be rectified and the QC forms resubmitted until no more issues were found.

Weighted response rates and NRBA
Regardless of response rate, all countries were required to conduct a basic NRBA. The basic analysis
evaluated the relationship of response status to available auxiliary variables and provided an indication of
the extent of non-response bias prior to weighting adjustments. It could be used to inform the choice of

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

436 
weighting variables. As noted in the previous section, the details of the basic NRBA were described in the
weighting QC form W-3.
As described in the next section, the Consortium computed weighted response rates for each country using
the official response rate formulae in Annex 4-1 of the PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines and the
data provided on the countries’ SDIF. If a country’s overall BQ response rate fell below 70% or the overall
assessment response rate was less than 67%, an extended NRBA was needed. The extended NRBA was
performed by the Consortium unless the country chose to perform the extended NRBA with support from
the Consortium. This analysis included the evaluation of the potential for remaining bias after weighting
adjustments were completed. It also attempted to evaluate bias directly in the proficiency estimates rather
than solely relying on auxiliary variables.

Sampling coverage and response rates
Coverage rates and response rates are important measures of the quality of the survey because they
reflect the representation of the target population. Countries attempted to reduce non-coverage and nonresponse bias, given that the main goal of PIAAC is to produce high-quality unbiased estimates,
representative of the target population, that are comparable across countries.

Potential for bias
Ideally, every eligible adult in the target population would have a non-zero chance of selection in a national
sample, would be located and would agree to participate in the study. In practice, these circumstances are
not realised in any survey population. There is potential for bias whenever part of the target population is
excluded from the frame, or sampled persons who did not participate in the survey have different
characteristics than those who did. For some important characteristics, the respondents may be
substantially different from the rest of the target population, resulting in biased outcome estimates.
The lower the response rates, the greater the potential for non-response bias. The extent of non-response
bias depends on how correlated the response propensity is with the survey outcomes. Therefore, it is
critical to evaluate the potential for non-response bias, as a quality check on the estimates. Similarly, noncoverage bias due to exclusions from the sampling frame can be substantial if the non-coverage rate is
high and the difference in potential survey outcomes between adults included in the sample and those
excluded from the frame is substantial. Given the relationships between bias and coverage and response
rates, countries had to keep the exclusion rates low and implement procedures to reduce the potential for
non-response bias and attain high response rates.
A maximum exclusion rate was set at 5% to guard against high non-coverage bias in PIAAC estimates.
Any exclusions to the core PIAAC target population, including those below this threshold, were reviewed
and approved by the Consortium. Even though up to 5% exclusions were tolerated, exclusions had to be
kept to a minimum. If the quality of the sampling frame was such that it could result in a non-coverage rate
of more than 5%, participating countries had to investigate ways to improve coverage.
To reduce the potential for non-response bias, countries had to plan and implement field procedures that
would lead to a high level of cooperation. It was critical to monitor the distribution of the sample during data
collection by key characteristics, such as age group membership, gender and region, to ensure steps were
taken to reduce the potential for bias as much as possible. Adaptive survey design was a key strategy
employed in this cycle to reduce the potential for bias. Countries were also required to identify auxiliary
data to reduce the impact of response propensities on the survey estimates. These auxiliary variables were
used in weighting adjustments to reduce non-response bias. Although sample weight adjustments based
on auxiliary data are effective in reducing non-response bias, they are not considered adequate
replacements for a vigorous effort to achieve the highest response rate possible.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 437
Coverage rates
The PIAAC target population is defined as all non-institutionalised adults aged 16 to 65 who reside in the
country at the time of data collection. The PIAAC Technical Standards and Guidelines require that the
sampling frame covers at least 95% of the PIAAC target population. Exclusions that is, persons who had
no chance of being selected into the sample, may not exceed 5% of the target population. There are, in
effect, two categories of exclusions in PIAAC – ex ante exclusions by design (frame exclusions) and ex
post exclusions following data collection (inaccessible persons). Both contribute to the overall noncoverage rate.

Exclusions by design
Exclusions by design, or frame exclusions, are of two types. First, exclusions may result from a decision
not to include certain population groups in the sampling frame. For example, the populations of remote
and isolated regions difficult to reach, or accessible at very high costs. Second, exclusions may result from
the rules determining which individuals are included in the list constituting the frame. For example, many
population registers include only those members of the population with valid residence permits and,
therefore, exclude undocumented immigrants.
The frame non-coverage rate is computed as the estimated population in the excluded groups divided by
the estimated core PIAAC target population. The rates by country are provided in Table 19.1. More
information on sampling frame non-coverage, including the specific groups excluded by each country, is
provided in Chapter 2.

Exclusions related to data collection
In addition to persons who are eligible under the international definition of the PIAAC target population but
were not included in the frame, persons who were included in the frame but in practice were impossible to
be interviewed could be treated as exclusions. Some registry-based countries experienced difficulties
locating and interviewing some or all sampled persons not residing at the address listed in the registry.
Such cases were classified into several categories, as shown in Table 19.2.
To arrive at an optimum and consistent approach across all registry-based countries, the Consortium
assumed that all countries attempted to locate the sampled persons and to interview them if they moved
into one of the PSUs in the sample or were in a location where PIAAC interviewers could visit and conduct
the interview and assessment. Some individuals are out of scope when the contact is attempted (e.g.
information is provided that indicates that they have died, moved to an institutional setting, or emigrated).
Others are “inaccessible” in that they cannot be interviewed because the information about their residential
address was incorrect or because they have moved to another location in the country. Finally, some
members of the sample are untraceable in that no information about their whereabouts is available. The
main advantage of classifying such cases in this manner was that the information about the inaccessible
cases could be used to reduce the bias associated with non-coverage and, thus, reduce inconsistencies
between countries’ data.
The inaccessible non-coverage rate was calculated as the inaccessible population divided by the eligible
population. The observed non-coverage rate had to incorporate sampling weights to account for selection
probabilities and to ensure that the observed rate was representative of those inaccessible in the frame. If
countries had an overall non-coverage rate (including frame and those inaccessible) greater than 5%, up
to 5% were reported in the non-coverage rate and the portion greater than 5% contributed as non-response
in the response rate calculations.2

information in graphical form, sorted by the overall non-coverage rate.

Response rates
The response rate is a valuable data quality measure and the most widely used indicator of survey quality.
A high response rate increases the likelihood that the survey accurately represents the target population,
and a low response rate reflects the susceptibility for notable bias in the outcome statistics.
The standard for including PIAAC countries in international indicators and reports based on response rates
was as follows:
•

National data with a minimum overall BQ response rate of 70% will generally be included in
international indicators and reports unless sample monitoring activities and/or non-response bias
analyses indicate serious levels of bias in the country data.

•

Unless problems resulting from response rates of between 50% and 70% are compounded by
other factors, such as undercoverage bias, results from countries with such response rates will
typically be included in international indicators and reports.

•

Results from countries with response rates below 50% will not be published unless the country can
provide the OECD Secretariat with evidence that the potential bias introduced by the low response

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

440 
rates is unlikely to be greater than the bias associated with response rates of between 50% and
70%.
Based on the non-response bias analyses, all participating countries were included in international
indicators and reports.

for the following stages of data collection:

overall.

The overall BQ response rate (ORR1) aligns with completed BQs (full BQ or doorstep interview). For
registry countries, ORR1 is equivalent to the BQ response rate. For countries with a screener
questionnaire, ORR1 is the product of the screener rate and BQ rate. The overall assessment response
rate (ORR2) aligns with completed assessments. For registry countries, ORR2 is computed as the product
of the BQ rate and assessment rate. For countries with a screener questionnaire, ORR2 is the product of
the screener rate, BQ rate and assessment rate.

Non-response bias analysis
Missing data can occur when some of the adults selected in the sample are not contacted or refuse to
participate (referred to as unit non-response), they fail to respond to a particular survey item (referred to
as item non-response), or because data collected from the sampled adults is contaminated or lost during
or after the data collection phase. Non-response bias can be substantial when two conditions are met:
1) the response rate is relatively low, and 2) the difference between the characteristics of respondents and
those of non-respondents is relatively large. This is reflected in the following deterministic non-response
bias formula:
𝐵𝑖𝑎𝑠(𝑦̄ 𝑅 ) = (1 − 𝑊𝑅 )(𝑌̄𝑅 − 𝑌̄𝑁𝑅 ),
where 𝑊𝑅 is the proportion of respondents, 𝑌̄𝑅 is the mean outcome for respondents, and 𝑌̄𝑁𝑅 is the mean
outcome for non-respondents. An alternative model of non-response assumes each sampled person has
a certain propensity to respond, and non-response bias in a characteristic is a function of the covariance
between the response propensity and the characteristic:
𝜎

𝐵𝑖𝑎𝑠(𝑦̄ 𝑅 ) = 𝑦𝑝 ,
𝑝̄

where 𝜎𝑦𝑝 is the covariance between the outcome variable and response propensity, and 𝑝̄ is the mean
response propensity. Based on this model, non-response bias is present if missingness is related to
proficiency, as measured by PIAAC.
Countries worked to reduce non-response bias to the extent possible before, during and after data
collection. Before data collection, countries implemented field procedures with the goal of obtaining a high
level of cooperation. Most countries followed the PIAAC required sample monitoring activities to reduce
bias to the lowest level possible during data collection. Finally, countries gathered and used auxiliary data
to reduce bias in the outcome statistics through non-response adjustment weighting.
A basic NRBA, along with a report of the results, was required for all countries. The basic analysis was
used to evaluate the potential for bias and to select variables for non-response adjustment weighting. In
addition, a more extensive NRBA was required if the overall BQ response rate (ORR1) was below 70%,
or the overall assessment response rate (ORR2) was below 67%. The Consortium performed both the
basic NRBA and extended NRBA unless the country chose to perform these analyses with support from
the Consortium.

Basic NRBA
The basic NRBA involved comparing survey respondents and non-respondents using auxiliary variables
available on the sampling frame, available from a previous data collection stage (e.g. screener data for the
BQ analysis), or coming from an external source that could be matched to each sampled unit. The auxiliary
variables must have been available for all eligible units and, as noted above, had to be related to
proficiency.
All countries were required to include the following variables in their analysis: age, gender, education,
employment and region. If any of these variables was not available for all eligible units, then a
corresponding area-level variable could have been used instead (e.g. the employment rate within small
geographic areas). Also, observational data on respondents and non-respondents collected during data
collection could have been used to evaluate bias, assuming the data was of sufficient quality. Cycle 2
offered a ‘curbside observations’ instrument that the Consortium prepared, and countries were encouraged
to consider using it when collecting data. The curbside observations instrument asked questions about the
type of dwelling unit, whether the dwelling unit was in a gated community, locked building or gated lot, and
the physical condition of the building or dwelling unit. Some of these items may have been useful for non-

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 443
response bias analysis and/or non-response weighting adjustments, depending on their completeness,
accuracy, interviewer variation, and association with response propensity or proficiency.
The basic analysis was carried out in two phases. The step of determining the basic NRBA variables in
the variable selection process was referred to as Phase 1. The Consortium provided countries with a
variable selection toolkit to assist them with this process. Phase 1 started with a pool of candidate predictor
variables gathered from various sources, and was carried out after the Field Trial. Proficiency proxy scores
were calculated from the Field Trial data for those countries that were able to conduct a regular Field Trial.
These proxy scores served as a proficiency-related measure, and countries had the option of using these
to evaluate the relationship between proficiency-related variables and the candidate predictor variables.
While some countries took this option, others used an alternative approach, such as basing the selection
of variables on past experiences. The outcome from Phase 1 was a set of proficiency-related variables to
be used in Phase 2. Phase 2 took the variables found to be related to the proficiency measures and
evaluated the relationship of those variables to response status. The goal was to use these variables in
the non-response adjustment during weighting. Phase 1 was performed by the countries, and, for most
countries, Phase 2 was performed by the Consortium.
Phase 2 of the basic NRBA was performed either using a classification tree algorithm to identify subgroups
with low response rates, or using logistic regression to model the relationship between response status
and the auxiliary variables. An additional basic NRBA method suggested by the Consortium involved using
chi-square tests to compare the distribution of auxiliary variables (correlated to proficiency) for respondents
and non-respondents.
The classification tree was included in all country analyses for which the Consortium performed the
analyses. Eight countries performed their own weighting, and these countries all performed their own basic
NRBA as well. These countries are Austria, Canada, Finland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden,
Switzerland and the United States. For the basic NRBA, each of these eight countries performed at least
a classification tree or logistic regression, and a few of them performed both. The exception is Austria,
which performed random forests and LASSO regression.
For most countries, all the required variables (age, gender, education, employment and region) were
included in the basic NRBA. However, 14 countries had at least one of these variables missing from their
analysis. In most cases, the failure to include the required variables in the analysis was due to the lack of
access to sources with reliable data for such variables. Where one or more of these variables was missing,
most countries included other variables correlated with proficiency, such as income or socio-economic
status.
Non-response weighting adjustments reduce bias in the outcome statistics to the extent that auxiliary
variables are correlated with proficiency. Typically, weighting adjustments are carried out by assuming
non-respondents’ proficiency levels are the same as the respondents in the subgroups created for
weighting adjustments using the auxiliary variables. This assumption is, of course, not true and the level
of bias reduction depends on the number of auxiliary variables used during weighting and the correlation
between these variables and proficiency.
The basic NRBA is a good initial assessment of non-response bias and is essential in identifying effective
weighting variables. However, it has its limitations. The analysis does not reflect the effect of weighting
adjustments on non-response bias, and the extent of bias remaining after non-response adjustments are
conducted. Therefore, for countries with lower response rates, a more extensive analysis was required to
assess the potential for bias remaining after non-response adjustment weighting.

Extended NRBA
A more extensive NRBA was required if the overall BQ response rate was below 70% or the overall
assessment response rate was less than 67%.
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

444 
Korea and the Slovak Republic achieved an overall BQ response rate of 70% or greater, and an overall
assessment rate of at least 67%, and thus did not require an extended NRBA. Korea is not included in any
of the tables in this section, since no extended NRBA was necessary for Korea. However, due to an issue
with its within-household rostering, it was decided that the Slovak Republic should conduct an extended
NRBA to assess whether this issue had any impact on potential bias. The remaining 29 countries did not
achieve overall BQ response rates of 70% and required an extended NRBA.
The main purpose of the extended analysis was to assess the potential for remaining bias in the final
weighted proficiency estimates after adjusting for non-response. Because the proficiency levels of nonrespondents are unknown, the NRBA is carried out by making assumptions about the non-respondents.
Therefore, it is necessary to conduct multiple analyses to assess the potential for bias since each analysis
has its own limitations resulting from the specific assumptions made about non-respondents. Together,
they were used to assess the patterns and potential for bias in each country’s data. The extended NRBA
included the following analyses:
•

comparison of estimates before and after weighting adjustments

•

comparison of weighted estimates to external totals

•

explained variability in proficiency estimates by auxiliary variables

•

comparison of estimates from alternative weighting adjustments

•

analysis of variables collected during data collection

•

level-of-effort analysis

•

non-response error susceptibility that remains.

Of the 30 countries that required an extended NRBA, 9 countries (Austria, Canada, Finland, Japan, the
Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States) opted to perform some or all of the
seven analyses themselves. The Consortium prepared programmes and documentation to conduct these
analyses and made them available to countries for use if needed. These analyses are described further
below.

Comparison of estimates before and after weighting adjustments
To better capture the effects of the weighting adjustments on unit non-response bias, estimates from the
full sample were compared to estimates from the respondents before and after weighting adjustments. If
the eligible sample estimates are closer to the non-response-adjusted estimates than the base-weighted
estimates, this indicates bias in the auxiliary variables was reduced through the weighting process. To
compare estimates before and after each step of weighting adjustments, the following comparisons were
made:
•

comparison of percentage distributions from BQ base weights for the total eligible sample of
persons with the BQ base weights for the BQ respondents to check for differences due to nonresponse to the BQ

•

comparison of percentage distributions from BQ base weights for the total eligible sample of
persons with that from the BQ non-response adjusted weights for respondents to check for
differences after the non-response adjustment process to the BQ.

The goal was to include at least one auxiliary variable that was not used in weighting adjustments in
addition to those used during non-response adjustment weighting. The inclusion of the non-weighting
variables shows whether the weighting adjustment was effective in reducing bias in other known auxiliary
variables, not just the weighting variables. Most countries included at least one non-weighting variable as
well as weighting variables in this analysis.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 445
In general, the analysis showed that the non-response adjustment was effective in reducing bias in
estimates of one or more of the auxiliary variables. The Netherlands used generalised regression (GREG)
in weighting adjustments, which combined non-response adjustments and calibration. Therefore, this
analysis was not informative for the Netherlands. Sweden used final weights instead of non-responseadjusted weights in their analysis. It showed that the combination of non-response adjustment and
calibration were effective in reducing bias in at least one of the auxiliary variables.
For adjudication purposes, information was compiled for each country about whether there were any
significant and notable differences remaining between the BQ base-weighted estimates for the total eligible
sample of persons and the BQ non-response adjusted estimates for respondents, for any of the auxiliary
variables or classes of variables used in the analysis. A notable difference was greater than 1.5 percentage
points.
There are two limitations of this analysis worth noting. First, the analysis only considers BQ non-response
and does not look at screener non-response. Second, the analysis does not consider the effect of the
calibration adjustment.

Comparison of weighted estimates to external totals
The second analysis compared estimates from PIAAC to external source estimates to assess potential for
bias in PIAAC outcome statistics.
To the extent possible, countries provided estimates from external sources that measured the same
characteristic for a similar time period. Some external source estimates were also subject to sampling
error. Whenever these sampling errors were available, the variance was considered when making
comparisons across estimates.
For many countries there were significant differences between the PIAAC estimates and the external
source estimates but, in most cases, countries were able to explain the reasons for discrepancies.
Possible explanations for the discrepancies included different data collection time periods, different
definitions (e.g. definition of employment), different modes of collection and coverage differences.

Explained variability in proficiency estimates by auxiliary variables
The analyses described thus far relied on auxiliary variables and did not directly measure bias in the
proficiency estimates. Bias in the auxiliary variables is indicative of bias in the proficiency estimates to the
extent that the auxiliary variables and proficiency estimates are correlated. Thus, R2 values from models
with auxiliary variables as independent variables and proficiency scores as the dependent variable can be
used to measure the explained variation in the proficiency variable. 3 For variables used in the weighting
adjustments, a low R2 value implies that using the variables in the weighting adjustments did little to reduce
non-response bias. On the other hand, a high R2 value implies a potentially high reduction in non-response
bias. However, it should be noted that the explained variation is based on respondents’ data, and the
relationship between proficiency and the auxiliary variables might be different for non-respondents.
Therefore, the R2 value could be different if a country’s response rate is very low, and if non-respondents
are different from respondents in terms of the relationship between their scores and the auxiliary variables.
The measure Explained Variation in Outcome (EVO) essentially uses the response rate and the R2 to
summarise the extent to which both types of respondent-derived information capture the information which
would have been obtained if the entire selected sample responded to the survey. The value of the EVO
measure can range from 0 to 1. A value of 0 can only be attained if there is a 0% response rate for the
survey and an R2 = 0, whereas a value of 1 can be attained if there is either a 100% response rate or if R2
= 1.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

446 
Variation in the outcome is “explained by” two components:
1.
The share of the sample for which outcomes are available (i.e. similar to the response
rate). This proportion is calculated using the base-weights.
2.
The effectively imputed values of the outcome for non-respondents, induced by
redistributing weight from non-respondents to respondents within a given response homogeneity
class (i.e. non-response adjustment cell), and through aligning to control totals through weight
calibration. This component is estimated using the 𝑅2 of the linear model predicting the survey
outcome of interest given the non-response adjustment cells and calibration variables.
The EVO statistic combines summaries of these two components of explained variation. In the case of a
single stage of non-response, the EVO statistic is defined as follows:
𝐸𝑉𝑂 =

∑𝑟 𝑤𝑖 + 𝑅2 ∑𝑛𝑟 𝑤𝑖
∑𝑟 𝑤𝑖 + ∑𝑛𝑟 𝑤𝑖

where:
𝑟 = set of respondents,
𝑛𝑟 = set of eligible non-respondents,
𝑤𝑖 = the base weight for case i, and
𝑅2 = 𝑅2 estimate for the model fit to respondents
In other words, 100% of the variation in outcome is explained for respondents in the sample. 𝑅2 × 100%
of the variation in outcome is explained for non-respondents in the sample through the non-response
adjustment variables. The numerator of the EVO statistic represents the amount of variation in the outcome
that is “explained” by observed respondents and non-response adjustments. The denominator represents
the total variation in the sample.
Note that the EVO statistic is outcome-specific. The value and interpretation of the EVO statistic will depend
on the outcome variable used in the model from component 2 above. For example, if literacy, numeracy
and adaptive problem-solving scores are all outcomes of interest, then the EVO statistic would need to be
calculated separately for each measure, and will need to be interpreted as the explained variation in
literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving, respectively.
The EVO measure can also be extended to cases with two stages of non-response as follows:
𝐸𝑉𝑂 =

∑𝑟 𝑤𝑖 + 𝑅12 ∑𝑛𝑟1 𝑤𝑖 + 𝑅22 ∑𝑛𝑟2 𝑤𝑖
∑𝑟 𝑤𝑖 + ∑𝑛𝑟1 𝑤𝑖 + ∑𝑛𝑟2 𝑤𝑖

where:
𝑟

= set of second stage respondents,

𝑛𝑟1

= set of first stage eligible non-respondents,

𝑛𝑟2

= set of second stage eligible non-respondents who were first stage respondents,

𝑤𝑖

= the base weight for case i,

𝑅12

= 𝑅2 estimate for the model fit using first stage non-response adjustment variables, and

𝑅22

= 𝑅2 estimate for the model fit using second stage non-response adjustment variables

If person-level base weights are not available for first stage non-respondents, they can be estimated by
taking the product of the first stage sampling unit base weight and the expected number of persons in a
first stage sampling unit.

Comparison of estimates from alternative weighting adjustments
For this evaluation, an auxiliary variable was recalibrated to known totals and estimates of average
proficiency, overall and for subgroups, were compared before and after the re-weighting. Re-weighting
was useful as an evaluation tool when:
•

The variable was not used in weighting (because it was not available) or was used with different
categories.

•

The variable is correlated with the outcome measure.

•

The variable is correlated with response propensity.

Any differences between estimates using the official survey weights and the re-weighted weights reflected
non-coverage as well as non-response bias, but if there was not a large change in the estimates, this was
further confirmation that non-response bias may not be a concern.
Of the 30 countries required to do this analysis, Switzerland was the only country not to perform the
analysis. In addition, the Netherlands and Sweden only evaluated the effect of the re-weighting on overall
estimates, not subgroup estimates. In summary, 10 countries found no significant differences between the
proficiency scores using final weights and when using the alternative weights. Another 11 countries found
at least one statistically significant difference, but none were considered notable differences. A statistically
significant difference was defined as having a p-value under 0.05, with a Bonferroni adjustment for multiple

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 449
comparisons, based on a t-test. A notable difference was defined as a significant difference for which the
absolute difference is greater than the standard error of the mean for the final weighted sample.
Eight countries found at least one notable significant difference, either overall or by subgroup. These
countries were Chile, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Singapore and Spain. For five
of these countries (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Singapore), these differences are likely to be
due to differences in timing, definition, coverage or collection mode of the alternative data source.
Considering this analysis overall, it presented very few concerns about the potential for non-response bias.

values for each proficiency domain. The table also lists the variables each country used in the alternative
weighting adjustment. Significant differences, both notable and non-notable, are identified in the table.

Analysis of variables collected during data collection
Disposition codes contain information on reasons for non-response. This analysis examined distributions
of sampled persons or households with known characteristics related to outcome (i.e. the literacy-related
non-respondent (LRNR) cases, which are cases that did not complete the survey due to language
problems, reading and writing difficulty or learning/mental disability). The demographic distributions of BQ
LRNR cases and other BQ non-respondents were compared using auxiliary data to evaluate if the two
groups differed as expected. For countries with a household sample, an additional comparison was made
between screener LRNR and other screener non-respondents. For example, LRNR might have been

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

452 
expected to be more highly concentrated in a particular region of the country. For this analysis chi-square
tests were performed to determine if there was a relationship between selected demographic variables
and the disposition codes (literacy-related or other) for incompletes. A special weighting adjustment for
literacy-related cases was conducted for all countries, except for Singapore. For Singapore, the BQ LRNR
cases together with the other BQ non-respondents were represented by BQ respondents, because there
were no literacy-related respondents. Therefore, in almost all countries, the existence of LRNR cases was
dealt with appropriately to reduce potential for bias. Note that Sweden had no BQ LRNR cases since they
used an interpreter for the BQ when needed. However, they did complete a similar analysis using these
interpreter-facilitated cases.
The analysis of disposition codes was conducted for all countries. Countries were asked to specify which
subgroups of the population they would expect to have higher rates of literacy-related non-response. These
expectations could then be compared to the results of this analysis. For some countries, the small number
of LRNR cases meant that a useful analysis could not be done. However, where the number of cases was
sufficient, most countries had no unexpected patterns in BQ LRNR characteristics. For all countries, the
conclusion was that the analysis did not raise concerns about the assignment of literacy-related disposition
codes or the treatment of LRNR cases in weighting.

cases with a non-zero final weight for analysis. The sample size includes both BQ respondents and BQ
literacy-related non-respondents (LRNR) with completed doorstep interviews (DI). The table includes a
breakdown of the counts of LRNR cases by category.

Level-of-effort analysis
Another way to evaluate bias in proficiency estimates is to compare proficiency estimates by the level of
effort required to reach respondents. Differences in proficiency scores by the number of contacts and an
insufficient number of contacts made could indicate non-response bias.
For this analysis, cumulative mean proficiency scores were calculated by the number of contact attempts
until a completed assessment. For most countries, mean scores generally increased with the number of
contacts. This type of analysis is often depicted in a chart that has the value of the estimate on the y-axis
and the effort measure on the x-axis. Figure 19.3 illustrates the relationship between the cumulative mean
literacy score and level of effort for all 30 countries for which this analysis was conducted. The y-axis is
the cumulative mean proficiency score. The x-axis is the maximum number of contact attempts until a
completed assessment. The figure shows that, for most countries, on average, the early respondents had
somewhat lower scores than those who completed the assessment after multiple contact attempts. There
are some exceptions to this pattern. For some countries, such as Austria and Croatia, the plot is relatively
flat, indicating that there is little difference between the proficiency scores of early respondents compared
to later respondents. There are also a few countries, such as England (United Kingdom) and Switzerland,
where early respondents have somewhat higher scores than later respondents. Austria and Finland had
their own paradata for the number of contacts, which differed from the number of contacts recorded on
their SDIF. The results using their paradata show a different curve to the plot below.
For countries for which the Consortium did the analysis, only the overall relationship between proficiency
scores and number of contacts was analysed. This was also true for countries that did their own analysis,
except for Canada. Canada did additional analyses to see if the relationship between low and high effort
respondents differed significantly by region, age, gender and education. There were no significant
differences by region, age and education, but there was a significant difference by gender, although the
directions of the plots were the same for males and females.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 455

Figure 19.3. Cumulative mean literacy scores by number of contact attempts

Measures of non-response error susceptibility that may remain
The final component of the NRBA is to evaluate the potential for bias remaining after weighting adjustments
under the scenario that non-respondents’ proficiency scores differ from the assumptions made during
weighting. See Chapter 8 for a description of the weighting process.
It is well known that non-response bias can be reduced to some unknown extent through sample weighting
adjustments when proficiency is correlated with auxiliary variables and auxiliary variables are correlated
with response propensity. The weighting non-response adjustments assume response probabilities are
constant within every group created for weight adjustment, the proficiency score has zero variance within
each group, and response propensity is uncorrelated with proficiency. It is known that these assumptions
are not correct, and the impact of weight adjustments is limited by the number and quality of variables
available for non-response adjustment, and the correlation between non-response adjustment variables
and proficiency. Also, it is not possible to measure the exact departure from these assumptions since the

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

456 
proficiency levels of non-respondents are not known. This analysis attempts to evaluate the potential for
bias that remains after the weighting process, by first computing a range based on the assumption that
non-respondents would all score at the 40th percentile of respondent scores within each weighting cell,
and in the other direction they would all score at the 60th percentile of respondent scores within each
weighting cell. The range of bias (RoB) was computed as the difference between the two estimates, while
accounting for the response rate and population size in the weighting cell.
The literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving scores’ first plausible value was used to compute
the range of scores within the responding sample and to predict the range of estimates for nonrespondents.
If the weighting classes were well defined, that is, each weighting class successfully contained a
homogeneous population in terms of proficiency scores, then scores would not vary much within a
weighting cell, so the true RoB would be small. On the other hand, the RoB is also affected by the response
rate. If the response rate is high, the RoB may not be high even when the respondents have a wide range
of scores in the weighting cell, because the non-respondents whose score will get filled in with the 40th or
60th percentile values make up a small proportion of the weighting cell. Thus, the range of bias analysis
measures the impact of response rate on the quality of final estimates as well as the effectiveness of the
weighting adjustments in reducing the potential for bias.
Once the RoB was computed, it was used to derive two Non-response error susceptibility (NES) scores
across countries. The NES scores by themselves are essentially meaningless, however, they can be used
to compare one country’s susceptibility to bias to that of another country.
•

NES Score 1 – It was computed as the RoB relative to the standard deviation. For this measure,
we divided the RoB by the country’s standard deviation of the 1st PV for literacy to remove the
effect of the standard deviation (e.g. mean assuming the 40th percentile minus mean assuming
the 60th percentile divided by the standard deviation). A higher value indicates a greater
susceptibility to bias, given the response rate and non-response adjustment cells.

•

NES score 2 – It takes the form of RoB / c. The numerator is based on the RoB metric using the
40th and 60th percentiles for non-respondents. For the denominator, we used a constant (c) for all
countries. This value was based on the median across the countries of the absolute difference
between the average literacy score for respondents on the first contact attempt and the final
average literacy score. In more simple terms, it basically scales down the range of bias values to
be between about .5 and 2. A higher NES score indicates a greater susceptibility to bias, given the
response rate, non-response adjustment cells and the standard deviation of scores among
respondents.

Table 19.9 presents the overall assessment response rate, along with the two NES scores, for each
country, while Figure 19.4 conveys the same information in graphical form. One can see that there is a
strong inverse relationship between a country’s response rate and the susceptibility to bias.
