Summary and conclusions of the NRBA
PIAAC standards were established with the main goal of producing reliable and comparable data across
participating countries. As a result, several standards and guidelines were developed to help countries

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

458 
achieve the highest response rate possible and, at the same time, reduce non-response bias to the
minimum achievable.
All countries were required to conduct a basic NRBA and report the results. In addition, a more extensive
NRBA was required if the overall BQ response rate was below 70%, or the overall assessment response
rate was less than 67%.
The basic and extended NRBA included several analyses. Each analysis was based on several
assumptions about non-respondents, limiting the utility of the results. Thus, multiple analyses were used
to assess the potential for bias in outcome statistics.
The explained variation in outcomes (EVO) measure is a good indication of the effectiveness of nonresponse weighting adjustment and calibration. Several countries with low response rates had relatively
high EVO values, implying more effective non-response and calibration adjustments than countries with
lower EVO values. However, data users need to be cautioned that the analysis is based on the strength of
the relationship between respondents’ proficiency scores and the weighting variables, as measured
through the 𝑅2 . That is, the analysis assumes that the same 𝑅2 exists for the remaining sampled cases
that have no scores.
Table 19.10 summarises the results of the NRBA for countries with response rates lower than 70%. The
analysis showed that non-response adjustment weighting and calibration were effective in reducing the
potential for bias in all countries. Countries that achieved higher response rates guaranteed a minimised
level of bias in outcome statistics, whereas countries with lower response rates had to rely on the auxiliary
variables available to them for non-response adjustment. Countries with relatively higher response rates
and highly effective non-response adjustment showed minimal potential for bias compared to countries
with lower response rates or those with low or moderately effective non-response adjustment weighting.
The analysis concluded that there was not enough evidence to indicate high levels of bias in the outcome
statistics across the countries. However, this conclusion was based on assumptions made about the
proficiency scores of non-respondents. Therefore, data users need to be cautioned when interpreting the
results of the NRBA for countries with very low response rates since different assumptions could lead to
different results. For example, a response rate of 50% would mean making assumptions about half of the
sample with no data. Multiple analyses, with different assumptions, were included in the NRBA to protect
against misleading results, however, the lower the response rate, the higher the risk of hidden biases that
are undetectable through NRBA, even when multiple analyses are involved.
The criteria for assigning adjudication outcomes are explained in Appendix 7 of this report.

Sample sizes and design effects
A high-quality survey produces estimates that have a low mean square error, which is a function of bias
and variance. The bias aspect was discussed in previous sections. This section will address the variability
aspect. Sample size is one of the main factors that affect the variability of survey estimates. The smaller
the sample size, the higher the variability of survey estimates. However, given the same sample size, the
survey estimates from a simple random sample often have lower variability than those from complex
sample designs. The effect of the sample design on the variability of estimates is usually referred to as the
design effect.
The actual sample sizes for each country, that is, the number of cases with non-zero final weight for
analysis, are provided in Table 19.7. In the following sections, we discuss the PIAAC design effects and
effective sample sizes.

Variability in sampling weights
A key component of the design effect is due to differential sampling weights. As mentioned in Chapter 8,
several PIAAC countries sampled certain subgroups of the population at a higher rate to obtain sufficient
precision for the analysis of the subgroups. For countries with a household sampling stage, people from
households of different sizes were also sampled with different probabilities. This led to unequal sampling
weights and an increase in the variability of survey estimates. In addition, sampling weights were adjusted
to account for sample non-response and undercoverage, which normally made the weights more variable.
The variability of weights can be expressed by the coefficient of variation (CV) of the weights. The CV is
𝜎

where 𝜎𝑤 is the standard deviation of the weights and 𝑤

Design effects and effective sample sizes
Many of the PIAAC countries used complex sample designs that involved clustered samples to meet cost
limitations and to be operationally feasible. For example, a sample may consist of 500 street blocks
(clusters) with 10 people from each block. Because people who live in the same block tend to have more
similar social and economic backgrounds than others, a simple random sample of 5 000 people is thus
likely to cover the diversity of the population better than a sample of 500 blocks with 10 people from each
block. Thus, the uncertainty (i.e. standard error) associated with any population parameter estimate will be
larger for a clustered sample than for a simple random sample of the same size. Furthermore, as
mentioned in the previous section, unequal sampling weights also increased the variability of survey
estimates.
The design effect is expressed by the ratio of the variance of the estimate obtained from the (more
complex) sample to the variance of the estimate that would be obtained from a simple random sample with
the same number of sampling units. Design effects can be used to evaluate the efficiency of the PIAAC
sample designs. In addition, the design effects from this study can be used to estimate initial sample sizes
for the next cycle of PIAAC.
The variance of PIAAC estimates can be estimated by using the replication technique, 4 which accounts for
the complex design, and a design effect can be computed for a statistic t using the formula:
𝐷𝑒𝑓𝑓(𝑡) =

𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑅𝐸𝑃 (𝑡)
𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑆𝑅𝑆 (𝑡)

where 𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑅𝐸𝑃 (𝑡) is the sampling variance for the complex sample for the statistic t computed by the
replication method, and 𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑆𝑅𝑆 (𝑡) is the sampling variance for the same statistic on the same data but
considering the sample as a simple random sample. The simple random sampling variance is computed
as the average of the simple random sampling variance for each of the 10 plausible values.
When computing design effects for statistics that involve plausible values, the notion of design effect as
given earlier needs to be extended to incorporate the imputation variance. This gives rise to five possible
design effect formulae that can be used to describe the influence of the sampling and test designs on the
standard errors for a statistic.
The variance for statistics that involve plausible values consists of two components: sampling variance
(𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑅𝐸𝑃 ), calculated using the corresponding replication method, and imputation variance (𝑉𝑎𝑟𝐼𝑀𝑃 ),

The five estimated design effects and the effective sample size for average proficiency scores for each
country and for each of the literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving domains can be found in
Appendix 5 of this report. Four countries had an effective sample size below 1 000. Chile had a high level
of clustering because of operational challenges due to its geography and high variability in person selection
probabilities. Croatia was not able to select as many PSUs as the Consortium recommended, and the
intra-cluster correlation was likely higher than expected. New Zealand oversampled some population
subgroups which led to high variability in person selection probabilities. New Zealand also implemented
deselection near the end of data collection, due to several logistical challenges encountered during data
collection. Portugal achieved a low final sample size, combined with a high level of clustering due to
selecting fewer PSUs than recommended, and due to unequal selection probabilities.

20. Data management and data-cleaning
procedures
Tim Daniel and Darrell Gwaltney, IEA Hamburg

This chapter details the data management and data-cleaning procedures
implemented to ensure high-quality, reliable data for PIAAC Cycle 2. It
describes the processes and tools used to standardise data handling
across diverse national contexts, including the IEA Data Management
Expert software. The chapter also outlines the roles and responsibilities at
both national and international levels, emphasising the importance of
collaboration among various stakeholders. Finally, it covers the steps taken
to verify, edit and protect the confidentiality of the data, ensuring its integrity
and analytical utility for reporting and analysis.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 465

Introduction
In PIAAC, as in any multi-national survey, it is essential to minimise total survey error, which can be
introduced during the stages of capturing, coding and processing data. All further steps in the survey’s
data processing and analysis depend on the quality of the data originally collected. Errors that occur during
data capture, coding and processing are difficult, if not impossible, to correct.
PIAAC is an assessment of adult skills, including a computer-assisted self-administered test and an
interviewer-guided collection of background data. The design, data structures and formats of PIAAC are
quite complex. For example, in addition to the raw responses, rich auxiliary and behavioural data, such as
response times and information about how respondents navigate through the assessment, were collected
and processed to support instrument validation, analysis and reporting.
Given these complexities – the timeline under which PIAAC was carried out and the diversity of contexts
in which it was administered – it was imperative to standardise the procedures related to national and
international data management. A comprehensive manual, training sessions, other supporting materials,
and, in particular, a mandatory data management software were designed to help National Project
Managers (NPMs) and their National Data Managers (NDMs) carry out their tasks, prevent the introduction
of errors, and reduce the amount of effort and time involved in resolving them. Approaches had to be
generally strict yet flexible in order to account for some idiosyncrasies and needs (e.g. with respect to
constraints of data sharing) as part of the country-by-country data management process. A variety of
quality control processes and procedures were implemented to prepare a high-quality database (i.e. one
that is valid, reliable and comparable) with the highest possible analytical utility.
This chapter summarises the collaborative efforts and processes among Consortium partners, national
teams and the OECD related to data management that led to the rich, standardised, international master
PIAAC database. It reviews key activities at the National Centres, describes the data extraction from the
PIAAC Delivery System and its integration into the IEA Data Management Expert software, and provides
an overview of all further data processing tasks within the National Centres. Furthermore, the chapter
provides insights into the data processing activities at the international level conducted by the IEA in
cooperation with the Consortium and the OECD, as well as an overview of all interim and final data
products for release. A special focus is given to the confidentiality edits and suppression workflows applied.

Tasks and responsibilities at the international level
The design and implementation of PIAAC were the responsibility of an international consortium of
institutions led by Educational Testing Service (ETS). In this Consortium, the International Association for
the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA) in Hamburg, Germany, had the primary responsibility for
designing, facilitating and supporting the data management at the national level, as well as the overall data
management at the international level. In particular, the IEA:
•

proposed standards, guidelines and recommendations for the data work in countries

•

created and provided software, codebooks and manuals to countries

•

organised and conducted data management trainings

•

conducted trainings on coding occupations and industry sector

•

supported countries during the national database buildings

•

developed and hosted the PIAAC dashboards

•

managed, processed and cleaned data at the international level

•

prepared analysis and dissemination databases for use by the Consortium, the OECD and
countries

•

provided data analysis software.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

466 
Conducting a study like PIAAC would not be possible without close cooperation and consultation among
all stakeholders. The partners involved in PIAAC and their roles in achieving a quality data product are the
following:
•

ETS – review, cleaning, quality control and support with respect to interview workflow as well as
cognitive response and log data (aggregate and full), release of data products to the Consortium,
countries and the OECD

•

Research Centre for Education and the Labour Market (ROA) – review, cleaning, quality control
and support with respect to BQ data, questionnaire flow and harmonisation of information from
national adaptations

•

Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences (GESIS) – review, quality control and support with respect
to BQ questions on education levels and highest attainment, as well as harmonisation of national
adaptations within these questions

•

Westat – review, cleaning, quality control and support with respect to sampling, weighting and
survey operations related data

•

OECD – overall review, quality control and support with respect to the resulting data products.

Tasks and responsibilities at the national level
Each participating country appointed a national project manager (NPM) to take responsibility for
implementing PIAAC at the national level. The NPM had to ensure that all required tasks, especially those
related to the production of a quality national database, were carried out as planned and in accordance
with the specified international standards and quality targets. The NPM was responsible for supervising,
organising and delegating all data management work. "Data management" refers to the collective set of
activities and tasks that each country had to perform to produce the required national database. This
included the adaptation of codebooks, integration of data from the national PIAAC delivery systems,
preparation of data packages for upload to the PIAAC dashboard, export/import of data required for coding
(e.g. occupation), data verification and validation, and eventually submission of the national PIAAC
database to the Consortium.
Because data-related tasks tend to be highly technical and require special skills, the Consortium
recommended that in addition to the NPM, each National Centre also appoints a national data manager
(NDM). The NDM was responsible for the day-to-day data management tasks within the country, was
expected to carefully review all provided information and instructions, participate in all applicable trainings,
supervise local data work, and, most importantly, communicate on data cleaning with the Consortium in a
timely manner. The NPM and NDM were expected to be supported by other staff or organisations. The
contribution that national technical personnel made was crucial to the survey's success and quality.

Key data management systems and integration processes at the National Centre
Data management software, manuals and training
To standardise the national data work, countries were provided with a customised and extended version
of the IEA Data Management Expert (DME) software. The IEA DME software supported data management
at the National Centre(s) after data collection. The IEA DME software was written in C# based on the
Microsoft.NET Framework 4.5, Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) and a variation of Microsoft SQL
Server, SQLite. Two versions of the software were created, one for the field trial and one for the main
study. The following list presents the key features of the IEA DME software and the customisation to the
PIAAC context:

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 467
•

maintenance of a single, multi-table, robust and relational database for the integration of all
sampling, response, workflow, log and coding data

•

documentation of the international as well as national record layout (codebook) and support for the
addition and adaptation of national variables within constraints

•

extraction, transformation and storage of data from the various sources in PIAAC, most importantly,
the delivery system

•

export and import to and from Excel; comma-separated and flat text files to interface with external
processes, for example, the coding of occupation or the import of sample design data

•

validation during import and on demand by using pre-specified validation rules by variable and
across variables and data sources using validity reports and statistics

•

support for work on separate computers for data integration via file merging

•

access control by using "roles" for managers in countries.

Countries were provided with a comprehensive data management manual detailing the processes to be
followed from the moment when the national delivery systems and case management systems were ready
for data collection until the moment when national databases were submitted and initial data cleaning was
completed.
Prior to the field trial and the main study, NDMs (or in their absence the NPMs) were expected to participate
in comprehensive data management trainings. Their participation in these trainings was vital to the success
of the project. These trainings focused on the setup and use of the provided IEA DME software, the way it
interacted with the assessment designs and delivery system, the incorporation of national adaptations
made in the BQ in codebooks, the integration testing between the national delivery system and the data
extraction logic, the import/export of relevant data stored in national case management systems or
resulting from coding processes, and the overall validation and verification of the database’s completeness
and consistency.

Codebook, database structure, record and value representation
Given the study’s design and involved technologies (e.g. the PIAAC Delivery System (PDS), the
international Case Management System (iCMS), IEA’s Data Management Expert (DME), the PIAAC
Dashboard or the Questionnaire Authoring Tool (QAT)), the data structures and formats were relatively
complex. A variety of data sources were combined to build the national and international analysis and
dissemination databases in PIAAC. The information in the database originated from the following sources
and processes:
•

sample design information (e.g. ID numbers and selection probabilities)

•

interviewers' input or automatic import for the case initialisation module

•

interviewers' input to the BQ module

•

respondents' actions in the tablet skills tutorial module

•

respondents' answers, actions and auto-assigned scores in the computer-based exercise

•

workflow information such as random assignments, disposition codes or timing information

•

behavioural and auxiliary information (e.g. selected answers, time spent per item, language
changes in the BQ, navigation, consistency edits triggered)

•

countries' coding of responses related to the ISCO and ISIC classifications as well as region,
language and country.

The PIAAC database included information from the sources above, but there was more to consider. The
interviews and exercises followed a variety of trajectories, data were generated for some respondents yet
not for others (e.g. any respondent who passed the locator stage was only administered two out of the
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

468 
three assessment domains), and some data were collected directly, whereas other data were generated
after data collection (e.g. derived occupation codes). Taking these into account, the Consortium organised
the data into a single relational database, though in multiple tables within this database. Each table
corresponds to one or more modules in the survey. Later, during the international data processing, most
of these sources and tables were combined to form a more familiar "flat" analysis file.
The key concepts used in the PIAAC data management and database structure were variables (including
their value and missing schemes), datasets and instruments. The combinations of information in these
entities form the PIAAC codebooks (elsewhere called metadata or record layout). In addition, data in
PIAAC is stored by means of data records and, eventually, data values.
Variables correspond to columns in the resulting database. A set of attributes defines each variable in
PIAAC. The IEA DME software "reused" variable definitions in several ways. Variables were defined once
and then referenced in the corresponding datasets or instruments in which they were assembled.
Secondly, value and missing schemes in the IEA DME software were defined only once and then
referenced by the corresponding variables rather than being defined multiple times. This recycling of
variables and schemes allowed efficient and consistent definition and adaptation of codebooks. Variable
attributes were defined using the two most commonly used packages for statistical data, SAS and SPSS.
Systematic and consistent variable naming conventions were applied for each component of PIAAC.
Whereas variables of the BQ followed a naming convention derived from work at Statistics Canada, naming
conventions for other assessment components followed a generic logic designed for PIAAC and took trend
aspects into account (e.g. item naming found in IALS and ALL). Note that variable names present in the
exported delivery system result files used a different naming convention and had to be renamed when
imported into the IEA DME database for further analysis.
There were 14 datasets used in PIAAC. Each of these 14 datasets comprised the information for specific
parts of the survey. A dataset is a logical collection of rows and columns where each column represents a
clearly defined variable identified by its unique name, and each row corresponds to a record of valid or
missing values collected for a case or sampled person. Table 20.1 below describes the type of information
they held, along with the respective sources in each of these datasets. Note that not all information was
stored as part of the country database. Full cognitive log information was stored in its native format (XML)
and provided to the Consortium at the time of data submission outside of the database maintained by the
IEA DME software.
Instruments, as used in the IEA DME software and database, are logical sets of variables, that is, a subset
of variables selected in a particular sequence from a larger set of variables. Instruments were used in
Cycle 2 solely for sequencing variables within a dataset.
Data records in the IEA DME software and database correspond to a single row in a dataset, identified by
one or more unique identifiers. Depending on a sampled person’s path through the interview, data records
for this person existed in multiple but not all datasets. Each data record in a dataset had the same set of
variables, and for each of these variables, either a valid value or a missing value was stored.

Each logical dataset corresponded to a physical table in the relational database managed by the IEA DME
software and had one or more identification variables in its first positions. Identification variables
corresponded to households or individual people in the survey. The identification variables used in the
PIAAC main study are described below.
•

CNTRYID – The country ID holds a 3-digit numeric code that follows the ISO 3166/UN M49
standard.

•

CASEID – This is the household operational ID. It was assigned at the sampling stage for countries
using a household sampling design.

•

PERSID – This is the sampled person’s operational identification number that uniquely identifies
them. The PERSID variable appeared in all datasets as assigned at the sampling stage. In the
case of household sampling, the PERSID was only assigned when within-household screening
was completed and persons were sampled. The PERSID included a mandatory check digit based
on approaches for universal product codes (UPCs). The check digit proved to be highly efficient
and effective in avoiding ID swaps or similar errors.

The following list provides a brief description of these datasets and the types of information they held:
•

o

The SDIF dataset held the required and optional variables as defined by the international
sampling standards. It included unique identifiers, sampling IDs, selection probabilities,
stratification information, screening information, demographic information, disposition codes,
information for variance estimation, raking dimensions and nonresponse adjustments
variables.

o

The SDIF dataset contained either one record for each sampled person for those countries
with a person/register sample or one record per case or sampled person(s) for countries with
household sampling and screening.
‒

In the first case (register/person sample), each data record was uniquely identified by the
combination of CNTRYID and PERSID. CASEID was blank in this case, as a household
identifier was not needed.

‒

In the second case (household sampling), each data record was uniquely identified by the
combination of CASEID and PERSID. If the within-household screening had not been

completed, the PERSID variable was blank. Multiple records with the same CASEID but
different PERSID existed in case two persons per household were sampled.

The delivery system maintained a log file of actions and events relating to the same modules
as described above for the BQR dataset. This log/audit dataset held information about the
interviewer’s actions during the CAPI, that is, any actions or variables that were explicitly shown
on screen. This dataset contained multiple records per person. Each data record included
information about the type of event, a timestamp, the item ID where the event occurred, and,
where applicable, a value associated with the event depending on the type.

according to their specific schemes and subject to double coding for 50% of the cases. The
purpose was to examine the coding accuracy.

Each of the above datasets included records per person or case depending on the trajectory through the
assessment. Each intersection of a variable and a record in the above datasets either held a valid or a
missing value. Valid values were the individual pieces of collected information conforming to the
corresponding variable specification, that is, the defined lengths, value schemes or ranges.
Most variables in PIAAC were numeric and had a value scheme assigned to them (e.g. “1” corresponded
to “Yes,” “2” corresponded to “No”). Wherever possible, value schemes define the possible values that a
variable could take. Missing data/values in a survey may occur when there are no data whatsoever for a
respondent (unit nonresponse) or when some variables for a respondent are unknown, cannot be known,
refused or otherwise not useful (item nonresponse). Missing data were distinguished semantically into
essentially two broad groups: i) data that were missing by design and ii) data that were supposed to be
there but were not provided or omitted. While missing data are inevitable in survey research, it is important
to describe it properly and use it as information to evaluate procedures, refine instruments or make
assumptions about the mechanisms responsible as well as the likely consequences for the validity and
possible bias of estimates. Analysis of item nonresponse is an important part of quality control, and
consistent use of missing values ensures that the PIAAC data files contain detailed enough information on
unit and item nonresponse.
Missing data in PIAAC can occur for several reasons:
•

Missing data by design (that is, it is known a priori that they will not be collected) for some or all
respondents because of the way the assessment is designed.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

472 

•

•

o

Respondents with literacy-related dispositions (see above) were not administered the
interview.

o

A small number of PIAAC participants did not participate in the international options.

o

Certain sections in the BQ were intentionally presented to subpopulations (domains) only with
reference to responses given to prior questions (“valid skip”).

o

Domain item clusters were assigned based on random allocation and previous proficiency
information collected.

Missing data due to the response process.
o

Respondents may have broken off the interview after it was started as a function of, for
example, time, motivation, fatigue or sensitive questions being asked.

o

Respondents may have explicitly refused to respond to questions in the BQ, or they may not
have known the answer to a question with sufficient certainty. These were coded in the data
as “refused” or “don’t know”.

Missing data due to logistics, processing or analysis.
o

Data were captured, yet CBA result files were lost during the transfer.

o

Erroneous routing in national versions of the BQ collected fewer data items for particular
respondents than intended.

o

Certain data items (variables and/or a subset of values) were not provided or suppressed due
to regulations relating to the confidentiality of information.

o

Respondents with literacy-related dispositions were routed to the doorstep interview.

o

A small number of values were obvious outliers, otherwise useless, or erroneously coded in
the original national databases.

The schemes to describe missing data in PIAAC during the time of data capture and building the national
database were relatively simple and distinguished only a few types of missing data.
The key missing value schemes used in PIAAC at the time of data integration are as follows. A description
of the missing values in the resulting public-use data products is presented in Chapter 12.
•

Default missing scheme – This scheme was used for many variables in PIAAC where a valid value
was expected for every data record or where there was no need to distinguish reasons for missing
data during capture and database building.

•

BQ missing scheme (numeric variables only) – All questions directed to the sampled person in the
BQ explicitly included the options "refused" and "don’t know.” This missing scheme, therefore,
distinguished the nature of the missing data and retained the information captured during the
interview. The scheme applied to all BQ variables as well as most coded variables:

•

o

Don’t know: The sampled person was responsible for this type of item nonresponse by
indicating “I don't know” or similar.

o

Refused: The sampled person was responsible for this type of item nonresponse by refusing
to answer the question.

o

Not stated /inferred: This is a systemic, catch-all nonresponse and was assigned if a variable
was expected to have a valid value, but the value was instead missing, out of range, otherwise
useless, and could not be reconciled or fixed.

Free-text entry (FTE) missing scheme – PIAAC used a number of free-text entry responses for
occupation, field of industry, country, language, foreign qualifications and some other fields in the
BQ. In order to retain the information provided by the respondents and/or the interviewer for later
analysis and disambiguation, the IEA DME software imported missing values for any free-text
entries in the CAPI system as string constants, that is, either “[REFUSED]” or “[DON’T KNOW]”.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 473
National adaptations and extensions
Along with the IEA DME setup, countries were provided with an international codebook template. The
international codebook for PIAAC included every variable and dataset related to the survey.
The general approach for national variables was to include all international as well as national data in a
country’s database to harmonise and map data post-collection. To do so, the international master
codebook had to be adapted to reflect the national BQ, where countries have typically adapted certain
variables to their national and cultural settings, and introduced additional national questions (extensions)
or adaptations in addition to the international ones. All adaptations and extensions in the national BQ had
to be reflected in the codebooks to parse and store the information captured by the delivery system. These
adaptations are related to the creation and specification of national variables and their associated value
schemes, as well as the adaptation of valid ranges for international variables (e.g. for currency units).
Adapting the international codebooks to reflect the national BQ was the responsibility of the NDM. This
task was performed according to instructions and guidelines provided by the Consortium. The NDMs used
the international codebook template as the starting point to which adaptations and extensions for national
use were applied through controlled interfaces in the IEA DME software. The key input for this work was
the national BQ itself as well as the agreed-upon Background Questionnaire Adaptation Spreadsheet
(BQAS). As a key strategy, any adaptations to BQ questions had to be reflected under a new national
variable name in order to clearly identify the potential need to harmonise, map or recode national to
international variables after collection. A naming convention was applied that uniquely identified each
national variable within and across countries. For example, a national variable for Germany that was based
on item XYZ would receive a name such as “XYZDE,” with the two-digit national country code (“DE” in this
example) added to the end of the international variable name. In the case of extensions, that is, questions
and variables unrelated to the domains and contents of the international BQ, a further variation using the
suffix “X” would have been used, resulting, for example, in a name such as “XYZDEX”. Nationally adapted
variables were then reflected in the national codebook with a special flag to denote them as adapted
variables. After all national adaptations were reflected in the codebooks, NDMs were responsible for
thoroughly testing the import and correct mapping of data from the delivery system, then submitting these
codebooks to the Consortium for further review, verification and preparation for international processing.

Data extraction from the computer-based delivery system
All data collected for PIAAC was integrated into a single national database managed by the IEA DME
software. The primary means of integrating the database were i) importing data from the national delivery
system or ii) importing data from national systems or processes. The bulk of the data in PIAAC naturally
originated from the interview sessions. It was stored in per-respondent result files in .zip format, each
including a sizable set of xml, json and csv format files for the various components of the assessment (BQ,
core cognitive modules, main cognitive modules and observation module). Table 20.2 below shows the
mapping of data captured in the PDS to datasets existing in the IEA DME.

The contents of the per-respondent result file archives were generally stored as single records and mapped
to the variables defined in the BQR, BQL and CBR datasets introduced earlier. In doing so, data were
extracted from the individual xml, json and csv files stored by the delivery system, transformed as
necessary, and then loaded into the respective target datasets (tables). Result data for the BQ was stored
in datasets BQR and log data in BQL; cognitive result file information was combined from multiple files to
form single records in datasets CBT, COMP, CBLO, CBRL, CBRN and CBRA. The transformation was
comprised of mostly one-to-one mappings of values. Yet, the data type was changed from the generally
used string types in the delivery system to numeric values in the target database. For example, originally
stored string literals such as “01” were stored as a numeric value “1”. Missing values were mapped as well,
from string literal “DK” for “Don’t know” to a numeric value depending on the length of the variables (code
7, 97, 997 and so on). A refused response (“RF” in the result files) was mapped to numeric codes 8, 98,
998 and so on in the database.
Additional transformations were applied in the following contexts:
•

For multiple-choice items allowing more than one response in the BQ, values stored under the
same name in the result files were mapped to individual variables.

•

For numeric values with decimal places, the thousand separators were stripped.

•

For the BQ and workflow log data, string literals for event types were mapped to a numeric value
scheme. For example, the event type “ANSWER_SELECTION” was mapped to the labelled value
“2” in the target dataset BQL.

•

For cognitive results, a name-mapping table matched long result variable names that were
idiosyncratic to the delivery system or sometimes not fully compliant with the naming conventions
to shorter names used throughout all subsequent data products and analysis, such as names
limited to eight characters in length.

These extraction and transformation rules contributed to the integrity of the result file archive. However,
given that some respondents broke off the interview and technical problems occasionally occurred, result
files were parsed and stored in a comprehensive way, meaning that the contents of the archives were
parsed (provided that the main BQ result file existed along with any other materials found in the archive).
As described before, NDMs were responsible for testing the integration between the delivery system, and
the IEA DME maintained a national database to make sure that i) all files, variables and values were
mapped as expected, and ii) all nationally adapted or extended variables in the delivery system were also
reflected in the national codebooks. Certain values in the result files were only of interest at the time of
collection and were not parsed and stored in the national database. For the most part, this is related to
strings for dynamic texts or interim values stored for some routing logic.
The full information in the native CBA log files (pertaining to respondents’ work on the cognitive assessment
items) was not parsed and loaded into the database. Instead, these were merely extracted from the result

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 475
file archives and stored in separate folders. Countries were requested to provide these log files to the
Consortium for further processing together with their initial data submission.

Import of sample design data from study management systems
The SDIF was a mandatory deliverable from countries to the Consortium; it was typically transferred as
part of the national database. Countries were required to make use of one of the three supported import
file formats (comma-separated, fixed length or Excel) to load SDIF-related data into the respective dataset.
The actual import of the sample design information data into the SDIF dataset, using the import feature,
was straightforward. Most variables in the SDIF were stored in a country’s study management system. To
import the sample design information, countries had to:
•

consult with Westat to identify the applicable variables to populate in the SDIF based on the
national sample design, plans for post-stratification and the like

•

export the variables of interest from the national study management system (or compile/merge
them from multiple data sources if applicable) into a single file in one of the import formats
supported by the IEA DME software

•

ensure that the data contained were complete, accurate and formatted as defined by the respective
codebook

•

ensure that variables not relevant to the national sample design were either represented by blanks
in fixed-length import files and empty cells in CSV and Excel or not included at all in the import file

•

ensure that all records in the import file were uniquely identified by a valid person ID and/or case
ID

•

ensure that numerical variables do not contain more decimals than specified.

The above-stated prerequisites, including file structure and variable definitions, were automatically
validated upon import. Given the different sample designs across countries, no checks for completeness
of SDIF data could be run. Sampling- and weighting-related data were reviewed by Westat following the
submission of national databases, and numerous corrections and additions were processed for a large
number of countries until a complete, valid and accurate SDIF could be finalised and approved prior to
weighting.

Import of coding data from external processes
Several free-text entry variables in the BQ were captured during the interview and then coded according
to the following schemes:
•

Occupation – ISCO 2008 at the four-digit unit group level

•

Industry – ISIC Revision 4 at the four-digit class level

•

Language – ISO 639-2/T (alpha-3/terminologic)

•

Country – UN M49 numeric

•

Region – TL2 level of the OECD classification of geographical regions.

The BQ variables that served as inputs for coding, as stipulated by the BQ framework, as well as the
corresponding validation and analysis plans, were documented as part of the data management manual.
Related advice and training were given to countries as part of data management training. Separate expert
trainings were held for the coding of occupations against the ISCO standard, and industry against the ISIC
standard. The respective coding schemes were included in the codebooks to facilitate validation at the
time of database integration.
More specifically, coding was required from countries in the following cases:

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

476 
•

•

Coding of occupations to ISCO 2008 and coding of industries to ISIC Revision 4
o

Four-digit codes from the 2008 ISCO-08 were used to code respondents’ occupations (current
and last job as applicable). The corresponding target variables in the BQC dataset were:
ISCO08_C (current job) and ISCO08_L (last job).

o

Four-digit codes from ISIC Revision 41 were used to directly code the sector in which the
respondent was working (current and last job as applicable). The corresponding target
variables in the BQC dataset were: ISIC4_C (current job) and ISIC4_L (last job).

o

The missing scheme for the variables ISCO08_C, ISCO08_L, ISCO88_C, ISCO88_L, ISIC4_C
and ISIC4_L was a special numeric scheme. Because the ISCO/ISIC variables were strings of
length 4, the missing codes were also strings of length 4:
Don’t know (code “9997”) was used if all of the raw responses were marked as “don’t know.”

‒

Refused (code “9998”) was used if one or all of the raw responses were marked as
“refused.”

‒

Not stated (code “9999”) was used if at least one of the provided raw responses was not
interpretable or otherwise useless and could not be reconciled or fixed.

o

The coding of occupations and industries to ISCO and ISIC was subject to quality control
implemented by IEA. As part of the data submission, countries were required to provide a
minimum of 50% of double-coded responses, as well as corresponding evidence and reports
on their double-coding exercise and use of (semi-)automated coding tools.

o

The PIAAC Technical Standards require a minimum agreement of 85% on the three-digit level.2
All double-coded responses were to be coded by a second coder.

o

Some countries were not legally able to disclose ISCO/ISIC data at the four-digit level and
submitted data only at the permitted level of detail.

Coding of language to ISO 639-2/T
o

For language-related free-text entries, the ISO 639-2/T alpha3 (terminological) scheme was
used.

o

The corresponding target variables in the BQC dataset were LNG_L1 (first language learned
at home and still understood), LNG_L2 (second language learned at home and still understood)
and LNG_HOME (the language most often spoken at home). By their very nature, ISO 639-2
three-digit alphanumeric codes for languages were defined as strings of length 3 in the BQC
dataset.

o

The coding of languages involved two steps:

o

•

‒

‒

mapping the numeric responses to the national closed-format language questions in the
BQ to the codes in ISO 639-2

‒

coding the write-in responses to the “other” language questions in the BQ to the codes in
ISO 639-2.

The missing scheme for the variables LNG_L1, LNG_L2 and LNG_HOME was a special
numeric scheme. Because the ISO 639-2 variables were strings of length 3, the missing codes
were also strings of length 3:
‒

Don’t know (code “997”) was used if the raw response was marked as “don’t know.”

‒

Refused (code “998”) was used if the raw response was marked as “refused.”

‒

Not stated (code “999”) was used if a raw response was given but not interpretable,
otherwise useless, not covered by the scheme, and it could not be reconciled or fixed.

Coding of the country to UN M49

 477
o

Countries coded the country names contained in various questions of the BQ using the
numerical codes of UN M49. In most cases, a country-specific list of countries was used that
covered the most relevant countries plus a category “other.” Both the “listed” countries, as well
as the “other” category were converted into UN M49.

o

The name of the country reflected the CURRENT name of the country in which the highest
qualification was attained or where the respondent was born, not the name of the country in
the past (regardless of whether the question related to the past, e.g. country of birth).

o

The corresponding target variables in the BQC dataset were CNT_H (country of highest
qualification) and CNT_BRTH (country of birth). UN M49 country codes were defined as
integers of length 3 in the BQC dataset.

o

‒

‒
