The missing scheme for the variables CNT_H and CNT_BRTH was the standard, numeric BQ
missing scheme. For the coding of countries, the missing codes were used as follows:
‒

Don’t know was used if the raw response was marked as “don’t know.”

‒

Refused was used if the raw response was marked as “refused.”

‒

Not stated was used if a raw response was given but not interpretable, otherwise useless,
not covered by the scheme, and it could not be reconciled or fixed.

Coding of the region to OECD TL2
o

Countries were required to code the geographical region corresponding to the respondent’s
address at the TL2 level using the OECD classification of geographical regions, for example,
“DE6” for a respondent in Hamburg, Germany. The corresponding target variable in the BQC
dataset was REG_TL2, and this variable was defined as a string in the BQC dataset.

o

The variable REG_TL2 was not derived from BQ responses but from sampling/survey control
data. Therefore, the missing scheme for the variables REG_TL2 was the default missing
scheme that only permitted “blank” as a missing value as data were expected to be available
for all sampled persons.

Data verification and editing at the National Centre
Validation, verification and record consistency checking prior to data submission
Each country was required to check the national database for errors and inconsistencies in the data. For
this quality control work, tools for applying the minimally required checks, as well as guidelines regarding
the within-country editing of data, were provided to countries. Automated validation checks to detect values
outside of the defined range for a variable, duplicate IDs, and double-punching checks to verify the
accuracy of the double coding were made available as part of the IEA DME software. These checks were
designed as an initial inspection to detect potential severe gaps or mismatches in the data. They were not
intended to replace the more thorough data-cleaning process at the international level. Countries were
required to run these on a regular basis.
Record consistency checks were also included in the software and consisted of 114 checks to identify
inconsistent records within and across data sets, as well as possible defects in the sample or survey control
file data. The checks were consecutively numbered and grouped by content:

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

478 
•

Checks 1 to 26 reported linkage problems between data sets, i.e. they listed PERSIDs which were
contained in a dataset but were missing from another one.

•

Checks 27-78 and 111-114 reported problems in the Survey Control File (SCF). The checks had
to be conducted for the SCF delivery to IEA in January 2023. They had to be conducted again for
final data delivery (to ensure consistency over the time of data collection).

•

Checks 79-110 reported problems in sampling-related variables during field administration time
and could only be conducted once completed interviews had been loaded into the DME.

In addition to the automated consistency checks, the IEA DME software contained functionality to review
descriptive statistics, including minimum, maximum, mean, median, variance, percentiles and sample
standard deviations, as well as to cross-tabulate variables for quality control purposes. NDMs were strongly
urged to review the frequency distributions of their data for plausibility and/or agreement with expectations.
It was also important to verify the completeness and integrity of the database with respect to the included
data records. Sampled persons in PIAAC followed a variety of paths through the interview, each generating
records in one or more datasets yet not in others. In addition, the existence of data records also depended
on whether the sampled person completed the entire interview or broke off before its end and consequently
didn’t work on all components. NDMs were advised and trained on the importance of checking the number
and IDs of data records existing in the various tables of the database against the known numbers from
survey records and case management systems.

Permitted and prohibited data editing and cleaning
Countries were required to run the checks described so far to ensure that the within-country data
integration accurately and authentically reflected the records provided by the sampled persons and/or the
interviewers. However, countries were asked to refrain from implementing any type of general datacleaning or dataflow editing on their own before submitting the data.
The Consortium partners requested original access to the types and the magnitude of outliers, implausible
values or implausible combinations of values, among others, to refine the instruments and/or to identify
problems with the translation of questionnaire items. However, countries were encouraged to make
corrections to the data that were clearly attributable to the survey process. They could also address data
integration issues or similar misunderstandings made, for example, by the interviewer. A common example
of these edits included the correction of incorrectly recorded disposition codes. This was considered part
of the normal and mandated data verification and checking. One exception, where a code was applied
rather than corrected after data collection, was the disposition code "90" if there were technical problems
in the PIAAC Delivery System (PDS) that made it impossible to recover data on site or only partial data
could be extracted from the PDS. Exceptions related to other possible error sources (e.g. residual BQ
routing errors or recoding errors) could be corrected using logical and verified correction procedures.
The Consortium received several requests to change/edit the data to make it more consistent across
variables or with other data collections. The Consortium’s position was that data collected during the
interview took precedence over assumptions (without any evidence) that the originally corrected data were
unreliable or invalid. Where no additional data was collected or additional information contradicted the
original information, no change was implemented or allowed. Exceptions were related to reproducible
errors (e.g. routing, recoding, etc.). A small number of exceptions were made but they required written
documentation and pre-approval by the Consortium.

Confidentiality review, editing and variable suppression
Some countries had regulations and laws in place that restricted the sharing of data with the Consortium
and/or the OECD. While this suppression of information aims to prevent the identification of individuals in
the microdata, it clearly reduces the analytical utility of the data. Thus, both goals of data protection and

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 479
high analytical utility had to be carefully balanced. As a general rule, the OECD encouraged all countries
to make available the largest possible set of information at the highest possible level of detail.
According to the technical standards1, each country had to notify the Consortium early on about existing
rules affecting the disclosure and sharing of PIAAC sampling, operational or response data. Furthermore,
each country was responsible for implementing any additional confidentiality measures in the database
prior to delivering it to the Consortium. Countries especially reviewed the sample design information
(dataset SDIF) and the BQ data (dataset BQR) to identify variables that might lead to the identification of
a respondent or otherwise sensitive information. Most importantly, any edits of the response values, to
ensure confidentiality, had to be applied prior to submitting data to the Consortium. The IEA DME software
only supported the suppression of entire variables. All other measures had to be implemented under the
responsibility of the country via the export/import functionality or by editing individual data cells.
The Consortium asked for complete and detailed documentation of any measures implemented to evaluate
the impact of data suppression on the analytical utility of the dataset, especially with respect to the
introduction of bias, attenuation of within-variable variance, or between-variable correlations as a result of
data suppression or perturbation. Perturbation involves adding random noise or slight modifications to
sensitive data to make it less identifiable while maintaining its overall characteristics. For example, you
might add a small amount of noise to numerical data or round values to the nearest integer. Most countries
suppressed data at the variable level and submitted a database excluding certain types of information,
such as country of birth, free-text entries by respondents, full log information or detailed earnings values.
These suppressions were carried forward throughout all subsequent data processing and analysis stages
and into the public-use data products. Perturbation of original values according to the documentation
known to the Consortium applied in a few instances.
A procedure for suppressing information in the public-use databases was implemented after processing.
The Consortium handled these additional suppressions in a standardised way. National teams identified
variables that contained sensitive information and could not be released publicly or could not be released
due to national laws on data protection. Generally, national teams requested a variable or variables to be
completely suppressed. However, countries were permitted to request a limited number of local
suppressions. Local suppressions refer to suppressing only individual cells/responses on a variable, while
releasing all other values for all other cases on that variable. Suppressed cases typically related to outlier
values in income variables or small cell sizes in coded variables (e.g. related to languages learned and
spoken at home, country of birth or region of residence, and detailed occupation or industry sector codes).
All suppressions were implemented by the Consortium on behalf of the countries and reviewed and
approved by the countries prior to public release. A few countries – Canada, Norway, and Sweden –
applied additional local suppressions after the data had been approved.

Data submission and required documentation
After the collection, integration and verification of main study data, each country was required to
electronically submit a set of materials to the Consortium, which included:
•

a single, integrated, verified, confidential and exported database per country in the IEA DME’s
format, using the adapted national codebooks, that is, including all national variables and values
(except for suppressions)

•

a single zip archive including all original cognitive log files extracted and stored as part of the data
parsing from the delivery system

•

a commented Record Consistency Checks Report produced by the IEA DME software, if
inconsistencies must remain. It was mandatory for countries to document all consistency checks
of the data, including those that did not lead to any changes in the data. Countries made use of the
automatically exported Excel documents that summarised the findings of all checks.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

480 
•

comprehensive free-format documentation of existing confidentiality edits and their impact on
univariate and multivariate properties.

•

comprehensive free-format documentation of any other issues that required the attention of the
Consortium during data processing and analysis. This could include, for example, out-of-design
cases (i.e. respondents who did not follow the assessment design as prescribed) or technical
problems.

The IEA DME software created a copy of the current national database. In this database, all values on a
variable that were marked as “suppressed” in the codebook were left blank. The database exported was
marked as non-productive and read-only.
Any data submission to the Consortium had to be made through secure channels. For this purpose, an
SSL/TLS-secured FTP site and a corresponding Web interface were set up. Document exchange folders
were created for each country. Access to such a country exchange folder was limited to authorised staff
members of the Consortium and the National Centre.

Data processing and editing at the international level
This section describes data processing from the moment countries submit their national databases until
the moment they produce a preliminary international database containing all national databases. This
process was conducted in three batches and lasted six months. The organisation of data submission into
batches became necessary due to issues achieving the required number of completed cases in many
countries. The Consortium opted to be flexible in arranging its procedures and workflows following the data
submission in order to best support countries in their efforts to reach the required number of cases, as well
as to foster the completeness and comparability of the data collected in all countries for further analysis
and final reporting.
The initial phase was used to clean data at the case level and with respect to all relevant fields to prepare
and flag cases for weighting that are valid and comply with the PIAAC definition of “complete.” The following
months were used for any residual data cleaning and/or for the processing of additional, revised or
erroneous data. Exceptions to this general timeline applied given the differing schedules in countries’ data
submissions and weighting work.
The main processing was done using IEA’s Data Processing Export (DPE), a desktop software utilising
Microsoft SQL Server to query and process data. The processing system was set up so that the different
steps, from importing to exporting data products, could be run again to include and reflect all changes and
edits. Missing values were represented using negative values throughout the cleaning process.
The steps were as follows:
1.
Data were read from the IEA DME formatted databases submitted by countries, merged
as necessary, and checked for structural integrity and deviations from the international variable
layout.
2.
Records and variables were checked for consistency, i.e. that no duplicate IDs existed,
that no unaccounted-for wild codes existed, and that the expected data pattern (given a case’s
pathway through the assessment, disposition codes, and locator pass status) matched the
observed data patterns.
3.
Any applied national adaptations that were not mapped to the international source
variables were recoded so that each national dataset followed a common variable layout across
countries.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 481
4.
The processing reimplemented the routing logic included in the international source BQ
and assigned ‘valid skip’ codes to any variable that was not in an interviewee’s path.
5.
Requested analysis variables (or those received from partner organisations and/or the
OECD) were derived and merged with the data, and then exported to SAS and SPSS format.

Import, structure check and recoding of national adaptations
The import of data typically followed the sequence of steps below.
6.
Received databases and documentation were renamed to match the convention expected
by the import process.
7.

Invalid variable names were reported and corrected (where possible).

8.
Variables defined in the codebook but not included in the respective data table (or vice
versa) were reported (and corrected where necessary).
The structure check stage performed several checks related to file and variable structure integrity. It
checked for changes in international variable definitions, availability of mandatory variables applicable to
all sample designs and contexts, as well as the validity of national variable definitions with respect to
naming conventions and in light of agreed-upon adaptations in the BQAS. All original missing values in
national databases were programmatically mapped to negative SQL missing values on import. At this
stage, validation checks for all numerical variables ran and ascertained that no unconfirmed out-of-range
values remained in the data. NDMs received standardised reports on any flagged inconsistencies for either
confirmation or resolution.
Questions in the PIAAC master BQ were designed to have the same meaning for respondents in all
participating countries, regardless of differences in language and culture. However, two sets of adaptations
or extensions had to be applied by countries in the process of translation/adaptation: mandatory
adaptations in the case of ISCED levels, country name placeholders, and the like, and specific adaptations
and extensions that reflected national research interest or were used to align questions with other data
collections. These national adaptations and extensions had to be processed along with data for nonadapted questions. While national extensions were processed, returned to countries for national use, and
referenced in the psychometric analysis, data collected from nationally adapted questions had to be
harmonised by recoding it to make it internationally comparable.
For this purpose, the IEA processed and reviewed all final BQAS files and documented all country
adaptations requiring attention during the international data processing phase by recoding national
responses back to the international response schemes and variables where needed. These “recoding
instructions” were discussed with the concerned country and finally reviewed by ROA, the Consortium
partner
initially
responsible
for
reviewing
and
approving
national
adaptations.
For all adaptations requested to questions on education levels, the consortium partner responsible for
approving these, GESIS, was consulted.
The recodings due to national adaptations were applied by default when processing countries’ data
according to the agreement found in the process described above. National variables affected by these
adaptations retained their original values throughout the whole cleaning process and were provided to
countries unchanged after data processing.
The Consortium reviewed the appropriateness of all applied recodings with respect to international
comparability of data by means of cross-tabulations using single or multiple source and target variables.
This also applied to exceptional cases where countries applied recodings prior to data submission, and
the source national variables were provided to the Consortium. For recodings where the original national
variables were not disclosed to the Consortium, no detailed validation of the recoding process was

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

482 
possible, and the Consortium informed the concerned countries that any error as a result of these
recodings was entirely the responsibility of the country. Nonetheless, the Consortium applied coarse and
technical plausibility checks of the resulting data. Countries were provided with the same frequency
distributions in the resulting data and were asked to check and verify them.

Data-cleaning process, systems, communication and reports
For the PIAAC main study, a comprehensive set of checks was implemented that allowed for a broad and
deep inspection as well as cleaning of data files. As stated earlier, this process of cleaning involved the
Consortium partners working on the database building, the OECD as the primary data consumer at the
international level, and the NDMs and NPMs in each country.
As part of the data-cleaning process, records and variables were checked for consistency. That is, the goal
was to ensure that there were no duplicate IDs, no unaccounted-for wild codes existed, and the observed
data pattern matched the expected data patterns (i.e. given a case’s disposition codes or data availability
in the assessments domains). Additional checks focused on the consistency of records and variables within
a dataset, the linkage of records between datasets, as well as repeating soft validation checks already run
during the interview. Any flagged issues had to be reviewed, verified, resolved or, where this was not
possible, at least commented on by countries. Extensive communication between the IEA and participating
countries on data inconsistencies and their resolution took place, detailed reports were provided to NPMs
and their NDMs on any such issues, and they were asked for confirmation or advice.
The overall observed quality of the submitted data was typically very good. There were no substantial
structural errors in databases and almost all cases matched between data sources. Very few cases had to
be removed or corrected because they were out of scope. The high degree of internal consistency of the
data can probably be attributed to three main factors: the fact that the PIAAC assessment was highly
standardised and computer-controlled so there was no possibility of following an incorrect path; the use of
strict ID validation in all components of the survey; and the diligent work of NDMs in identifying the few
mismatching cases and allocating data as appropriate. Where data did not match the expected design,
narrative reports from countries indicated that this was due to interviewers not following the intended
workflow.
Other potential issues were mostly related to incidental, variable-level errors. These were too diverse and
too sparse to be reported here in any detail. Recurring issues across countries included but were not limited
to:
•

incorrect or inconsistent disposition code assignment, often in cases of breakoffs;

•

incomplete or incorrect mapping of national adaptations where this was the country’s responsibility;

•

discrepancies between age and gender as recorded in sampling frames, collected via screeners,
entered or loaded during case initialisation, or reported by respondents in the field;

•

incomplete loading of sample design data for non-interviews, that is, individuals who refused to
take the interview, language-related nonresponse, or absences;

•

incorrect loading of other sample design data given a country’s plans for nonresponse adjustment
and raking;

•

incomplete data for double-coding reliability analysis; and

•

incorrect, incomplete or unreliable coding – for example, concurrent mapping and coding of country
of birth responses, agreement of occupational distributions with external data sources, or handling
of occupation/industry codes as numerical.

In many cases, such issues could be resolved by reviewing the original data and reviewing registry
information and/or feedback from field operation, coding staff or interviewers.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 483
General edits and the iterative integration of derived variables
After the cleaning phase, the state of the data reflected the data collection as accurately as possible, and
any individual or structural inconsistencies were removed to the extent possible and known to the
Consortium. During this post-cleaning phase, general structural changes were made to the data for all
countries based on the now cleaned original values.
Most importantly, the processing systems reimplemented the routing logic included in the international
master BQ and assigned “valid skip” missing values to any variable that was not in the respondent’s path.
It should be noted that this was done comparably for all countries and only considered original or recoded
responses to any international BQ variables. “Valid skip” missing codes were generally only assigned to
respondents who started the BQ. In the case of breakoff during the BQ, the “valid skip” recoding was only
implemented up until the last known valid value. All subsequent values were coded as “not stated.” Further,
“valid skip” codes were carried forward to any coded variable (e.g. second language learned) if the
referenced original variables were previously coded as “valid skip.”
In a few cases, countries not only adapted questions but were permitted to adapt the routing rules
implemented in the international master BQ. This resulted in a few instances where too little or too much
information was collected in comparison to a route that a “standard” respondent would have taken through
the BQ. Excess data collected due to national routing was overwritten with “valid skip” codes in the process
described above for reasons of international comparability because respondents affected were not
supposed to have data observed according to the international routing rules. In cases where too little
information was collected, and thus missing data were present yet not expected, there was usually no way
to recover. Such data cells were coded as “not stated.” The overall number of affected cases was very
small, but it nevertheless shows the risk and possible impact of excessive national adaptations to already
complex international collection instruments.
This processing phase was further used to derive or merge reporting variables, weights and scale scores.
The process of deriving variables was highly iterative and depended on the progress of the weighting and
analysis. The derivation and integration were observed in the necessary sequencing conditions. For
example, scripts for the coarsening of variables had to be based on revised original and/or derived
variables.
•

Derivation of variables from sample design and case initialisation data
o

A number of sample-design-related variables were derived from sample design, case
initialisation and BQ information. Except for some special settings in some countries, the
derivation of these variables was done according to standardised scripts that were consistently
applied with each pass of the data for all countries. The most important derived variables in
this segment were:
‒

Three final, combined disposition codes for the case initialisation and BQ phase
(DISP_CIBQ) and for the main assessment (DISP_MAIN).

‒

Resolved age (AGE_R) and gender (GENDER_R) taking into account frame information
but giving precedence to observed data during the interview, further incorporating collected
age and gender in the case of literacy-related nonresponse.

‒

A completion flag (COMPLETEFLG) set according to technical standards definitions in
relation to assessment components and/or key items.

‒

A weighting flag (WEIGHTFLG) computed from the disposition codes and/or literacyrelated nonresponse information.

‒

An interim code (SCENARIO) derived according to a set of rules intended to identify cases
earmarked for weighting yet with insufficient information or vice versa.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

484 
o

•

Integration of weighting and variance estimation variables
o

•

Once valid cases were flagged for weighting and analysis, weights and scale scores were
merged into countries’ data files as they became available. Weights were computed by either
the concerned countries or Westat and were merged into the files. Countries had to sign off on
the weights produced by Westat prior to the merge.

Derivation of variables from the BQ data
o

•

The key Consortium partners responsible for identifying valid cases reviewed the outcomes of
the above assignment in regular online meetings and revised the weighting and completion
flags as well as aggregate disposition codes in a small number of cases depending on whether
sufficient information was available to assign a weight and/or analyse the cases.

A vast number of variables were derived from original responses to the BQ. These variables
relate to a set of broad groups, namely the respondent’s background, education/training,
earnings and skill use.
‒

Most of these variables were computed automatically during each pass over the data.
These were based on definitions provided by the OECD and other partners of the
Consortium.

‒

Derived earnings variables were directly derived in the case of detailed responses or
imputed from broad categories and merged into the files.

‒

Skill-use derived variables were based on IRT estimation procedures, computed, and
merged into the files.

o

A set of coarsened variables was scripted at the IEA in response to countries’ need to protect
the confidentiality of respondents’ information in the database. For these variables (suffix “_C”),
one of three types of coarsening was applied: i) top coding, ii) categorisation, or iii) collapsing
existing categories into a smaller set.

o

Finally, a set of “trend” variables was scripted by the IEA (suffixes “_T”, “T1” and “TC1”). These
trend variables relate to variables collected in the same or similar way as the ALL and IALS, or
the PIAAC Cycle 1 surveys; PIAAC variables were recoded to match the metric or coding
schemes used in ALL and IALS to be comparable across surveys.

Derivation of scale scores
o

PIAAC cognitive item responses were calibrated, analysed and scaled. This process resulted
in a set of ten plausible values for each domain (literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem
solving).

Production of the preliminary national and international databases
The data finalisation phase transitioned data from the internal IEA processing systems to data products
ready for further use by the Consortium, the OECD or the participating countries. The final processing
phase further repeated many of the checks implemented at earlier stages to ensure that automated or
incidental data editing did not introduce any inconsistencies, for example, out-of-range codes, into the data.
In addition, a set of additional checks was conducted that ensured data integrity after all cleaning steps
had been run through and before export to the different final formats took place. For example, checks
ensured that the variable widths and types in the codebooks were defined wide enough to hold the data in
the national master database.
At this stage, a single international codebook was used to describe and document the data. Widening
conversions were applied consistently across all countries in case one or more countries extended the
width of a variable in their national database’s codebook (e.g. currency values). The final international
master database held 3,422 international variables for each participating country. Codebook information

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 485
for nationally adapted or extended variables was taken from the national databases originally submitted
by countries.
In all, the 14 datasets present in the IEA DME software and database at the time of data capture were
processed. Eventually, they resulted in the following export file types, each produced in both SPSS as well
as SAS format:
•

PRGxxxMS.sav/.sas7bdat – The main analysis file with all originally collected and derived
variables, international as well as national.

•

PRCxxxMS.sav/.sas7bdat – An auxiliary file holding raw responses in string format collected in the
field.

•

PSDxxxMS.sav/.sas7bdat – A flat file encompassing sample design variables. This file included a
true subset of variables as well as all records from the PRG file and was mainly used by Westat or
countries in the process of weighting.

•

PRLxxxMS.sav/.sas7bdat – A flat file for the CAPI event log.

Data files were exported separately by country. This allowed for the provision of files to the Consortium as
well as to individual countries on a rolling basis. The placeholder “xxx” used in the file names above
corresponds to operational country identifiers based on ISO 3166.
The SPSS data files were standard, Windows-based .sav files and encoded in Unicode (UTF-8). SPSS
data files included full dictionary information from the applicable metadata maintained in the codebooks,
including variable types and formats, variable labels, value labels (including any labels for missing values),
missing value definitions and variable measurement levels.
The SAS-formatted files were standard, compressed .sas7bdat data files for Windows environments and
encoded in Unicode (UTF-8). Variable types, widths, decimals and labels were assigned to all variables
according to the labels defined in the metadata. SAS does not provide a way to store value labels in the
file permanently. Therefore, each file in SAS format was accompanied by an equivalently named .sas file,
which could be used to assign formats (value labels) to working files. Missing values represented as SAS
missing values were programmatically mapped to either numerical missing values in the case of SPSS or
a reduced set of special missing values in the case of SAS.
To allow for the export of data products for the various data users and stakeholders, data files could be
produced according to three export profiles:
•

•

•

Profile 1 for international analysis, weighting and archiving
o

This export profile retained all international variables originally submitted or derived on the data
file.

o

These full information files were made available only to the Consortium partners who required
access to the data as well as the OECD. These files were kept strictly confidential and were
not shared beyond the group of organisations and individuals involved in the analysis and
weighting.

o

This profile included all records originally submitted by a country.

Profile 2 for the release of national databases to countries
o

This export profile maintained most international variables. It excluded a small set of internal,
interim or redundant variables produced as part of the scaling and analysis process and was
only relevant for archiving.

o

This profile was provided only to the concerned countries.

o

This profile included all records originally submitted by a country.

Profile 3 for public use

Each data exported was uniquely identified by an export data and an export version variable in the data
files. These two variables allowed analysts to compare the data version underpinning the current work. In
terms of data flow, the IEA, as a subcontractor, provided all data products exclusively to ETS, followed by
quality control. Subsequent data releases to other Consortium partners, the OECD, and participating
countries were managed by ETS. An alternative data exchange protocol was used in Canada to account
for special regulations pertaining to data security.

Data review and finalisation
Following the initial data-cleaning process described above, an iterative process of data review and
corrections began within the Consortium, which eventually involved the participating countries and the
OECD Secretariat. Integrating, verifying and, where necessary, updating the data and implementing
countries’ feedback on their national databases required multiple data send-outs and rounds of review.
The general principle in this process was that data, cleaned or derived by one party (e.g. a participating
country or a Consortium partner), was reviewed by at least one other partner as well as by the country to
which the data belonged. Thus, reviewing and finalising the national and international databases was a
collaborative process involving survey designers, stakeholders and national project teams.
The key data products resulting from the process of reviewing and finalising national and international
databases of countries are the following:
•

Preliminary international database – The IEA provided a preliminary international database to the
Consortium for internal review. This review had to ensure that all processes and procedures for
analysing main study data were in place. This database included originally submitted, initially
cleaned, and, where applicable, perturbed data. Further, this database contained the design
weights provided by countries. A series of country-by-country updates to the preliminary
international database and initial versions for late-submitting countries were issued in parallel with
data cleaning and initial weighting efforts.

•

First international database – IEA provided the first international database for analysis to the
Consortium. This database included weights, replicate weights, and a basic set of scripted derived
variables.

•

Second international database – The Consortium completed the initial data analysis and generated
the majority of derived variables and plausible values. This database was shared with the OECD
to serve as the basis for the international reporting.

•

Release of preliminary national databases – The Consortium then released the cleaned, weighted
and analysed national data (i.e. containing the products of analyses like the plausible values, the
z-scores for the social and emotional skills, the skill-use indices, etc.) to countries for review and
approval. The microdata files were accompanied by summary data tables and metadata
information. For completeness and transparency, all scripts applied to the data during processing
were shared with Consortium partners, the OECD and the participating countries. These scripts
were used to i) address country-specific data issues, ii) apply systematic recordings of international
variables for all countries, and iii) create derived variables in a standardised way.

•

Review of preliminary national databases – Two months were planned for countries to review
records and variables included in their cleaned, weighted and analysed national databases. Based
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 487
on these country reviews, as well as on the Consortium’s and OECD’s observations, the
Consortium and the OECD agreed on data changes and error corrections to be applied commonly
for all or just individual countries to improve the validity and quality of the data. These data
corrections sometimes required re-analysis of BQ variables that contributed to the population
model for a country, resulting in updates to plausible values. Countries were further asked to
identify variables for suppression based on a preliminary list of variables earmarked for inclusion
in public-use files.
•

Release of restricted international database through the Data Explorer – The database was shared
with the participating countries via an initial, secure version of the PIAAC Data Explorer. Access to
this version of the Data Explorer was restricted to countries, the OECD and the Consortium
partners.

•

Release of preliminary national public-use files – Following the earlier corrections, the IEA
produced a preliminary public-use file for each country that reflected the respective national
suppressions. Countries were asked to verify the contents and the suppressions.

•

Release of the international report and a public-use international database – The public-use version
of the international database was scheduled to be released in parallel with the international report
for PIAAC.

21. Generating results for PIAAC
Mathew Kandathil, Jr. and Lokesh Kapur, ETS

This chapter details the procedures for preparing and analysing PIAAC
data. It describes the conversion of SPSS data files into ASCII text files and
XML data dictionaries to facilitate various analytic tools. It presents the
steps for receiving, processing and updating data, including the creation of
derived variables and quality control measures. It also explains the use of
Python-based procedures for merging data from multiple sources and the
verification processes for analysis results using the PIAAC International
Data Explorer. Finally, it covers the dynamic report system for generating
and publishing analysis reports, ensuring efficient and accurate data
handling and reporting.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 489

Preparation for PIAAC data analysis: SPSS to ASCII integration
The Consortium’s data analysis systems are set up to process the PIAAC data in both SPSS file format
and “flat” file ASCII text format. SPSS data files are completely self-documented, containing variable labels,
data value labels and missing value definitions in addition to the data. Yet, many of the scaling and analytic
tools used by the Consortium required the input data to be represented in “flat”-file ASCII-text rectangular
format, where each data field must occupy the same position in every record in the file.
To address this need, the Consortium developed procedures to convert SPSS files into two parts:
•

an ASCII text file containing the data

•

a proprietary XML data dictionary file containing metadata such as labels, formats and definitions
for missing values.

Before using any programme or procedure with the ASCII data file, the XML dictionary file must be
processed. This step maps the contents of the data file to the corresponding set of variables for analysis
or processing.

Preparing the PIAAC analysis database: Data receipt and derived variables for
analysis
When data files were delivered to the Consortium via secure, confidential file transfer protocols (i.e. FTP
site), files were unzipped and placed in a date-tagged folder before transfer to the operational folder.
Many of the data variables in the survey component were long text responses that could not be reduced
to numeric codes and needed to be retained in the database for future interpretation. These responses
were usually encoded in the native language of each country and could contain extended ASCII codes
(Unicode) to represent certain characters. When placed in an ASCII file, these codes corrupt the
rectangular structure of the data file and cause errors in processing the data. Because these responses
have no analytic utility, they were identified and stripped from the SPSS data files before transfer to the
operational folder.
Some variables need to be created or derived from existing variables, which the Consortium uses to identify
or track the data throughout the analytic processes. As these variables have no analysis value outside of
these processes, they were not provided to the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational
Achievement (IEA), the data management contractor, for the master database or any related data product.
Instead, such variables were only created and retained in ETS operational data files. An SPSS macro was
implemented to automatically create and add these variables to the SPSS data files as they were
transferred to the operational folder.
After the SPSS files were transferred to the operational folder, the last step in the process was to produce
the ASCII extract data file and its accompanying XML data dictionary file.

Preparing the PIAAC analysis database: Updating and adding data
The results of several analytic processes at ETS produced new variables (or new data for existing
variables) that were merged into the operational data files for internal quality and consistency checking
before addition to the master database. These various data sources included, but were not limited to, the
following activities:
•

the production of scale scores for literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving

•

the development of indices for the skill-use constructs

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

490 
•

the modifications and cleaning of cognitive data by applying ‘Not Reached’ item codes, removing
outliers and adding recovered process data information for cognitive items

In addition to the above procedures, ETS also provided code for the derivation of variables to be used for
trend analyses with the IALS and ALL surveys and other derived variables to IEA for implementation. ETS
added these variables, and those created by other contractors, such as imputation of income variables by
ROA and education-derived variables by GESIS, to the quality control checks implemented on the data
files.
ETS developed a Python-based procedure that iteratively processes the data files for each country in order
to efficiently, consistently and accurately perform the merging operations using a variety of input data
sources. Each application of the procedure only required a parameter file as input that specified the
operations to be performed and the folder and file names for the input and output files.
The critical outputs for each application of this procedure were:
•

an SPSS file containing the new or updated variables

•

an SPSS file containing the merge of the operational file and the new or updated variables

•

data and dictionary extracts of the merged SPSS file.

Once these files were verified and approved by ETS’s analysis and psychometrics teams, the SPSS file
containing new or updated variables was delivered to the data management contractor to update the
master database. Then, the updated merge files were used for further operational analysis.

Verifying analysis results: The PIAAC International Data Explorer
The process of populating the PIAAC International Data Explorer (IDE) database is summarised in Figure
21.1 below. This process was applied separately for each country and used to verify the results provided
by ETS Data Analysis teams.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 491

Figure 21.1. PIAAC database population and quality control

The Base SPSS File contained the data that was given to each country for its analysis and reporting.
The Add_Data procedure creates two files from the Base file: an ASCII text rectangular file containing the
data values extracted from the Base file and an XML file containing information about the extracted data
variables (location, format, labels). This Data Set Layout (DSL) XML is structured in a proprietary ETS
schema.
The PDExtract programme used the information from an input parameter file to process the data from the
Extract file and metadata from the DSL file to produce a series of text files suitable for loading into the
appropriate tables in the IDE database. The programme also produced an SQL script that is customised
for performing the loading of these tables and contains a procedure for forming the data tables used by
the IDE.
The PIAACSDT programme also used the information from an input parameter file as well as a list of data
variable names to calculate and produce summary data tables (SDT) – one analysis for each scale score.
Each table in the analysis was a one-way tabulation of various statistics for each category of a given
variable. The statistics pertained to a scale score and included the categorical percentages, average
scores and percentages within the benchmark levels. Each statistic was accompanied by the standard
error estimate, degrees of freedom, number of cases used to calculate the statistic and number of strata
on which the standard error was based. All these results were stored in an HTML document with full
precision. This document may be viewed with any of the popular Internet browsers when accompanied by
the appropriate Cascading Style Sheet (CSS) document. The document may also be parsed or translated
to produce Excel workbooks and report quality tables, among others, which ETS provides.
In the QC Robot procedure, the resulting HTML document from the PIAACSDT programme was used to
generate analysis requests for the IDE, one for each variable, and the results returned from the IDE were
compared with those in the HTML document. The results of these comparisons are posted to the internal
ETS QC Report document, where differences in the above-specified criteria are flagged and subsequently
examined.

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

492 
The only statistics that can be reported in the IDE that cannot be calculated by the PIAACSDT programme
are the percentiles. Because the calculation of the percentiles within the IDE uses more resources than
the other statistics, only a subset of critical variables was selected for quality-assurance analysis. The IEA
IDB Analyzer reads data from the Base SPSS file, uses SPSS macros to calculate the desired percentile
statistics, and writes the results to an XML file. The QC Robot procedure processed this XML file in the
same way as the HTML file from the PIAACSDT programme and added the comparison results to the QC
Report file.
Prior to the first execution of the procedure described above, the IEA IDB Analyzer and the PIAACSDT
programmes were extensively calibrated with each other to ensure that the Merged SPSS and Merged
Extract files were isomorphic and produced identical results for the statistics common to both programmes.

Verifying analysis results: The PIAAC Dynamic Report System and Analysis
Reports
The PIAAC dynamic report translation and publication system streamlined the report and form generation
by separating the data extraction and statistical computation process from the report design layouts and
generation of publication formats. The generation process is shown in Figure 21.2.

First phase: Data extraction and statistical computation
In the first phase, the IDE, IDB Analyzer, and procedural language applications performed data extraction
and statistical computation across the entire PIAAC database. It provided data files containing the numeric
results for BQ and cognitive items in the tagged language (XML, HTML) formats. As a result, numeric
computations are done once, and the numeric results are available for the second phase for efficient
repurposing for quality control and report generation processing.

Second phase: Report design and publication
During the second phase, the publication system accepts report design and layout templates that are
created with common desktop applications and rendered XML structures based on those templates. Using
these well-formed XML reporting structures, the system then applied XML-XSLT style sheet language or
PYTHON-based scripts to transform the numeric results into viewable and publication-ready formats (PDF,
RTF, Excel, HTML, and so on) for distribution. By increasing flexibility for rapid report generation
customisation through XML translation processing and the availability of a common numeric results
archive, this two-stage phase approach to reporting dramatically reduced technical resource requirements
and delivery times, enabling PIAAC to accommodate iterative data cleaning cycles while maintaining fixed
publication delivery timelines.

PIAAC summary data tables, item analyses, tables and graphical displays for possible inclusion in
international and national reports, as well as compendia, are generated by the Consortium using the PIAAC
dynamic report translation and publication system. The following are descriptions and examples of each
of these tables. All, except for the compendia, are secure and not available for public view.

Analysis reports: Summary data tables (SDT)
Via a secure FTP site, the Consortium delivered sets of files individually to each country containing
summary data tables (SDT) that provided descriptive statistics for every categorical background variable
in the respective country’s PIAAC data file. For each country, the SDT included both international and
idiosyncratic national background variables. The Consortium and the countries the SDT were used for
quality control and validation purposes: plausibility of 1) distributions of background characteristics and 2)
performance results for groups, especially in the extent to which they agree with expectations or
external/historical information.
For each variable, these tables contain weighted summary statistics, including variable identification,
sample size, number of valid cases, weighted percentages of individuals corresponding to each valid
response option, and weighted percentages of individuals for whom none of the valid response options
were selected. Each categorical cell also contained the average score on one of the three PIAAC scale
score domains (literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem solving). Standard errors were included where
applicable. An individual set of tables was also provided for each of the three scale score domains. The
SDT were provided in Excel format to countries.
Two files were provided for each of the three cognitive scales – literacy (LIT), numeracy (NUM), and
adaptive problem solving (APS) separately by the set of international variables (INT) and the set of national
adaptations and extension variables (NAT). The “INT” SDT files include the original BQ variables, any
Consortium-derived categorical variables, and the quintile categorical variables derived from the skill-use
indices (some variables may be excluded due to limitations imposed by the number of categories within

SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

494 
that variable). The “NAT” SDT files include the original idiosyncratic national BQ variables. Each file
consisted of one worksheet for each variable in the analysis, using the variable name as the name of the
tab and a sheet named Table of Contents that contains hyperlinks to the individual worksheets. Each
variable-named worksheet contains the analysis results in tabular form.

Analysis reports: Item analysis tables, weighted and unweighted
Similar to the summary data tables, the item analysis tables contain summary information about the
response types given by the respondents to the cognitive items. They contain, for each country, the
percentage of individuals choosing each option for multiple-choice items or the percentage of individuals
receiving each score in the scoring guide for the constructed-response items. They also contain the
international average percentages for each response category. The item analysis tables were used by the
Consortium and the countries for quality control, verifying data structure accuracy and validation purposes.
A brief description of the details of the calculation of item statistics for the PIAAC data follows.
In PIAAC Cycle 2, the direct assessment was completely tablet based (TBA). No paper booklets were
offered for the current cycle. All respondents were provided with a quick tutorial section at the beginning
of the assessment to familiarise them with the type of features they would be using in the cognitive sections.
The TBA direct assessment was given to all respondents able to communicate in the test language
regardless of skills and background. Despite this, simple statistics such as the proportion of correct
answers across respondents are not possible. The reason is that test-takers follow different adaptivetesting paths depending on their performance on the assessment. However, some respondents followed
a linear path of the assessment instead of the adaptive path. Statistics for the items administered in the
linear path can be used to examine and validate item performance within a country because of the random
assignment of respondents to this path. In each country, approximately 25% of the respondents were
randomly selected to follow the linear path of the direct assessment. Since the comparability of the item
analysis (IA) reports for respondents taking the adaptive path of the assessment is limited, the IA reports
provided to countries were based on those respondents taking the linear path of the assessment.
All respondents with non-zero weights were included in the item analysis. Item analysis of cognitive data
involves the calculation of a set of statistics to describe the data in terms of quantity and quality before a
measurement model is applied.
Unweighted item analysis results are particularly useful for verifying the accuracy of the data structure.
Seven worksheets are provided in each Excel item analysis file for unweighted and weighted items: literacy
locator items, numeracy locator items, literacy items, numeracy items, APS items, reading component
items and numeracy component items.
Each worksheet has eight columns unless there are polytomous items in a set. Each row represents a
unique item, identified in the first column entry with the item ID used throughout all phases of PIAAC. Due
to the matrix sampling design, each respondent was given only a fraction of the items in the item pool. By
design, these missing responses were termed “not administered.” In some cases, respondents were given
tasks they did not attempt or reach during the assessment. For typical paper-based assessments,
consecutively missing responses at the end of a block are also treated as “not administered” and termed
“not reached.” For the TBA items, the position of an item is not nearly as informative as the duration of
time each respondent spent on it and/or the number of interactions (e.g. touch selecting, dragging and
dropping, scrolling, tapping, numeric entry) with the item by the test-taker. Clearly, skipping items without
any interactions is not a good indication of the respondent’s skills. A heuristic decision was made that items
with a missing response were treated as “not administered” when less than five seconds were spent on
them, and no interactions were recorded (aside from those required to skip the item). This was the case
even when the item was followed by a valid response later on. Omitted responses were treated as incorrect
responses. The total is the sum of the correct and incorrect (including omitted) responses. Percent correct
SURVEY OF ADULT SKILLS 2023 TECHNICAL REPORT © OECD 2025

 495
is calculated as the number of respondents with the correct response divided by the total number of
respondents who attempted the item.
Because statistically equivalent samples received the linear portion of the assessment, item statistics are
comparable within a country; that is, an item with a percent correct of 0.4 was more difficult than another
item with a percent correct of 0.65 for the population.

Analysis Reports: Compendia
Using the public-use files (PUF) as the source data, the compendia are sets of tables that provide
categorical percentages for both cognitive and background items. The compendia are essentially redacted
versions of the summary data tables. The purpose of the compendia is to support PUF users in exploring
the contents of the PUF and to ensure that they are performing PUF analyses correctly. The item statistics
reported in the compendia differ from the item analysis tables in two ways: 1) for confidentiality reasons,
some countries have altered data or removed respondent records from their PUF files, and 2) the
compendia do not use the routing methods employed in the item analysis (i.e. only using the linear portions
of the sample). As a result, comparing compendia item statistics across countries for reporting purposes
is not appropriate. The compendia reside on the OECD Website and are based only on those PUFs that
were made publicly available by national teams.

The 2023 Survey of Adult Skills, a product of the OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), provides a
comprehensive overview of adults’ literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving skills – skills that are fundamental for personal, economic and
societal development. These key information processing skills provide the foundation for access to employment, higher wages and continuous
learning, while enabling individuals to navigate the complexities of their personal and civic lives.
The Survey of Adult Skills 2023 Technical Report provides a detailed account of the methodology underpinning the survey. It describes the assessment and the sampling design of the survey and outlines the process of developing the cognitive skill measures and the questionnaires used
to collect background information on respondents. It explains the approach to scaling the cognitive data and creating the proficiency scales for
reporting results. It presents tools for analysing the data and details all operational aspects of the implementation of the survey, including field
operations, quality control and data management. In addition, the report explains how the results of the 2023 Survey are linked to those of the first
survey cycle, conducted between 2011 and 2018, as well as to previous adult skills surveys.
